events.title: Revolut’s valuation jumps 53% to $115B in new share sale as it prepares to launch US bank
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Revolut’s investors have completed a secondary share sale that values the British fintech at $115 billion, 53% more than the price tag it had gained in another share sale a year ago, as the company prepares to launch a U.S. bank in 2027. Investors including Glade Brook Capital Partners, Coatue, Durable Capital Partners, T. Rowe Price Associates, and Baillie Gifford led the share sale, which brought no new money into Revolut. The company declined to say how much stock was sold. Founded in 2015 by Nik Storonsky and Vlad Yatsenko, Revolut has grown from a money-transfer app into a financial services platform with more than 80 million retail customers across over 40 countries. It has established banking operations across Europe, and launched banks in the U.K., Mexico, Australia and New Zealand this year, as well as secured banking licenses in France, Colombia and Argentina. The company also began rolling out financial services in India earlier this year, and has received conditional approval from the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency to establish a national bank, which it plans to launch in the first half of 2027, subject to final regulatory approval. The London-based company has grown increasingly profitable, achieving profit margins of 38% on revenue of $6 billion in 2025. Even though Revolut has built much of its business around consumers, its business banking division, launched in 2017, has become an increasingly lucrative endeavor. The division accounts for about 20% of Revolut’s gross profit, James Gibson, head of Revolut Business and a partner at the company, told TechCrunch in a recent interview. Available across Europe, the UK, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, and the U.S., Revolut Business processes more than £36 billion (about $48.6 billion) in transactions each month, including over £1 billion (around $1.35 billion) in the U.S. alone. The division generates more than £950 million (about $1.28 billion) in annualized revenue and holds more than £18 billion (roughly $24.3 billion) in customer deposits, the company told TechCrunch. Nearly half of Revolut Business’ new customers in the U.S. are newly incorporated companies, the company said. Revolut is looking to bring its business banking services to more markets, including Mexico, Brazil and India, Gibson said, though he did not specify when the company expects that to happen. The fintech also aims to grow its business customer base from over 800,000 businesses to a million by 2027, he said. The company’s rising valuation comes as it weighs a public listing. Storonsky has considered a dual listing in New York and London and indicated a preference for a primary listing in the U.S. However, an IPO, which could reportedly value Revolut at $200 billion , would come no earlier than 2028, depending on market conditions. events.title: CVS confirms it will split pharmacy business from insurance
events.summary: CVS Health confirmed Tuesday night that it would split in two, reversing the 2018 deal that brought together insurance behemoth Aetna and the 9,000-store retail pharmacy chain into a $117 billion empire . That deal ushered in a new era of healthcare consolidation, lacing together huge swaths of a highly regulated industry into a conglomerate critics said led to less competition and higher prices for consumers. Now, these companies are facing increasing regulatory scrutiny and political pressure in Washington, which is only expected to grow after Democrats regain control of Congress in January. “We believe based off of where we are and how we’re performing, the businesses are best served by splitting, ” CVS Chief Executive David Joyner told The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday. — Shelly Banjo

events.title: Tesla and SpaceX shares drop after Elon Musk's election bet backfires
events.summary: Both SpaceX and Tesla are headquartered in Texas. Michael Yanow/NurPhoto via Getty Images Elon Musk's election night bill keeps getting bigger. Tesla and SpaceX shares both fell premarket after a string of Democratic victories in Texas. Musk reportedly spent over $200 million in a failed mission to keep Texas red. It's looking like the election might become even more expensive for Elon Musk. Shares in Tesla and SpaceX fell as much as 6% and 7% premarket on Wednesday after the Democrats won a string of midterm victories in Texas, where both companies are based. The Texas results, which saw James Talarico beat Republican nominee Ken Paxton to the Senate seat and Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa unseat longtime governor Greg Abbott, will be especially painful for Musk. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO spent roughly $224 million backing Republican candidates in Texas, according to The New York Times, including $158 million in September alone. Should the share drops for SpaceX and Tesla hold at market open, Musk's companies would lose more than $200 billion in combined market value. Both companies had pared some losses as of 9 a.m. ET. Musk, who moved SpaceX's HQ from California in 2024 after criticizing the state's lawmakers, now faces the prospect of his two public companies once again being regulated by Democratic officials. Texas is the home of Tesla's Austin gigafactory, and the company's robotaxi service operates in multiple cities across the state. SpaceX, meanwhile, launches its Starship rocket from its Starbase facility in Boca Chica, near the Mexican border. Dan Ives, a Wedbush analyst who is bullish on SpaceX and Tesla, said in a Wednesday note that Musk "needs to find the path forward with Texas now with a Democratic win on both the Senate and Governor race." Musk donated at least $446 million to Republican candidates and groups in the run-up to the election and clashed with Talarico, who called out the billionaire in his victory speech on Wednesday. The world's richest man reacted to the nationwide tsunami of Democratic victories in the midterm elections on X, writing that SpaceX's plan to build data centers in space looked "pretty appealing right now." "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," Musk added. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Dollar falls while gold and US Treasury bonds rally as markets react to Democrats’ midterm election victory – business live
events.summary: European shares power ahead; bond yields decline European shares are powering ahead! The FTSE 100 index in London has surged 207 points to 10,845, a near-2% gain. The Dax in Frankfurt is up by a similar amount, while the French and Italian markets have jumped more than 2% and the Spanish exchange has soared 3.2%. The pan-European Stoxx 66 has gained 1.8%. Wall Street is expected to open higher in less than half an hour, after Democrats secured sweeping victories in the midterm elections and secured control of US Congress Investors are hoping that it will be able to limit Donald Trump’s scope for sharp policy shifts, and keep a lid on government spending and borrowing. The yield, or interest rate on the benchmark 10-year UK gilt is down 6 basis points at 5.18%, while the corresponding US Treasury yield has fallen 5.1bps to 4.91%. Oil prices are down sharply , easing inflation fears, with Brent crude falling towards $100 a barrel. It is currently trading $2.72 a barrel lower at $100.87 a barrel, a 2.67% decline. Eurozone yields nudged higher after inflation in the eurozone hit 4% last month, the highest in three years, and up from 3.8% in September. The core inflation figure, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, remained at 2.5%, also in line with economists’ expectations, according to the flash estimate from the eurozone’s statistics office Eurostat. 6m ago European shares power ahead; bond yields decline 3h ago Sterling hits seven-week high against dollar 4h ago Cryptocurrencies recover from earlier losses 5h ago US Treasuries rally on prospect of reduced government spending 5h ago European shares rise as Democratic sweep lifts clean energy and bank stocks 5h ago US stock futures turn positive 6h ago Democrats' Texas win spells trouble for datacentres, analysts say 6h ago 'Blue wave washes over US, futures recover', analysts say 7h ago Introduction: Dollar falls while gold and US Treasury bonds rally as markets react to Democrats’ midterm election victory Ion Jauregui , market analyst from the UK-based brokerage ActivTrades, says the sharp decline in Nasdaq futures earlier was an overreaction, but they have since recovered strongly. Although we know that having a Democrat-run congress will increase the likelihood of increased scrutiny for AI, data centres and increased investment into technology, this does not mean that there will be a significant reduction in spending. Big tech companies will be concerned about their valuations. People are beginning to question just how much they are investing in AI and how long until they see returns. Adding regulation concerns into the mix, this looks more like a re-rating. Big tech stocks, AI infrastructure, datacentre developers and some of the semiconductors are likely to be the most vulnerable to a Democratic Congress. Cryptocurrencies and some financial stocks are also likely to face a more difficult regulatory environment. Renewable Energy, Utility and clean energy investment companies may see benefits from the positive political environment. Healthcare is likely to be more of a mixed bag due to the impact of regulation on drug pricing and insurance. European clean energy and bank stocks have rallied on the result. However, for now, I would say that it is mostly a repositioning. Clean energy stocks are seeing benefits from the more positive political environment. European banks are also seeing benefits from increased risk appetite. However, this is based on expectations. To make this sustainable, we will need to see if there are real changes to fiscal, energy or regulatory policies due to the new political landscape in Washington. Turning to the pound, which has gained 0.6% against the dollar to $1.3492 today, he said: Sterling has gained significantly vs the dollar, nearing $1.35. This is largely due to the weaker dollar and lower US Treasury yields. However, interest rates in the UK will still be driven by domestic inflation and Bank of England policy. In terms of trade, having a Democrat-run Congress may limit further expansion in US fiscal policy but is unlikely to have a quick impact on the general protectionist approach. George Saravelos , global head of currency research at Deutsche Bank, has sent us his thoughts on the midterm elections. 1. Risk positive. We agree with the rebound in global equities and risky currencies overnight. The combination of a large Democratic majority in Congress and president Trump’s statement that he is willing to work with the opposition should act as a break on extreme policy outcomes and bring down risk premia. The market is increasingly likely to interpret surprising policy shifts from the executive as time-bound by the next presidential election or the new domestic political configuration. 2. No news is good news on Iran. Over the last 48 hours, president Trump stated that no attack on Iran is imminent and has acknowledged that the Iran war drove part of the election outcome.

events.title: Essential workers being priced out of rental market, report shows
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Essential workers struggle to afford vast majority of rental listings, report reveals A new report has found almost all rental properties are unaffordable for essential workers. ( ABC News: Floss Adams ) Anglicare's annual Rental Affordability Snapshot has revealed key professions can only afford a small percentage of rental listings across Australia. Of 16 occupations surveyed, only three saw an increase in affordability since last year. Anglicare is calling on the federal government to deliver more social and affordable housing. Essential workers are being priced out of Australia's private rental market as affordability plummets, new research shows. Anglicare's annual Rental Affordability Snapshot has revealed key occupations, including retail workers, social workers and cleaners, can afford fewer than 1 per cent of rental listings. Other essential jobs, such as nursing and teaching, are not faring much better, with just 1.1 and 3.3 per cent of listings deemed affordable, respectively. Social worker Allie Thompson is about to move into a new rental in inner north Brisbane for $740 per week, which will take up about half of her income. The single mother has chosen to stop taking some of her medications to be able to afford the shift. "I just avoid going to the doctor's as much as I can unless it's absolutely urgent, and I haven't been to the dentist in probably 10 years," she said. "My son is the priority, so he gets the dentist, he gets the medical appointments and the mental health appointments. "I'll choose that any day, but that means I've had to cut back on those other things that are still important." Nurse Silvia Laing says she has cut back on luxuries to afford rent. ( Supplied. ) Silvia Laing has worked as a nurse for more than 40 years, and now supports cancer patients living at home. The 64-year-old pays $550 a week for rent in Albany, WA, which she splits with her partner. Ms Laing said that constitutes about a third of her income. "Holidays are one thing that I've had pretty much cut, and going out for meals has reduced considerably," she said. "Accommodation and health are on the top priority list, and everything that's somewhat luxury is just not going to be afforded." Anglicare's own staff are not immune to the impact of rental prices in the north west of WA. Meenaaz Adams is the organisation's new Pilbara Service Manager and has only just found a rental, eight weeks after moving to the town of Karratha. Ms Adams was provided with a month of accommodation but did not realise how difficult securing a long-term home would be. Meenaaz Adams works for Anglicare and has also found difficulty securing a rental. ( ABC News: Amy Rossbach ) "We thought that 'oh we'll secure something in four weeks'," she said. "No, we were declined three times, something I've never experienced." Increased demand from resource companies had put pressure on the local market, with the average weekly rent sitting at around $1,700. The Anglicare report surveyed 48,776 rental listings across Australia, measuring each property against the full-time minimum wage for workers in 16 essential occupations. There are no affordable rental properties for a hospitality worker in the Northern Territory, the report shows. ( ABC News: Monish Nand ) Of the jobs included in the research, only three saw an increase in affordability compared to 2025, while the other 13 either decreased or remained stagnant. For a hospitality worker in the Northern Territory, there are no affordable rentals available in the state. Elsewhere, only 338 listings remained. Anglicare Australia executive director Kasy Chambers said wage growth had not kept up with rent increases in recent years. Kasy Chambers says wages have not increased at the same rate as rents. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) "We would have had a social contract or an understanding some years ago that if you worked full-time, if you trained for these kinds of jobs, you would be able to find affordable housing," she said. Data from real estate analyst Cotality showed unit rents have increased by 44.3 per cent in the last five years, while house rents have gone up by 36.6 per cent. Ms Chambers said wages have increased by less than half that rate in the same period. "For those who are paying in the private rental market, sadly, most of that increase has just been swallowed up by rents." Ms Chambers said the growing disparity between wages and rental affordability was due to an over-reliance on the private market to deliver housing. "Over the last 40 years in Australia, consecutive governments have stopped building and funding housing," she said.

events.title: CVS to split off drugstore business in major breakup of healthcare giant
events.summary: CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half of 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history, the company announced Wednesday. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release. It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs. "From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer engagement, affordability, and care coordination," Joyner said in the release. CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion. The two new companies would both be publicly traded. The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said. Existing CVS shareholders will own shares in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans. The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion. CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period. Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's health care benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year. On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home-visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business. CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits. It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units. Even so, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split "feels like a complete shock" in a Tuesday note. But he said that the retail pharmacy business has been performing well, winning market share from competitors and seeing stabilizing gross margins thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year. "In this context, perhaps the outlook for a standalone retail pharmacy (still with meaningful scale and leverage on its own) is stronger now than before," Cherny wrote. He added that "the rationale could also be to avoid what has been relentless state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration." The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. PBMs, which negotiate drug prices and manage prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers, have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies. Congress enacted PBM reforms in February, including provisions to change how PBMs are compensated under Medicare Part D. Meanwhile, states have increasingly moved to restrict PBMs' ownership of pharmacies.

events.title: US voters roundly reject data centers in ballot measures
events.summary: American voters roundly rejected data centers nearly anywhere they were on the ballot Tuesday, a rebuke sure to rattle investors already growing skittish about the AI buildout. Residents in more than 30 localities across nine states voted for moratoriums, outright bans, and other measures, some in direct response to specific projects underway. Edgewater, Fla. overwhelmingly voted to embed a data-center ban in the city’s charter, and voters in Perry, Ohio passed a measure placing financial and operational constraints on hyperscalers seeking tax breaks. Democrats running in more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races aired anti-tech or anti-data center ads this cycle, one analysis showed. The pressure pushed some Republican candidates including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, an AI booster just a few months ago, into promises of tougher regulation; he lost anyway. Banks and asset managers financing the buildout have already begun treating local opposition as a credit risk, while hyperscalers are rushing to hire community liaisons . Meanwhile, tech companies bracing for the vibe shift are trying to rebrand the data centers as “ compute campuses ” with mixed results, Semafor’s Ashley Gold reported. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: SpaceX signs deal with Qualcomm to provide network technology for U.S. mobile service
events.summary: SpaceX struck a multiyear deal with Qualcomm to build out base stations for its U.S. mobile carrier, Starlink Mobile, which is trying to take on Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile. Qualcomm said the deal represents its largest 5G initiative to date. SpaceX, which currently beams Starlink broadband internet to millions of subscribers in the U.S. via satellites in low-earth orbit, is turning to Qualcomm for terrestrial expansion. SpaceX announced a deal with chipmaker Qualcomm to provide key network technology for Elon Musk's Starlink Mobile service, a challenger to Verizon , AT&T and T-Mobile . Qualcomm said on Wednesday that the terrestrial network it will help SpaceX build will "complement Starlink's satellite capabilities," with a planned rollout to begin next year. Financial terms of the multiyear deal weren't disclosed. "Together with SpaceX, we are building world-leading cellular infrastructure in the United States, advancing 5G today, with an opportunity to lay the foundation for AI-native 6G in the years ahead," Durga Malladi, an executive vice president at Qualcomm, said in the statement. Starlink is a critical piece of SpaceX's business, accounting for 36% of the company's revenue in the third quarter and 85% of its operating profit. But to date, the company's consumer business has been limited when it comes to mobile direct-to-device services as its satellite network can't provide all the voice, video and data coverage that competitors offer on popular smartphones. Now SpaceX is snapping up spectrum and forging partnerships to take on the major mobile carriers. Last month, the company announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio in the 800 MHz band. The news sent shares of U.S. carriers reeling. Earlier this week, the Washington Post reported that SpaceX is in talks to acquire EchoStar's Boost Mobile. SpaceX went public in June in the largest IPO on record and is now valued at close to $2 trillion. With Qualcomm, SpaceX will be using the chipmaker's Dragonwing cellular infrastructure hardware and software in base stations to enable high-capacity coverage for Starlink Mobile. Qualcomm has a long history of making chips for cellular networks, but is best known for making the modems and radios that go inside devices, not base stations for running a wireless network. The company has targeted carriers and other infrastructure companies since it made a bigger push into the 5G infrastructure market in 2020 . SpaceX represents one of Qualcomm's highest-profile customers or partners in 5G infrastructure, following earlier deals with Verizon, Dish, and Europe's Vodafone. While SpaceX plans to use Qualcomm's technology to establish tens of thousands of new cell sites, it hasn't announced partners among cell tower companies or said how many new towers may be required. Mobile carriers generally lease space from companies such as American Tower and Crown Castle , which commonly host multiple carriers from one site. SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's request for additional information. -- CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed reporting. WATCH: SpaceX most undervalued opportunity

events.title: UK interest rates increase expected after services sector activity accelerates
events.summary: Purchasing manager’s index at eight-month high, bolstered by spending on AI as firms regain momentum since start of Iran war The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday after a closely watched survey showed growth across the UK’s services sector leapt last month to an eight-month high, bolstered by spending on artificial intelligence. S&P Global’s survey of the services sector in October showed businesses regained much of the momentum they lost after the start of the Iran war, but also felt the impact of a renewed spurt of input price inflation, which accelerated to a five-month high. Officials at the Bank have become concerned about inflation after the consumer prices index (CPI) rose from 3.1% in August to 3.5% in September . While the nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC), which sets interest rates, has been split in recent months , a majority is expected to vote on Thursday for 0.25 percentage point increase to 4%. Tim Moore, the economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said a survey of the manufacturing sector earlier this week also showed businesses facing strong price pressures. He said: “These signals underscore the near-certainty of a Bank of England rate hike in November and collectively raise the likelihood of further Bank of England policy tightening into 2027.” Financial markets expect three further increases in the cost of borrowing, although most City economists believe inflation is likely to peak in the spring of next year, allowing the Bank to limit the number of extra interest rate rises to one or two. Moore said service providers indicated the fastest upturn in activity since February and “a solid rebound in new orders”. The S&P Global services purchasing manager’s index (PMI), which gauges growth across sector, rose from 52.1 to 52.8. A reading above 50 indicates a period of expansion. Bigger workloads prompted businesses in the services industry to take on additional staff in October, the survey found. This ended two years of continuous job cutting across the sector, with many businesses during that period saying that they were responding to higher labour and business costs, or not replacing employees who left. Moore said the survey suggested an “increase in economic resilience despite challenges from geopolitical tensions, elevated cost pressures and subdued consumer confidence.” “Greater workloads were attributed to an improved pipeline of sales opportunities, particularly those linked to AI investment spending,” he added. The sector has benefited from the demand for AI applications and software services associated with the boom in datacentre construction. Matt Swannell, the chief economic adviser to the economic forecasters the Item Club, said official data also pointed to a surge in activity in the IT and professional services sectors. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning He cautioned that growth in business-to-business services was not being matched on the high street, which has continued to be badly affected by a dip in consumer confidence. “With at least some of that strength reflecting businesses’ rapid adoption of AI technologies, we expect pockets of strength to sustain momentum into next year. But in a two-speed economy, consumer-facing services will come under increasing pressure as households’ spending power is squeezed,” Swannell said. He added: “An interest rate hike looks nailed on at tomorrow’s MPC meeting. And today’s data only adds to the weight of evidence.” Moore said about four in 10 of the services sector survey panel reported an increase in their input prices, while only 1% experienced a decline. It is unclear how much services firms will pass on higher input costs to consumers, pushing up inflation. Some members of the MPC have said they are prepared to wait for more evidence while others have indicated they will vote to quell even modest increases in prices. Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said there was a sign that services businesses were absorbing costs, but not by enough to prevent a rate rise. The services output price balance dropped to 56.9, from 57.8 in September. “We estimate this is consistent with underlying services inflation rising about 4.1%, down from the latest official reading of 4.4% but still too high for the MPC to stand pat,” Wood said. Meanwhile, inflation in the eurozone rose to a three-year high of 4% last month on surging energy and food costs, up from 3.8% in September. The increase makes a rate rise in December by the European Central Bank more likely after it left borrowing costs unchanged last week.

events.title: Prediction markets win big on election night
events.summary: Prediction markets emerged as big winners of the midterms. Kalshi and Polymarket correctly called the Democratic sweep of Congress by wider margins than most polling models, as well as key battleground races, though they missed surprises like Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s loss and Democratic Senate victories in Iowa and South Carolina. Trading volume on down-ballot elections grew nearly fivefold from the 2024 cycle to this year’s midterms to $1.8 billion, according to a Semafor analysis of the sites’ public data feeds. Sports and crypto bets still dwarf election contracts across both platforms, and the 2026 midterms attracted less trading interest than the presidential race. Prediction markets have been racing to win over the sports-betting and gambling industries’ customers, executing aggressive ad campaigns to expand their influence. Kalshi has struck business partnerships with media outlets including CNN and Dow Jones, and its ad campaign on Meta rivals super PAC spending ; Kalshi and Polymarket have also aired a slew of star-studded ads. But it’s one thing to bring in revenue, it’s another to do what the prediction markets say they do well: predict. — Jake Angelo

events.title: UK Officials Said AI Would Add £400 Billion to the Economy. That Figure Mainly Came From Google
events.summary: For the last two years, the UK government has been telling the British public that the country could receive an economic boost of £400 billion, thanks to AI, a figure intended to calm fears that the technology would lead to sweeping job losses and even an economic crash. But the UK AI minister admitted last week that figure was significantly higher than the government’s actual projections after it was revealed that assessment came solely from a report commissioned by Google, and that its own estimation of AI’s economic benefit was less than a third of that £400 billion figure. n AI minister Kanishka Narayan, answering a parliamentary question on the issue, said that AI adoption and data investment could add £55 billion to £140 billion to the UK economy by 2030, bringing the central estimate to £120 billion. But even this “more recent assessment,” he said, was a “hugely uncertain” estimate. Narayan said the £400b figure “was drawn from a publicly available 2023 report commissioned by Google and produced by Public First,” a British consultancy firm now referred to as PF Global. Responding to WIRED’s questions about the difference between the figures, PF Global’s head of economics, Jonathan Dupont, said the disparity was partially because of what they saw as the government’s slow adoption of AI. “AI is a very fast moving technology, and, as we learn more, we inevitably have to update the assumptions lying behind our models. Compared to our older model, the numbers the government uses assume a much slower rate of adoption than looked possible back in our model that was created in 2023.” Government departments and agencies used Google’s £400 billion figure for almost two years, under two governments. Ministers have had the lower estimate since at least November 2025, almost a year before this week’s admission, yet Skills England, a government agency responsible for apprenticeships, was still publishing the old figure four months later. Nayaran’s parliamentary answer is the first recorded evidence WIRED could find of the government setting the two numbers side by side, or saying that the report was commissioned by Google. The answer did not withdraw the £400 billion figure or say it had been wrong. Dame Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, told WIRED: “The government is right to promote the potential for technology like AI to improve public services. However, these reports highlight one of the central barriers to delivering the digital transformation of public services my committee has identified: hype. “Economic projects inevitably rely on assumptions, but overstating the benefits of technology risks undermining the case for change. The government needs to be realistic about what technology like AI can deliver and be transparent with the public about potential savings.” PF Global highlighted more top-down adoption of AI and integration into civil service workflows as examples of how take-up could improve. “While we haven’t changed our view on the overall potential of technology, given the slower rate of adoption we’ve seen in practice, our central estimate for the amount of potential likely to be achieved by 2030 is much closer to the Government’s number—with growth ramping up in the next few years after that.” Lord Holmes of Richmond, the Conservative peer who asked ministers in January 2025 about the origins of the £400 billion claim but did not receive a response, told WIRED: “It is unfortunate that the figure used repeatedly by the government, and then, unsurprisingly, by multiple other organizations has now been significantly and rightly adjusted. It would have been better for the government to clarify this much sooner and more directly.” He added: “Robust data is critical, not least as billions of pounds of our money and how the government chooses to deploy it depend on it.” The spat over these two numbers—£120 billion and £400 billion—is part of a wider debate over the line between government support and boosterism. Former technology minister Peter Kyle also used the £400 billion while promoting the benefits of AI, while many parliamentarians outside of government raised questions about potential issues around the technology. “The government’s revised estimates for how much AI could add to the economy are welcome—but it’s concerning that they come after almost two years of ministers citing a figure from research that was paid for by Google,” Sumedha Deshmukh of the Ada Lovelace Institute told WIRED. “This reflects a wider pattern. Figures about AI that look precise often have assumptions and incentives built into them, and industry often funds or shapes the research behind them. “The government should test the numbers it is given before it builds policy on them, fund independent research, and measure whether promised gains are delivered.

events.title: Private companies added 86,000 jobs in October, slightly higher than expected, ADP says
events.summary: Private sector companies added 86,000 jobs in October, unchanged from the prior month, payrolls processing firm ADP reported Wednesday. Gains came across the board, with trade, transportation and utilities leading. Professional and business services lost jobs, as did information-related firms. Job changers saw significant pay gains, coming as the level of job quitters increased. Private sector job growth held steady in October, with gains spread across sectors, as the labor market showed fresh signs of stabilization, ADP reported Wednesday. The payrolls processing firm said companies added 86,000 jobs during the month, the same as the downwardly revised total for September and slightly ahead of the Dow Jones estimate for 75,000. Employment gains came mainly in the service sector. Trade, transportation and utilities led with 39,000 new jobs, while education and health services added 28,000, and leisure and hospitality contributed 19,000. Other sectors showing gains included financial activities (15,000), construction (13,000) and other services (10,000). However, some of the gains were offset by a decline of 27,000 in professional and business services and a loss of 8,000 in natural resources and mining. Information services, a sector potentially impacted by the artificial intelligence buildout, lost 2,000 jobs. Salaries continued to show gains, particularly for those changing jobs — those workers saw a 4.8% annual gain. A report Tuesday from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that the number of people quitting their job, a sign of labor market mobility, hit its highest level since March 2025. Workers overall saw a 3.2% base pay gain, while gross pay increased 4.7% annually. Pay for those staying in their jobs rose 3%. "Employers of all sizes were hiring last month, and our data suggests that job-changers were lured by a combination of bonuses, overtime, and more hours in addition to higher base pay," said ADP's chief economist, Nela Richardson. "Taken together, earnings growth for these workers hit its fastest pace since March 2024." Companies with between 50 and 499 workers added 33,000 jobs. Large businesses added 24,000, while small firms increased rolls by 28,000. The ADP report serves as a precursor to the BLS nonfarm payrolls count to be released Friday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones are looking for the BLS report for October to show a gain of 59,000 after September's modest growth of 29,000.

events.title: How big money lost the 2026 midterms
events.summary: Liz’s view After the presidential election exactly two years ago, Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy rode into Washington as protagonists of a new type of politics, running the short-lived Department of Government Efficiency. Last night, both suffered the worst defeats of their political careers. Musk had moved many of his businesses to Texas and spent more than $200 million to hold the state for Republicans — part of a 2026 blitz that dwarfs any political spending by a single donor in a single election cycle — with returns that were diminishing, if not outright negative. Senate candidate Ken Paxton’s numbers faded the more Musk spent. Ramaswamy lost his bid for Ohio governor, where his Republican predecessor won four years ago by 25 points, a bigger swing than can be explained by Trump’s unpopularity and the blue wave that crested nearly everywhere. The two seemed to embody a new type of hard-edged conservative politics that lives at the intersection of Twitter and money, driven by wealthy and successful businessmen who believed their wealth and success would translate into political victories and personal popularity. I watched last night’s results from Ramaswamy’s gloomy election night party at an upscale Marriott in Columbus, Ohio, where a prayer circle was going in the women’s bathroom by 9:45 pm. The outcomes suggest that money and its purest embodiments will be forced to slip politely back behind the curtain, to support more relatable public figures. Ramaswamy’s fellow anti-woke traveler and fringe Wall Streeter, James Fishback, lost even earlier, in the primaries for Florida governor. The biggest money in American corporate history — the huge new investments in AI — also had a hard night, as Trump’s embrace of the technology helped doom his party. Now they have to find new ways to recast their projects as pro-worker and community-friendly to make sure the AI buildout actually happens — and to find spokespeople more appealing than the DOGE twins. events.title: Uber beats on revenue even as mobility and delivery units miss estimates
events.summary: Uber reported better-than-expected revenue for the third quarter, but the company missed estimates in its two core units. The mobility business was challenged overseas by rising fuel costs and lower driver availability. Uber plans to have over 2,000 fully driverless vehicles available on its platform by the end of 2027. Uber reported revenue for the third quarter that topped analysts' estimates, but the company missed expectations in its two key businesses. Here's how the company did versus analysts' estimates compiled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 25 cents vs. 96 cents expected Revenue: $14.77 billion vs. $14.69 billion expected Revenue increased 10% from $13.47 billion a year earlier. events.title: Americans have said 'NO TO WAR,' Iran speaker says as Democrats take Congress
events.summary: Ghalibaf said that "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message." The Iran war has been a central issue for voters in the midterms, after U.S. President Donald Trump launched joint strikes with Israel against the Islamic Republic in February. Should Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress, they could push through a binding War Powers Resolution, which will then direct Trump to end the conflict with Iran should Congress not authorise it. Iran's speaker of parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Americans have said "NO TO WAR," as projections from U.S. midterm elections showed that Democrats have flipped both houses of Congress. Posting on X after projections showed that Democrats will have a majority in the House and Senate over the coming two years, Ghalibaf said that "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message." "If the [U.S. government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare." The X account of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei posted: "The process of the US's collapse has accelerated." "If there are still those who entertain the slightest hope that the hegemonic system may change behavior or shifts in its political parties may bring about change, or that by making concessions to the US, they can persuade it to abandon its hostility, they're gravely mistaken," the account added. Last Saturday, Khamenei had called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response." The Iran war has been a central issue for voters in the midterms, after U.S. President Donald Trump launched joint strikes with Israel against the Islamic Republic in February. The conflict has pushed up energy prices across the U.S., which has led to cost of living concerns. Trump is also blaming the Iran war in part for the Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress, telling the Wall Street Journal that "Iran was a piece of it" when asked if the war contributed to the Republicans losses. However, he maintains that prosecuting the war was the right decision, saying, "I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again." Washington has not explicitly stated it plans to resume attacks on Iran, but reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the midterm elections. With their new majorities, Democrats might be able to push through a War Powers Resolution, which will direct Trump to end the conflict with Iran should Congress not authorize it. In June, both chambers — which were then Republican controlled — passed a concurrent resolution to end the conflict, although a concurrent resolution is not binding and does not have the force of law. Previous attempts to impose a binding War Powers Resolution had been defeated. events.title: Elon Musk's millions fail to deliver Texas for the Republicans in fierce midterms
events.summary: Americans are electing members of Congress, which is made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate. All 435 House seats are up for election. In the Senate, only 35 of 100 seats are being contested because senators serve six-year terms. This results tracker shows both the races being decided now and the 65 seats that are not up for election this year - 34 held by Democrats and 31 by Republicans. Democrat James Talarico's resounding victory in the Texas Senate race caused a major upset in the midterms for Republicans - and for Elon Musk. According to the Financial Times , external , the billionaire's political action committee (Pac) contributed $47m (£35m) to Republican candidate Ken Paxton's campaign, on top of the $158m he gave the Senate Leadership Fund in September. The money was not enough to stop the seat from turning Democrat for the first time since 1988. In his acceptance speech, Talarico said: "We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas." "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," Musk jokingly wrote on X , external . Democrats take control of US Congress as voters resoundingly reject Trump's Republicans Talarico's victory marked a key turning point in the midterms, helping solidify the Democrats' control of the US Congress in a wave of wins across the US . Musk has increasingly made Texas the hub of his companies, from Tesla's Austin headquarters to SpaceX's Starbase launch site. As well as backing Paxton through outside groups, the X owner took to his own platform to spread conspiracy theories about the Democrat, posting: "There is something deeply wrong with Talarico" after he briefly disappeared from the campaign trail in October. "There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator," Talarico posted in response. On top of contributing to one of the most expensive Senate races ever, the SpaceX owner also became the top individual donor in this year's midterms overall , contributing an estimated $446m in backing Republican candidates. Musk's money went through Super Pacs, groups which can raise unlimited sums but can't give directly to candidates or coordinate with their campaigns. Individuals, parties and traditional groups face legal limits on direct donations. Super Pacs get around this by spending independently, such as on ads backing a candidate. Musk became one of the Republican Party's biggest donors in 2024, pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Donald Trump's winning presidential campaign. A similarly eye-watering amount was not enough to do the same for Paxton this time around. events.title: Democrats’ win won’t mean a major US-Africa shift
events.summary: Yinka’s view Last night’s sweeping Democratic victory in the US midterm elections heralds a shift in vibes rather than policy. As John “JT” Tomaszewski, the National Endowment for Democracy’s senior director for Africa, told me, African countries will “still struggle” to get on the agenda because of the competing domestic priorities battling for lawmakers’ attention following a chastening electoral rebuke to President Donald Trump. There will, however, be more scope for congressional scrutiny of his administration’s policies. Democrats will likely be keen to use hearings and investigations to revisit the dismantling of USAID and the human costs of cuts to foreign assistance. Some of that would be welcomed because there are still key questions about the administration’s decisions that probably deserve public answers. They will certainly embarrass the White House, which is kind of the point, says Cameron Hudson, a George W. Bush-era official. But I am less convinced that the theater of hearings will translate into meaningful changes in US-Africa policy. Veteran Democrats understand this challenge. A former US ambassador under Joe Biden told me he would like to see — but doesn’t expect — a more assertive Democratic agenda setting out what the US relationship with Africa should actually look like. But, this person suggested, there isn’t any political appetite left for restoring traditional development assistance: “Everybody’s moved on from that.” Meanwhile, African governments have more immediate concerns. One African ambassador, who asked not to be identified, noted visa bans and restrictions currently affect more than half of sub-Saharan African countries , questioning how Washington can keep promoting “commercial diplomacy” while making it harder for African business leaders to travel to the US. “How can the US keep talking about moving to do commerce with Africa when its business leaders can’t visit?” the ambassador asked. There may be a new mood in Washington, but for now, African governments will have to judge Washington by what it does, not what Democrats say about what Trump has done. As the ambassador said: “We’ll welcome the changes so we can have more soberness.” Notable South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the outcome of the US midterm elections signals a shift in the geopolitical landscape that could open the way for a reset in Pretoria’s strained ties with Washington.

events.title: Hebron’s Israeli rooftop settlers threaten the city’s Palestinian identity
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Israeli settlers have expanded in Hebron’s Old City, with Palestinian residents and business owners’ presence under threat. Hebron, occupied West Bank – Yusef al-Khatib, 65, never expected that the building that housed the tailoring shop he inherited from his father, and where he has spent most of his life, would be swallowed up by an illegal Israeli settlement in Hebron’s Old City. He continues to practice the trade that has been part of his family’s history for decades. But the settlers in newly erected prefabricated structures on the rooftops over his shop have created uncertainty about the future of his tailoring business. list 1 of 3 US midterms present a test for Republican redistricting in Texas and beyond list 2 of 3 Palestine weekly: Election deadlock meets West Bank sieges, Gaza killings list 3 of 3 Palestinians return to ruined Hebron homes after Israel’s 10-day siege Yusuf said his father began working at the business about 80 years ago, and when he was just five years old, he began helping in the shop. Nearly 60 years later, he is still working there. “This shop is my livelihood and the livelihood of my family. It enabled me to raise my children and provide them with an education,” he told Al Jazeera. Hebron’s Old City has had a settler presence since 1978, but these illegal outposts have extended since then to cover a wider area. About 500 settlers live in the Old City, despite it being illegal under international law, with Palestinians living there fearing that they will eventually engulf the whole of Hebron. Over the years, Yusuf has witnessed major changes in the Old City, from the closure of markets and streets to Palestinians to the establishment of Israeli settlement outposts right in the heart of Hebron. The Palestinian businesses located on Shalala Street, the main entrance to Hebron’s Old City, are adjacent to Shuhada Street, which has been closed to Palestinians since 1994, after an Israeli settler killed 29 Palestinians as they prayed at the city’s Ibrahimi Mosque. Settlers, present in hundreds, are continuing to find ways to expand into the Old City area and force Palestinian residents to leave. On October 29, settlers placed mobile structures on the rooftops of commercial buildings in the area, which are expected to accommodate 20 new settler units, which activists say will change the Palestinian character of the area. This includes building housing on top of Yusuf’s tailoring shop. In the face of this pressure, his response is to keep his shop open, to maintain the legacy left behind by his father. “It is an inheritance I received from my father, and I will continue to protect it and hold on to it, despite my fear of the settlers on the rooftop above the shop and the threats we may face.” Bader al-Daour al-Tamimi, who has four children at university, has seen settlers take over the rooftop above his shop and turn it into a new outpost. He fears that one day, he will lose access to his shop and the only source of income he has to support his children in their education. “Shop owners have come to expect that they may not be able to open their shops the following day, because of the constant threats from settlers and soldiers,” he said. “Our presence here is not just about business; this is the home of our fathers and grandfathers, and part of our history.” For Adel Mustafa al-Shuyukhi, 67, the shop represents another story of a longstanding connection to the Old City. He inherited it from his father and has spent about 50 years working there, becoming intimate with every inch of the neighbourhood. “I know every corner of it, and I know the shop owners here one by one,” he told Al Jazeera. He, too, has witnessed the changes to the Old City throughout his working life, watching the closure of markets and the raising of military gates at the entrances of neighbourhoods. He remembers when Israeli authorities began issuing restrictions that have stopped Palestinian customers and business owners from reaching stores. But al-Shuyukhi believes that keeping his shop open is not just a financial necessity but also essential to maintain the Palestinian identity of the Old City. He wants his children to continue running the shop when he dies, just as his father left it to him. “Despite all the restrictions, we are standing firm and do not want to leave our shops,” he said. “I have told my children that if anything happens to me, they should come and open the shop so that it remains open and we do not abandon it.” From the division of Hebron to expansion Issa Amro, 46, an anti-settlement activist and founder of the Youth Against Settlements group, places the current expansion in a broader historical context dating back to the 1994 Ibrahimi Mosque massacre and the agreements that reshaped control over Hebron. Before then, the Old City housed a bustling market, filled with vegetables, poultry, camels and carpentry.

events.title: Business leaders react as a 'blunami' sweeps America
events.summary: Brad Gerstner and Reid Hoffman are two of Silicon Valley's most prominent elite investors, hedge fund managers, and venture capitalists. Bloomberg and JP Yim/Getty Images Business and tech leaders across the US are reacting after the Democrats took full control of Congress. LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, Brad Gerstner, and Elon Musk are among those reacting to the blue wave. Data centers and California's ballot measure targeting billionaires are in the spotlight. The 2026 midterm elections delivered shocking wins for Democrats on Tuesday evening, reshaping the balance of power in Washington. Business leaders, tech executives, and investors are now assessing what the new political landscape could mean for their industries as Democratic candidates flipped key Senate and House seats. This includes Texas, where James Talarico won his Senate race despite over $150 million in funding from Elon Musk for his Republican rival, Ken Paxton. After the results, some of the tech and business leaders who sought closer ties with President Donald Trump ahead of his return to the White House could face new congressional scrutiny. In California, the results of the nation's first-ever ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with net worth exceeding $1 billion could have major implications for the state's elite, though as of around 7 a.m. ET, the "No" vote held a strong lead. Here's how powerbrokers in business and tech reacted to the midterms results amid the blue wave sweeping across the country: Reid Hoffman, LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman is a Democratic megadonor. JP Yim/Getty Images for Clinton Global Initiative Reid Hoffman , the cofounder of LinkedIn and a Democratic megadonor, reacted to the party's big wins in a post on X Tuesday evening. "Voters made clear they demand a different kind of country. Americans want an economy that can compete globally and deliver for them at home. And they made clear that they want leaders they can trust to fight for their constituents," he wrote. "This night blew the doors off our expectations. From Texas to Ohio, Kentucky to Iowa, and South Carolina to Indiana, voters rejected the status quo. Tonight's lesson: Never discount any voter in any place," he continued. Hoffman has been active in politics and vocal about his support for Democrats, spending tens of millions this election cycle. He also spent millions to support Kamala Harris's campaign in 2024. Hoffman has previously said the Democratic Party had alienated Silicon Valley and was partly to blame for its shift to the right. Elon Musk, SpaceX and Tesla CEO SpaceX CEO Elon Musk Mark Schiefelbein/AP Elon Musk , who spent hundreds of millions to support Republicans, broke his silence late on election night with two short X posts. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said, referencing concerns that Democratic wins could mean more scrutiny on data center development. "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," he joked in a quick follow-up post. Musk, the world's richest person, spent more money than any other individual in the midterms, donating a whopping $446 million, mostly in Texas, the state he calls home along with his companies Tesla and SpaceX. In addition to Talarico's Senate seat, the Texas governorship was also won by a Democrat, Gina Hinojosa. It was the first time in decades a Democrat won a statewide race in the Lone Star state. Dara Khosrowshahi, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi at Uber's America250 celebration in July. Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Uber Dara Khosrowshahi , the CEO of Uber, shared his thoughts on the midterms in a Wednesday morning interview with CNBC. "I think the people of our country sent a message regarding change," he said. "I think that continuous inflation really has taken a mark on the consumer." "I think it's up to businesses and up to our politicians and leaders in Washington to respond, and I hope that they do, because it was a very clear message that was sent out." Khorowshahi, who is Iranian by birth, was a vocal critic of Trump during his first term, but donated $1 million to the president's inaugural fund after the 2024 election. Keith Rabois, Khosla Ventures managing director Keith Rabois. Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images Keith Rabois held executive roles at PayPal, LinkedIn, and Square, before becoming managing director at Khosla Ventures. As the results came in overnight, he posted on X: "Another reason to move to Miami." It came shortly after the Associated Press called Florida's US Senate race for the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, who held on despite a strong Democratic swing. While two of the city's three main congressional districts elected Democrats in huge swings, the one that covers downtown Miami looks set to narrowly reelect the Republican incumbent, with 99% of the vote counted. Rabois is married to Jacob Helberg, Trump's undersecretary of state for economic affairs, and their wedding ceremony was officiated by Sam Altman. Last year, The Wall Street Journal reported the couple was selling their Miami Beach home for $65 million as Helberg relocated to Washington, DC, although Rabois planned to stay based in Miami. Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner Bloomberg/Getty Images Brad Gerstner , CEO of Altimeter Capital, had thoughts on how the US data center buildout would be affected by the elections. In a guest appearance on the All-In podcast livestream Tuesday evening, Gerstner said fears that a "blue tsunami" could make it difficult to build new data centers are "overblown." But he said that election results could slow down the development of the centers, and candidates like Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who won the Texas gubernatorial race Tuesday, could "issue a moratorium on new data centers." He said this could be "really challenging for the AI infratrade." Gerstner also said that Republicans and the AI community have "struggled with the messaging" over AI as the affordability crisis has weighed on Americans' minds. The investor is the architect of "Trump Accounts," the investment vehicle for children in the country that launched in July. Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis Dylan Patel, founder of SemiAnalysis, speaks during the Raise summit in Paris, France, on Tuesday, July 8, 2025. The annual conference gathers global leaders and key speakers in tech and AI. Photographer: Nathan Laine/Bloomberg via Getty Images Nathan Laine/Bloomberg via Getty Images Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, hinted at what he believes a blue wave could mean for the AI buildout. "I am now bullish space datacenters," Patel said in a post on X alongside a screenshot of results out of Texas that showed Hinojosa with an early lead over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. events.title: Why a company donating $20,000 a month counts for more than $240,000 once a year in the eyes of customers
events.summary: Repeated giving may give the impression that companies care more. useng/iStock via Getty Images Plus People tend to think more highly of companies that give to charity on a monthly or weekly basis rather than donating an annual lump sum worth the same amount. This is what I and five other marketing researchers found when we conducted seven studies involving more than 150,000 people . The Journal of Marketing Research, which is peer-reviewed, published our article on the results in early 2026. My co-author Alexander B. Park and I led the team. Our goal was to discover whether the way a company communicates with the public about its donations affects how much credit it gets from consumers for those gifts. Across seven studies, we found that companies earn more goodwill when they give consistently – say, US$20,000 a month – instead of making a single $240,000 gift. On average, consumers also said they were more likely to buy from those companies. To test this premise, we did two real-world studies. First, we partnered with GiftAMeal , a U.S. company that runs a free app for diners. Each time someone takes a photo of their meal at a participating restaurant and shares it on social media, GiftAMeal donates to a local food bank. We ran two versions of GiftAMeal’s Facebook ad, which together reached 67,576 people. One said the company “donated 25,000 meals every month” last year. The other said it “donated 300,000 meals” last year. Both were true, and everything else about the ads was the same. We found that people who saw the monthly version were about 21% more likely to click on the ad. Next, we worked with Salt + Smoke , a Midwestern barbecue restaurant. When we emailed 75,514 customers who subscribed to its newsletters, half read that the company would give $5,000 a month from September through December to a small, local charity that supports early childhood education programs. The other half read that it would make a one-time donation of $20,000. Subscribers who read about the monthly donation pledge were nearly twice as likely to click through to the restaurant’s website as those who read about the one-time gift pledge even though the total was the same. Then we ran online experiments with more than 7,400 people to learn why and when consistent giving makes people view a company more favorably. We found that, on average, when a company gives monthly, people see its charitable support as a more genuine commitment to the causes. Why it matters U.S. companies gave nearly $44 billion in 2025 alone. And this kind of giving is popular with the public. In a 2022 survey, 88% of Americans said it’s important for companies to make the world a better place. Companies frequently promote their donations with the largest numbers they can muster. For example, Microsoft announced that the software giant and its employees donated $256 million in 2025; Walmart and its foundation say they have donated $2 billion in 2026. Yet boasting about big numbers may not impress people as much as emphasizing the consistency of donations . This may help explain why companies often struggle to convey their charitable efforts in ways that win people over. Even if companies give only once a year, they can indicate that they are engaged in a steady pattern of giving. For example, they can make their annual gifts on Giving Tuesday every year. Donating on the same day or as part of the same fundraising campaign every year can signal an ongoing commitment, not a one-off. What still isn’t known We don’t yet know how long the reputational boost companies may get from recurring donations might last, or whether those donations can translate into long-term customer loyalty. It’s also possible that what we found would not apply during emergencies. For example, consumers might be happy to see a company make one big gift right after a hurricane when a local community’s needs are immense. What’s next Along with Park and Cynthia Cryder , a Washington University in St. Louis marketing professor, I’m now studying other ways that corporate philanthropy can affect how much credit companies get for doing good. So far, we’ve found that companies may earn less goodwill when they ask customers to chip in to their charitable campaigns. People seem to expect companies to carry more of the load themselves. The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work. Yanyi Leng does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

events.title: Weil Gotshal is a canary in the legal coal mine
events.summary: Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse last week has set off a blame game over what made the storied law firm uniquely vulnerable. But focusing on Weil’s particular circumstances misses the bigger point. The legal profession’s traditional business model is under enormous strain, and its outdated taboo against outside capital must be reconsidered if firms of all sizes, from New York’s white-shoe giants to regional players across the country, are to remain competitive. Law firms have always had to live with the risk of top talent departing. If partners lose confidence in their firm’s future, or decide they can do better elsewhere, they head for the exits. If enough leave, the firm’s very survival can be at stake. What is different now is that this inherent instability, a feature of the partnership model rather than a bug, is being pushed to a breaking point by two converging forces: generational turnover in law firm leadership and the upheaval brought on by artificial intelligence. A generation of law firm leaders is approaching retirement, forcing firms to confront difficult questions about succession. At the same time, AI is transforming how legal work gets done, calling into question the hourly billing model that long seemed untouchable. Lawyers no longer need to spend days reviewing thousands of contracts for diligence issues that software can flag in minutes. Discovery that once required armies of lawyers can now be narrowed with far greater precision. Research that used to take days can increasingly be completed in hours using AI-assisted platforms that identify precedents, summarize rulings and surface relevant arguments. Adapting to these changes while navigating generational turnover can be treacherous. Advanced AI systems, cybersecurity infrastructure, workflow automation and data platforms all require substantial investment. So does providing liquidity to retiring senior partners and setting up the next generation for success. One promising solution is the management services organization, or MSO, a model that my firm, Uplift Investors, has been at the forefront of bringing to the legal industry. MSOs allow outside investors like us to finance technology, operations and other nonlegal functions while lawyers retain control over the practice of law. The appeal is straightforward. Firms gain access to capital and professional management without having to surrender their independence. They can invest in technology and improve efficiency while freeing lawyers to focus on serving clients rather than running a business. For investors, the attraction is a large, fragmented industry with substantial room for modernization. And for clients, the potential payoff is better service at a lower cost. Unfortunately, opponents of MSOs are threatening to cut off this lifeline. They argue that outside investment violates rules prohibiting nonlawyers from interfering with a lawyer’s professional judgment. What they conveniently gloss over is that MSOs are designed to preserve those very safeguards by separating business operations from the practice of law. Lawyers remain bound by strict professional obligations, and their duty to clients does not disappear because a firm adopts a different capital structure. Properly structured, MSOs can help firms modernize without compromising professional independence. To be sure, the model is not a one-size-fits-all solution, and certain segments of the legal profession will need to explore other avenues for accessing outside capital. We believe MSOs are a natural fit for personal injury law, for example, where firms face significant upfront costs to pursue cases, often wait years to get paid and need substantial resources to compete effectively. That is why we have focused exclusively on personally injury to date. Still, despite MSOs being particularly well suited to certain areas of the law, critics paint with a broad brush, lumping together different forms of outside capital and dismissing them wholesale as a “workaround” to existing rules. The stakes are not academic, and they extend far beyond the fate of any single law firm. Across the country, millions of Americans live in legal deserts, where individuals and small businesses struggle to find affordable counsel. Smaller and regional firms are often best positioned to serve these communities, but many lack the resources to invest in technology, expand their reach and lower costs. Denying them access to growth capital leaves underserved communities with even fewer choices and threatens to make legal services more expensive and less accessible to those who need them most. This makes the growing patchwork of conflicting state rules governing MSOs particularly troubling. Firms in some jurisdictions can access capital to modernize and expand, while competitors elsewhere are denied the same opportunity. Clients will feel the consequences not as abstract regulatory distinctions, but as higher bills, slower service and fewer choices. The irony is hard to miss. In the name of protecting the profession, these restrictions shield the largest incumbents from the very competition that would make those incumbents and the industry more durable. The future of law is arriving whether the establishment likes it or not. Weil should be a wake-up call. The wrong lesson to draw is that even the most prestigious firms can disappear. The real lesson is that an industry facing unprecedented change can no longer afford to be denied the capital needed to adapt. Protecting professional independence is essential. Protecting an outdated business model at the expense of the profession’s future is indefensible. events.title: Iran hails US voters rejecting war while Khamenei warns hostility won’t end
events.summary: Iranian officials see Republican midterm losses in a positive light, but supreme leader says US policy will not shift. Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has said that anyone expecting a shift in the United States’ policy towards his country is “seriously mistaken”, hours after midterm elections dealt a blow to President Donald Trump. His comments came as other Iranian officials struck a more optimistic tone on Wednesday, following the results of the US vote, which saw Democrats score a major victory by taking control of both chambers of Congress. list 1 of 3 Iran commander sets out five conditions for regional security list 2 of 3 Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes list 3 of 3 Who determines Iran’s fighting and negotiating position amid US threats? “Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Khamenei said in a written statement published on his website. He said that Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz had shattered the “myth of America’s invincibility”, and warned that any renewed US attack would draw a far wider response . Trump himself has acknowledged the US-Israel war on Iran that began in February likely impacted his Republican Party’s poor performance in the elections, saying voters were probably not ready “for the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline”. Khamenei said Iran’s confrontation with the US had reached a point where “every day and every hour” had become a time of resistance against “the Great Satan”. His message was to mark the National Day of the Fight Against Global Arrogance, which falls each year on November 4, the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the US embassy in Tehran. The supreme leader described Iran’s management of the Strait Of Hormuz, through which one fifth of world’s oil and gas passed before the war, and what he called the elimination of US military bases in regional countries as a reaction to US “aggression and crimes” during the conflict. “In the event of repeated transgressions, it will take on much wider dimensions,” he said. The supreme leader struck a “cautious” note on Wednesday, warning that a party shift in the US would not persuade Washington to abandon its hostility against Iran, noted Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas, reporting from Tehran. This contrasted with a more celebratory mood among other Iranian officials reacting to the Republican defeat, Atas said. “Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” said Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator with Washington and his country’s parliament speaker. “If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” he added on X. Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser and assistant to the supreme leader, said Trump had been “slapped in the face by his own people”. “The true winner in this arena was Iran, which transferred the cost of the war into the United States,” he wrote on X. Judiciary chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei wrote on Telegram: “Trump was defeated both in war and in politics; we will certainly impose further defeats on him; this is still only the early outcome.” He added that November 4 “has always been a day of defeat for the Americans” and honoured “the dear martyred students of Minab”. Mehdi Tabatabaei, deputy head for communications at the president’s office, said Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, “blind adherence” to Israel’s interests and the “futile war” with Iran had handed the Republicans their biggest defeat. Atas said Iranians believe a Democratic-controlled Congress could restrain Trump and make him “less reckless” over the war, with some Republicans wary ahead of the 2028 elections. But some in Tehran fear that because officials have framed the result as a defeat imposed by Iran, Trump could “personalise the matter” and launch a new round of war “in an act of revenge”. The US has warned it could carry out a short but intensive military campaign against Iran after the midterms. Hamidreza Moghadamfar, an adviser to the commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said Iran would hit targets beyond US bases if Gulf states allowed Washington to launch attacks from their territory. Speaking at a rally in Bandar Abbas, he named the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain and said Iran would respond with a “new doctrine and new technology”.
