events.title: McDonald's earnings beat, but traffic to its U.S. restaurants falls
events.summary: McDonald's quarterly earnings topped expectations, but its revenue fell short of estimates. The chain's U.S. same-store sales declined, but CEO Chris Kempczinski said its domestic performance is improving. McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years. McDonald's on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results as traffic to its U.S. restaurants fell, leading to a slight decline in domestic same-store sales. The fast-food giant reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. restaurants that have been open at least 13 months. Even so, the segment performed better than the 0.5% decline that Wall Street anticipated, according to a survey of analysts by StreetAccount. At the company's investor day in September, executives said that same-store sales in July and August were slightly negative but they expected September to return to same-store sales growth. "In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement. Kempczinski said in August that the company's U.S. business was falling short on execution, particularly on the implementation of its value offerings. Like many restaurants, McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years. Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.57 adjusted vs. $3.38 expected Revenue: $7.16 billion vs. $7.29 billion expected The company reported third-quarter net income of $2.49 billion, or $3.51 per share, up from $2.28 billion, or $3.18 per share, a year earlier. Excluding restructuring charges and other items, McDonald's earned $3.57 per share. Net revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion. The company's same-store sales rose 1.5%, lifted by its international segments. That topped analysts' expectations of a 1.3% increase, according to StreetAccount. McDonald's international developmental licensed markets business, which includes Japan and China, reported same-store sales growth of 4.2%. Wall Street was forecasting same-store sales to rise 2.1% for the division, based on StreetAccount estimates. The company's international operated division, which includes top markets like Australia and Germany, saw same-store sales growth of 1.4%. Still, the business underperformed Wall Street's expectations. Analysts were projecting same-store sales would rise 2.1%, according to StreetAccount. France was a weak spot, McDonald's said.

events.title: Democrats win chance to take on energy costs
events.summary: Democrats' big night gives them a chance to turn voter anger over high energy prices into legislative action and congressional oversight, but divisions within the party could complicate their plans. Why it matters: This was an energy election . High gasoline prices, record diesel costs, and rising power bills fueled discontent with President Trump and his party. Voters' rebukes of data centers could slow the buildout of power-hungry AI infrastructure. The latest: Stunning Senate wins in red states and House wins nationwide propelled Democrats to control of both chambers, and flipped several governor's mansions. Energy costs were prominent in key races, such as Democrats hitting GOP rivals over farmers' bills in Iowa, Kansas and Ohio. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) bashed Greg Abbott (R) over his prior embrace of data centers in the state where developers are planning big projects. The data center backlash also featured in Ohio and Pennsylvania, where Sherrod Brown defeated Sen. Jon Husted (R) and Paige Cognetti unseated Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R). Both Republicans faced criticism over their support for data centers. State of play: A detailed Democratic energy agenda hasn't emerged, but there are early clues. Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer tied Republicans to electricity costs in his first comments after returns came in. Likely Speaker-in-waiting Hakeem Jeffries has vowed to quickly push an affordability agenda, with energy as a key pillar. He tasked Reps. Nikki Budzinski (D-Ill.) and Mike Levin (D-Calif.) with leading a "Gas and Utilities Affordability Working Group" that crafted ideas, though they remain under wraps. Another potential source of ideas: Hundreds of proposals backed this year by the 100-plus member House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition. Some could gain bipartisan backing, like support for advanced nuclear power. But other areas would be largely symbolic, like restoring some IRA tax credits. Catch up quick: In the Senate, Schumer has offered broad areas of focus around grid development, affordability and consumer protections, and clean energy. He has vowed to restore clean energy tax credits, while pledging "systematic protection for consumers from rising prices." Other ideas include more support for energy efficiency and greater transparency in utility bills. The intrigue: Democrats did not make climate change a midterm messaging focus. Watch whether progressives push to revive an explicitly climate-focused agenda. My thought bubble: Don't expect Democrats to bring back their select committee on climate change, which Republicans disbanded after winning House control in 2022. There has not been a decision announced. But the party's shift away from messaging focused on climate is reason to be doubtful, even as global warming marches on. What's next: The most immediate thing to watch is how the results may affect the politics of the bipartisan permitting deal in the lame duck. Some House progressives have argued that Dems could get a permitting deal more to their liking next year. But backers of the current bill see almost no chance of a political opening to craft a more liberal bill that Trump would sign or could even clear the Senate. The permitting fight has also opened rifts within the Democratic coalition, with multiple unions and the clean energy industry backing the bill, while many environmentalists are undecided or flatly opposed. The debate also highlights broader divisions between the "abundance movement" and progressives who want a harder line against fossil fuels Those divisions could extend well beyond the lame duck permitting fight, influencing future legislative priorities and the policy agendas of presidential hopefuls as 2028 jockeying begins in earnest. The bottom line: One thing already clear is that Democrats are lining up energy-focused oversight of Trump's diesel agreement with Moscow, offshore wind policies and much more. events.title: Uproar over missing 'pop' as Rice Krispies changes its recipe
events.summary: Published 4 November 2026, 01:14 GMT Rice Krispies and Coco Pops, long-standing staples of the family breakfast table, will no longer be made of whole rice grains in the UK, after Kellogg's said it was changing its recipe. Instead the tiny toasted puffs will be made using corn flour and rice flour, and will also now contain wheat gluten as an ingredient. A Kellogg's spokesperson said the reformulation was due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies of some grains and cereals. The cereal giant said the new versions had been "carefully assessed for taste, appearance and texture", but fans complained online they no longer made the famous "pop" sound and said their children would no longer eat them. Some expressed dismay that the taste and texture were "totally different" and dubbed the change "grim" and "disgusting". "There's no snap, crackle and pop in these," a parent named Dani wrote on TikTok. "My toddler won't eat them." Lauren, also posting on TikTok, added that she had been eating Rice Krispies every day for breakfast "for years and years". "I had a bowl of the new recipe and you can immediately tell the difference," she said. "They don't have the snapping sound when you put in the milk." Jessicake meanwhile said they tasted "weird and stale". The "Snap, Crackle and Pop" - made when milk is added to the puffed rice - has been a centrepiece of the brand's marketing since the 1950s. Recipe changes are notoriously difficult for big brands. Chocolate makers are constantly accused of reducing cocoa content in their products and debates rage constantly online over whether ketchup recipes have changed. When Scottish fizzy drink Irn Bru cut its sugar content in 2018, fans famously stockpiled crates of the old version. No changes are being made to Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada. Kellog's said the recipe change in the UK will help "maintain consistent quality" as extreme weather takes a toll on crops and pushes up ingredient prices. Rice Krispies, launched nearly a century ago, are sold around the world and come in variations such as vanilla and strawberry flavours in some markets alongside the widespread chocolate-flavoured Coco Pops version. "We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration," Kellogg's said. The cereals have already undergone some change, with reductions in salt content in the 1990s and lowered sugar in 2018. The company said Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food. A backlash against processed foods in recent years, especially those low in fibre and high in sugar, has put cereals generally under the spotlight from healthy eating advocates. Kellogg's stressed the cereals contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same. However, the new recipes mean packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning. Previously packaging said the products "may contain gluten" because they were made in a factory handling other cereals and there was a risk of cross-contamination. Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather? Published 21 August Kellogg's said it has not changed the recipe for any of its other cereals. Most of the world's rice comes from Asia, many parts of which has been affected by droughts, floods and heatwaves due to the El Niño weather phenomenon. The weather event is expected to severely impact crop production from South East Asia in particular. The region produces more than a quarter of the world's rice. The World Meteorological Agency expects the record-breaking El Niño will last until at least 2027. The company separated into two distinct firms in 2023. The largest is Kellanova, which focuses on snacks, cereals, noodles and other food products like Eggo, Pringles and Pop-Tarts sold globally. It is now owned by Mars, which makes confectionery and pet food. The other business, WK Kellogg's, operates in North America and has since been taken over by Italian chocolate giant Ferrero . events.title: The Download: blended meat, restored sight, and the agentic web
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat  In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge served hungry students steaming marinara sauce and meatballs. The students loved them: 92% of those who tried them wanted them on the menu. Few could guess that mushrooms had been mixed into the meat. Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the biggest challenges of the climate crisis: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef. Joyn is among a wave of startups creating “blended meat,” which combines plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat. Get a taste of the startups betting on greener beef . —Meghan McCarron This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration More than 5 million people have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which retinal cells die off. Until now, no treatment could restore their vision. A system called PRIMA changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients could read, do crosswords, and use their phones. Find out how the sight-restoring implant works . —Linda Marsa MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts. This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Democrats have dealt tech billionaires a major midterm setback The results could bring tougher scrutiny of AI and data centres. ( CNBC ) + Musk poured millions into Texas, but both his candidates lost. ( Wired $) + Several winners promised to restrict data centre construction. ( FT $) + Stock futures slid as Democrats won big. ( NBC News ) + The tech left said it’s ready to “wipe the floor.” ( Vanity Fair $) 2 Google is shutting off Search for schools that reject AI The company said AI and Search can no longer be untwined. ( CNN ) + Critics accused Google of pressuring schools to adopt AI. ( NBC News ) + AI is the end of search as we know it. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 The Binance hackers used fake job interviews in their record heist They targeted an engineer through LinkedIn. ( NBC News ) + Researchers had repeatedly warned about the tactics. ( TechCrunch ) + The breach could boost demand for specialist crypto custodians. ( CNBC ) 4 Materials maker 3M will pay $7.35 billion to settle “forever chemicals” lawsuits The suits involve PFAS in firefighting foam. ( WSJ $) + New tech could help rid water of PFAS. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Finland is opening a nuclear waste vault built to last 100,000 years It will bury spent fuel 400 metres underground. ( New Scientist $) + It’s time to make new plans for nuclear waste . ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Russia wants underground data centers after Ukrainian strikes Drone attacks have disrupted services used by millions. ( Ars Technica ) 7 Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity FlashProve uses cryptography to verify a model’s outputs. ( TechCrunch ) + “Personhood credentials” could prove you’re human. ( NYT $) 9 Dinosaur blood has been found in fossils for the first time The discovery advances research into ancient biomolecules. ( Guardian ) 10 Chernobyl’s dogs appear to be evolving Scientists found differences linked to DNA repair and immunity. ( Wired $) Quote of the day “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time ” —Elon Musk tries to laugh off a costly loss on X after the Republican candidates he spent record sums supporting got drubbed in the US midterm elections. From the China-US rivalry and model breakthroughs to public sentiment and the impact on jobs, here are the index’s key findings on the state of AI today . —Michelle Kim We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. events.title: Hackers tried to literally boil blood in France
events.summary: France's national blood service said three of its sites were affected. Universal Images Group via Getty Images A cyberattack targeted refrigerators storing blood plasma in France. The blood service's alarm system recognized the rising temperatures, and no equipment was destroyed. Over the weekend, a cyberattack hit refrigeration systems at dozens of grocery stores across Europe. Hackers have come for blood. France's national civilian blood service, the EFS, said its refrigerators were hit by a cyberattack on Monday that raised temperatures to "very high levels." The attack hit three sites, affecting equipment storing blood samples and plasma used in transfusions, the EFS said in a press release. Hospitals often use frozen plasma for patients who are hemorrhaging or otherwise losing a lot of blood. Hackers targeted a refrigeration equipment supplier, not the EFS itself, the release said. The EFS' monitoring and alarm systems identified the rising temperatures, and people responded to the attack before any samples or products were compromised or destroyed. Products at the facilities were "preventively transferred to other facilities," the EFS said. The attackers aimed to raise temperatures from -22°F to 230°F, according to the French publication Le Canard enchaîné. The EFS did not comment on the temperatures reached, and said it is working with France's cybersecurity agency and the Ministry of Health to investigate the attack. A spokesperson for the EFS told Business Insider that the organization has "strengthened" temperature monitoring of all refrigeration equipment, and that blood collection and distribution are "fully ensured." Europe's refrigerators feel the heat The attack on blood plasma fridges is the latest in a wave of incidents involving internet-connected fridges and freezers. From Sunday into Monday,  hackers targeted refrigeration systems  at dozens of European supermarkets. Fridge and freezer temperatures rose at stores in countries including Sweden, Belgium, and Estonia, with one Swedish retailer saying temperatures were set to 122°F in a Facebook post. Some stores were forced to throw away food. Employees throw away bags of spoiled refrigerated food outside an ICA supermarket in Stockholm. Fredrik SANDBERG / TT NEWS AGENCY / AFP via Getty Images Last month, another cyberattack hit hundreds of French grocery stores, causing retailers to throw away thousands of dollars worth of food. The director of a store in Normandy told Business Insider that his freezers were set to 122º F and that he lost $112,000 worth of food. It is not clear who is behind the refrigeration attacks or whether any of them are connected. Commercial refrigeration systems are connected to the internet so that engineers can monitor them remotely for maintenance. The defrost settings allow them to clear ice buildup, but have been overridden by hackers to dangerously high levels. Many of the targeted systems have out-of-date software. The string of incidents comes amid a broader wave of cyber anxiety in recent weeks, including over a $6.3 billion crypto heist and newfound vulnerabilities in a programming language that supports up to 70% of websites. U.S. same-store sales – or sales at locations open at least a year -- fell 0.2% in the July-September period, the Chicago burger giant said Wednesday. While that was not as bad as the 0.5% drop Wall Street had expected, it was the first retreat for McDonald's since early 2025. McDonald’s restored in-app deals and its marketing was focused on value during the quarter, which helped push same-store sales into positive territory in September. But the shift in focus at McDonald’s shows how challenging the economic environment has become for U.S. fast food companies. Third-quarter foot traffic fell 2.6% across the entire fast food sector in the U.S., according to Revenue Management Solutions, a restaurant industry consultant. “This is the environment that we’re in right now. You have to be on your game and deliver that value,” said McDonald’s Chairman and CEO Chris Kempczinski during an investor presentation last month. “The pressure around cost of living isn’t going away.” Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Captain identified after deadly Florida Learjet crash 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Globally, same-store sales rose 1.3% in the same period that U.S. sales fell. Strong sales in Germany and Australia helped offset weakness in France, which was rocked by protests that began in September. Revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion for the quarter, short of Wall Street expectations of $7.28 billion. Net income rose 9% to $2.49 billion. Adjusted for one-time items, the company earned $3.57 per share. That beat analysts’ forecast for a $3.38 per-share profit. events.title: AI data center stocks and Musk's SpaceX decline as Texas governor result raises risks of a slowdown
events.summary: Several AI-linked stocks fell as election results came in showing a convincing win by Democrats of both houses of Congress. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race after campaigning for tougher limits on data center development. Investors are weighing whether state-level data center restrictions could delay projects in major buildout markets. AI data center stocks came under pressure as Democrats — seen as proponents of moratoriums on the buildout — won big in midterm elections and in key technology hubs like Texas. Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow, analysts said. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants to enact an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state, won over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State. The midterm elections will slow the pace of data center buildouts across the U.S., Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning. "There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," he said. He added that the election in Texas was the "biggest worry" of the night for tech investors and the AI trade because that's where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from. SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 7% and 6%, respectively. Peer Nebius Group was down 3% and Oracle shed 4.3%. Nvidia shares were slightly in the red. Tech giants Alphabet , Meta and Microsoft mostly bucked the trend and were higher. The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing. "We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week. Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo. Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end. "Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."

events.title: Why are Europe’s governments struggling to respond to growing protests?
events.summary: Protests intensify as governments prioritise security measures over addressing underlying social and economic concerns. Protests across Europe show no sign of abating. They subside on certain days, only to flare up a few days later. Largely led by young people, demonstrations have swept across at least eight European countries, driven by grievances ranging from school conditions and the cost of diesel to a deeper sense of insecurity about the future – and the feeling that opportunities are increasingly out of reach. list 1 of 3 UK to double wait for permanent residency, with exemptions for care workers list 2 of 3 California’s Bay Area debates data centres ahead of US midterm elections list 3 of 3 ‘Going hungry’: Garment workers in Bangladesh say wages barely cover needs “They are plural and uncoordinated, with no single leader or programme,” said Alberto Alemanno, professor of European Union law and policy at HEC Paris Business School. “So it’s less a rejection of one policy and more a signal that people no longer trust the system to deliver. That’s why they are so critical.” For governments, addressing discontent is proving difficult. Experts say there is no easy fix, and that many have so far struggled to offer answers beyond a show of force. The protests are likely to continue, they warn. “Where there has been a reaction, the focus is on public order and security,” Alemanno said. “Part of the reason is that, like any popular protest, these movements include or attract small violent minorities . They dominate the headlines and risk undermining legitimate claims.” Rallies continue because they are increasingly about more than individual grievances, said Donatella della Porta, a political science professor at the Scuola Normale Superiore in Florence. While governments have tried to address some of the protesters’ material demands, they have failed to grasp the broader political concerns driving the demonstrations. “At this point, protests are no longer just about investing more in the school system. There are also fundamental issues, including military spending, governments’ alliance with [United States President Donald] Trump, the rising cost of gasoline and the war in Iran,” she said. “ The issue of Palestine is also very central to these protests.” This week, protesters have continued to blockade several high schools and universities in France, where students have been pushing for better conditions, more teachers and the replacement of Parcoursup, an admission system that some say is discriminatory. In Germany, metal and electrical workers have gone on strike while students have demonstrated over fears of the return of conscription. In Belgium, firefighters marched through Brussels, demanding more staff and better equipment. And on Friday in Italy, the USB union brought tens of thousands of people together, calling for a reduction in military spending. France’s Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Monday that some measures to meet students’ demands have been adopted, including capping class sizes to 28 for the first year of high school, creating 10,000 places in higher technician programmes, and transforming Parcoursup. Other measures require in-depth work between now and the end of December, he said on X. But the announcements have failed to quell the protests. On Tuesday, dozens of schools remained blockaded and several universities were disrupted, according to French media. A nationwide strike over wages, the cost of living and public services is also expected on November 5. In Spain, massive protests swept through the country for weeks over a housing crisis, triggered by the eviction and subsequent death of an 87-year-old pensioner from her lifelong home. On Tuesday, police dismantled a sprawling tent camp in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square. Officials said the eviction took place overnight “without incident or episodes of violence”, reporting that 334 people were removed and two arrested. In a post on Telegram, protest organisers lamented “a violent police operation” that they said left several people injured. The government has approved new housing measures, including limits on rent increases and temporary protections against eviction for some vulnerable tenants. But these promises have done little to dissuade protesters, who are planning a general strike over housing rights and the cost of living on November 11. In Italy, after violence broke out during protests two weeks ago, the government of far-right leader Giorgia Meloni tightened security measures. “Violent participation” in a demonstration – by joining a group of five or more people and throwing stones, firecrackers or sticks – was made a criminal offence that could result in up to five years in prison and a fine of up to 20,000 euros ($22,500). Italy also made parents liable for damage caused by their children and adopted a policy of preventive detention of children.

events.title: U.S. midterm elections in pictures: Democrats' sweeping victories deliver rebuke to Trump
events.summary: Democrats scored sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections on Wednesday, flipping key Republican-held seats in Congress. The party was projected to regain control of both chambers of Congress. Democrats scored sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections on Wednesday, flipping key Republican-held seats in Congress and securing historic wins in traditionally conservative states, as voters delivered a setback to President Donald Trump. The party was projected to gain control of both chambers of Congress, with victories across several battleground states threatening to constrain Trump's legislative agenda for the remaining two years of his presidency. Here are some of the scenes from polling stations, campaign headquarters and election-night celebrations across the United States. Among the biggest surprises was Texas, where Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton to become the state's first Democratic U.S. senator since 1988. Fellow Democrat Gina Hinojosa also unseated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the state's first Latina governor and ending more than three decades of Republican control of the office. In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a Republican-held Senate seat after defeating Trump-backed Michael Whatley. Cooper will succeed retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who announced his departure after clashing with Trump over his tax and spending legislation. In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff secured reelection against Trump-backed Republican Mike Collins, while former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor's race, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state. Meanwhile, in Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown staged a political comeback, defeating Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a closely watched Senate race. The elections were widely viewed as a referendum on Trump's second term, with concerns over the cost of living, inflation and the war in Iran weighing on voter sentiment. —CNBC's Danielle DeVries contributed to this article.

events.title: The midterms won’t ease borrowing costs. Here’s what CFOs should do now
events.summary: Good morning. What do the U.S. midterm election results mean for finance leaders? With Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress, companies could face greater scrutiny of issues such as AI investment and data center development. But the broader financing challenges facing finance chiefs extend beyond the shifting political landscape. “CFOs should go into 2027 expecting sustained higher borrowing costs,” Josh Putnam, EY-Parthenon’s global and Americas corporate finance leader, told me. Financing conditions are also likely to remain volatile, regardless of which party controls Congress. Growing deficits, strong capital demand, inflation volatility, and policy uncertainty are putting pressure on long-term rates, Putnam said, making disciplined capital allocation, debt management, and investment decisions increasingly important for finance chiefs. His advice is to stress-test investment hurdles, evaluate debt maturities, and protect balance-sheet flexibility. Companies must understand which investments can generate returns above their cost of capital and redirect resources when they cannot, he said. Planning for fiscal uncertainty Political gridlock could add risk, but on its own it does not necessarily mean higher long-term borrowing costs. A divided government “would not automatically push term premiums higher,” said Gregory Daco, EY-Parthenon’s chief economist. But repeated budget disagreements, shutdown risks, debt ceiling stress, and greater fiscal uncertainty “would reinforce upward pressure,” he said. Daco recommends testing investments against a range of financing costs and maintaining hurdle rates that reflect a structurally higher and more volatile cost of capital. For companies, however, the risks extend beyond long-term interest rates. Political uncertainty can also affect access to credit and the cost of short-term financing. “Markets respond to uncertainty by charging more, whether the risk originates in Washington, D.C., or on Wall Street,” said Mark Williams, a master lecturer in finance at Boston University’s Questrom School of Business and a former bank examiner for the Federal Reserve Bank. Williams said that banks react to elevated risk by tightening credit terms and reducing lending. “Legislative gridlock can create volatile funding cycles and cause short-term borrowing costs to spike,” he explained. Companies relying on commercial paper, a form of short-term corporate borrowing, should consider longer-term funding, diversify financing sources, and secure credit lines across multiple banks, he said.  Because a divided government can increase the risk of shutdowns, which can delay the release of economic data, CFOs should also develop internal models to fill those gaps, Williams said. Government contractors, meanwhile, should evaluate how potential payment delays could affect cash flow. The rising cost of the AI boom AI investment could face particularly intense financial scrutiny as financing costs rise and regulatory uncertainty increases. Voters on Tuesday sent a clear message about the AI buildout: the costs of data centers are now a political issue. Candidates in both parties who campaigned on rising electric bills won key races, and at least 14 Ohio towns passed restrictions on data center development, Fortune reported . The results underscore the growing regulatory and political uncertainty facing AI and data center developers, which could drive up costs and complicate project financing, Williams said. Private credit funds, the primary lenders in the space, would demand higher interest rates, he said, and prices on outstanding AI bonds could fall as yields rise.  But the market was already recalibrating AI risk before the election, Williams noted. He recommends returning to corporate finance fundamentals, including more conservative net present value assumptions, multi-variable scenario analysis, and stress testing against higher borrowing costs and stricter lending covenants. Daco also sees a political dimension. With affordability central to the election, “a backlash is likely if households see AI investment raising power costs while its benefits remain concentrated,” he said. CFOs should prioritize projects with measurable productivity gains, account fully for power and infrastructure costs, and pair technology investment with investment in workers and skills, Daco said. The financial discipline required to navigate the next economic cycle remains vital. As Putnam put it, “Companies that demonstrate they can put capital to work effectively will be best positioned to pursue growth.” Sheryl   Estrada Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Ad industry dealmaking is heating up. M&A pros think these 9 companies could be the next big buyers.
events.summary: David Steinberg's Zeta Global could pursue further acquisitions, according to ad industry analysts and insiders. Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images A version of this post appears in CMO Insider. Sign up for Business Insider's marketing newsletter . It's shopping season in the advertising industry, and I'm not just talking about the holidays. After a somewhat sleepy period, the M&A market is stirring back to life, with strategic buyers loading up their carts. In the past couple of weeks alone, Publicis Groupe completed its $2.2 billion acquisition of the data company LiveRamp ; Salesforce announced a $5.7 billion deal for the customer-engagement platform Braze; India-based Affle said it's buying fellow adtech firm Perion for $420 million; and advertising holding company Stagwell picked up Freestar, a platform that helps publishers sell their ad space. Jay MacDonald, CEO of the investment bank Digital Capital Advisors, has a simple rule for predicting where M&A could strike next: follow the ad dollars. He pointed to areas including influencer marketing, retail media, and connected TV. He added that geography-focused acquisitions could help companies gain a larger share of wallet. The AI boom is also causing strategic players to rethink ad businesses they may have once overlooked, said Ana Milicevic, cofounder of Sparrow Advisers. "Adtech has been innovating with real-time decisioning, identity, and all these component parts that in a much more automated world are very relevant," Milicevic said. CMO Insider polled nine ad industry bankers, investors, executives, and consultants about which strategic buyers they thought could splash out on more acquisitions in the coming months. Their answers ranged from Accenture to Zeta. We've listed the highlights in alphabetical order. Accenture The consulting firm said last month it plans to spend around $5 billion on acquisitions in its 2027 financial year. Ad industry pros expect its highly acquisitive marketing services division, Accenture Song , to remain an active buyer. Karsten Weide, principal at W Media Research, said Accenture's recent purchases of the creator and social agency Whalar and the data firm Sagacity demonstrate its appetite for marketing technology, customer intelligence, and creative capabilities. "Additional acquisitions could help Accenture Song assemble a more integrated marketing offering spanning data, AI, creative production, commerce, and campaign execution," Weide said. Adobe Fresh off its $1.9 billion acquisition of the search engine optimization platform Semrush this year, Adobe, soon to be helmed by new CEO Anil Chakravarthy, could be on the hunt for more companies to help strengthen its marketing and creative stack. Sanja Partalo, general partner of S4S Ventures, said Adobe's competitive environment is getting more challenging by the day, with creative AI companies like Higgsfield, Runway, and Canva vying for its Creative Cloud customers. (Both Adobe and S4S invested in Runway's Series E round this year.) "As brands need to produce more content for more channels, I'd expect Adobe to keep looking for tools that connect creation to campaign execution and measurement, as well," Partalo said. "I believe M&A is a tool they will continue to deploy to strengthen their offering." Havas Holding company Havas completed eight acquisitions in the first nine months of 2026, and its CFO François Laroze said last month that additional deals could close before year-end or in early 2027. "Publicis' acquisition of LiveRamp increases the incentive to strengthen Havas' data, identity, retail media, and AI capabilities, although its established strategy favors smaller, targeted acquisitions," W Media Research's Weide said. Digital Capital Advisors' MacDonald said Havas could pursue targeted acquisitions in the $50 million to $200 million range, compared with Publicis' billion-dollar-plus deals. Omnicom On ad giant Omnicom's third-quarter earnings call last month, CFO Phil Angelastro said the company is getting back into acquisition mode, having completed its $9 billion mega-merger with IPG and some disposals across its portfolio. Industry insiders predicted retail media acquisitions could be high on Omnicom's list of potential targets. That would bolster its Acxiom data and Flywheel commerce assets. Nick MacShane, senior managing director at the investment bank Progress Partners, described Omnicom as a company that needs "to answer other people's M&A," pointing to the Publicis-LiveRamp deal. Omnicom "still lacks the commerce stack Publicis built with Epsilon, CitrusAd, and Profitero," said Andreas Roell, CEO of the advisory firm Evros Group. OpenAI OpenAI is scaling its ad business at lightning speed. The company said last month that more than 100,000 advertisers had run ChatGPT ad campaigns over the eight months since its ad platform's debut. It's also launched a slew of adtech integrations, including with Criteo, Kargo, Pacvue, and StackAdapt. Industry insiders said partnerships can sometimes signal that buyers are road-testing a company's capabilities ahead of a potential acquisition. OpenAI could move to purchase an ad-buying platform that has baked-in advertiser and agency relationships, Sparrow Advisers' Milicevic said. "The biggest value is the advertising know-how," she said. "Hiring a larger team that already functions well with each other and knows how to speak to buyers, and knows what transactions are valued, can really accelerate their go-to-market." M&A will largely depend on what happens with OpenAI's forthcoming initial public offering , said Joshua Wepman, a managing director within Houlihan Lokey's technology group. "Anything they're working on, they'll slow roll it with the S-1 process," Wepman said. Publicis The highly acquisitive French agency group shows no signs of slowing down after buying LiveRamp, and said earlier this year it expected to resume incremental bolt-on acquisitions once that deal was completed. events.title: China expands overseas mining stakes, tightening grip on critical minerals
events.summary: Chinese firms will likely double their outbound investment over the next five years to expand mineral supplies overseas. A state-coordinated push could curb competition among Chinese firms and strengthen their position against foreign competitors. China's "near-monopoly" in rare earth separation and refining could be strengthened by a growing overseas mining presence. China is mobilizing state-linked companies to take bigger ownership stakes in mines overseas, seeking to strengthen its stranglehold over the metals vital for electric vehicles, semiconductors and jet engines The state-led push could give Beijing greater leverage over global supplies of critical minerals and who gets access to them, analysts say. "China is rolling out a state-coordinated global mining strategy" to replace firm-level decision-making, said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia, adding that the model would allow for larger, better-aligned global mining investments. In April, a dedicated overseas bureau was set up to oversee investments abroad by central state-owned enterprises. Several government agencies, ministries and policy banks have been mobilized to steer overseas mining deals. Later in July, a mining investment vehicle was created to coordinate overseas deals, advising Chinese companies on compliance, risk management, and market conditions as they face growing geopolitical tensions and regulatory hurdles abroad. The push for greater centralization could curb disorderly competition among Chinese firms and strengthen their hand against Western competitors and newer entrants, such as Saudi Arabia and India, Wang said, though a longer review and approval process could also raise corruption risks and weigh on investment returns. Chinese firms have invested heavily in overseas mining for two decades, making big bets in places avoided by Western miners, from Tajikistan to the Democratic Republic of Congo. The push has gained urgency as governments increasingly view critical minerals as a source of geopolitical leverage. Chinese mineral acquisitions abroad reached $8.8 billion in the first three quarters this year — already the highest annual total since at least 2018, according to a Rhodium Group report released Wednesday. "Acquisitions have mostly been concentrated in minerals that China lacks domestically," said Armand Meyer, senior research analyst at Rhodium, naming lithium, nickel and cobalt during the electric-vehicle boom in the mid-2010s and gold in recent years. Outbound investment in upstream critical minerals will likely roughly double from the 2021-2025 period, according to Eurasia, as China doubles down on overseas push to secure access and reserves that it lacks domestically. Beijing treats 70% import dependence as an implicit red line – which puts copper, lithium, cobalt, nickel, bauxite and iron ore under a hard national security constraint to expand supply abroad, Wang said. Even where reliance is lower, Beijing wants more. For gold, which sits within the 50% "safe" range, the government still seeks additional access to high-grade resources, Wang said. That pursuit of scale and "ultimately geopolitical strength" could override decisions over investment risk and profitability, she added. But the push is facing growing resistance as host governments demand more local processing, a stage China dominates and has turned into a key supply-chain chokepoint. More resource-rich countries are restricting exports of unprocessed minerals and requiring foreign partners to refine them locally. Countries have long shipped rare earths to China for processing because refining carries high environmental costs, allowing Beijing to build out massive processing capacity across the country. The U.S. has abundant supplies of rare earths, but it relies on China to refine them. China now produces about 92% of the world's refined rare earths, according to the International Energy Agency. That gives Beijing the ability to withhold supply or flood the market to influence prices and project power, said Brad Handler, director of Energy Finance Lab at the Payne Institute. "If a rival builds a new refinery, China can produce more, oversupply the market and push prices below economic levels," he said. China has curbed exports of seven medium and heavy rare earths since last year, requiring exporters to obtain licenses. Japan has been among the hardest hit, reportedly coming within months of running out of yttrium. The element, used for screen displays and semiconductors, is produced as a byproduct during the extraction of other rare earth metals. China's exports of yttrium oxide to Japan collapsed to 4,000 kilograms in September from 51,000 kilograms a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. And the oxide's price reportedly surged to about $1,150 a kilogram outside China — roughly 179 times its level two years earlier — compared with about $9 a kilogram inside the country.

events.title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
events.summary: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem. Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows. events.title: Business winners and losers from the 2026 midterm elections
events.summary: The midterm elections sent millions of Americans to the polls. Here's what we learned from the early results. Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images The midterms ended on Tuesday, sending a fresh batch of lawmakers to Washington and state houses. Americans also decided on ballot measures. Those decisions could determine future business projects. AI companies and the stock market have been some of the biggest losers of the night. There's a new set of power brokers in government, and it's creating winners and losers when it comes to companies, industries, and policies. In the 2026 US midterms , which ended on Tuesday, voters handed the Democratic Party control of the House and the Senate. Voters also cast ballots in governor races, state legislative races, and on ballot measures. Those results will help determine which projects receive funding, which companies face new regulations, and which policies are blocked over the next two years. From affordability candidates to mega-donor Elon Musk, here are the winners and losers in the 2026 midterm elections. Winner: Candidates running on affordability Hakeem Jeffries made affordability a key part of his campaign. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images The Democratic Party will control Congress, with majorities in the House and Senate. The result is a surprisingly strong showing for Democrats, many of whom put affordability at the center of their campaigns. The cost of living frequently came up as a key issue for voters , with Americans shelling out more at the gas pump than a year ago as the war in Iran has pushed up prices. "We will fight hard to lower the high cost of housing and groceries and gas," said Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who will likely become Speaker of the House in January, in a Tuesday night speech. While many Republicans also ran on affordability policies, President Donald Trump acknowledged in a call with Fox News that midterm voters weren't willing to pay more for gas . "I don't think it's the war, I think it's the gas prices," Trump said. Loser: Elon Musk Musk was the biggest disclosed individual donor in the midterms race. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Musk spent more than $400 million trying to keep Republicans in power. It wasn't enough. He put the cash behind Republican-aligned groups this cycle, making him the biggest disclosed individual donor in the midterms. His biggest bet was on Ken Paxton's Senate campaign in Texas, where Musk-backed groups spent about $212 million. Democratic lawmaker James Talarico defeated Paxton anyway, helping Democrats take the Senate — and undercutting Musk's effort to preserve Republican control in the state he has made home to Tesla and SpaceX. Musk also used X, his social media platform, to tout Republican candidates, especially in Texas. "The fate of Texas and America is at stake," he wrote on X while endorsing the state's Republican Senate candidate, Ken Paxton. Meanwhile, he called James Talarico, Paxton's opponent, "a creep." Texas is also a personal political battleground for Musk. Tesla moved its corporate headquarters to Austin in 2021, while Tesla and SpaceX both reincorporated in Texas in 2024. SpaceX is now based at Starbase, Texas . He said he moved the companies to the Lone Star State for more favorable tax, land acquisition, and corporate legal policies. Loser: AI companies Data center buildout was a key mandate in the midterm polls. Kaylee Greenlee/Bloomberg via Getty Images AI companies are likely to face a tougher political environment. Democrats are expected to use their new control of Congress to scrutinize the costs of the AI race: the power and water consumed by data centers, rising household electricity bills, and whether tech companies are keeping enough of their promises about local jobs. That could mean more investigations and scrutiny of companies such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, and the firms building the data centers that support them. But the results won't necessarily mean a crackdown on AI. The president, who is pro-AI development and pro-AI infrastructure, can veto major legislation. There is also bipartisan agreement on AI regarding national security, competition with China, and economic growth. Pending: The stock market US stock futures fell after the Democratic sweep became clear on early Wednesday. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images Initially, investors were not fans of the "blunami" that has swept election results. US stock futures fell after the Democratic sweep became clear, with S&P 500 futures down about 1% and Nasdaq 100 futures down nearly 2% in early trading. The dollar also weakened sharply against most major currencies as investors braced following a strong Democratic showing. AI-linked stocks were among the hardest hit, as investors weighed the prospect that Democratic control could mean tougher oversight of Big Tech and its data center spending. However, S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures both reversed into gains of about 1% each as of 6:30 a.m. ET as the market digested the latest results. Loser: People counting on $5,000 checks from Trump Those waiting for Trump's proposed $5,000 "dividend" might have to keep waiting. Trump made the promise conditional on Republicans keeping control of the House and Senate, an outcome voters have rejected. Even if Trump revived the idea, he would need Congress to authorize and fund it since the president cannot unilaterally spend more than $1 trillion on nationwide checks. Democratic control makes this even less likely. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Mortgage rates drop for the third straight week, but homebuyers are still leaving the market
events.summary: The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, decreased last week to 7.3% from 7.37% Refinance demand was 60% lower year-over-year. Homebuyer applications were 19% lower than a year ago. After a brief bounce the week before, mortgage demand continued its slide last week, despite falling mortgage rates. Total application volume dropped 1.2% week to week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, decreased last week to 7.3% from 7.37%, with points declining to 0.75 from 0.76, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. "Mortgage rates drifted down to their lowest level since September 2026 last week in the wake of the Federal Reserve's decision to hold on additional rate hikes at its October meeting," said Mike Fratantoni, senior vice president and chief economist at the MBA. Refinance demand was essentially flat for the week, rising just 0.1%. It was, however, 60% lower than the same week one year ago. Mortgage rates, despite falling for now three straight weeks, are still about a full percentage point higher than they were at this time last year. That gives borrowers very little incentive to refinance. Get Property Play directly to your inbox CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox. Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell 2% from the previous week and were 19% lower year over year. The housing market shows no signs of thawing, after the sharp rate increase in September sent it into a deep freeze. The share of adjustable-rate mortgages, which offer lower rates but carry the risk of eventually resetting higher, continued to climb. The average rate on a 5/1 ARM dropped to 6.29% from 6.41% the previous week. "As we have highlighted in recent weeks, more borrowers are choosing ARMs in this environment to lower their initial payments, with the ARM share at its highest level since September 2025," added Fratantoni. Mortgage rates moved slightly higher to start this week, according to a separate survey by Mortgage News Daily. That came after a hotter-than-expected report on job openings. "All else equal, stronger labor market data tends to put upward pressure on rates. Tech stocks were also modestly higher [Tuesday], and weakness in the tech sector has been a key factor driving persistently lower rates over the past several weeks," wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily. Correction: Total application volume dropped 1.2% week to week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. An earlier version misstated the figure.

The election also sharpened the political fight over data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure. Democrats decisively took control of Congress Tuesday night, delivering a stinging rebuke to President Donald Trump and his economic record as voters voiced deep frustration with rising prices, government corruption and the AI data center build-out . The party scored an extraordinary pair of victories in traditionally Republican Texas. James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the state in nearly four decades. Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Gov. Greg Abbott, making her the first Democratic governor of Texas since Ann Richards left office in 1995. Texas became the clearest measure of how far the blue wave reached: Democrats swept the state's marquee races in a Republican stronghold long considered beyond their grasp. Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results The victories were part of a broader wave of Democratic gains. In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews upset Darline Graham in a race Republicans had expected to win. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Democrats also flipped Senate seats in Iowa and North Carolina and won key races in Georgia and New Hampshire. The results marked a striking collapse for Trump's candidates. Paxton, Graham and Husted were among the president's prominent picks who lost after he made dozens of endorsements. Elon Musk, the world's richest man and the cycle's largest individual political donor, spent record sums in a failed effort to help Republicans retain power, including in Texas. Musk's spending may have become a liability as voters raised concerns about government corruption and the growing influence of billionaires in exit polls. Talarico repeatedly attacked Musk on the campaign trail, accusing him of trying to buy "his very own personal United States Senator." "Tonight's results are a wake-up call for corporate special interests and billionaires who have been rigging the economy," said Rep. Chris Pappas, who defeated former Republican Sen. John Sununu to win an open Senate seat in New Hampshire. The outcome is poised to reshape the technology sector's relationship with Washington. A more adversarial Congress is likely to intensify scrutiny of tech companies and the AI data center build-out. Markets reacted as the scale of Democratic gains became clear: Dow futures fell and S&P 500 futures slipped Tuesday evening. Economic frustration was also central to Democratic gains. Many voters blamed Trump's tariffs and the war with Iran for worsening their economic situation, while the cost of living remained a persistent strain. Democratic control of both chambers gives the party a powerful check on Trump in the final two years of his term, including the ability to block parts of his agenda and intensify congressional oversight. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Public Accounts Committee talks of 'broken promises' and 'chaos' as 'thousands' of retired folk miss out on money Capita set to miss legal deadline on 93,000 civil servants' pension fixes, claims union 19 days ago UK spending watchdog opens investigation into Capita's pension fiasco October 2, 2026 Sopra Steria widens legal challenge to Capita's Whitehall outsourcing deal October 1, 2026 UK government vows to reclaim services from outsourcing giants September 28, 2026 Sopra Steria's £370M Capita spat heads for 2028 courtroom showdown August 26, 2026 Capita has repeatedly "broken" promises to resolve the "chaos" engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) following its takeover of the administration – a move that left thousands of retired public sector workers unpaid. So says Parliamentary spending watchdog, the Public Accounts Committee, which this week launched an inquiry into the handover of the ten-year £239 million contract in December from previous incumbent MyCSP. As The Register exclusively revealed , the troubles began early on as members of CSPS – which manages pensions for 1.7 million people – complained of unrecognized passwords and usernames on the portal Capita developed. Capita said it inherited 132,100 complex remediation cases, and claimed the work-in-progress backlog from the prior system was more than double the 37,000 items when it won the deal in 2023 . Capita ran to Microsoft for support , and promised the use AI and automation, in addition to its 500 full-time employees working on the project, would resolve the issues by March. It missed this deadline, as well as one set for June 30 and is set to miss March 2027 . The government subsequently withheld a £10 million payment to Capita over the CSPS fiasco. The National Audit Office, a spending regulator, has already launched its own probe into the failures and is now joined by the PAC, which says thousands of civil servants and their families have struggled to on and collect their pensions The PAC has already held three evidence sessions on Capita and the government’s efforts to ameliorate the situation. The law was changed in the Budget 2026 to mitigate the impact of administrative delays in CSPS on bereaved families. Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair at the PAC, said in a statement: "In response to the alarming reports of hard-working civil servants being thrown into financial uncertainty following Capita’s takeover of the CSPS, we have held a number of evidence sessions with both the top leadership of Capita, and the civil servants and ministers of the Cabinet Office who have ultimate responsibility for overseeing the contract. " Over and over again, promises have been made and broken by Capita, to our faces in formal evidence sessions, that they will get a grip on what has gone wrong. As a result, we are launching an inquiry, which will be informed by the authoritative factual basis provided by the NAO, which supports the scrutiny work of this Committee." The inquiry will draw on the finding of the NAO's forthcoming report on the switch of CSPS to Capita, and will take into consideration the status of the scheme at go-live date, how Capita has performed, and the effect on CSPS members, plus take a look into the way the Cabinet Office has overseen the prior scheme and the switch to Capita. The Register has asked Capita to comment.

events.title: Riyadh parents stuck in war-time limbo
events.summary: The Scene Houthi strikes on the Saudi capital have created an eerie echo of the COVID-19 period: Schools have gone online and many businesses have sent staff home, spurring an economic slowdown similar to that during the pandemic . And like six years ago, there is no foreseeable end. Parents in Riyadh have been stuck in limbo for almost a month, waiting and wondering when they will be able to send their children back to school so they can get on with work. The frequency of strikes on the city has not slowed over the past month since that side of the conflict started, with missile alerts still ringing multiple times a week, sometimes multiple times a night. There was a brief moment of hope last week when authorities tried to bring students back to classrooms. The education ministry divided Riyadh into 10 zones and planned a staggered return, which would have seen schools reopening neighborhood by neighborhood. The experiment lasted just three days after which officials reversed course, sending students back online without offering a new date for schools to reopen. The decision is now up to individual schools, with the majority opting to remain online. Meanwhile, the city’s business hub, King Abdullah Financial District, remains largely deserted, and office towers above 10 floors are still closed. Some expats who asked to work from abroad were told that there was no need to leave. The message: Keep calm and carry on — things are fine. But the restrictions have made it impossible for many to work from their offices and nobody seems to know how long this arrangement will last. For months, Riyadh maintained a veneer of business as usual despite the war, but this has become harder to sustain with the city postponing events, from tennis tournaments to conferences, and now doing a U-turn on schools. For residents, the question is no longer just whether the Houthi attacks will stop, but how long will this suspended version of life continue. Saudis are coping with humor, as they have throughout this war and past ones. One joke circulating online describes remote schooling as a wise precaution with one unintended consequence: The Houthis now face their deadliest threat yet, mothers trapped at home with their children, directing their prayers against them. Notable Consultants are driving into Riyadh from Oman and Bahrain to keep face time with Saudi clients as flights falter , and the attacks may be speeding up what the kingdom’s headquarters policy always wanted, fewer Dubai commuters, and more staff living in the kingdom , Bloomberg reported.

events.title: Can Democrats stop Iran war, reverse Trump’s tariffs after midterms win?
events.summary: Democrats can block Trump’s legislative agenda and launch investigations, but they have no two-thirds majority to override a presidential veto. Democrats have taken control of the United States House of Representatives and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections in a scathing defeat for US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party. The Congress that will convene in early January will be radically different from the first two years of Trump’s second presidential term, which saw Republicans holding majorities in both chambers. list 1 of 3 Who determines Iran’s fighting and negotiating position amid US threats? list 2 of 3 Key takeaways from the 2026 midterm elections in California list 3 of 3 GOP’s redistricting gamble backfires in Florida as Democrats hold ground While Democrats will have greater power to scrutinise Trump’s policies and obstruct any legislation they oppose, there is still a lot a president can do without congressional approval. Here is a look at some pressing political issues and how a Democratic majority in both chambers might affect them: Trump has acknowledged the role the war on Iran has played in Republican losses in the midterm elections. “I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time, people understood the importance of what I’ve done with Iran,” Trump said during a telephone interview with Fox News. Frustration among voters about inflation, and the rising cost of fuel and groceries have been among the main factors behind their rebuke to Republicans. Democrats tapped into this by campaigning heavily on affordability and domestic spending. Trump embarked on the war on Iran with Israel in February without congressional authorisation. He could still order attacks, but he could also face constraints from the new Congress. Lawmakers could use their power to deny additional funding when the current government-funding bill expires on December 11, presenting a critical budget constraint on Trump’s military decisions. However, James Boys, research fellow at the Centre on US Politics at University College London, said that while Congress may wish to cut off funding, it may not be straightforward. “With troops in theatre, this would prove to be highly problematic and be seen to be placing American lives at risk,” he said. Analysts also said the War Powers Resolution is unlikely to succeed in reining Trump in. Previous attempts to use the 1973 federal law have been defeated or rendered ineffective. The War Powers Resolution states that a president can repel an imminent attack, but military actions must end within 60 days unless Congress declares war. The president can then issue a veto, which can only be overcome by a two-thirds supermajority in both the House and Senate. The projected breakdown of the newly elected Congress shows that Democrats are well short of those supermajority thresholds. Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the UCD Clinton Institute in Dublin, Ireland, said that while Congress is constrained without a two-thirds majority, what it could do is propose legislation by “working with some Republicans who might distance themselves from Trump” after the resounding declaration of dissatisfaction voters have given the president in these midterm elections. For example, he said, “JD Vance, the vice president, opposed the war and has done so from the start.” Last week, Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief in a reported effort to revive talks and avert further attacks. “[Will] he now push even harder to end the war?” Lucas asked. However, Boys said the fact that Trump no longer faces election himself because the US Constitution requires him to leave office at the end of his second term may make the president instead feel that “he is now unleashed to act with impunity on the world stage”. “Indeed, given his weakened domestic political circumstances, one can easily imagine Donald Trump escalating policies in the Middle East as he seeks to establish an indisputable presidential legacy,” he added. Last year, Trump unleashed tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on about 90 countries with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. The move, which rattled global markets, was struck down by the Supreme Court in February, but the Trump administration has found workarounds to that ruling. Days after the Supreme Court’s 6-3 vote, Trump doubled down on the tariffs, quickly signing an executive order based on a different statute and raising them from 10 percent to 15 percent. However, those tariffs are limited to 150 days unless they are extended by Congress. Democrats have blamed Trump’s tariffs for exacerbating the rising cost-of-living crisis as tariffs ultimately fall back on US importers who pass them on to consumers. They accused Trump of “pickpocketing the American people”.

events.title: UK Supreme Court hears appeal against Palestine Action’s proscription
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Rights activists say UK decision against Palestine Action is a ‘misuse of terrorism powers’. An appeal challenging the designation of Palestine Action as a “terrorist” organisation has begun at the United Kingdom’s top court, as police arrested demonstrators who gathered outside to protest against the group’s proscription. The two-day hearing at the Supreme Court in London began on Wednesday. Huda Ammori, cofounder of Palestine Action, said ahead of the hearing that she would argue the ban is having a disproportionate effect on freedom of speech and the right to protest. list 1 of 3 UK denies entry to Swedish academic due to speak at Palestine event list 2 of 3 What can a global strike of dockworkers achieve for Gaza? list 3 of 3 London police arrest 139 as hundreds protest Palestine Action ban The direct action group was proscribed by the UK government under then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer in July last year. The decision has since been denounced by rights groups, including Amnesty International and Liberty. Palestine Action describes itself as a “direct action movement committed to ending global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime”. Its designation as a “terrorist” organisation puts it on the same list as armed groups such as al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS). Those found guilty of belonging to or supporting Palestine Action risk up to 14 years in prison. As the hearing got under way, protesters gathered outside the court. Some expressed support for Palestine Action, while others opposed the group’s proscription, which many view as an affront to civil liberties. One demonstrator held a placard reading: “God help us Jews who support Palestine and Palestine Action”. About 25 protesters were arrested, according to the Press Association; the final person detained carried a sign saying: “God help us who are not married to the UK’s national security adviser who support Palestine and Palestine action.” It’s understood this is in reference to journalist and author Sarah Helm, who is married to the UK Prime Minister’s national security adviser, and who had earlier posted a similar line on X but did not face prosecution. “Today was another demonstration of the chaos wrought by the Government’s grave misuse of terrorism powers to proscribe Palestine Action,” Tom Southerden, Amnesty International’s UK Law and Human Rights Director, said in a statement issued after Wednesday’s arrests. “The sight of musicians, politicians and celebrities being arrested for peacefully holding placards is a grim one. That they were arrested for using the same language that Sarah Helm didn’t face arrest for, shows how dangerously vague our terrorism laws are.” Amnesty is one of several organisations calling for the UK government to lift the ban on Palestine Action. “Whatever the Supreme Court ultimately decides, it’s long past time for the Government to admit they got this badly wrong, end the proscription of Palestine Action and put a stop to these appalling arrests,” Southerden said. The UK government’s crackdown on pro-Palestine voices has come under intense scrutiny since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza more than three years ago. Last week, Swedish academic Andreas Malm was prevented from entering the UK after the government said his presence was “not conducive to the public good”. Malm is a vocal supporter of Palestine and has spoken out against Israel’s assault on Gaza. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said before taking office in July that the Labour Party had “got it wrong” on Gaza. However, his comments have come under renewed scrutiny after Malm was refused entry to the UK last week.
