events.title: Tenerife’s Jesus de Miguel remembered in moving tributes by football world
events.summary: The football world is paying tribute to Jesus de Miguel , as it mourns the loss of the Tenerife forward, who died on Tuesday following an on-field collision during a Spanish second division match. The 30-year-old was challenged by Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono , whose knee appeared to strike de Miguel in the chest. Medical staff tended to him on-field before he was sent to a hospital, where he suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance. list 1 of 4 Chinese state TV continues Real Madrid blackout after Mbappe-Mao meme row list 2 of 4 Coventry fan, 14, hands himself in after Bradley Lowery taunt in Sunderland list 3 of 4 AFC reschedules Asian Cup 2027 in Saudi Arabia amid regional conflict list 4 of 4 Carrick says United players are committed despite poor run “There are no words of comfort. There is absolutely nothing to mitigate this feeling full of sadness,” Tenerife said in a statement as they confirmed his death on Tuesday morning. The club announced six days of official mourning during which all club activity would be suspended. Its players, staff and officials will attend de Miguel’s funeral, which will take place in the village of Navahermosa, Toledo, in central Spain. Tenerife will hold a tribute for de Miguel at its home ground, Heliodoro Stadium, on Saturday at 6 pm local time. The Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) postponed all domestic matches on Tuesday as a sign of respect and later extended the suspension until Friday, November 6. European football’s governing body, UEFA, announced that a minute’s silence would be observed at all Champions League matches this week. “We have searched for words and found only silence. In that silence, our hearts and thoughts are with his family, his teammates, everyone at CD Tenerife, and all those who mourn this tragic loss,” UEFA said in a statement. The tributes began with Barcelona and Aston Villa on Tuesday night, where victims of last week’s train accident in Toledo that killed 69 people were also remembered. The Champions League anthem was also not played as a mark of respect. “Wherever [de Miguel] is, I hope he finds his way,” Barcelona forward Raphinha told the media after his side’s 3-0 win. “I want to send his family strength … and today, not talk about football.” “After I saw the news, I didn’t feel good. In the end, he was a fellow football player. This could have happened to any of us. It could have happened to me,” he added. “It’s very difficult to go out and play a game in these circumstances. He was a player who was the same age as me. Maybe that’s why it affected me so much.” Ahead of the match between Atletico Madrid and Bayern Munich, a screen showed a portrait of de Miguel, smiling with his arms outstretched as he ran on the pitch. Social media was flooded with condolences from football clubs and fans across the world as they honoured de Miguel. Several football giants currently playing for Spanish clubs paid tribute too, including Lamine Yamal, Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior, Ferran Torres and Pedri, alongside veterans such as Paul Pogba. Hundreds of fans laid flowers, lit candles and pinned up photographs of de Miguel outside gate 9 of Estadio Heliodoro, where the collision happened during his final match. Andorra goalkeeper Owono released a statement on Tuesday night saying he was devastated by Monday’s incident that would stay with him “for the rest of my life”. “I want everyone to know that I never intended to hurt anyone. It was a terrible accident, something I wish with all my heart I could take back,” he said in a post on social media. “No words can express the pain, guilt and heartbreak I feel right now.” Local police have opened an investigation into the incident, though it is unlikely that Owono will face criminal proceedings, despite calls from some football fans for involuntary manslaughter charges to be brought for his role in the collision. Following the incident, Owono did not turn back to look at de Miguel but immediately began walking towards the touchline, anticipating the red card which Manuel Angel Perez Hernandez swiftly brandished. Videos posted online showed Tenerife fans in the stands chanting “assassin” at Owono as de Miguel was transported on a stretcher to an ambulance. The incident was a painful reminder for former French defender Patrick Battiston, who faced a similar challenge from a West German goalkeeper during the 1982 World Cup semifinal. He was knocked unconscious in the collision and had to be administered oxygen on the pitch before slipping into a coma. Unlike this week’s incident, goalkeeper Harald Schumacher showed no remorse, nor was he sent off, and the match resumed as normal. He later apologised in person to Battiston, who went on to make a full recovery and resumed playing. “It really shocked and moved me,” Battiston told French outlet L’Equipe when asked about the incident. “Especially to see his teammates and opponents take their heads in their hands. What happened is terrible.”

events.title: McDonald’s US sales decline for first time in six quarters despite value push
events.summary: Over the last two years, McDonald’s has rolled out a series of offers such as an under-US$3 (S$3.80) menu and a US$4 breakfast meal as higher living costs force consumers to opt for cheaper alternatives. McDonald’s US comparable sales fell 0.2% in the quarter to Sept 30, its first decline in six quarters, as cash-strapped diners cut back on eating out. The chain has pushed value deals, including an under-US$3 menu and a US$4 breakfast meal, but traffic still fell 4.6% and stayed weak in October. CEO Chris Kempczinski said the company was “encouraged by improvement” after value changes. Global sales rose 1.5%, and adjusted earnings increased to US$3.57 a share. McDonald’s reported a bigger-than-expected decline in US sales as financially stretched consumers cut back on dining out, extending a slowdown that has tested the burger chain’s efforts to win back lower-income diners with value meals. Over the last two years, McDonald’s has rolled out a series of offers such as an under-US$3 (S$3.80) menu and a US$4 breakfast meal as higher living costs force consumers to opt for cheaper alternatives from rivals, convenience stores and home-cooked meals. Comparable sales in McDonald’s largest market fell 0.2% in the quarter ended Sept 30, missing analysts’ expectations for a 0.1% fall, according to data compiled by LSEG. It was the company’s first such decline after five quarters of growth. Customer traffic remained under pressure in the third quarter, and visits to McDonald’s restaurants fell 4.6% in the three-month period from a year earlier, according to data firm Placer.ai. Traffic also remained below year-ago levels in October despite the return of McDonald’s Monopoly promotion and Halloween-themed Boo Buckets. CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement on Nov 4 that the company was “encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value.” Chief financial officer Ian Border had told investors at a Sept 23 event that US sales would likely be negative for the quarter, but that September would likely be positive. Rival Burger King’s parent Restaurant Brands International topped sales expectations last week, helped by discounts and promotions. Yum Brands said on Nov 3 that Tex-Mex chain Taco Bell’s sales have returned to growth following a food safety-related hit. McDonald’s global comparable sales rose 1.5%, in line with expectations. Adjusted earnings rose to US$3.57 per share from US$3.22 a year earlier, helped by a roughly 4% decline in operating costs and expenses. REUTERS

events.title: M&S boss bemoans last week’s budget as ‘whole lot of nothing’
events.summary: Stuart Machin hits out at Labour but welcomes expected UK-EU food deal as retailer reveals half-year results The chief executive of Marks & Spencer has called John Healey’s first budget as chancellor a “whole lot of nothing” and bemoaned an “onslaught of taxation and regulation” from the Labour government despite welcoming an expected deal on EU border checks. Stuart Machin said he was disappointed at last week’s budget statement, adding that it “didn’t really address the issues we need to focus on growth”. He said the chancellor’s “real terms” freeze on business rates, for example, would lead to an additional £10m on M&S’s existing £170m rates bill. Machin also criticised plans for the “most ridiculous” deposit return scheme under which retailers must install machines for the return of cans and plastic bottles in stores in England and Scotland from next October in order to drive up recycling rates. In Wales, the scheme is to also include glass bottles. The M&S boss said he was “very supportive” of a new food trade deal between the UK and EU , which is expected to be completed later this month. Machin said this would help reduce a £10m post-Brexit hit to the retailer caused by the paperwork, packaging and logistical costs involved in sending goods to the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland. He added that the deal would also help UK exports of food to mainland Europe. The comments emerged as M&S said a sustained cyber-attack that forced it to shut down its website last year had continued to hurt clothing sales over the past summer. The retailer said profits bounced back to a better-than-expected £355m in the six months to 26 September from only £3.4m a year before, as it partly recovered from the hack. The attack, which began over Easter 2025, forced M&S to shut its website, which sells clothing and homewares, for more than six weeks. Total sales over the half year across the food to fashion group rose 16.2% to £9.2bn. M&S said sales and profit from its clothing and homewares arm remained below that of two years ago as “availability was constrained due to the longer-than-expected impact of manual ordering processes following the incident, while profitability was diluted by an increased mix of online sales, which have higher fulfilment costs”. The retailer has previously explained that its team of buyers had to calculate demand and make orders to suppliers without the help of their usual technology and detailed information last year. Machin said: “We are broadening our appeal and the brand is in good health, but the results fell short of their potential and show there is a lot more to do.” He added that the manual ordering meant that in some clothing categories M&S did not stock enough everyday products, such as denim and knitwear, over the summer. Profits were also hit by more people shopping online during the “long hot summer”. Machin said the impact of the cyber-attack “lasted longer than we expected”, but added: “That’s now behind us.” M&S said it had been able to take its biggest ever share of a declining clothing market despite the availability problems, which were now resolved but added: “Market conditions remain challenging.” Machin said the UK clothing market was down by 11%, with £1bn in clothing sales lost across the industry in the last six months as the hot weather, low consumer confidence and a shift away from spending on nonessentials hit sales. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning He added that the industry was still “heavily discounting” and M&S was trying to avoid that trend by pricing its goods affordably. M&S clothing, beauty and homewares sales rose 17.5% to almost £2bn in the half year compared with the same period last year, which was affected by the hack. Performance is expected to improve in the second half as M&S said availability has now recovered “creating a better balance between core and seasonal stock”. Its food business powered ahead, increasing sales by almost 14% to £5.2bn in the half year as it opened seven new stores and expanded or refurbished others. The group’s Ocado joint venture also swung to a half-year profit of £25.6m from a loss of £3.1m a year before as sales rose 16% and it improved the efficiency of its deliveries M&S said it expected to cut £120m in costs this year across technology, logistics and stores. Machin said the retailer would not be making redundancies but was likely to be cautious on hiring new workers as it tried to offset new costs, including £35m related to a new packaging levy.

events.title: Elon Musk's Texas-sized midterms failure
events.summary: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk bet big on keeping Texas "red." Win McNamee/Getty Images SpaceX CEO Elon Musk donated at least $446 million ahead of the 2026 midterms. Musk and allied super PACs spent $224 million on Texas alone. In the end, he could not prevent the once unthinkable. Texas turned blue. Elon Musk was the 2026 midterms' largest donor. He's already one of its biggest losers. Musk, the world's richest person, donated at least $446 million ahead of the midterms. The biggest recipients of Musk's largesse were America PAC, his super PAC, and the top super PACs of Senate and House Republicans. Musk chose to make his biggest play in Texas, his adopted home state and the headquarters of Tesla and SpaceX. In September alone, Musk donated $158 million to Senate Republicans' main super PAC, which was quickly routed to a super PAC supporting GOP candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. In addition to those donations, Musk's America PAC has spent over $47 million against Democratic nominee James Talarico. All told, The New York Times reported that Musk spent roughly $224 million in the state. Talarico won the Senate race, flipping the seat to the Democrats, per the Associated Press. At 4:17 a.m. on November, the Associated Press called the gubernatorial race: House Rep Gina Hinojosa, also a Democrat, will be the state's next governor. Democrats' decadeslong dream — and Musk's nightmare — came true: Texas is blue. Democrats have also won control of both the House and Senate, according to the AP. Talarico, who had increasingly targeted Musk, compared his victory to the biblical tale of David defeating Goliath. "The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world, and the entire Washington D.C. establishment," Talarico said during his victory speech. "David wasn't as big or as strong as Goliath. He didn't have as many weapons, but he had hope. He had faith, and he had a slingshot." Musk's bets reflect his statements that the midterms offered Republicans a chance to build up a defense to Democrats potentially sweeping control of Washington in 2028. In such a scenario, Musk said he is worried that Democrats will grant Washington, DC and Puerto Rico statehood and push far-left policies like offering legalization to people living in the country illegally. "This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word," Musk wrote on X on October 30. Once an Obama supporter, Musk has swung hard to the right in recent years. He has quickly surpassed the Koch brothers, Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein, and other megadonors to become the biggest spender in the GOP. Musk has also indicated that he's aware Democrats are eager to haul him in front of Congress. "Live by the sword, die by the sword," Musk wrote on X in October. "Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets …" Musk's ROI has been mixed In the 2024 elections, Musk spent more than $290 million , the vast majority of which was directed to helping President Donald Trump retake the White House. For his efforts, Musk later became the effective leader of the White House DOGE office. In early 2025, DOGE's sweeping mandate helped make him one of the most powerful people in the entire government. Musk returned to the campaign trail in 2025, spending over $20 million between himself and allied super PACs on a Wisconsin state Supreme Court election. He even donned one of the Green Bay Packers' famous cheeseheads. This time, Musk's spending wasn't enough. His favored candidate lost by more than 10 points. Musk's midterm spending has confirmed his continued support for Republicans, something he briefly threw into question during his falling-out with President Donald Trump . In June 2025, Musk threatened to create a third party, called the America Party, but never seriously followed through on his plans. He won't have to wait long for his next opportunity. Few races are more tantalizing for donors than presidential elections. History also shows that a big donor (even one with fewer zeros in their net worth) can keep a struggling candidate afloat long after it appears their campaign is dead in the water. Now that the midterms are wrapped up, the 2028 presidential primaries are around the corner. Musk may want to get his checkbook ready. Aditi Bharade contributed additional reporting. events.title: The podcast boom is hitting a messy reality for CMOs
events.summary: Some marketers are hitting pause on podcast ads. Jens Büttner/picture alliance via Getty Images A version of this post appears in CMO Insider. Sign up for Business Insider's marketing newsletter . Podcasting's growth story is facing a CMO reality check. Cluttered, repetitive ad breaks and a lack of consistent measurement standards are factors giving some marketers pause about continuing to pour budgets into podcasts. That's according to a new report from the podcasting ad agency Oxford Road, which was shared exclusively with CMO Insider. More than half (57%) of the marketers Oxford Road polled said measurement gaps were holding back their podcasting investments. For brands with annual media budgets of $100 million or more, 90% said measurement was a top concern. "The exposure side, the attribution side — they're both a bit of a mess, frankly," said Oxford Road EVP Giles Martin, referring to how marketers assess podcast audiences and measure the success of their campaigns. The podcast market operates across multiple platforms, from RSS feeds to Spotify, Apple, and increasingly YouTube . Each has its own audience metric: downloads, streams, or views, which are calculated differently. Attribution is just as fragmented, with marketers relying on an imperfect mix of promo codes, pixels, geo-testing, and media mix modeling to gauge what worked. "It makes it harder for advertisers to buy, it makes it harder for sellers to sell, and it can make it harder for creators to get the money they deserve," Martin said. That could go some of the way toward explaining why 40% of marketers in the report said other channels deliver a better return on investment than podcast ads . More ads, more problems Growth in the podcast advertising market appears to be slowing. While 40% of the marketers surveyed by Oxford Road anticipated increasing their podcast and audio budgets in 2027, this was down from the 59% of brands that said they increased those budgets this year. That tracks with other industry spending forecasts. EMARKETER expects US advertisers to spend $3.76 billion on podcasts next year, up 10.4% year over year, but a slowdown from the 16.8% annual growth it estimates for 2026. "There's a significant disconnect between audience attention and advertising investment," said Patrick Dolan, head of display and audio at the media agency The7Stars. The pitch to advertisers is that podcasts offer highly engaged audiences who are selecting the shows they want to listen to, often around specific topics that align well with brands' business objectives. Host-read ads can offer an added degree of connection. "A good host read sounds like advice from a friend," said Byron Tassoni-Resch, CEO of the performance marketing agency WeDiscover. Yet for some marketers, podcast ad breaks have evolved to become too messy. More than 40% of the marketers polled by Oxford Road cited the "advertising environment" as a reason they were putting off podcast investments. Marketers said they were concerned about growing ad loads, ad repetition, and other quality-control issues, such as inauthentic, "ho-hum" host-read ads, or even ads that cut off mid-sentence. Oxford Road's report was based on a July survey that polled 41 marketers, a group it said represents $400 million to $500 million of podcast ad spend, including three of the top 10 podcast spenders. Marketers need a multi-pronged podcast strategy Media buyers said marketers need to adopt a more sophisticated approach to extract greater value from their podcast investments. Martin of Oxford Road said brands should consider treating podcasts as a deeper, multi-format partnership, combining host reads with creator social posts , short-form video, newsletters, and, where useful, lower-cost pre-recorded podcast ads that build reach and brand recall. The7Stars' Dolan said that bolder approaches to podcast plans create a "true value exchange" between the podcast creator and the advertiser and foster a more authentic partnership. "These more long-term approaches stop the short-term, high-frequency 'standard' read that lacks the passion we seek from our podcast creators," Dolan said. Media buyers made a similar case for measurement, where combining different methods is the best approach. "Brands buy podcasts like TV, but they measure them like search," said WeDiscover's Tassoni-Resch. Relying on promo codes alone, for example, is an imperfect science because it only counts the people who remember them. A podcast ad might have helped drive a sale, but it often doesn't get credit for it. Tassoni-Resch recommends brand-lift studies to show how awareness changes after a brand is mentioned on a podcast. Marketers should also combine methods such as holdout tests and media mix modeling to demonstrate how podcasts are additive to search and social ad spending, he said. "When CMOs can see this value, they invest more to improve the message and scale the channel," Tassoni-Resch said. "Good measurement turns a one-off podcast test into a long-term partnership." The podcast industry is pushing for unified standards to address fragmented metrics across audio and video platforms. Last year, Oxford Road convened the Alliance for Measurement in Podcasting, a group of industry executives across podcast platforms and media owners, advertisers, agencies, publishers, and talent and measurement firms. This year, it released the "AMP Accords," calling for a universal definition of a podcast, standardized cross-platform impression metrics, and a consistent approach to advertising attribution. "There's so much ambiguity here," Martin of Oxford Road said. "We need a little bit more clarity in terms of what it is, how you count the exposures, and then how you measure the ROI." events.title: Treasury yields fall after Democrats win House and Senate majorities
events.summary: Treasury yields moved lower on Wednesday as investors weighed big wins from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield fell 3 basis points to 4.917%. The 30-year bond yield slid 4 basis points to 5.289%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield declined marginally to 4.606%. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another. Democrats obtained majorities in both the House and Senate . The party is projected to win at least 250 House seats and at least 54 in the Senate. Democrats flipped Senate seats from Republicans in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Maine and Texas. They also won key gubernatorial races in Ohio and Texas. The resounding victory by Democrats could rein in government spending from the Trump administration, as it makes it harder for the White House to push legislation through Congress. Traders at JPMorgan said one of the issues Wall Street is focusing on after the midterms is "reduced deficit spending." "This can be achieved by asserting power over the budget and likely wading through a government shutdown," they said.

events.title: Data centers are in the midterm meme spotlight as posters joke about turning them into daycares and community colleges
events.summary: Data-center memes spread across X after Democrats’ midterm wins, as the industry faces growing political opposition. Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images X users joked about slowing the AI boom and converting data centers after the Democrats' midterm wins. Users suggested turning them into community colleges, daycares, and homeless shelters. The Democrats are generally less in favor of data centers, which were a key ballot issue in many states. After Democrats' midterm wins , data-center memes spread across X as users joked that the buildings powering the AI boom could face a tougher political climate. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, while candidates who called for tighter rules on data centers won several governors' races . Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms called for a statewide pause on new development, while Texas’s Gina Hinojosa campaigned against the rapid expansion of data centers. Ohio’s Amy Acton backed a conditional moratorium that would require developers to meet standards, including covering their own utility costs. The world's richest man, Elon Musk, was among those posting about the results. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," he wrote on X. events.title: America is heading for two years of constitutional brinkmanship
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections A Democratic Congress will not bring conventional gridlock. It will set the stage for a volatile struggle over presidential power. Republican political strategist, foreign policy analyst and former surrogate for Donald Trump’s 2016 and 2024 presidential campaigns. To understand the coming collision between President Donald Trump and a Democratic Congress, one must first discard the textbook formulas of US governance. The United States is about to witness a political experiment for which there is no modern precedent: a purely transactional populist, entirely unmoored from traditional ideological orthodoxy, forced to share power with a legislative branch unified in partisan hostility. The conventional wisdom predicts immediate, paralysing gridlock. That is a misreading of the terrain. Trump does not view politics through the lens of conservative dogma or constitutional restraint; he views it through the lens of the deal. Consequently, his governance will not be characterised by passive stagnation, but by an aggressive, volatile mix of transactional bipartisanship and raw executive unilateralism. Domestically, the ideological lines will blur. For decades, the Republican Party was defined by its commitment to limited government and free markets. Trump has spent a decade dismantling that consensus. Confronted with a Democratic House of Representatives and a Democratic Senate, he will feel no tribal loyalty to standard conservative policy. Instead, expect him to seek out areas of populist overlap. When it comes to massive infrastructure spending, protectionist trade policy and aggressive state intervention to protect domestic manufacturing, Trump is often closer to the Democratic centre-left than to the ghost of former President Ronald Reagan. He will dare the opposition majorities to vote against legislation that pours millions of dollars into their districts or levies tariffs that protect their blue-collar constituents. It will be an unholy, ad hoc alliance — issue-by-issue, fleeting, and transactional — designed to deliver the optics of victory for both a populist president and a vulnerable congressional majority. Where such transactions fail, however, the venue will shift from the legislative chamber to the administrative state controlled by the executive. Trump will not accept the traditional boundaries of a divided government. If necessary, he will govern by decree. Executive orders, emergency declarations and expansive interpretations of federal statutes will be deployed to bypass a stubborn Capitol Hill. The administration will dare the Democratic leadership to tie up the government in the federal courts, turning the slow wheels of the judiciary into a political weapon. Yet, the true test of this fragile constitutional architecture will not occur on the domestic stage. It will happen abroad, specifically in the volatile expanses of the Middle East, where the executive branch enjoys its greatest constitutional latitude. The immediate flashpoint is Iran. The Trump doctrine rests on a foundation of maximum economic pressure backed by highly unpredictable, asymmetric tactical deterrence. It is a posture designed to keep adversaries off balance. But a Democratic Congress, historically wedded to the framework of multilateral diplomacy and deeply wary of congressionally unauthorised foreign entanglements, will view this unpredictability not as a strategic asset but as an existential danger. The US is likely headed for a historic constitutional showdown over the War Powers Resolution of 1973. Democratic majorities will also aggressively use the power of the purse to place statutory fences around the commander-in-chief, attempting to defund military manoeuvres or explicitly prohibit unilateral escalations against Tehran. Trump will treat these attempts at legislative constraints with open contempt. Asserting an absolute, almost unrestrained reading of the Constitution’s Article II executive authority, the president will argue that modern geopolitical threats require executive agility, not governance by congressional committee. When the rockets fly, the president will act unilaterally, leaving Congress to meaningless academic debates. Hanging over this entire drama is the ultimate constitutional weapon: the threat of impeachment by Congress. In a Washington where both the House and the Senate are controlled by the president’s opponents, oversight will cease to be an instrument of governance and become an engine of partisan political destruction. Democratic congressional committee chairs will launch a relentless, multifront campaign of subpoenas and investigations. Every member of Trump’s cabinet will live in a permanent state of interrogation; every foreign policy decision will be audited for high crimes and misdemeanours.

events.title: Poundland owner in crunch talks as retailer's collapse looms
events.summary: Published 4 November 2026, 00:03 GMT Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the US-based owners of Poundland on Wednesday as the government hopes to save the retailer from collapse. The discount chain is on the brink of insolvency and Gordon Brothers, which bought it for £1 last June, has rejected a takeover bid which could have saved the 12,000 jobs currently at risk. A meeting was due to be held on Thursday but has been brought forward as the scramble to secure a rescue deal for the firm intensifies. Gordon Brothers has previously said Poundland faces multiple economic challenges from rising inflation, increasing staff costs, and "severe levels of shoplifting". Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of the business has not been made. Meanwhile, MPs say they have called in Poundland's owners for questioning to explain their role in the discount retailer's looming insolvency. Liam Byrne, chair of Parliament's business committee, said: "Every report suggests Poundland is a viable, profitable business with a future ahead of it and without good reason to let it crash and burn - and then to break it up and sell it off piece by piece. "We are asking Gordon Brothers to appear before Parliament to explain themselves and tell us just what it is that's preventing them from accepting the fully-funded deal on the table to save more than 12,000 jobs." Business Minister Kate Dearden and union representatives are also meeting Poundland's managing director Barry Williams later today. Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its lenders until next Thursday. Adam Turner: We would lose "a few million" if Poundland went under The meeting comes after a major Poundland supplier has said it will lose millions of pounds if the retailer goes bust. Adam Turner, sales director at Bradford-based Highcrest Retail Brands, said Poundland was one of its biggest customers and its collapse would cost it "a few million" in lost sales. The family owned business mainly sells confectionery to Poundland and turns over about £50m. Turner said the firm becoming insolvent would leave a substantial gap in its balance sheet next year. Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", Turner said. But he warned other medium and small suppliers to the retailer have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they". This echoes a warning from Poundland founder Steve Smith on Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse. Not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall, he told the BBC on Wednesday. He said he was "amazed" Poundland was being put into administration, pointing to the profitability of the company. "Also, there's two offers on the table from some really good people," he added. "All I'm asking is for Gordon Brothers to see if they can put a deal together." Gordon Brothers said Walsall-based Poundland is "still not cash generative at a sustainable level" because of the economic issues it faces. If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises. However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present – meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed. Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm Published 2 days ago If Poundland goes under, suppliers will be getting "pennies in the pound" back from the administration, he said, which is "very upsetting" – although he still hopes a deal can be done so Poundland can remain solvent. Poundland owners Gordon Brothers will be a secured creditor, which means they are first in line to get their money back, and suppliers "who have done nothing wrong" will take the financial hit. "It's sad. It's a nightmare for us all to be honest with you. It's not just the suppliers, it's the staff at Poundland, some of these guys have been there for many years. "It's from the warehouse staff all the way to the shop staff to everybody within head office. It's a massive ripple effect through the supply chain," he added. Turner said he had no knowledge of whether Gordon Brothers had deliberately timed the process of Poundland going into administration so it could take advantage of having high stock levels, which it can then sell. One of the ways Gordon Brothers makes money is through stock liquidations – selling off stock from collapsed businesses. One insider familiar with the situation told the BBC that the timing of Poundland facing collapse was "odd" – most retailers don't fall over in the run-up to Christmas. Dearden has said the government doesn't want to interfere with "current ongoing commercial negotiations", but that ministers want "clarity" on the plans for the retailer.

events.title: A town's creative way for homeowners to tap into the short-term rental market could be a blueprint for others
events.summary: Matthew DeFeo for BI This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Boulder is finally embracing short-term rentals … on a short-term basis. The city is lifting its long-standing ban on most Airbnbs, allowing permanent residents to rent out their homes during four weeks spanning January and February. It's a potential model for other cities looking to dabble with the short-term rental market again. Boulder's shift is due to the arrival of The Sundance Film Festival. The college town is replacing Park City as the host of the iconic independent film festival for the next decade. But with roughly 100,000 expected visitors and only 3,000 hotel rooms, the local government needed to get creative. Now residents are hoping to lure film enthusiasts into their homes, erasing some mortgage payments in the process. BI's James Rodriguez has the full rundown on the Boulder community's crash course on the short-term rental business . Some residents are already having an Instagram-vs-reality moment when it comes to pricing their abodes. They're eyeing five-figure stays despite their homes not necessarily fitting the bill. "I think people need to get over that idea that they're going to just make their retirement on the first year of Sundance coming to Boulder," Juli Kovats, a longtime real estate agent there, told James Boulder's success would show how a city can allow residents to benefit from Airbnb without swallowing up housing supply. Short-term rentals have been a hotly debated topic for years , especially as the housing market has worsened. Many cities have banned or enacted strict regulations to prevent investment properties from sitting dormant while hopeful homebuyers struggle with limited inventory. The market hasn't been a cakewalk for investors either. Vacation homes, once viewed as almost a fool-proof play in real estate, have proven to be a nightmare to sell , James previously reported. Rentals based around specific events come with their own issues. Owning a rental property near a big stadium is great when the team is crushing it. The appeal drops if it's a losing team that struggles to fill the stadium, making it harder for you to book guests. Boulder's approach could be a happy medium. Permanent residents have the chance to cash in on specific events without turning the community into a bunch of rental properties that risk sitting empty most of the time Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Wall Street seeks shelter in Treasuries as midterms threaten to throw Washington into a fiscal gridlock
events.summary: With only a couple of seats left to be called in the midterm elections, a “blue wave” is preparing to wash through Congress. Voters made it clear they were unhappy with Republicans in the first two years of President Trump’s administration, with 54 Democrats elected to the Senate and 44 Republicans, as of this writing, per CNBC . Consumers will want to see action on issues close to home from their newly elected officials, namely affordability and inflation . Military conflict with Iran has pushed up oil prices and, as a result, gas prices. That action came after Trump’s tariff scheme, which targeted exports from foreign countries, but economists say it resulted in increased costs being passed back to consumers. While Main Street has a checklist of action it wants to see, Wall Street is hedging on how the new power dynamics on Capitol Hill will play out. In the early hours of this morning, yields on longer-dated bonds trended downward as demand inversely rose. 30-Year Treasuries pushed below 5.3%, while the 10-year pushed down toward 4.9%. Demand for the securities shows bonds remain the destination of choice in a market flight to safety—a question which seemed to hang over the market this summer as yields rose over 5%. A more divided government increases the likelihood of government standoffs, particularly over spending. “Fiscal gridlock seems the likely default,” UBS’s Paul Donovan told clients this morning. “President Trump has seemingly retreated from an earlier pledge to veto everything the Democrats suggest, Treasuries have initially strengthened on the results.” Beyond a shield against volatility, investors have additional motivations to look to bonds in the current political climate. President Trump and his team may now find it harder to push through policy packages that might require more spending and, as a result, more government borrowing. Likewise, Democrat spending packages could face roadblocks from a still sizeable Republican presence in Congress and Trump’s veto power. Markets are also bracing for near-term volatility in equities, as UBS’s chief investment officer, Mark Haefele, noted to clients, “particularly in tech and other areas sensitive to greater regulatory scrutiny.” With AI driving stock gains this year, investors may seek to balance any hiccups with the dependable asset of Treasuries. While spending gridlock may frustrate policymakers, it might calm the nerves of debt hawks. Concern over the fiscal trajectory of the U.S. is mounting, owing to federal deficits of between 6% and 7% of GDP, and interest payments on the national debt now demand more than $1 trillion a year. A gridlock could slow the path of any spending bills, allaying some concerns about the U.S. budget picture. As Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid noted this morning: “There’s been a rally for U.S. Treasuries … given that divided government has generally made it harder for fiscal stimulus to be passed. So that’s eased concerns on the fiscal trajectory a bit.” Timeline for answers Policymakers’ appetite for a conversation on fiscal responsibility may be gauged sooner rather than later. The current federal government funding package runs out on December 11 and will require bipartisan support to prevent a government shutdown. While the officials elected in the midterms won’t be in office until the New Year, a shift in the tide may give Democrats more motivation to hold the line or make bolder demands in return for support. The odds of a government shutdown jumped to 45% overnight on the prediction market platform Kalshi , up from around 30%. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Current price of oil as of November 4, 2026
events.summary: At 7 a.m. Eastern Time today, the price of oil sits at $105.84 per barrel, using Brent as the benchmark (we’ll explain what that means shortly). That’s a decrease of $4.61 since yesterday morning and $41 more than at this time last year. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $110.45 -4.17% Price of oil 1 month ago $106.48 -0.60% Price of oil 1 year ago $64.84 +63.23% Will oil prices go up? Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices The price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges. Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve In the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets disrupted. It’s not a permanent fix, as it’s more meant to provide immediate support for consumers and ensure critical parts of the economy like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and so on can keep operating. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Both oil and natural gas play key roles as major sources of energy. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by proxy. If oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, increasing the demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil Oil prices are often measured by two key benchmarks: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Between the two, Brent is a better representation of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the best way to review historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now leans on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. When you look at the Brent benchmark across multiple decades, you’ll see that oil has been anything but consistent. It has experienced spikes driven by wars and supply cuts, as well as crashes linked to global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s brought the first big oil shock when the Middle East cut exports and imposed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices dropped in the mid-1980s for reasons such as weaker demand and more non-OPEC oil producers entering the industry. Prices spiked again in 2008 with rising global demand, but soon crashed alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand collapsed like never before, bringing prices to under $20 per barrel. In short, oil’s historical performance has been far from steady. It’s massively affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: Strait of Hormuz closure has cost Europe an extra $142 billion Ryanair’s CEO says fares could rise up to 20% next year because of the Iran war As Trump eyes new attack, Iran vows to retaliate beyond the Mideast Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: ‘The opportunity outweighs the challenge’: Bahrain leads drive to restore tourism in the Gulf after eight months of conflict and collapsing visitor numbers
events.summary: Gulf states are preparing to launch a joint global tourism campaign as the region seeks to rebuild traveler confidence following months of conflict with Iran.  Bahrain’s minister of tourism, H.E. Fatima bint Jaffar Al Sairafi, told Fortune that the campaign would encourage international visitors to travel across several Gulf countries on one vacation. Bahrain proposed the initiative at a Gulf tourism meeting in Manama, the kingdom’s capital, in September, where it secured approval. “All the countries are on board and the plan will be implemented very soon.” Al Sairafi said at the Gulf Gateway investment forum in Bahrain. Tourism in the Gulf states generated nearly $131.9 billion in 2025. But since the war began, the World Travel & Tourism Council estimated in March that the region was losing around $600 million per day in tourism revenues.  Read more: ADNOC to expand AI use across its operations to strengthen resilience “[We want to] promote our countries in terms of multi-destination itineraries rather than solo itineraries, that’s actually where our strength is,” Al Sairafi said. Gulf tourism leaders had been “very disheartened” by the Iranian attacks after years of expansion in the sector, she added arguing that closer regional cooperation offered a way to rebuild.   The initiative would bring together Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, and Kuwait as they seek to restore confidence in a tourism market where visitor numbers have collapsed.   In 2025, the region welcomed 75.7 million international tourists, according to UN Tourism, representing a 4.9% increase on the previous year.   The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) publicly announced approval of a tourism recovery plan on Sep. 10, and Al Sairafi confirmed that the global campaign was close to launch.   Al Sairafi said that the conflict had accelerated cooperation between Gulf tourism authorities, turning the region’s shared exposure to disruption into an incentive to market destinations together. “I really believe that the recent developments that have happened over the past few months are one of the main drivers for us to actually combine our effort,” she said.   Her model is based on the multi-country European vacation. Visitors making a long journey from Europe or Asia, including China, will be encouraged to explore neighboring Gulf states using the region’s road and air connections.  “Rarely do we only visit one country,” she said of trips to Europe. “We want to create a destination where people enjoy all the cultures of all the GCC states and spend time and money equally.”   Making those trips easier to book will also require coordination. Al Sairafi said that aligned tourism calendars, better transport connections, and cooperation between airlines, hotels, and booking platforms would be needed.   The research agency, ORF Middle East, said that support for tourism businesses and efforts to restart events could become harder to sustain if the conflict drags on. With increased tensions and potential renewed disruption, the joint promotion offers no guarantee of a return to previous tourism numbers.   Al Sairafi pointed to Bahrain’s international conference calendar as evidence that confidence was returning. Business visitors were extending their stays and booking guided tours, she said, bringing spending beyond the events themselves.  According to the ministry, Bahrain’s visitor numbers increased more than 50% between the launch of its tourism strategy in 2022 and 2025, while tourism revenue rose more than 30%. Al Sairafi says recovery would mean renewed annual growth in arrivals, revenue and overnight stays.   “I believe that the opportunity that we see outweighs the challenge,” she said.   This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: AI-generated data found on Nigeria voter roll
events.summary: The News Nigeria’s election authority is under pressure to address the discovery of AI-generated voter information and ID photos on a draft electoral roll, which has sparked concerns about the integrity of January’s presidential vote and risks further undermining faith in the politics of Africa’s largest democracy. With just over 10 weeks to go until the vote, President Bola Tinubu is locked into a re-election battle against a slate of familiar rivals in campaigning that revolves around economic and security issues . More than 103 million Nigerians registered to take part in the poll, according to the Independent National Electoral Commission, but its numbers and overall preparations have come under intense scrutiny. Advocacy groups, technology analysts, and former INEC officials have led calls for an independent inquiry to identify how fabricated information came to be included. Many have warned that the false data would add to the cynicism about the organizer’s commitment to a fair election and weaken voter participation. Nigerian elections have often struggled with low turnout: At just 27%, the 2023 vote saw the lowest turnout since the country’s return to democratic government in 1999. INEC, responding to the backlash, said the contentious register is a temporary document open to review for errors, and that it would look into “possible technical or procedural lapses ” that allowed AI intrusions. A senior official blamed rogue staff, and said the commission “ doesn’t know why ” they would use their logins to tamper with the roll. Know More These responses have been unsatisfactory given the gravity of the situation, analysts say. “INEC wants to make light of it to say that they are doing a cleanup,” Kolawole Oluwadare, a senior official at Lagos-based rights group SERAP, told Semafor. “This goes beyond what INEC can handle in house, which is why we are calling for an audit” by an external body, he added. Martin Uwakwe, a US-based technology analyst who reviewed the draft roll, found several errors in the register beyond the AI-generated issues, including duplicates and the presence of people who had died. He said the electoral commission could use Nigeria’s existing identity database to authenticate voter data and ensure integrity. “These things are very easy to do but I don’t know why we are still having this conversation in 2026,” he told Semafor. Resolving issues with the register is critical for voting to be credible on election day. With each election cycle, Nigeria has increased the role of digital technology, including biometric tests, in the voting process to improve transparency and efficiency. But the present qualms around AI manipulation of voter data may make people skeptical of the reported outcome. For example, the portable electronic devices that will be used to accredit voters on election day (known as BVAS) could be manipulated by those who have access to the back end potentially disenfranchising unwanted voters. “If the people with access are compromised, it becomes an issue,” Uwakwe said. Step Back The hope that technology would drastically transform Nigerian elections to make them vastly more credible did not materialize in the 2023 election. BVAS devices malfunctioned en masse, while poor cell signals and other system failures delayed voter accreditation and result availability across the country. Only around a third of results could be viewed on INEC’s website two days after voting ended, fueling tensions that threatened to spill over. Legal challenges to Tinubu’s victory ultimately fell through because courts determined that it was not mandatory for INEC to publish results electronically. A repeat of these issues could have damaging long-term effects on Nigeria. “When citizens perceive elections as flawed or manipulated, confidence in democratic institutions diminishes, leading to political apathy , protests, and even violence,” Agathus Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, a Nigerian political analyst, wrote for the Abuja-based Center for Democracy and Development in a recent post. Notable INEC boss Joash Amupitan said his agency embraced the use of AI but warned that bad actors could use the technology to impersonate officials by, for example, making false announcements.

events.title: Musk makes light of defeats after record spend on Republican candidates
events.summary: Tesla and SpaceX founder Elon Musk is the world’s richest man and the largest individual donor in the US midterms. Elon Musk has joked online about the Republican defeat in the US midterm elections after spending nearly half a billion dollars to bolster the party’s campaigns. Republicans were decisively routed by Democrats in Tuesday’s polls, losing control of the Senate and the House of Representatives, while racking up losses in states long seen as Republican strongholds, such as Texas and Kansas. list 1 of 3 ‘We defeated Goliath’: Texas Democrat James Talarico wins Senate seat list 2 of 3 Republicans fuming after Democrat Talarico flips Texas Senate blue list 3 of 3 Democrats win control of House and Senate: Key US midterms takeaways “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” the Tesla and SpaceX founder wrote on X, which he owns, on Wednesday. Musk reportedly spent $446m supporting Republican candidates in the elections, making him the top donor. His donations have mostly gone to his own Republican-leaning political action committee, America PAC, and to the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) super PAC. The SLF used Musk’s $158m in donations in September to support Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas, who lost to Democrat James Talarico. Voters rejected Paxton’s plan to make Texas the centre of the country’s artificial intelligence (AI) industry by rapidly building data centres. Talarico campaigned for tighter regulations on their development. Musk took to X to joke: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now”. The South Africa-born entrepreneur has moved the headquarters of his companies Tesla, SpaceX, and X to Texas. Talarico explicitly referenced Musk in his election victory speech, saying his campaign had taken on “goliaths” including “the richest man in the world” and won. Musk, who became a trillionaire in June when his company SpaceX went public, supported the Republican campaign for governor of Texas, a race which the Democrats also won. Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Governor Greg Abbott despite a $5m donation by Musk to the Republican candidate. Huge campaign donations by billionaires have become part of the political reality in the US since a 2010 Supreme Court ruling that the government could not limit political spending by corporations, unions, and other groups if they spend it independently of candidates.

events.title: Wayfair sales jump 10% as furniture retailer says it's winning share of sluggish market
events.summary: Wayfair said its sales jumped 10% in the third quarter as the retailer posted its strongest quarter since the pandemic. The company also reported double-digit revenue growth in the U.S. CFO Kate Gulliver told CNBC the growth is largely due to the company continuing to take market share in what's been a sluggish housing market. Wayfair on Wednesday said it posted its strongest quarter of sales growth since the pandemic as the furniture retailer continues to win over customers and take market share. The company said it saw double-digit revenue growth in the U.S., reaching about $3 billion, an 11.4% increase from the year prior. Still, international net revenue for the quarter decreased 2.3% year over year to $380 million. The report comes as the housing market remains sluggish. But the furniture and home goods retailer has reported consistent growth over the past year. CFO Kate Gulliver told CNBC that Wayfair's momentum is building as it takes market share. "We see the overall consumer in the U.S. in this category, we think it's roughly flattish, and so that's our [market] share momentum continuing to build," Gulliver said. She added that shopper loyalty, the opening of new stores, the company's luxury furniture business and an emphasis on value has allowed the company to win more consumers. Customers are also continuing to spend, whether at the company's value prices or on the luxury side, she added. "We've been highly promotional for the last few years, and the promotional activity this year is actually very consistent with last year," she said. "It maintains this sort of momentum on promotional activity this year." Here's how the company performed in its third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 93 cents adjusted vs. 79 cents expected Revenue: $3.42 billion vs. $3.38 billion expected For the period ended Sept. 30, Wayfair reported net income of $62 million, or 45 cents per share, compared with a loss of $99 million, or a loss of 76 cents per share, the year prior. Total revenue grew 9.7% year over year, reaching $3.42 billion. The company said its active customers grew 4.7% year over year, reaching 22.2 million. It also saw a 12.2% increase in orders delivered during the quarter to about 11 million. As the company looks ahead to the holiday season and the fourth quarter, Gulliver said it's maintaining promotional activity similar to last year. She added that the company is confident that its range of prices and products will appeal to a broad base of consumers. "We've seen that growth play out," Gulliver said. "We've seen that flow through to EBITDA, ultimately to net income positive this quarter, which is really another key piece in the story and the momentum here, so we feel very good about the quarter of the performance."

events.title: Netflix just hired an adtech operator who knows how to solve 'gnarly problems'
events.summary: Former colleagues of Darshan Kantak, Netflix's new VP of its ads platform, said he's used to solving complex problems. Courtesy of Darshan Kantak A version of this post appears in CMO Insider. Sign up for Business Insider's marketing newsletter . Netflix knows its ad business needs to move faster, and it's bringing on a well-regarded adtech operator to pour on the accelerant. The company said this week it's hired Darshan Kantak, a Google, Snap, Meta, Microsoft, and Yahoo alum — he's just missing Amazon on his résumé — as VP of its ads platform. Former colleagues of Kantak told me he's a detail-oriented leader accustomed to solving complex problems and willing to get his hands dirty. The first major item on his to-do list will be getting Netflix's adtech stack into gear. Last month, Netflix cut its annual advertising revenue forecast by $300 million to $2.7 billion, citing delays in rolling out ad products and partner integrations. (Netflix still expects its ad business to grow by 80% this year.) Andrew Buckman, the CEO of the digital ad firm Publisher Collective, said Kantak, with whom he worked at Yahoo, has the chops to help figure out the snags. Buckman recalled how Kantak came to his aid at Yahoo two decades ago. The company was rolling out a new search advertising platform , and Buckman was responsible for reconfiguring search-term pricing across all its European markets. Buckman had missed one integration. "I broke Finland," he said. Kantak, who was responsible for the entire global rollout, with Finland accounting for a tiny slice of overall revenue, sat next to Buckman's computer for two hours as they pored over the data together to fix the problem. "I always had the feeling that he was the biggest brain in the room but would never actually admit it," Buckman said. "He was always open to working through different problems, rolling his sleeves up, and figuring out the right solution with you as you go along." At Meta, former colleague Graham Mudd , who is now an SVP of product at Mozilla, said Kantak was instrumental in building some of the products that helped shift Facebook toward a data-driven performance advertising business, having previously mostly focused on brand advertising. That should bode well for Netflix as it seeks to diversify its advertising customer base, Mudd said. "He knows the playbook," Mudd said. "If you want someone who knows exactly what to do and how to motivate people to get there and the experience to know, 'if we do X, Y will happen,' he's a great person for that." In a statement, Kantak said he was drawn to Netflix for the chance to use technology to ensure ads feel "relevant and welcome for members, and technical tools that make advertising even more innovative and effective." As for Kantak's specific tasks ahead, Netflix said on its latest earnings call that its advertising priorities include rolling out new ad formats and increasing the availability of measurement and reporting tools. And next year, it plans to expand its ad-supported tier to 15 new countries. Iván Markman , Yahoo's former chief business officer, said he recalled Kantak as leading on "gnarly problems requiring a lot of brainpower," such as Yahoo's growing marketplaces business and the development of early programmatic advertising products after its acquisition of the Right Media exchange in 2007. "When I think about CTV, premium video, and the marketplace more broadly, all of these players still have a lot of cloth to cut in terms of how you build out both the experience and the marketplace in a thoughtful way, globally," Markman said of Netflix's ad opportunity. "Darshan's been there and done that." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: These races matter if you care about money, Musk, and the AI boom as Democrats rack up shocking wins
events.summary: Michael Gonzalez/Getty; Brandon Bell/Getty; BI The midterms will be, in part, a referendum on AI and Big Tech backlash. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk bet big on the Texas Senate race. His candidate lost. Democrats also won a key race in Ohio, and retook control of the Senate. The 2026 midterms have arrived, and results are rolling in. Democrats have won control of the House and Senate. They scored a stunning victory in Texas, where Democratic nominee James Talarico flipped a Texas Senate seat in a race that saw SpaceX CEO Elon Musk donate over $150 million to Republican candidate Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Beyond control of Congress, Tuesday's election will illustrate the extent of Silicon Valley's political power and the breadth of the AI backlash. In addition to the candidates, there are big ballot questions looming, none more so than the California wealth tax fight. Here are some of the key results, and what we're still watching for. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk Mark Schiefelbein/AP Texas Senate What happened: Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico has flipped a Texas Senate seat, per The Associated Press. Talarico's defeat of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is a stunning development that some Republicans feared ever since Paxton emerged from a bitter primary and subsequent runoff. Sen. John Cornyn warned that if Paxton beat him, his fellow Republicans would need to spend gigantic sums of money to hold the seat. Enter Elon Musk. The world's richest man has been frequently trashing Talarico on X. More importantly, Musk has donated at least $158 million that has been routed to a pro-Paxton super PAC. The victory means Democrats are now within striking distance of flipping the Senate, a thought that was considered unlikely just months ago. Ohio Senate Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican from Ohio, walks past President Donald Trump Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images What happened: Former Sen. Sherrod Brown is returning to Congress. Per the AP, Brown has prevailed over Sen. Jon Husted, a former lieutenant governor, who was trying to hang on to former Vice President JD Vance's Senate seat. Brown, a former three-term senator, criticized Husted for his previous support for data center development. Husted has said the issue should be left to communities and no longer supports offering tax incentives for new data center construction. Earlier this summer, Senate Republicans' campaign arm warned AI labs that if Husted goes down "and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one." Pennsylvania 1st District What happened: Bucks County commissioner Bob Harvie has defeated five-term Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, per the Associated Press. Harvie focused his first ad of the general election on his call for a data center moratorium. He also blasted Fitzpatrick over the Republican's previous support for a massive Amazon data center in Falls Township, which is in Bucks County. In 2024, Trump narrowly lost the district, but Fitzpatrick still easily won reelection by nearly 13 points. Michigan Democratic US Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed Jeff Kowalsky/ AFP via Getty Images Michigan Senate What happened: Former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, has defeated Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican, per the Associated Press. No race compares to the drama of the Michigan Senate race. On Sunday, Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed after a bitter primary, reversed herself and issued a last-minute endorsement of Rogers. Beyond the headlines, the race offers some interesting policy contrasts. Echoing Sen. Bernie Sanders (and Trump), El-Sayed has called for the government to take equity stakes in AI companies. El-Sayed also wants to force tech giants like Microsoft to divest from AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. Rogers, the Republican hopeful, has called for a pause on data center development in the state. Michigan has not elected a Republican senator since 1994. Design software maker Canva is cutting 22% of its staff, amounting to 1,271 people, amid a growth slowdown. The company’s co-founder and CEO, Melanie Perkins, in a note to employees said while Canva has scaled so far, it needs to change to address slowing growth. “Over the past thirteen years, we’ve turned a dream in a pitch deck into a platform used by hundreds of millions of people. None of it would have been possible without the talent, imagination, and care of every single person who has been part of this journey. Yet success in our first chapter doesn’t guarantee success in the next. This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade,” Perkins wrote. Canva is reshuffling its organizational chart and merging its product, growth and platform teams to reduce communication friction. The company is also reducing “subspecialisation,” which means its employees might be asked to take up more responsibilities. The company is also moving towards hybrid work and asking people to work from an office a few days a week. The company has been shipping its own AI models to reduce costs and reliance on third-party models, but it still had to cut its revenue growth forecast to 20% from 30% to address ballooning AI costs. This also resulted in Canva’s early investors cutting its valuation to about $35 billion earlier this year. Canva is also facing increasing competition from AI startups and general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini, whose image generation capabilities allow people to easily put together posters and presentations. events.title: BMW warns on profits as it counts cost of plan for 8,000 job cuts
events.summary: German carmaker slashes profit margin to between -0.5% and 0.5% this year in face of competition from China The German carmaker BMW has issued its second profit warning in a year, blaming the costs of a restructuring programme including significant job losses in the face of continuing competition from China. The company is the latest to issue a profit downgrade in the German car sector, after Mercedes-Benz last week cut its profit outlook. Western automakers have struggled to keep pace with lower-cost Chinese rivals, which has led to reduced sales in China and a rise in Chinese exports to Europe . BMW signalled a potential for losses after slashing its profit margin to between -0.5% and 0.5% this year and blamed fourth-quarter costs tied to the restructuring that includes 8,000 job cuts in its home market . At the beginning of the year, BMW had considered a margin of 4-6% would be possible. It reported an 11% drop in third-quarter pre-tax earnings on Wednesday to €2.1bn (£1.75bn). Sales in China fell 22% in the first nine months of the year, which BMW said was in line with a broader downturn ⁠in that market. The chief executive, Milan Nedeljković, said: “Current developments in our industry call for decisiveness and swift implementation. We will therefore specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures.” China “remains a key focus”, Nedeljković added, with the group’s Neue Klasse ​revival of its model offering beginning in ​China this month with the launch of the iX3. BMW follows Volkswagen in making painful restructuring costs caused by the rapidly changing market. Because of the rapid launch of its new generation of electric vehicles, the company is writing off parts of its previous vehicle and technology generations and pricing in the costs of the redundancy programme. The operating ‌margin in BMW’s core ‌automotive business narrowed to 3.4%, beating analysts’ forecast of 3.1% but declining from 5.2% a year earlier. Excluding restructuring charges, the margin would be above 2%, within its previous forecast range, the company said. BMW said it planned to cut management functions more quickly under its restructuring drive. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Revenue fell 6% to €30.4bn in the third quarter, hurt by the declining sales in China. While BMW’s ​rival Mercedes-Benz also reported lower profits in the third quarter, Porsche rebounded slightly, but only after steep charges last year as it overhauls its model lineup and retreats from China. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Attackers reportedly set cold-room controls to 110°C, but safeguards prevented stock losses FBI pins $6.3B Binance crypto heist on North Korean hackers 2 days ago Japanese virtual desktop cloud hacked so hard it asks to be banned 8 days ago Ransomware gets personal: 'We-know-where-you-are kind of stuff' 21 days ago Imagine there's no Shiny Hunters – AI could make human hacking crews obsolete 23 days ago FBI confirms 'multiple' arrests related to ShinyHunters hack 29 days ago Attackers tampered with cold-storage settings used by France's civilian blood service after compromising a refrigeration supplier, the organization said. The French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed the incident on Tuesday, saying its own systems had not been directly targeted. Safeguards prevented any loss of blood products. The affected equipment stored blood samples and frozen plasma, including plasma intended for transfusion. "The EFS' monitoring and alarm systems enabled the rapid identification of these anomalies and the implementation of necessary measures to ensure that no blood samples or products were compromised," it said. "Thus, depending on the circumstances, as soon as the incident occurred, the affected equipment was either brought under control without impacting the products and samples, or neutralized; the products stored in these cold rooms were preventively transferred to other facilities." The EFS did not name the supplier publicly. According to reports, attackers changed cold-room temperature settings from -30°C to 110°C. That does not mean the equipment or its contents reached the higher temperature. The organization added that it notified the country's cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the Ministry of Health. News about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration devices across Europe emerged on Monday morning after retailers arrived to work, only to find puddles on the floor after cyber criminals activated defrost modes. Reports of the supermarket attacks describe remotely activated defrost cycles and temperatures as high as 50°C, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food. The attackers have not been identified. More retailers have reported disruption since the initial disclosures on Monday. Stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden were the first to report issues, although cases from Estonia, Finland, Germany, Portugal, Romania, and the Netherlands have since been confirmed. Richard Horne, chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), told BBC Radio 4's Today program on Wednesday that he was aware of "a couple of impacts" in the UK's own food supply chain. No affected UK businesses have publicly identified themselves, although the British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC that some of its more than 300 members had become "collateral" in the attacks, with two reporting that their fridges had begun defrosting. The latest wave of cold-store attacks comes a month after the first, which affected French supermarket chains Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others. Both supermarket waves involved remote interference with refrigeration controls, causing stock losses. Whether the attack affecting EFS used the same access route remains unclear. Some affected chains identified Danfoss controllers in their systems; others said they did not use the company's equipment. CERT-FR published an advisory at the time of the attacks urging organizations to remediate vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers. The attacks in France followed reports of compromises at US military commissaries, which also led to food wastage in August.
