events.title: Reed Jobs’s Yosemite raises $350 million second fund to make cancer non-lethal
events.summary: Reed Jobs isn’t trying to cure cancer. For Jobs—an investor and, yes, Steve Jobs’s son—the aim’s far more precise: To make cancer non-lethal. The rhetorical distinction is important.  “I don’t think you’ll cure cancer because we’re human,” said Jobs. “Any human cell could become cancerous, right? And we’re not going to stop having human cells. So, the idea that none of them could ever become cancer is preposterous. That risk’s never going away.” And medicine, however advanced it may be, seldom makes diseases vanish. But there’s a path to a world where cancer is much less intractable. Consider, Jobs says, the trajectory of AIDS as a guide to what might be possible for cancer treatment.  “There’s no vaccine for [AIDS], unfortunately,” he said. “I’d love for there to be, but in the absence of that, it’s a far less scary disease now in the United States because it’s non-lethal. With a cocktail of drugs, you can actually prevent mortality. In many ways, I think that’s a massive victory and, in some ways, the most essential victory. Because it’s victory over death, and that’s what I want for cancer patients.” For Jobs, this has been his life’s work—he started working in cancer labs as a teenager when his father got sick (Steve Jobs would pass away in 2011). Today, he’s a VC, the founder of venture firm Yosemite, which he started after spinning out of Laurene Powell Jobs’s Emerson Collective in 2023. Yosemite (and Jobs) are devoted to cancer-focused investing, both in startups and via scientific grants.  Yosemite has now closed its second fund at $350 million, a serious jump from January’s first close at $200 million, Jobs exclusively told Fortune and the Term Sheet Podcast . Jobs’s LPs include Amgen , AbbVie , MIT, Memorial Sloan Kettering, and VC legend John Doerr. Yosemite’s model is unique: Jobs, in some ways, is operating in a traditional venture model, investing in startups early and taking sizable stakes en route to an exit (he’s clear the goal is venture-scale returns). But Yosemite also offers philanthropic grants to scientists.  “With philanthropy, we can fail really cheaply,” said Jobs. “That’s the real wisdom behind this… One of the difficult and suboptimal things about my industry is how slow it is. And look, that’s really important from a regulatory standpoint. But it also means you can waste a lot of money on things that aren’t going to work, which is obviously really bad. What we’ve learned is that we can test new ideas really quickly and cheaply in universities with grants. And before we waste a lot of time, money, and resources, we can kind of flip over that first card.” Yosemite’s first fund, closed in 2024 at $263 million, included AI drug discovery startup Chai Discovery, cervical cancer screening company Teal Health, epi-therapeutic medicine maker Tune Therapeutics, and care navigation startup Sage Care. This variety reflects how Jobs believes the healthcare system and science will ultimately have to evolve.  “I don’t think a company alone is going to make cancer non-lethal,” said Jobs. “I think it’s going to be a consortium of things. It’s going to be a really long push, probably cancer by cancer, more likely than not.”  When Jobs started Yosemite in 2023, biotech was in a slump, one that’s turned around substantially in recent years. The biggest changes are scientific advancements over the last three years, he said.  “You couldn’t have told me four years ago that we’d be sitting here today and we would have the advancements in GLP-1s, in immunotherapy, in vaccines now, and against pancreatic cancer that we’ve achieved,” said Jobs. “Those things have happened and have been titanic for the industry.” I asked Jobs what advice his father would have for him. “I think he’d say stay on the path, because something we have in common is we’re really good long-term builders,” said Jobs. “Yosemite is not going to, as you know, reach its zenith of success in the next year or two. This is a long-term play that’s going to take my whole life.” See you tomorrow, Allie Garfinkle X: @agarfinks Email: alexandra.garfinkle@fortune.com Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . events.title: My daughter is French and American. Choosing a name that reflected both her cultures was difficult.
events.summary: The author decided to name her daughter Romy. Courtesy of Virginie Romary I'm French, and my husband is American. My 9-year-old daughter has dual nationality and is Franco-American. Selecting a name for her turned out to be more complicated than we anticipated. For many parents, choosing a first name for a child can be a stressful experience, as it significantly influences their identity and shapes first impressions. For me, this process was particularly challenging because my child holds dual nationality. I had to consider various practical and cultural factors to ensure that my daughter would feel comfortable with her name in both countries. It needed to be easy to pronounce and spell in both languages Since my daughter has an American family name , we decided to choose a French first name to reflect both of her cultures. However, it needed to be easy to pronounce in English, especially since we live in the US. I often see panic in people's eyes when they attempt to say my name here, and I didn't want my child to experience the same. I believe that a simple name is better for fostering confidence and developing social connections than a name that requires repeated attempts to get the pronunciation right. Consequently, I had to reject many French names I love, such as Victoire or Manon , because they aren't common in the US and might be difficult for Americans to understand and pronounce. I also wanted a name that is spelled the same way in both countries to avoid administrative issues and prevent my daughter from constantly having to correct it. Therefore, names like Chloé had to be excluded from the list as well, since they are sometimes spelled with a 'K' here, and the accent could introduce complications. Traditions and trends in both countries matter I noticed that in the US, people often refer to others by using a diminutive of their first name. I still don't understand how William became Bill and why David is often shortened to Dave . French people don't use diminutives so easily and only restrict them to close family and friends. I didn't want my daughter to be called anything other than the name I chose . Josephine would have been Josie, which is why we declined a longer name and opted for a shorter one that is structurally difficult to shorten further. Trends in France and the US also differ. What is considered chic and trendy in the US is often seen as outdated in France, such as Isabelle or Sophie, which are names associated with older generations. While we didn't specifically want a trendy name , we also wanted to avoid giving our daughter a name that might be perceived as a "granny name" or as odd in one of her cultures, to prevent any teasing. Choosing a name for her daughter was more difficult than she thought. Courtesy of Virginie Romary Despite all these careful considerations, my daughter's name remains confusing After weighing the practical and cultural differences, we opted for the first name Romy . It's an elegant and stylish first name in France, popularized by the famous actress Romy Schneider from the 1950s, who was celebrated for her natural grace and beauty. It's also a nod to my family name . I remember the differing reactions from our French and American friends when we announced it; the French were charmed by it, while many people here looked at us, stunned, wondering what kind of name it was. Only a few people heard of the actress, and while it's a well-known name in Europe, it has not crossed the Atlantic yet. It wasn't until after my daughter's birth that I realized how unfamiliar and potentially confusing the name is here. People also often expect to see a boy with it, while in France, it is strictly feminine. Even though it is a simple name, the pronunciation differs slightly, and the last letter is frequently misspelled. I never anticipated this outcome, despite all my previous concerns. Choosing a name is a tricky job, regardless of the effort we invest. What matters most today is that my daughter is proud of her name and that it represents her family and culture. events.title: Democrats will face a health care stress test
events.summary: Democrats will be able to take plenty of messaging votes on health care after their blowout wins Tuesday — but they'll face too many limits and internal disagreements to force all of the big policy changes they want. Why it matters: They'll have a tough time repealing Medicaid cuts or restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies while President Trump is still in office, and their own divisions will hold them back on other issues. And Medicare for All ? Last night gave the idea a big boost, but don't hold your breath. Friction point: With control of both the Senate and House, Democrats will have powerful new leverage — but that leverage will also expose fault lines. Until now, progressives backing Medicare for All and centrists favoring more incremental changes were united in opposing Trump administration policies and blaming the president and the Republican Congress for the health affordability crisis. They'll try to use their power in the next Congress to promote sweeping changes with an eye toward the 2028 elections while also advancing more piecemeal policies, hoping to force some deals with Republicans. But they'll still face divisions over how to expand the federal government's role in the health system, or how to bend the steep health cost curve. Driving the news: House Democrats have already signaled their opening moves with a 100-hour/100-day agenda agenda that prominently features health policies like reinstating the enhanced ACA tax credits that expired at the end of 2025. There will also be votes to roll back the steep cuts to federal Medicaid spending that Republicans included in their "One Big Beautiful Bill," per an 84-page memo from a health care working group to Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.). Other near-term agenda items include expanding Medicare drug price negotiations to private insurance, restoring withheld National Institutes of Health research funding and ending the use of AI in authorizing certain services in traditional Medicare. Within the first year, the blueprint also envisions votes on Medicare for All, a government-run public insurance option and plans to let many Americans under 65 buy into Medicare. There will also be a heavy dose of oversight, with multiple committees intent on using their subpoena power to examine details of Trump's drug pricing deals and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s vaccine policies. Reality check: Little of this would reverse the rising cost of care. And Democrats could spend a lot of energy next year playing whack-a-mole trying to target various expenses, like hospital spending, insurance premiums and the cost of insulin. Some policies, like site-neutral hospital payments , could generate billions in new savings to pay for coverage expansions, and even generate some bipartisan support at a time when more lawmakers are fed up with hospital consolidation and prices. There's also growing interest in how surprise billing disputes are driving up costs. But Democrats won't be the only ones looking for fixes. An aggressive Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services under administrator Mehmet Oz is sure to continue pursing fraud and waste in federal health programs and cutting federal spending on subsidies. Between the lines: The biggest winner Tuesday may be the progressive wing of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Strengthened by the Senate victory of left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the critical swing state of Michigan, the progressives can make a national case for Medicare for All — though the definition may be squishy. Expect many lawmakers to offer assurances that Americans can keep their health care if they want it, with a consensus likely forming around compromises like a Medicare buy-in. Actual dealmaking will largely be driven by big legislative vehicles, like bills to keep the government funded and address the debt ceiling, that could be magnets for health policy changes. There also are certain must-do's, like a "doc fix" to shield physicians from scheduled Medicare reimbursement cuts and a reauthorization of Food and Drug Administration user fees to fund new product reviews. The latter could also be a way for Democrats and Republicans to respond to growing concerns about China challenging U.S. dominance in drug development. What we're watching: Whether a "govern from the center, message from the left" strategy binds a caucus that isn't truly aligned on health care, or whether it quickly exposes rifts between establishment Democrats and the ascendant populist wing.

events.title: ‘Call me senator’: How Abdul El-Sayed beat Trump’s hate to create history
events.summary: The 42-year-old Democrat has defeated Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim senator in the US. Abdul El-Sayed had an uncomfortable message for US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance as he celebrated his historic election victory in Michigan. They had used a range of racist labels and rhetoric to target El-Sayed ahead of the midterm elections, which he was contesting against Trump’s handpicked candidate, Mike Rogers. Trump mocked his name, and said that as president, he could call the Michigan physician and former public health official anything he wanted. Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist”, while Vance described him as a “psychopath”. list 1 of 3 Trump says US will stop giving Israel aid after year-end list 2 of 3 Rogers, El-Sayed urge turnout for critical race list 3 of 3 Firsts for women and minorities in US midterm elections Now, the 42-year-old winner of the Michigan race pointed out, they would soon need to address him as a senator. “JD, habibi [Arabic term of endearment], it is an irony – you are constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January,” El-Sayed told cheering supporters in the early hours of Wednesday, shortly after he was projected to win the highly contested race. “Donald, I know you struggle with my name, so when JD swears me in, you can call me ‘senator’. May we never have to see the likes of you in Michigan again.” The Democrat’s victory over Republican Rogers on Tuesday made him the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, following a campaign marked by attacks on his faith and criticism of his opposition to US military adventurism in the Middle East, and Washington’s support of Israel. “To all the parents who struggled to explain why the president openly mocks someone for their name or how they pray, let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost,” he said in his victory speech. Political analyst Rami Khouri says Abdul El-Sayed’s election to the US Senate could mark a historic turning point in attitudes towards Muslim and Arab Americans. Khouri, a non-resident Senior Fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, said El-Sayed’s victory alongside New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s electoral success last year demonstrated the growing influence of Muslim and Arab American politicians. “This is going to have huge implications for driving down anti-Arab, anti-Islamic sentiments,” Khouri told Al Jazeera. But beyond the historic significance of his election, El-Sayed has focused on his promise to challenge economic inequality, healthcare and the cost of living in the country. “Michigan, it just shouldn’t be this hard. It shouldn’t be this hard to buy a second bag of groceries or to fill your tank,” he said. “It shouldn’t be this hard to pay your taxes and know that that money is going to be spent on you and your kids instead of dropping bombs on somebody else and their kids.” The physician and public health official is set to win more than 52 percent of the vote with more than 95 percent of votes tallied. His victory is seen as a breakthrough for progressives in the Democratic Party, who have increasingly challenged the party’s status quo over economic inequality and US wars abroad, including steadfast support for Israel. Moreover, his win carries particular electoral significance, as Michigan is seen as a swing state that Trump won comfortably just two years ago. El-Sayed was born and raised in the Detroit metropolitan area of Michigan and is of Egyptian descent. He has often described his upbringing as that of a typical kid in a “brown” family of immigrants — he was expected to be high-achieving and successful at everything he did. El-Sayed studied at the University of Michigan, where he was valedictorian of his 2007 graduating class. At his commencement, guest speaker and former President Bill Clinton praised the incoming senator for his speech focusing on inclusivity and equality. “I wish every person in the world who believes that we are fated to have a clash of civilisations, and cannot reach across the religious divides, could have heard you speak today,” he said. He went on to become a Rhodes Scholar at the University of Oxford in the United Kingdom. He also earned a medical degree from Columbia University in New York. Before entering electoral politics, El-Sayed built his career in public health , working as an epidemiologist and eventually leading Detroit’s Health Department as its executive director. He later became director of the Wayne County Department of Health, Human and Veteran Services. The incoming senator is married to Indian-American psychiatrist Sarah Jukaku, with whom he has two daughters. El-Sayed first sought elected office in 2018, when he ran for governor of Michigan on what many considered a progressive platform. He campaigned on expanding healthcare access and challenging corporate influence but lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer, who subsequently won the governorship.

events.title: South Africa downplays AGOA blow
events.summary: The News South Africa moved to contain fears of major economic damage after the White House’s decision to exclude it from a US preferential trade program, saying its biggest mineral exports never relied on the duty-free program and the tariff increase on affected goods is manageable. Washington announced plans this week to remove South Africa , along with Rwanda, from the African Growth and Opportunity Act from next year. South Africa’s fruit and nut exporters have benefited from the 26-year-old program that allows thousands of products from eligible sub-Saharan countries to enter the US market duty-free. The US, explaining its latest move, cited concerns ranging from barriers to American trade and investment to corruption and foreign policy. Farmers and exporters warned, however, that the wine and citrus sectors could face job losses as their products become less competitive The decision deepens a rupture between Pretoria and Washington, entangling a trade dispute with the two countries’ wider political differences, raising the prospect of a prolonged standoff that gives South African an incentive to pursue opportunities in markets including China. It comes weeks after the US imposed travel restrictions on unidentified officials. These were introduced over South Africa’s race-based business and land policies, which seek to address the inequities of apartheid, as part of an escalating campaign that has included false claims by US President Donald Trump of a genocide against Afrikaners. Even so, South African government officials say much of the country’s biggest trade with the US is already outside AGOA protection. President Cyril Ramaphosa’s agriculture envoy Wandile Sihlobo told Semafor that losing the program was not a “train smash.” The country’s exports already face a 12.5% US tariff, meaning the loss of duty-free access adds an estimated 3.4 percentage points to the average levy, Sihlobo said. “It’s not necessarily as catastrophic as we have faced in the past,” he wrote in a note shared with Semafor. Eckart Naumann, an economist at Trade Law Centre, a South African policy think tank, struck a similar note, calling South Africa’s removal from AGOA regrettable but “ does not spell doom for South Africa ”. South Africa exported about $1.7 billion of goods to the US under AGOA in 2025, representing around 10% of the country’s sales to the country and roughly 1% of its global exports. But some of South Africa’s largest exports sit outside AGOA. Platinum group metals, which account for roughly a third of exports to the US, already enter duty free because they are deemed important to the economy. A Trade Law Centre analysis found that about 80% of South African exports by value are exempt from the current 12.5% tariff . South African-built cars effectively lost much of their AGOA advantage when Washington imposed a 25% tariff on vehicle imports in 2025. Addressing the diplomatic dispute, Deputy Trade Minister John Steenhuisen told a local radio station that South Africa had been “very generous” in trying to resolve the tensions but some US objections collided with Pretoria’s red lines. He said land reform and racial transformation were non-negotiable. The latest US demands extended to corruption, and “who we trade and do business with in the rest of the world,” Steenhuisen said. “It’s been pretty much a moving target. Trade and politics have collided and are so deeply enmeshed that it’s going to be difficult to separate them.” The pressure could push South Africa further into China’s orbit. Trade Minister Parks Tau, in a statement, said the loss of AGOA would accelerate South Africa’s search for opportunities in other markets including China, even as the US cited Pretoria’s relations with “governments of concern” among the reasons for withdrawing AGOA benefits. Know More Pretoria has for the past 18 months tried to mend relations with the US, appointing an Afrikaner as an ambassador to Washington, offering to buy up to $12 billion of US liquid natural gas over 10 years, and lifting the avian-flu related ban on US poultry. But the dispute has increasingly moved beyond trade, with Tau saying Washington had introduced “new issues” that had not formed part of negotiations that began in 2025. “This decision does not define the broader relationship between South Africa and the United States, however a solution depends on the willingness of both parties to find solutions,” Tau said. Steenhuisen acknowledged the US decision would have “sectoral impacts — particularly in some parts of the agriculture sector.” The government has promised to support affected industries, but has yet to spell out what that assistance will entail. Washington’s decision to eject South Africa from AGOA came on the eve of the US midterms, after Trump spent much of his second term tuning his false Afrikaner-genocide narrative which plugs into pre-existing politics of white victimhood on parts of the American right. Tiisetso’s view South Africans can probably live without AGOA. The more troubling question is whether the country’s deteriorating relationship with the US stops there. It hit a low point with the May 2025 Oval Office showdown and went downhill from then. The preferential trade program was already losing economic significance for South Africa, with only 1% of its total exports going to the US under AGOA last year. Cars, previously among the biggest beneficiaries, have their own 25% tariff problem. PGMs, which account for a far bigger chunk of US-bound exports, don’t rely on AGOA for favorable access. So far, so manageable. But Washington has advertised its willingness to go further. When the US imposed visa restrictions in September, Ambassador L. Brent Bozell III called them the “first step in a series of escalatory measures.” Seven weeks later, Washington moved to remove South Africa from AGOA, citing, not only trade and investment barriers and corruption, but US national security and foreign policy interests. It would be a leap to conclude that Washington intends to target South African mineral exports next. Nobody is saying that. But once trade policy becomes part of a wider political fight, their favorable treatment becomes more interesting Losing AGOA may turn out to be the tariff fight Pretoria could afford to lose, but the biggest risk is discovering that Washington has not finished looking for pressure points. Room for Disagreement The Citrus Growers Association, a Cape Town-based trade body, described South Africa’s exclusion as a “serious blow,” and warned of employment losses. Meanwhile, the Exporters Western Cape, a lobby group, told Ramaphosa before the decision that the province’s exports to the US had already fallen 41% with particularly steep declines in juice, grapes and citrus. Notable South African vehicle exports to the US fell 83% in 2025 after a 25% Section 232 tariff, which Naamsa says “nullif[ies]” AGOA’s benefits, Freight News reported.

events.title: Texas just went blue, and the tech bros are sad
events.summary: Tech bros headed to Texas to find redder pastures. Democrats just flipped the governor's mansion and a Senate seat. Elías Valverde II/The Dallas Morning News via Getty Images, Brandon Bell/Getty Images, Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images Texas drew in tech moguls — including many who wanted redder politics than Silicon Valley. Well, it just turned pretty blue. We're starting to see the anger from tech execs trickle out. Texas — with its cowboy hats, slow-smoked barbecue, and de-regulatory stance — was supposed to be the California antidote for tech bros fed up with Silicon Valley's Democratic politics. Well, Texas just got a lot bluer. On Tuesday, voters handed Democrats control of the House and Senate. In Texas, they selected James Talarico for the Senate and Gina Hinojosa for the governor's mansion, despite massive Republican spending backed by Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk . Now, the tech-world frustration is starting to trickle out . "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote on X. Jason Calacanis, a tech investor and co-host of the "All-In Podcast," had a similar reaction. "I never expected Texas to turn blue," he wrote on X. "Ugh, I moved here to get away from the left lunacy!" It was clear over the past year that President Trump was going to lead the GOP off the cliff because of ice, the war, tariffs, the other war and inflation. … but I never expected Texas to turn blue 🤯 Ugh, I moved here to get away from the left lunacy! https://t.co/VTFzfXchHp — @jason (@Jason) November 4, 2026 Chamath Palihapitiya, another "All-In" co-host, was more dire during a Tuesday-night livestream. "There's only one thing that sinks the US economy," he said. "That's the AI trade. And the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers. And the only way to sink the data centers is to sink the power. And all the power that matters right now is in West Texas." Alex Cohen, the Texas-based CEO and cofounder of AI healthcare company Hello Patient, had a blunter response on X: "RIP AI it was fun while it lasted." The Lone Star State had not elected a statewide Democratic candidate since Ann Richards won the governor's race in 1990. Talarico is the first Democrat to win a Texas Senate election since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. Not everyone in tech is angry at the results. LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, a prominent donor for Democrats , called the midterm elections, including the Texas results, "an overwhelming wave against Trump and his cronies," in a post on X. As of publication, several outspoken Texas-based tech figures — including David Sacks, Travis Kalanick, and Blockchain co-CEO Lane Kasselman — had not posted about the results. events.title: ‘Seismic shift’: World reacts to US midterm election results
events.summary: Iran’s top negotiator says US voters sent a “NO TO WAR” message, as Trump’s Democratic opponents take Congress. Democrats in the United States have scored a major victory in midterm elections, taking control of both chambers of Congress in a stinging rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. The results are being carefully watched outside the US, as foreign leaders consider how the new political reality in Washington could affect US foreign policy – from the conflict with Iran to the Russia-Ukraine war and trade relations. list 1 of 3 Republicans fuming after Democrat Talarico flips Texas Senate blue list 2 of 3 Key takeaways from the 2026 midterm elections in California list 3 of 3 Democrat Troy Jackson unseats Republican Senator Susan Collins in Maine Trump himself has acknowledged the US-Israel war on Iran likely impacted his party’s poor performance in the elections, saying voters were probably not ready “for the short-term consequence of the price of gasoline”. Here are the latest reactions from world leaders, as the scale of the Democratic victory continues to emerge: European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose said the US results left her “cautiously optimistic on Europe’s behalf”. “Not because everything now ⁠⁠changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and ⁠⁠relations with the rest of the world,” said Schaldemose in a post on X. “But the EU must continue the course of standing stronger and standing on its own two feet. That’s not up for debate,” she added. Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is also the chief negotiator in talks with the US, said voters had rejected conflict. “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” wrote Ghalibaf in a post on X. “If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” he added. Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile, said partisan shifts in Washington would not alter the US’s “hostility” towards Tehran. “If there are still those who harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system could change through party or factional shifts, or who believe that making concessions to the US could persuade it to abandon its hostility towards the Iranian people, they are gravely mistaken,” said Khamenei in a statement shared by Iranian state media. There was no immediate reaction from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a Trump ally whose coalition lost its own majority in Israel’s parliament in elections last week. However, opposition figure Yair Golan, whose party is in a coalition seeking to replace Netanyahu , said the US vote reveals “just how toxic Netanyahu has become” among US Democrats and Republicans alike. He warned that if Netanyahu and his far-right government remain in power, Israel would be on “a path toward international sanctions, global isolation, and a confrontation with the United States – our most important friend and ally.” Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid, also part of the anti-Netanyahu coalition, said the US vote effectively ruled out “any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu”. Health Minister James Frith stressed that the UK would maintain steady, strong ties with Washington despite an apparent “seismic shift in domestic politics for the Americans”. “The change of emphasis of power in the States is frequent,” Frith told British media. “But the mainstay of the relationship with the UK Government, as its closest ally, is unwavering and unchanging.” “So I don’t expect it to change the nature of the relationship at all; it remains very strong,” he added. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said France would wait to see whether Trump, who remains in control of US foreign policy, adjusts his approach. “Either he decides to rise above the fray – acknowledging that ‌‌changes are necessary, particularly regarding gasoline prices, which directly ‌‌affect people – and, I might add, he tones down his international involvement, or he does not,” Lescure told French TV. “Frankly, this is something we will need to keep an eye on in the ⁠⁠coming days.” Left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the US Democrats’ landslide victory was emblematic of the “unravelling” of the global far right. “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will soon happen in Spain,” said Sanchez, whose own premiership is at stake in snap elections he called for November 29 . Sanchez said US voters had rejected policies that “only ‌‌impoverish”, as well as hate, sexism, climate change denialism and “the privileges of the elites”. Government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis said US-Greek relations would not be affected by the election results. “Greek-American relations will remain strong,” he told local media. “The United States is our strategic ally, and this will continue for major projects ⁠⁠and all major agreements.

events.title: Dario Amodei wants ‘a country of geniuses in a data center.’ Realizing that vision requires risky financial mechanics, Anthropic’s IPO filing shows
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has written about creating AI powerful enough that it will be like “having a country of geniuses in a data center.” But the company’s recently-unveiled IPO prospectus sheds new light on the kind of precarious financing Anthropic will require to turn that vision into reality. This week the company updated its prospectus to include its third quarter financial results , which showed a squeeze on the company’s margins as computing costs have risen. The company also revealed additional data center spending commitments. The company has now pledged to spend a whopping $895.4 billion stretching out to 2045. Some of the companies selling Anthropic the chips and cloud services it needs are also helping it finance those very same purchases. Broadcom has agreed to absorb losses under a $63 billion equipment-financing arrangement if Anthropic defaults, with its maximum potential liability reaching about $43 billion once the equipment is deployed. Such backing helps Anthropic obtain computing capacity without paying the full equipment cost upfront. Google and AMD also tie some funding to Anthropic leasing or deploying their hardware. Suppliers providing guarantees could face payouts to lenders and developers they backstop just as weaker AI demand reduces their own sales and market valuations. Who bears the risk? In the $63 billion transaction announced on Oct. 26, Bank of America , Citi, Morgan Stanley and Blackstone will finance a newly formed company that buys Broadcom chips and networking equipment and leases them to Anthropic. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2027. Anthropic will pay rent for those chips over time, providing the income financiers rely on to recover their investment.  If Anthropic defaults on its lease, however, Broadcom has agreed to cover the difference between 72.5% of the amount still owed under the lease and what the equipment sells for. For example, if $100 remains owed and the equipment sells for $60, Broadcom would pay $12.50.  Gil Luria, the head of technology research at D.A. Davidson tells Fortune that Broadcom basically has to cut a deal like this in order to make sure it doesn’t lose sales to rival Nvidia , which has also offered to backstop some of its biggest chip buyers. “In order to stay competitive with Nvidia’s support of its customers, other large semis companies like Broadcom and AMD have had to step in to support their customers as well,” Luria said. Luria upgraded Broadcom to buy on Oct. 27.  Financiers’ ability to recover money after a default also depends on whether other customers can use the chips. Comparing Nvidia GPUs with Google’s specialized AI chips, known as TPUs, which are built by Broadcom, Andrew Giudici of credit-rating agency KBRA told Fortune , “Custom TPUs generally have greater re-leasing risk than Nvidia GPUs because they are designed for a more specialized ecosystem and have a narrower pool of potential users”. Residual-value support, such as Broadcom’s agreement,  can help financiers recover money when equipment cannot be sold or re-leased for as much as expected, Giudici said. “However, it effectively transfers a portion of that risk to the support provider.” That makes the supplier’s creditworthiness, the enforceability of its commitment and the extent of its coverage important to assessing the financing, he said. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan. Broadcom has agreed to backstop Anthropic in a financing deal that will allow the AI company to purchase TPUs, a kind of AI chip, produced by Broadcom. David Paul Morris—Bloomberg via Getty Images Cash-rich suppliers with substantial businesses outside AI have capacity to absorb losses, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a professor of real estate and finance at Columbia Business School, said. But weaker AI demand could hit those partners’ hardware sales, cloud revenue and investment values at the same time as calls on their guarantees. “Separate contracts can transmit the same underlying demand shock across multiple balance sheets,” he said. “Individual loans can become safer while the broader system becomes more concentrated but also harder to assess.” Anthropic’s IPO filing says its ability to expand computing capacity may depend on a small number of cloud providers, partners and financiers remaining willing and able to support them. Two of the most important, Amazon and Google, are also spending more cash on their own AI buildouts than their operations bring in. Amazon reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the preceding 12 months, primarily because of increased AI-related equipment investment. And Google’s parent Alphabet free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion in the third quarter. Both still generate substantial cash and can borrow readily, but their spending means that continued support for Anthropic increasingly competes with their own buildouts for capital. CEO Dario Amodei has described how an AI company could grow extraordinarily quickly and still buy more computing capacity than it could afford. In a February interview with podcaster Dwarkesh Patel, he illustrated the financial danger with a hypothetical company buying computing capacity on the assumption that revenue would grow tenfold annually. Even fivefold growth could leave it unable to afford what it had ordered. The market could become enormous and still develop too slowly for the purchases made in anticipation of it. “If you’re off by a couple years, that can be ruinous,” he said. Complex funding conditions Under a March 2026 agreement, Anthropic can issue up to $42 billion in convertible notes to Broadcom to cover eligible quarterly rent, preserving cash it would otherwise need to pay out. Interest increases the debt, and the holder can choose to convert it into Anthropic shares at a discount. Notes issued under the facility normally carry 9% interest, with the interest added to the debt, and with the notes deemable for stock at 90% of the market price. But notes issued when specified revenue conditions are unmet carry a 13% interest rate and convert at 85% of market price, giving noteholders more shares for each dollar and further diluting existing shareholders. Sustained failure to meet the agreement’s conditions can end access to further funding. Anthropic says the revenue-growth thresholds are significantly below its recent actual growth rates. The company reported 45% quarterly revenue growth in its third quarter financial results, and a year-over-year growth rate in excess of 1,000%.  Google and AMD also tie funding to hardware commitments: certain Google funds become available as Anthropic takes on TPU lease obligations, while AMD’s investment becomes available as its GPUs reach delivery and deployment milestones.  “Hardware-linked equity investments expose Amazon and AMD without making them blanket guarantors,” Van Nieuwerburgh told Fortune . If Anthropic cannot pay, Broadcom and Google bear losses within their backstops’ contractual limits

events.title: Trump says midterms voters weren't willing to pay more for gas: 'I understand that'
events.summary: President Donald Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Florida. Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images As the Democrats scored a wave of key midterm victories, Trump says gas prices are to blame. Fuel prices have soared about 36% on average compared to last year amid the Iran war. Trump called the higher fuel costs a "short-term problem but for long-term gain." President Donald Trump said voters were unwilling to pay higher gasoline prices that shot up because of the Iran war, as Democrats swept the midterms on Tuesday. "I don't think it's the war, I think it's the gas prices," Trump said on a phone call with Fox News as he reflected on the results. "People agree with what I'm doing in Iran, but they really, probably weren't willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline." "And you know, I understand that," he continued. "I don't agree with it, and I would say to people, you know: 'It's a short-term problem but for long-term gain." The president congratulated the Democratic congressional leaders and said he would accept the results. Democrats have won the majority in both the House and Senate, meaning Trump would have to face a fully opposition-controlled Congress. "I don't like to consider it a defeat for me, I wasn't on the ballot," said Trump, adding that he felt "badly for a lot of very good Republicans, a lot of very good patriots that lost tonight." Fuel costs have surged since February, when the US and Israel began launching airstrikes on Iran, after which Iran began mining and attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. The disruptions to the strait, through which 20 to 25% of the world's seaborne oil previously flowed, have constrained global supply and sent energy prices soaring worldwide. Regular gas prices in the US are now about 36% higher on average, or about $1 higher per gallon, compared to a year ago, per AAA's Fuel Price Tracker on November 3. Some states saw far higher jumps. In Michigan, where Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican incumbent Sen. Mike Rogers, gas prices have jumped 52% compared to a year ago. Diesel prices, meanwhile, have risen about 70% on average in the US, reaching record highs this fall in all but three states. The White House has said that it expects oil prices to drop significantly once the war in the Middle East ends. Though hostilities have largely toned down since the beginning of the war and both sides have repeatedly tried to broker ceasefires, the fighting continues on a limited scale. Several media outlets reported that the US had carried out an unpublicized campaign of several small-scale strikes on Qeshm, an island in the Strait of Hormuz, in the last few weeks. The Wall Street Journal was the first to report on the strikes, which included one attack on Monday. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Behind the Curtain: The Trump obliteration
events.summary: Make no mistake: Democrats won by epic, sometimes historic margins across red and blue states, up and down ballots, obliterating almost everything President Trump, and a Republican Party remade wholly in his image, built over the past decade in American politics. Why it matters: Trump and Republicans are left with a mostly white, mostly old House and Senate minority, confronting a younger, more diverse ascendant Democratic Party with power and margins it hasn't held in 18 years, since the dawn of the Obama era. The results speak louder than any words we can write: Democrats won Senate races in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Ohio, and perhaps Mississippi en route to what could be a 55-seat majority. Democrats won swing districts all across red America, with national average margins of victory of roughly 13 points, according to a New York Times estimate . Texas is now a Democratic state, top to bottom — unthinkable mere months ago. James Talarico crushed Ken Paxton ( 55% to 43% ) like it was Connecticut. State Representative Gina Hinojosa will become the first Democratic governor of Texas in 32 years . Pastor Adam Hamilton is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas in 94 years. North Carolina looks like a true-blue state after Democrats flipped the Senate seat and likely ousted Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.), chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) — meaning he led the GOP drive to keep the House. North Carolina's congressional delegation could swing from 10R-4D to 5R-9D. Georgia was even worse for Republicans, where they lost all power at the state and U.S. Senate levels. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) predicted on X that the losses were so widespread, so deep, so severe that Republicans might not "have a shot at Senate control until 2032." How to think about last night more broadly: This is a 50-50 nation with fast, whiplash shifts in power at the federal level due to persistent discontent with the party in power. So, on one hand, this isn't terribly surprising. On the other, Republican losses were so deep, so wide, so everywhere that it would be foolish to see this as anything but a massive repudiation of Trump, his agenda, his style, his rhetoric and his presidency. If anything, what's left of the Republican Party is more pro-Trump and less likely to challenge him. His critics, even the timid ones, were ousted long before the general election. So Republicans are left with two more years of riding a very unpopular leader managing a very unpopular war. A trapped, embarrassed Trump is even more unpredictable. Democrats have the numbers to investigate Trump, his family and supporters, and the power to set the agenda in the House and Senate. The bottom line: Voters nationally said government corruption was a "crucial issue" in their vote for Congress. Democrats will spend months trying to rehab a party that, despite its victory, remains deeply unpopular as a brand. Expect a vigorous fight between Mamdani-like socialists and Schumer-like center-leftists. Top takeaways from Axios' Zachary Basu.

events.title: ADNOC to expand AI use across its operations to strengthen resilience
events.summary: Welcome to this week’s Fortune Gulf Brief. We’ll be covering:   Abu Dhabi’s flagship energy conference champions AI Saudi Aramco profits jump 35% as it targets full production capacity Why Bob Diamond is optimistic about Bahrain Oman and China strengthen commercial ties, establish $800 million joint investment fund  And, the three we enjoyed reading this week Many of the biggest names in the oil and gas industry have converged on Abu Dhabi this week to attend the emirate’s flagship annual energy conference, ADIPEC , with energy security a priority as the industry grapples with ongoing supply disruptions amid heightened geopolitical tensions. Concerns over renewed U.S. strikes on Iran and the prospect of retaliatory action by Tehran have gripped oil markets in recent days. They also led both Exxon’s CEO Darren Woods and Chevron’s upstream president, Clay Neff, to withdraw from attending ADIPEC , citing security concerns. But overall, the turnout has been strong, with heavyweights such as BP’s CEO Meg O’Neill, Baker Hughes CEO Lorenzo Simonelli, and Halliburton’s chairman and CEO Jeff Miller, all flying in to speak at the event. Shell , TotalEnergies , Eni, ExxonMobil, Chevron , and Occidental Petroleum were also present among the 2,260 exhibiting companies. More than 120 U.S. companies are exhibiting this year, second only to China in number. In total, the event is expected to draw around 239,000 visitors from 170 countries.  Dr Sultan Al Jaber, UAE minister of industry and advanced technology and Group CEO of ADNOC, took to the podium during the event’s opening ceremony on Monday to set the tone for the days ahead.  “Energy leadership is not measured by what you produce in good times, it is measured by what you deliver in hard times,” he said. “The choices we make today will determine the energy landscape a decade from now.”  He urged increased investment in energy infrastructure and AI to strengthen the industry’s long-term resilience against future disruptions, noting how AI has become essential to ensuring operational continuity. “AI must be built in, not bolted on,” he said. “In a crisis, the speed of insight and the speed of decision-making is the difference between continuity and disruption.” Earlier that morning, ADNOC signed a deal with OpenAI and G42, an Abu Dhabi-backed AI firm, to become the world’s first energy company to deploy OpenAI’s Frontier platform to build and manage AI agents. It plans to use the technology to transform its oilfield development, well management, and commercial operations. Referring to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was seated in the front row at the ceremony as guest of honor, Al Jaber said: “Sam, from the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI. And now, together, we will find out what AI can do for energy.” BP’s CEO Meg O’Neill also outlined her company’s focus on AI in a speech delivered on the first day of ADIPEC.  “Understanding the macro impact of these investments and technologies, and what it means for global energy demand is really important, and we spend quite a bit of time on that, trying to sift through the myriad of forecasts which range from gentle growth to something that is astronomical and hard to figure out, and how they underpin our investment decisions,” she said.  O’Neill explained that the two main areas where BP is focusing its AI efforts are sub-surface analysis, including seismic processing and reservoir management, and the application of physical AI to improve facility operations, reduce costs and maximise resource flows through its systems. Nine out of 10 energy leaders (89%) increased their AI spending over the past year , while 63% expect returns from existing investments to match or exceed their costs, according to the Powering Possible report, the third annual study conducted by ADNOC, its international investment arm XRG, and Microsoft . The report, published last week, also noted how the proportion of energy leaders ranking AI among their top two corporate priorities has increased to 62%, up from 42% a year earlier, as the industry increasingly embraces agentic AI. In addition to AI and energy security, conversations over the last few days have focused on addressing some of the sector’s most pressing challenges, including shifting trade routes to rising electricity demand and the investment needed to build resilient energy infrastructure. Speaking to  Fortune  contributor Inzamam Rashid on the sidelines of ADIPEC, Dr Carole Nakhle, CEO of Crystol Energy and Secretary General of the Arab Energy Club, described the scale of this year’s energy disruption as “unprecedented”. “We are all sailing through a very thick fog,” Nakhle said. “Resilience doesn’t get parachuted in overnight; it requires investment over years and decades.” Melissa Hancock And as ever, thanks for reading, and do keep in touch with your thoughts and ideas. melissa.hancock@fortune.com   This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Funding to help poorer countries cope with climate crisis has stalled, says UN
events.summary: Report reveals financial support promised by rich nations for adaptation measures is well behind the pace that is needed Flows of money to help poor countries cope with the climate crisis have been flat or falling since 2022 , despite growing impacts from extreme weather and warnings from scientists that global heating may be accelerating . A new UN report has revealed that financial support for adaptation – which includes measures such as stronger infrastructure, early warning systems, flood protection and drought-resilient irrigation – is woefully short of what is needed and far behind even the inadequate promises that rich countries signed up to in 2021 in recognition of their far greater responsibility for the crisis. The world’s 155 developing nations will need $305bn (£226bn) annually by 2035 to adapt to heatwaves, fires, floods, storms, droughts and rising sea levels that are made more intense or more frequent as a result of decades of burning fossil fuels, mostly in wealthy global north nations, according to the UN Environment Programme . Yet finance flows from rich to poor countries were at most $32bn in 2024, the latest year for which data is available. That was only a billion up on the previous year, and down from the peak of 2022, partly because many governments in Europe are devoting more of their budgets to defence spending. This is well behind the pace required to meet the goal of hitting $40bn by 2025, though some of the shortfall is expected to have been made up last year by multinational development banks, the report said. At the Cop30 global climate talks in Belém , Brazil, last year, wealthy nations agreed to triple adaptation finance for developing countries by 2035. This increase to between $85bn and $120bn would reduce the gap, but still meet only 20-29% of needs, the report said. The world’s least developed countries (LDCs) and small island states are disproportionately affected by the climate crisis and least able to pay for upgrades to infrastructure, such as more sea barriers and firefighting equipment. The UN estimates these countries need $40bn to $50bn each year in adaptation finance, which is about 3-4% of their gross domestic product – double the relative burden for upper-middle-income developing countries. Despite this, LDCs received 16% less in adaptation financial support in 2024 than two years earlier. Between 2020 and 2025, low- and middle-income countries accounted for 99% of all the 765 million people affected by floods and landslides. Some of the worst impacts on human health and natural life support systems are unaccounted for because developing nations are less likely to have monitoring systems in place to assess heat-related deaths or damage to ecosystems. A recently established loss and damage fund is already overwhelmed. In its first round, 119 developing countries submitted requests totalling $2.8bn, far outstripping the initial funding of $342m. The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential Inger Andersen, the UNEP executive director, said a global temperature overshoot of 1.5C above preindustrial levels was now locked in, making climate impacts more intense, frequent, and unpredictable. “For the countries that contributed the least yet suffer the most, this is an unavoidable reality,” she said. “Adaptation finance is a vital investment in global resilience. Delivering on these commitments protects frontline communities, prevents forced displacement, safeguards global food security, and ensures no one is left behind. Now is the time to honour commitments in full. Delays not only increase long-term costs, they also strain our near-term capacity to cope as our systems reach their limits.” Climate justice groups say adaptation finance is the most urgent issue at the upcoming COP31 UN climate summit, which will be hosted in Antalya, Turkey, from 9 to 20 November. As well as a faster, bigger flow of funds, the priority, they say, is for grants or concessionary loans rather than high-interest loans, which are difficult to pay back on sea walls, heat shelters and other projects that do not generate direct revenue. The UN report underscores this, noting that debt and equity costs can more than double the budgets of adaptation projects. While wars are diverting resources and attention away from climate action, Anderson said it was important to view the interlinked nature of the world’s crises: “While some might view climate action as a separate issue, ignoring it only increases national and regional vulnerability, especially as many climate impacts unfold beyond national borders. Failing to invest in mitigation and adaptation only exposes nations to greater risk. Climate change directly threatens people, economies, and the ecosystems that sustain us – and why adaptation is a direct investment in national security and resilience. The two are fundamentally inseparable.”

events.title: Abnormal AI's new CMO says 'safe is boring' and is ditching the B2B marketing playbook
events.summary: Don Jeter is joining Abnormal AI and has ambitions to make the brand a "household name." Courtesy of Don Jeter A version of this post appears in CMO Insider. Sign up for Business Insider's marketing newsletter . Cybersecurity startup Abnormal AI wants its marketing to be anything but ordinary. Abnormal AI exclusively told CMO Insider on Wednesday that it has appointed Don Jeter as its chief marketing officer. In an interview, Jeter said he has big ambitions to use unconventional marketing techniques as part of a plan to build Abnormal AI into a "household name" brand. "I want my nephew, who is 14, and my parents to know Abnormal," Jeter said. "I want to be the most talked-about cybersecurity company in 2027." Jeter said that's why he intends to throw out the traditional business-to-business marketing playbook, which often focuses on features and functions, and instead plans to create "cultural moments" that will capture the attention of all kinds of consumers beyond its CISO target audience. Founded in 2018, Abnormal made its name using behavioral AI to detect email security threats. It has since expanded the technology to help companies spot unusual activity in employees' digital accounts and logins, and is increasingly applying the same approach to securing organizations' use of AI tools. The company was valued at $5.1 billion after a $250 million Series D funding round in 2024. One of Jeter's near-term challenges is resetting the narrative that Abnormal is only an email security company. He'll be attempting to do so in a noisy market, competing for mindshare against the marketing heft of trillion-dollar tech giants and buzzy frontier AI companies , as well as the cybersecurity vendors jostling for chief information security officers' budgets. "Right now, in this market, you've got to build trust and awareness before the sales conversation starts," Jeter said. "If you do brand marketing correctly, everything else gets easier; it signals to the market you are winning." While he wanted to keep his specific plans under wraps for now, Jeter said out-of-home advertising and other IRL activations are likely to play key roles in Abnormal AI's marketing mix. "We want to create stuff that people naturally want to share and participate in," Jeter said. "With great marketing, you never have to ask your employees to 'please share and retweet.'" B2B brands are increasingly taking a more business-to-consumer marketing approach. Salesforce and Adobe hold their glitzy Dreamforce and MAX conferences. Autodesk has a string of major sports team partnerships and splurged to advertise on the Las Vegas Sphere . Elsewhere, Ramp enlisted former pro skater Tony Hawk for a comedic campaign that culminated with him dropping in and skating on a ramp during a live event outside the New York Stock Exchange and around the trading floor. "A B2B buyer is still a person who remembers a great story, and in a category where nearly every company is promising smarter AI, tighter security, or faster results, IRL connection gives people a reason to remember one brand over another," said Steve Nottingham, CEO of the commerce experience agency RSM&, about Jeter's plans for Abnormal AI. Nottingham said CMOs who want to execute these kinds of activations need to start with a clear objective, an idea that could only come from their brand, a defined audience, a parallel content strategy that allows for amplification, and measurement that clearly connects the buzz to brand awareness and the sales pipeline. "Done thoughtfully, a real-world moment can work harder than almost any other line in the budget, because the conversation it starts keeps going well beyond the day itself," Nottingham said. Jeter has experience in this area. As CMO of cybersecurity startup Torq , he built the brand through deliberately offbeat marketing campaigns. Torq sponsored Monster Jam's nationwide tour for its "Torq, not torque" campaign, then brought a 20-foot inflatable skeleton and an on-site tattoo bus to the 2026 RSAC cybersecurity conference. "B2B marketing, in general, has played it safe for a very long time, and what we are seeing is that's no longer working in today's culture and scarce attention economy," Jeter said. "Safe is boring, and boring is invisible." Read the original article on Business Insider

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Very nearly 30something environment gets spruced up… and there's a new Trinity, too Architect creates open source replacement for VM migration tool VMware has hidden 1 day ago Linus Torvalds says Linux kernel is out of 'stabilization phase' and using 'much healthier model' for AI contributions 2 days ago 'Mother of all editors' Emacs is 50 3 days ago AlpineBSD announced – an AI-free FOSS OS 4 days ago Ubuntu 27.04 may bring a preview of the long-awaited Core Desktop 5 days ago Fresh on the desktop this week is a new version of Enlightenment as well the continuation of noughties hero KDE 3, the Trinity Desktop Environment, for those who prefer things a little old school. Enlightenment version 0.28 is the latest release of one of the older Linux graphical environments, which first appeared in 1997. Version 0.28 arrives nearly two years after the previous release – we reported on Enlightement 0.27 in January 2025. If you're not familiar with this venerable window manager, often referred to as just E, we refer you back to that article, which also explains Enlightenment's slightly strange version numbering scheme. Last time around we noted that its single-line release notes really didn't give us much to write about. The development team has made up for it this time, with some 68 lines of changes. It's both the same old E, and simultaneously a modern tool: it is still an X11 window manager, but it can also act as a Wayland compositor if you prefer. It offers conventional stacking resizable windows, but also can act as a tiling window manager if you prefer. On recent distros, it can now talk to the Pipewire audio server, and it can also work with NetworkManager to control network connections. This version delivers preliminary support for NetBSD too. This isn't really a tool for newbies or those looking for a simple easy desktop. A sign of its age is that the first-run wizard asks if you want windows to activate as soon as you move the mouse pointer over them. This was traditional 20th century Unix behavior, and in the early days of Linux it was called "focus-follows-mouse," but it's rarely seen today. E isn't a full desktop environment: it only offers a few of its own optional tools, such as the Ecrire text editor, Ephoto picture viewer, Evisum task manager, and Rage video player. Even its taskbar is optional. It is more like a basis for experienced users to customize and build their own environment around. The Trinity Desktop Environment has a rather lower learning curve: TDE is a port of the final version of KDE 3 to modern Linux. Proving old school is still cool, the project – which keeps the look and feel of 2005-era KDE 3.5 alive – has just announced TDE release 14.1.7 , with dozens of bug fixes and plenty of new features. Among these is a tweak to the kicker/taskbar: you can now scroll the taskbar using the mouse wheel, flicking through your open applications.This release drops support for Ubuntu 24.10 "Oracular Oriole" but adds support for the latest 26.10 "Stonking Stingray." Forks of older versions by users disenchanted with new versions are a recurring feature of the FOSS world, but they often tend to peter out after a while. TDE is one of the exceptions: we first reported on a new release in 2021 and again in 2023 .

events.title: ‘I will not delete my posts’: Inside Uganda’s crackdown on online critics
events.summary: Uganda’s online critics allege abductions and intimidation as families search for missing relatives. Kampala, Uganda – Praise Aloikin Opoloje walks into the visitors’ waiting room at Luzira Women’s Prison wearing an oversized yellow-and-black striped dress and a broad smile. Detained since September 26, 2026, she was charged with the alleged unlawful use of a SIM card registered in her mother’s name. Her case has drawn attention to the risks faced by Ugandans who use social media to criticise powerful political and military figures. Opoloje appeared before the Buganda Road Chief Magistrate’s Court on September 28, charged with using another person’s SIM card to carry out illegal activity. She denied the charge under Regulation 29 of Uganda’s 2024 Regulation of Interception of Communications Regulations. Opoloje says her detention followed a video in which she declared that she was not afraid of General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Uganda’s military chief and son of President Yoweri Museveni. A video, an arrest and an alleged threat Opoloje says she was lured to a Kampala police station by a false accusation that she had stolen a carpet. She alleges that six men then forced her into a Toyota HiAce van, locally known as a “drone”. “We are going to show you what we do to people who insult our president,” one of the men allegedly told her. She says the men beat her, threatened to rape her and drove towards Entebbe. She feared they were taking her somewhere she might be tortured. According to Opoloje, a phone call prompted the men to turn back towards Kampala Central Police Station. Her account of the alleged abduction and mistreatment could not be independently verified. Asked whether she would cease speaking out, Opoloje said, “Me? Never. In fact, when I get out, if I do, I will start from where I stopped. I cannot keep quiet seeing what is going on in the country.” Opoloje says she feared being taken to a basement where, she believes, people are tortured and raped. “Being in here in prison is better than being in the basement that they were taking me to,” she says. Since Al Jazeera’s interview with her, Opoloje was granted bail on October 14, with court permission required before travelling internationally. She also alleges that men have threatened her mother, telling her they knew where she lived. Opoloje says her detention has affected her family, including her three-year-old daughter. “I don’t think my mother or my three-year-old daughter should pay the price for my actions,” she says. A father searches for his missing son For Emmanuel Baliza, 59, the uncertainty is different: he says he does not know where his 17-year-old son, William, is being held. Emmanuel says armed men took William from their home after the teenager expressed an intention to protest against police brutality and Uganda’s education system. According to Emmanuel, a stranger first lured him away using a pretext involving land. He says about six men wearing military uniforms and face coverings were waiting in a Toyota HiAce van and searched his phone. “I told them, that’s my son, 17-year-old William Baliza,” Emmanuel says. He alleges that the men took William, claiming they were arresting him for planning to protest after the elections. They reportedly told Emmanuel they were taking his son to the Special Investigations Unit, which handles serious and high-profile crimes, but did not provide a reference number. Emmanuel says he later heard that William might be held at a military detention facility in Kasenyi near Entebbe. He says officials denied holding his son, leaving the family without confirmation of his whereabouts. According to Emmanuel, his daughter told him William had posted a message on TikTok reading: “Uganda is bleeding.” Reporting on the powerful, facing the consequences Journalist and human rights activist Andrew Tabandama Natumanya says his reporting on a security operation involving properties linked to former Parliament Speaker Anita Among brought scrutiny from security personnel. In May, officers searched properties linked to Among amid investigations into allegations including corruption and money laundering. Media reports said luxury vehicles, including a 2025 Rolls-Royce Cullinan, were seized. Andrew says he posted real-time updates about the operation on X, formerly Twitter. He believes the attention his reporting attracted stemmed partly from questions about how he obtained information from within security agencies. “Their main discomfort was, ‘How is he getting this information? How is he aware of what is happening at the Criminal Investigations Department? Who is giving me these updates?’” he says. Andrew alleges that on June 17, 2026, a stranger lured him to a washing bay, where armed personnel forced him into a van. He says he was taken away, assaulted and humiliated. According to Andrew, officers placed his head beneath one officer’s feet before stripping him naked and photographing him.

events.title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?
events.summary: Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise UK interest rates for the first time in more than three years at their next meeting. Most analysts believe the Bank rate will go up from 3.75% to 4%, following holds at the previous six meetings. Before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, rates had been expected to fall this year, but the economic fallout from the conflict has pushed up inflation across the globe. Interest rates affect mortgage, credit card and savings rates for millions of people. What are interest rates and why do they change? An interest rate tells you how much it costs to borrow money, or the reward for saving it. The Bank of England's base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings. The Bank moves its base rate up and down in order to keep UK inflation — the rate at which prices are increasing — at or near 2%. When inflation is above that target, the Bank typically puts rates up. The idea is to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises. What is happening to UK interest rates and inflation? The Bank of England's base rate rose to 5.25% in August 2023. It remained at that level until August 2024, when the Bank started cutting. Five cuts brought rates down to 4%, before the Bank held rates at its meetings in September and November 2025. It then cut in December 2025 before holding rates steady in January, March, April, June, July and September 2026. Meanwhile, the main UK inflation measure, CPI, has fallen significantly since the October 2022 high of 11.1%, which was caused by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. However, the rate has been heading back up and is expected to go higher. It was 3.5% in the year to September 2026 , up from 3.1% the previous month and well above the central bank's 2% target. The Office for National Statistics (ONS), which tracks UK inflation, blamed the acceleration on sharp rises in petrol and diesel prices. The US-Israel war with Iran has put up energy and fuel costs around the world, which has increased the pace of price rises more generally. What is happening to UK prices? Published 21 October What is expected to happen to UK interest rates? At the start of the year, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates twice in 2026, with the first drop predicted to come in March or April. However, the increase in fuel prices and inflation after the outbreak of the conflict has upended all of this. Oil prices initially rose sharply as a result of disruption to supplies in the region, but dropped back when various ceasefires were agreed. Oil prices rose again when the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July. UK household energy bills rose after the increases in the price cap in July and October, while global oil prices have risen again recently. Given the uncertainty, many analysts think UK interest rates will rise at the November meeting and again early next year. What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Published 28 September Why are UK fuel prices rising again? Published 2 October How do interest rate changes affect mortgages, loans and savings rates? Just under a third of households have a mortgage, according to the government's English Housing Survey , external . About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate. Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost would go up by about £31 a month if the Bank raises the base rate by 0.25 percentage points, but it depends on the size of people's loans. An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) would wait to see if their lender chose to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise. But the vast majority of mortgage customers - some 87% - have fixed-rate deals. While their monthly payments aren't immediately affected by a rate change, their future deals are. Most lenders have already priced in a rise in the Bank rate in November, so this is already reflected in any rates being offered. As of 4 November, the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate was at 5.96%, while the average five-year rate stood at 5.99%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts. The average two-year tracker rate was 4.67%. About 800,000 fixed-rate mortgages with an interest rate of 3% or below are expected to expire every year, on average, until the end of 2027. Borrowing costs for customers coming off those deals are likely to rise sharply. You can see how your mortgage may be affected by future interest rate changes by using our calculator: How much could my mortgage payments change?

events.title: Euro zone inflation hits 4% for first time in three years as interest rate hike looms
events.summary: Euro zone inflation rose to 4% in October, its highest level in three years, according to a flash estimate. Energy inflation accelerated to 20.8%, adding to price pressure across the currency bloc. The reading keeps attention on whether the European Central Bank will raise rates again at its final meeting of the year. Inflation in the euro area jumped to a three-year high of 4% in October, a flash estimate showed on Wednesday. The reading is in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and was up from 3.8% in September . Officials said the increase was largely due to surging energy costs, with energy inflation rising to 20.8% from 18.9% in September. Europe, a net energy importer, is vulnerable to external energy shocks and has seen prices rise steadily since the start of the Iran war. October marked the first time inflation in the euro zone has hit or exceeded the 4% threshold since Sept. 2023's reading of 4.3%. Inflation also varied across the 21 euro zone economies, with Lithuania recording the hottest inflation rate of 6.1% while Malta's was the lowest at 2.3%. All euro zone countries saw inflation hold above the European Central Bank's 2% target. The euro was up 0.6% against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday morning, although the greenback fell against a basket of major currencies as counting continued in the U.S. midterm elections, while the yield on the 10-year German bund — broadly seen as a benchmark for euro zone bonds — was marginally higher. Policymakers said underlying inflation and wages were broadly stable, despite inflation sitting at a three-year high. Rate hike looms — but French turmoil could complicate policy The European Central Bank kept its key interest rate at 2.5% last month, following a hike of 25 basis points in September. Shortly before Wednesday's inflation print, markets were pricing in a 71.8% chance of a hike at the ECB's final meeting of the year in December. Following the data release, markets were pricing in more than a 72% chance of rates rising. Robert Mertens, global capital markets senior analyst at Validus Risk Management, cautioned that "ongoing turmoil in the French bond market is placing constraints on ECB policy" and the bank's capacity to get inflation under control. "Should we see an easing in French political unrest, the ECB could potentially pursue a more aggressive hiking path," he said. "If the ECB can deploy more aggressive tightening relative to the Federal Reserve, we would see increased Euro support and upside versus the Dollar."
