events.title: 'Thick, orange water' safe to drink, woman told
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts TasWater's aging pipes in question as 'thick, orange' water seen in Hobart homes Sandy Bay resident Emma Thornley says she was initially told by TasWater that the water was safe to drink. ( Supplied: Emma Thornley ) Residents in the Hobart suburb of Sandy Bay say thick, orange water spurted from their taps on Tuesday after a water main burst. One resident says TasWater told her the "thick and viscous" liquid was fine to drink. TasWater says it is investing in infrastructure upgrades. When Hobart resident Emma Thornley put a load of whites in her washing machine on Tuesday morning, she was not expecting it to come out covered in dark-orange stains. "I ran to my kitchen tap, and [the water] was very dark browny-orange," she said. Ms Thornley let the water run for a while, which cleared it, but a few hours later she filled up the kettle straight under the tap. "I didn't watch the water going into it, which in hindsight was a bit silly, and then realised that the water in my cup of tea was really gritty and had a really foul taste," she said. It persisted on and off throughout the day. An sms sent by TasWater advising residents of Sandy Bay and South Hobart of the possibility of discoloured water being discharged from taps. ( Supplied: Emma Thornley ) The culprit was a 60-year-old burst water main on Regent Street, Sandy Bay, near Ms Thornley's house. Water issues are not uncommon in her Hobart suburb. "I think I've had about eight text messages [from utility TasWater] to alert me that the water quality would be affected or it might be cloudy or discoloured while they were doing work, but we usually get those texts in advance or ASAP when there's an issue," she said. Ms Thornley tried to report Tuesday's issue over the phone but was told the water was fine to drink. She took a bottle of the orange liquid to show the TasWater crew on her street, who advised her not to drink it. A Sandy Bay resident captured some of the murky water in a jar. ( Supplied: Emma Thornley ) "I don't want to drink it and I'm pretty sure they wouldn't either." ASIC fines Mona owner David Walsh's company for late financial report Topic: Business, Economics and Finance NSW man in court over alleged ice seizure at Tasmanian beach car park Lobster fishers rail against salmon industry's antibiotic plans Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Glen Christensen also had issues with his water on Tuesday, despite living about 2 kilometres from the emergency works. He said he was trying to run a bath for his two-year-old granddaughter, but the water that came out was dirty with sediment. "The first time I called [TasWater], I was told to run the tap closest to the meter, which is my outdoor tap," Mr Christensen said. The Sandy Bay resident took to social media about the TasWater response to her concerns. ( Supplied: Emma Thornley ) He followed the advice, but it did not help. "We ended up resorting to a shower, at least that way she wouldn't be sitting in it, and whilst the shower was running there was a significant drop in water pressure, after that the water came clear," he said. Another resident commenting on social media also reported bath water running "brownish" in the evening. TasWater said its crews responded to the burst water main at about 9.45am and had restored supply to the majority of affected properties by 11.30am, with all properties restored by 5.30pm. Australia's national drinking water guidelines state that water should be aesthetically pleasing and pleasant to drink. "Many customers equate aesthetics with the safety of drinking water, so every effort should be made to meet the aesthetic guideline values," it states. TasWater's head of communications and engagement, Liz Hafner, said it was not uncommon for sediment to settle in pipes after an outage, and that crews routinely flush pipes once water has been restored to clear it. Water pipe leaked for nine months next to Barbara's home It took nine months to identify a damaged pipe belonging to state water utility TasWater as the cause of a leak damaging Barbara Turner's Launceston home. Two years later, she can't get rid of the mould. "Our initial advice provided to the customer was that the water was safe to drink [which] reflected the information available at the time," she said. "Once we became aware from the customer of the level of discolouration, we updated our advice and carried out further flushing." Some affected customers received text messages from TasWater, and the utility said it provided live updates on its website throughout the service interruption.

events.title: Liverpool owner FSG holds talks over buying majority stake in Cadillac F1 team
events.summary: Cadillac are jointly owned by Mark Walter Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group , has held talks about buying a majority stake in the Cadillac Formula One team for more than £2bn as Mark Walter continues to sell off his sporting assets amid allegations of insurance fraud. Cadillac entered F1 this year as a joint venture between General Motors and Walter’s TWG Global, which sold its controlling interest in the NBA’s Los Angeles Lakers and a 13% stake in Chelsea this summer, and is also looking to sell Los Angeles Sparks, the WNBA team. Walter is under investigation by the US Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission over alleged fraud involving the management of funds at his insurance companies Delaware Life, Clear Spring, and EquiTrust. TWG has said “there has been no fraud”. How do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts? In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications. If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version. If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'. The 66-year-old Walter is also the controlling owner of Major League Baseball’s Los Angeles Dodgers and insists they will not be sold. TWG has denied that a sale of Cadillac is imminent, but the Guardian has learned it has had talks with a number of interested parties including FSG, whose sporting investments also include majority stakes in the Boston Red Sox and the NHL team Pittsburgh Penguins. A source with knowledge of FSG’s plans disclosed that it is looking at other sporting investments after selling 38% of Liverpool this summer to a consortium that includes the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin, whose group has also secured the option to complete a full takeover at Anfield before August 2027. A move by FSG to buy into Cadillac could have implications for its position at Liverpool , which is valued at £5.5bn after this summer’s partial sale, presenting it with the opportunity to make a huge profit after it paid £300m for the entire club in 2010. FSG has a history of investing in motor sport through its 50% stake in the Nascar team RFK Racing, with the source adding that it has been attracted to F1 by the sport’s remarkable growth over the last decade, particularly in the US. F1’s annual revenue has more than doubled to $4bn (£3bn) since it was bought by Liberty Media in 2017, and the value of its TV rights continues to increase. The size of TWG’s and General Motors’ respective stakes has never been made public. Cadillac are bottom of the constructors’ championship in their debut season and have yet to win a point. FSG declined to comment on its investment plans.

The stand-off deepens a year-long dispute between Wingtech and Dutch authorities, as the company faces an impending delisting deadline at home, while Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten prepares for an official visit to Beijing in the spring. In a statement on Tuesday, Wingtech said the court-appointed administrators overseeing Nexperia had submitted a proposal based on a “two circles” structure.

events.title: How Texas went Democratic
events.summary: Texas woke up red on Tuesday and went to bed blue. Why it matters: Just months ago, Democratic campaigns in the MAGA heartland appeared quixotic — obligatory more than realistic. Now those Democratic candidates have swept to power, led by two state representatives from liberal Austin — James Talarico , soon to be seated in the U.S. Senate, and Gina Hinojosa , who will take her place in the new year in the governor's mansion. Zoom in: The Democratic victories were comprehensive. State Rep. Vikki Goodwin (D-Austin) unseated three-term Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, per the Associated Press. Democrat Nathan Johnson, a state senator from Dallas, defeated Republican Mayes Middleton, state senator from Galveston, in the race for attorney general. What they're saying: "We shocked the world tonight. With a Texas chip on our shoulder, we showed the world that anything is possible tonight," Hinojosa said. "We just took back Texas," Talarico told his supporters. What happened: An unpopular president and high gas and grocery prices deep-sixed red-state GOP candidates across the country. But the Texas GOP was further hampered by an unpopular U.S. Senate candidate (even members of his own party impeached him) — Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. And Greg Abbott, who had served as governor since 2015, was unwilling to debate his gubernatorial opponent. Meanwhile, the Democrats were disciplined, with Talarico and Hinojosa staying on message about affordability even as their Republican opponents tried to make the race about social issues. Amid a crush of cameras and security personnel, Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico toast at an Austin Whataburger after their victories Tuesday night. Photo: Brandon Bell/Getty Images Follow the money: Republicans went down despite a rescue mission from Elon Musk, who gave north of $150 million in support of Paxton's campaign in a single quarter this year — and gave at least $5.5 million to Abbott's campaign this cycle. The big picture: The Democratic wins have huge implications for the 2028 presidential race. Democrats have proven, after years of flailing, that they could win statewide in Texas, potentially putting the Lone Star State and its 40 electoral votes in play. Political pundits will be wondering: Was this a one-off wave amid a terrible midterm climate for Texas Republicans — or a sign of foundational change? The bottom line: Fireworks were shooting off in Austin Tuesday night, and state agencies so long occupied by the GOP will now be run by Democrats, opening the way for wide policy changes in long-conservative Texas.

events.title: Crypto dips on Democrat midterm wins, Binance hacks dent optimism
events.summary: Sentiment has also been hurt by the US$6 billion hack of the Binance platform last week, the largest heist in history. Crypto prices fell after Democrats won both US midterm chambers, raising fears of slower deregulation and weaker support for industry-friendly laws. Bitcoin briefly hit a six-week low, while the wider market lost about US$300 billion in October and bitcoin is down around 41% from its October 2025 peak. A US$6 billion Binance hack and heavy customer withdrawals hurt trust, as experts warned of security risks and pressure on future crypto legislation. LONDON/HONG KONG – Cryptocurrencies briefly dipped on Nov 4 as Democrats won majorities in both the Senate and House in the US midterm elections, a potential blow to an industry that has pushed for faster deregulation for digital assets. The sector has spent more than US$300 million (S$383 million) backing crypto-friendly Democrats and Republicans in roughly equal measure during the current and previous election cycles, hoping to pass legislation US crypto companies say will put them on a solid legal footing and allow them to thrive. Bitcoin briefly touched a six-week low before recovering to trade roughly flat by 07.15 GMT (3.15pm Singapore time) at US$78,070. Ether traded at US$2,292, up just 1%. Bitcoin has fallen by around 41% since hitting record highs above US$122,000 in October 2025, bringing the value of the broader crypto market to around US$2.61 billion, according to CoinMarketCap. The market has lost some US$300 billion in value in October alone, as deepening concern about future returns from AI and the strain of rising borrowing costs pushed investors into less risky assets such as government bonds and safe-haven currencies. Sentiment has also been hurt by the US$6 billion hack of the Binance platform last week , the largest heist in history. On Nov 3 , Binance customers had withdrawn a net US$4.72 billion from the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened following the hack at the weekend. “The market may be re-evaluating the risk-reward profile of crypto assets. On one hand, the string of security incidents is forcing investors to re-examine the industry’s security infrastructure and custody risks,” Tim Sun, Senior Researcher at HashKey, said. “On the other hand, potential shifts in the US political landscape could stall the progress of structural crypto legislation and institutional framework development. All of these factors leave the crypto market facing strong headwinds,” he said. Trump, who vowed to make the United States the “crypto capital of the world” during his 2024 presidential campaign, has made his own forays into digital assets, with the launch of his “Trump” meme coin, plus his family’s World Liberty Financial crypto platform, among other ventures. The sector has seen sweeping reforms in the almost two years since Trump returned to office, including lighter enforcement, the creation of a strategic bitcoin reserve. Washington has also allowed for easier access to banking and exchange-traded products and passed a federal stablecoin law that could help these assets move into the mainstream payments and money transfer systems. events.title: US midterms: What investors can expect after Democrats shatter Republican strongholds
events.summary: The US Democratic Party picked up 53 Senate seats and 222 seats in the House of Representatives as at 3pm on Nov 4, Singapore time. Democrats won both houses of Congress, a major rebuke to President Donald Trump. They took 53 Senate seats and 222 House seats. Markets expect more policy gridlock, less chance of big tax or spending changes, and possible tariff fights. US futures fell, while Asian shares recovered after the result. Investors will watch Treasury yields, the Fed, the US dollar, oil and gold. DBS said Singapore Reits, developers and aviation stocks may gain from the Democratic win. SINGAPORE – The US Democratic Party took control of both houses of Congress in a dramatic win in the US midterm elections. Seen as a rebuke of President Donald Trump’s policies, a sea of blue has picked up 54 Senate seats and 220 seats in the House of Representatives as at 9pm on Nov 4, Singapore time. Voters sent a strong message about their unhappiness with the state of the US economy, the Iran war and inflation to kick Republicans out of even traditional “red” strongholds. The elections, held on Nov 3 , determine control of all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and about a third of the Senate, midway through Trump’s four-year presidential term. Its implications will be felt far beyond the US’ borders as it raises the prospect of opposing forces between the White House and Congress. What does this mean for global markets? Equities: The Democratic sweep could make it harder for Trump to push through major legislative changes, potentially limiting further fiscal stimulus. Analysts at BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, said Trump would likely face significant legislative resistance and policy gridlock, although he could continue pursuing policies through executive orders. BMI also warned that a sharp slowdown in data centre construction and artificial intelligence investment could lead to a greater-than-expected decline in overall investment, weighing on the US economy. US equity futures fell as Democrats gained ground, with S&P 500 equity futures down about 1% at the time of BMI’s commentary. Technology stocks also faced pressure amid concerns over AI valuations and the prospect of tighter regulatory scrutiny. Congressional aides said that while a rollback of tariffs is expected, Trump will remain undeterred in his zeal for more tariff actions. In Asia, stocks started on Nov 4 down but retraced decisively after news of the Democrats’ win. Singapore’s Straits Times Index lost 76 points in the morning, but was down just 0.66 point at 5,268.63 at the close. Interest rates and bonds: The election outcome could influence US Treasury yields through expectations for fiscal spending, government borrowing and inflation. Greater constraints on government spending could ease concerns over additional borrowing, although political disputes over fiscal policy may also create uncertainty. BMI flagged the US debt ceiling negotiations in 2027 as a major risk, warning that talks could become contentious at a time when Treasury yields are already elevated and fiscal risks are mounting. DBS Group Research strategist Philip Wee noted on Nov 2 that the midterms, falling oil prices and the US employment report on Nov 6 could prompt investors to reassess the Federal Reserve’s tightening outlook. The market-implied probability of a December rate hike had fallen to 73.5% from a peak of 90.8% on Oct 19, he said. Currencies: The US dollar weakened as investors assessed the implications for fiscal spending and monetary policy. Wee noted that the week’s developments could extend the dollar index’s retracement from its mid-October peak. For Singapore investors holding US dollar-denominated assets, movements in the greenback against the Singapore dollar could affect investment returns when converted into local currency. C ommodities: Oil and gold prices are also worth watching, particularly against the backdrop of the Middle East conflict. Gold fell 0.5% to US$3,925.25 an ounce in New York trading on Nov 3 , as investors weighed the prospects of a diplomatic resolution to the conflict. The precious metal had already slumped nearly 7% in October, falling below US$4,000 an ounce. Lower oil prices have eased inflation concerns, although rising bond yields have weighed on gold, which does not pay interest. The midterm results could increase policy uncertainty, although this may not necessarily translate into higher gold prices. What does this mean for Singapore stocks? DBS Group Research believes that November presents an opportunity for investors to buy on market weakness, with Singapore real estate investment trusts (REITS), property developers and aviation-related companies among the potential beneficiaries of a Democratic win.

events.title: Democrats’ big night has the internet joking that DEI is back
events.summary: With a blue tsunami, some are joking that DEI is back. TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images Midterm election results show a huge Democratic surge across the country. Delighted X posters are now semi-jokingly declaring that DEI is so back. A leftward political shift could reignite DEI focus in companies, reversing previous trends. If election night results are any barometer, it might be time for everyone to get more woke. The country saw a blue tsunami Tuesday night, with traditional Republican strongholds chipped away at — or even flipped — by Democrats. Jon Ossoff won reelection in Georgia handily; South Carolina's Senate seat flipped to blue; and Democrat James Talarico is Texas' next senator. The Associated Press called the race, saying the House and the Senate had flipped to Democratic control. The internet has come to its own (somewhat joking) conclusion: DEI is so back. Delighted X users spent the evening joking that pronouns will return to email signatures, whether workers like it or not. "YOU HAVE TWELVE HOURS TO PLACE THE PRONOUNS BACK IN YOUR EMAIL OR YOU WILL BE REPORTED," one X post read . Another joked that should Democrats win 53 or more Senate seats, pronouns would have to return to email signatures. New York City Council member Chi Ossé wrote "PRONOUNS BACK IN BIOS NOW" in response to favorable projections for Texas Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico before his win was called. And yet another X post declared that there would be a new gender with every seat Democrats won. Of course, these are flippant meme fodder, but they get at a potential vibe shift. In the wake of President Donald Trump's 2024 victory, both the federal government and, in turn, companies across the economy cracked down on DEI initiatives. Some firms did indeed tell workers to remove their pronouns from their email signatures; others publicly pulled back on DEI initiatives and goals, leaving some workers feeling disheartened and others affirmed. Overall, it was a rapid about-face from 2020-era rhetoric and initiatives that centered on racial equity and inclusion, and a pivot that many companies embraced in an effort to not attract the ire of Trump and the federal government. Now, though, the political landscape has been thrown into another seismic shift with the leftward turn in the midterms. For the firms that have stuck with their DEI initiatives , that might be welcome news, as voters embrace a new group of leaders. And, of course, DEI never fully went away: Many companies still quietly embraced diverse hiring practices, but shirked away from the term. There's also always the possibility that the likely Democratic gains lead to new innovation; as one X poster wrote , "We're doing double pronouns now!" Read the original article on Business Insider

Sovereign AI raises the stakes on every infrastructure decision. When data residency, operational control, and compliance requirements limit where workloads can run, there’s far less room for error. A site that looks viable on paper can become a costly problem if cooling, airflow, or resiliency assumptions don’t hold up under real operating conditions. That’s why early validation matters. The Cadence Reality Digital Twin Platform helps teams create high-fidelity digital representations of AI infrastructure to evaluate power, cooling, thermal performance, site conditions, and operating scenarios before deployment. In one case, a data hall appeared sound in review, but once leakage and a cooling failure were modeled, more than half the cabinets ran too hot. The design itself hadn’t changed, only the assumptions behind it. Inside, you’ll see how teams can uncover issues like these early, before they turn into expensive constraints. This eBook shows how physics-based validation helps teams make better siting decisions, avoid preventable retrofits, and sustain performance over time. events.title: Beyond The Chip: How AI Is Reshaping Semiconductor Design And Manufacturing
events.summary: While AI is transforming nearly every industry, one of its most significant impacts is happening behind the scenes, inside the semiconductor factories responsible for building the chips that power today’s AI revolution. During a recent presentation at the Global Semiconductor Alliance (GSA) European Executive Forum, I discussed how the conversation around AI scale is evolving. For years, the semiconductor industry focused primarily on transistor scaling. Today, however, the biggest challenges facing AI designers extend far beyond the transistor. Power delivery, connectivity, advanced packaging, and supply chain resilience are emerging as the primary constraints on AI scaling. At Intel Foundry, we’re addressing these challenges on two fronts. First, we’re developing advanced process and packaging technologies that help customers build increasingly capable AI systems. Second, we’re using AI and machine learning (ML) throughout our technology development and manufacturing operations to improve quality, accelerate yield learning, and help customers bring products to market faster. Three forces shaping the future of semiconductor design Three major AI trends are shaping what modern silicon must deliver: Agentic AI introduces multistep reasoning workloads that are far less predictable than traditional computing. Autonomous agents place new demands on power delivery and high-performance connectivity, making efficient scaling increasingly important. Physical AI brings intelligence to edge devices and real-world systems. Scalable AI-enabled automation and modeling are essential for cost-effective, high-yield manufacturing. The foundry industry increasingly views both agentic AI and physical AI as significant long-term growth drivers. Sovereign AI initiatives are increasing demand for secure, resilient, and geographically diverse manufacturing and supply chains to support both business continuity and national security needs. By maintaining Intel Foundry’s production capabilities across North America, Europe, and Asia, customers gain flexibility in determining where their products are manufactured while improving supply chain resilience and security. Multi-dimensional scaling: The new path forward A decade ago, the semiconductor industry largely focused on the system-on-chip (SoC) model, where a single chip integrated as much functionality as possible. Today, innovation has shifted toward a system of chips, using chiplet architectures that combine multiple specialized dies, memory stacks, and accelerators into a single solution. This approach provides greater modularity, scalability, and faster innovation cycles while enabling the performance required for advanced AI workloads. At the same time, scaling is no longer simply a matter of shrinking transistors. The industry is increasingly focused on optimizing performance across the entire system, from compute and memory to packaging and interconnects. Advanced process technologies such as gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, including Intel 18A with RibbonFET GAA technology, provide improved electrostatic control and support scaling beyond traditional FinFET architectures. Power delivery also has been reimagined. Intel 18A uses PowerVia, our backside power delivery technology that routes power through the back of the wafer rather than sharing frontside interconnect layers with signal routing. By separating power and signal paths, PowerVia reduces resistance, voltage drop, and power delivery noise. Combined with high-density metal-insulator-metal (MIM) capacitors, the architecture improves power integrity. PowerVia delivers up to a 10% increase in cell utilization¹ and a 4% improvement in ISO-power performance.² Connection to the transistor layer is enabled through innovative nano through-silicon vias (TSVs) that are approximately 500 times smaller than conventional TSVs. While backside power adds manufacturing complexity, Intel Foundry optimized the overall cost structure by maintaining 32 nm lower-metal pitches on the frontside, enabling direct-print patterning rather than more expensive multi-patterning approaches. This balanced architecture allows Intel 18A and Intel 18A-P to deliver improved performance-per-watt and more efficient power delivery for AI-era workloads while remaining cost competitive. Intel 18A with PowerVia can provide approximately 18% performance-per-watt improvement versus Intel 3.³ Now in risk production, Intel 18A-P is expected to deliver an additional 9% performance-per-watt improvement over Intel 18A⁴ (see the Intel 18A family technical brief for details). As systems become increasingly modular, chips must communicate efficiently with one another. This is where Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) plays a critical role. UCIe provides a standardized interconnect for high-bandwidth, low-latency communication between chiplets, simplifying integration and enabling more scalable heterogeneous systems. Advanced packaging serves as the glue that connects all these technologies together. A complete AI package may combine I/O dies, advanced logic silicon, HBM, 2.5D integration, and 3D integration. Intel Foundry supports these designs through technologies including Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge-T (EMIB-T), Foveros, and Foveros Direct. EMIB-T incorporates power-transfer capabilities directly into the bridge structure, helping improve power delivery efficiency and reduce inductive power droop in multi-die AI systems. It can also reduce package material requirements by eliminating the need for a full silicon interposer in many applications. Foveros Direct uses hybrid bonding to enable 3D integration, allowing designers to stack leading-edge compute dies on optimized base dies. This approach helps customers balance performance, power efficiency, and total cost of ownership (TCO) by placing each function on the process technology best suited to its requirements. Using AI across the semiconductor manufacturing lifecycle While AI is creating new challenges for chip designers, it is also helping solve many of the challenges associated with manufacturing advanced semiconductors. At Intel Foundry, AI and ML are already deeply integrated into our manufacturing workflows, actively supporting how we develop and manufacture leading-edge process technologies (see Figure 1). One area where AI is delivering value is design technology co-optimization (DTCO). Advanced process nodes involve enormous design spaces with countless tradeoffs between power, performance, and area (PPA). AI helps engineers explore these possibilities more efficiently and identify optimal solutions. Fig. 1: Intel Foundry’s deployment of AI and ML efforts across the manufacturing flow. AI’s role extends beyond product design and into every stage of the manufacturing lifecycle, transforming how we identify and correct manufacturing issues. events.title: Choosing The Right Power Transistor: Why Application Fit Matters More Than Technology
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Silicon MOSFETs, IGBTs, SiC MOSFETs, and GaN HEMTs each offer meaningful advantages, but those advantages do not carry the same value across every converter, motor drive, or power stage. Selecting a power transistor has become less about identifying a universally superior technology and more about matching device behavior to the demands of the application. Silicon MOSFETs, IGBTs, SiC MOSFETs, and GaN HEMTs each offer meaningful advantages, but those advantages do not carry the same value across every converter, motor drive, or power stage. The decisive factors are the electrical and thermal realities of the design: bus voltage, current profile, switching frequency, allowable temperature rise, control strategy, commutation behavior, PCB parasitics, and system cost targets. The discussion begins with the switching and conduction mechanisms that shape the behavior of every power transistor, including crossover loss, inductive switching, parasitic capacitance, reverse conduction and charge-recovery behavior, and the practical distinction between hard-switched and soft-switched operation. These operating modes create different selection priorities: hard-switched stages are often strongly influenced by turn-on loss and commutation behavior, while soft-switched stages depend on the charge to be commutated, the available current, and the ability to maintain soft switching across the operating range. On that basis, it compares silicon MOSFETs, IGBTs, SiC MOSFETs, and GaN HEMTs in terms that matter to designers working on real hardware: voltage range, current capability, switching performance, gate-drive implications, thermal behavior, and implementation sensitivity. The discussion then moves into application context, including PFC, resonant conversion, synchronous rectification, and motor-drive design decisions, where lower device loss alone does not guarantee the best overall result. Thermal margins, board design, control choices, and total system cost all influence whether a given device technology improves the converter in a meaningful way. The application examples also show when direct transistor substitution can address the dominant limitation and when a topology change or hybrid implementation offers a more effective path. The role of simulation is also considered, showing where modeling is useful for relative comparison and where hardware validation remains essential before a design decision is finalized. The result is a practical framework for choosing among silicon, IGBT, SiC, and GaN technologies based on application fit rather than technology fashion, enabling power-electronics designers to select the device, and where appropriate the topology, that best aligns with the converter’s actual operating conditions and design priorities. events.title: Blog Review: Nov. 4
events.summary: Cadence’s Mick Posner introduces a physical AI sub-project workstream to extend the OCP’s Foundation Chiplet System Architecture’s data center, cloud, and server-centric baseline with the specification requirements to satisfy real-time, safety-critical physical systems, while retaining everything FCSA already defines. Synopsys’ Charlie Matar considers how design focus is shifting from the server to the rack , with silicon behavior shaping rack-level power and cooling requirements, while rack constraints influence decisions inside chips and packages. Siemens’ Harry Foster warns that while verification complexity has been managed by dividing large problems into smaller pieces, new challenges are emerging as the number and diversity of interactions influencing correct SoC behavior grows. Arm’s Zenon (Zhilong) Xiu examines how quarter-tile and structured sparsity outer product instructions make the SME2 programming model better suited to small, dense, quantized, and sparse matrix workloads in modern AI software. Keysight’s Linas Dauksa digs into AI data center infrastructure, including key components, energy demands and power density challenges, the array of liquid cooling technologies available, and what differentiates hyperscale facilities. SEMI’s Sungho Yoon considers factors related to a forecasted increase in wafer shipments , including rising process material sales and a high number of new and upcoming production lines. Plus, check out the blogs featured in the latest Systems & Design newsletter : Technology editor Brian Bailey poses the age-old question for anyone involved in the verification of semiconductor systems: in the age of AI, who verifies the verifier ? Axiomise’s Vidya Chandran Darbari and Ashish Darbari dig into what biological reasoning can teach us about verifying silicon systems. Keysight’s Chris Mueth explains why applying the appropriate level of simulation and abstraction at each stage of the design process is needed for effective thermal analysis. Siemens EDA’s Emma-Jane Crozier explores how self-verifying agents validate their decisions and why physics-based engines are the authority on correctness. Arteris’ Leon Brown looks at which products may fall within the EU Cyber Resilience Act’s scope and what information may need to be provided to customers. Movellus’ Aakash Jani and Siemens’ Henrique Mendes and Robert Wilcox separate false failures caused by voltage droop from real structural defects. ChipAgents’ Zackary Glazewski demonstrates how to deal with difficult bugs while intelligently deciding what to investigate, what to rerun, and where to spend compute. Vinci’s Hardik Kabaria examines why physics-based analysis becomes more consequential as chips, packages, boards, and systems are designed together. Cadence’s Reela Samuel breaks down how to orchestrate multi-step engineering workflows to reduce repetitive effort and explore more design options. Synopsys’ Anand Thiruvengadam outlines how autonomous engineering agents pursue an objective requiring hundreds or thousands of reasoning steps while maintaining context, evaluating results, and adapting along the way. The post Blog Review: Nov. 4 appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.title: Neural Super Resolution
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Insight into how neural graphics can improve image quality and performance while simplifying deployment on power- and bandwidth-constrained devices. As AI becomes an increasingly important part of the graphics pipeline, Neural Super Resolution (NSR) offers a new approach to generating higher-quality images without the cost of rendering every pixel natively. This white paper explores how Imagination’s NSR technology uses neural reconstruction to upscale lower-resolution frames into higher-resolution outputs, combining current-frame data, temporal history and learned inference to deliver high visual quality with reduced bandwidth, power and memory demands. Unlike approaches that rely on separate AI accelerators, NSR runs directly within the GPU, enabling graphics, compute and AI workloads to work together in a unified execution environment. Readers will learn the principles behind neural super resolution, the role of Converged Acceleration in modern GPU design, and how Imagination’s E-Series architecture integrates matrix acceleration and neural processing into the graphics pipeline. The paper also explains the importance of data locality, microtiling and Self-Compression in achieving efficient neural rendering, while examining the performance, bandwidth and energy benefits of GPU-native super resolution. For graphics architects, developers and SoC designers, it provides insight into how neural graphics can improve image quality and performance while simplifying deployment on power- and bandwidth-constrained devices. events.title: Democrats ride inflation wave back into power in Congress
events.summary: James Carville's mantra rings in my ears every election cycle: "It's the economy , stupid." The famed political strategist coined the phrase in 1992 but it's still relevant now, with the Democrats on track to retake both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, gaining powerful oversight roles over Donald Trump 's presidency. The result will probably have a profound impact on the data centre buildout and other sectors. As results trickled in late into the night in Washington - and during the morning rush hour in Abu Dhabi - it became clear that this week's vote was a referendum on Mr Trump's performance as well as Americans' pocketbooks. Early results from NBC News's exit poll showed nearly half of voters saw the midterms as a rebuke of the US President, with the economy again being a key frustration. Mr Trump made sweeping promises during the 2024 election, when Americans chose to send him back to the Oval Office. Those promises included slashing energy costs, reining in price pressures and a pledge to “make America affordable again”. By most metrics, the economy is on solid footing. US manufacturing activity picked up in October despite uncertainty over policies from the Beltway and rising prices from the Iran war. Layoffs fell to their lowest level in 18 months, while job openings surged. The nation's GDP accelerated at a 3.4 per cent clip in the third quarter. Consumer spending is resilient. The unemployment rate continues to hover around a historically low 4 per cent. However, Mr Trump ran into the same problem that drove Democrats out of power in 2024 : inflation. For Joe Biden, it was a post-Covid inflationary surge exacerbated by a round of stimulus cheques that drove headline inflation to 9.1 per cent in 2022. The portrayal stuck with Kamala Harris, the Democratic party's nominee for president after Mr Biden unexpectedly dropped out of the race. For Mr Trump, it is the war in Iran , and the greatest oil shock in history, that has driven up energy prices amid an AI buildout. Headline inflation rose at a 3.7 per cent annual pace in September, compared to the 3 per cent rate in January 2025. The Federal Reserve has reversed its rate-cutting cycle and raised interest rates by a quarter point in August. It could do so again in December. Yields on the 10 and 30-year Treasuries recently climbed to their highest levels since before the 2008 global financial crisis. And while the share of voters who said inflation had weighed on them is similar to 2024 levels, roughly two-thirds of voters said the President had made the economy worse. Separate exit polls from NBC said 44 per cent of voters said their financial situation was worse than two years ago, compared to 18 per cent who said it was better. About 38 per cent said it is “about the same”. Seventy-five per cent of voters said they were either “dissatisfied” or “angry” about the country today, compared to 18 per cent who said they were “satisfied” and 7 per cent who said they were “enthusiastic”. Recent moves by the President suggest he understands he needed to regain control of prices, chief among them a disputed deal that allows the sale of Russian diesel to US and global markets. Mr Trump made a final appeal to voters on Tuesday, telling Fox and Friends that “inflation was solved”. Despite the millions of dollars spent on campaign finance this season, no messaging was stronger than the sticker shock consumers faced while filling up their cars and grocery carts. Traders on Wall Street took notice, too. Futures on the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite were all in the red, while investors rushed into bonds for safety. The dollar extended its losses. Mr Trump spent his first two years in office touting deregulation, the data centre roll-out and a range of business-friendly policies. Now comes the reckoning.

events.title: GOP's redistricting firewall pummeled by blue wave
events.summary: Republicans tried to save their House majority with a bold wave of mid-cycle redistricting. It failed in spectacular fashion on Tuesday. Why it matters: Republicans not only fell short of winning seats in several districts they redrew to favor their candidates, they put some GOP incumbents in danger of losing by spreading their support thin. Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.), who has mostly won landslide reelections since entering Congress in 2010, trailed his Democratic opponent by 200 votes, according to the Tennessee secretary of state's unofficial final results . Republican state legislators carved up his district in an effort to shore up neighboring Republicans, making his district nearly 20 percentage points less GOP-leaning. State of play: While Republicans succeeded in picking up a Democratic district in Tennessee to make up for that loss, they largely failed to pick up the seats they tried to make reliably Republican in other states. Florida: Republicans are set to go 0-for-4 in redistricted seats, failing to unseat Democratic Reps. Darren Soto, Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz, or capture a new seat that Democrat Pia Dandiya won. Texas: Republicans are set to narrowly win just one of the five districts they redrew heavily in their favor, with Democrats easily hanging onto several Rio Grande Valley and San Antonio-area seats. Ohio: Democratic Reps. Greg Landsman and Marcy Kaptur held on despite Republicans drawing them into more hostile territory. Alabama: Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures is also set for a comfortable win in a district Republicans had planned to fall into their hands. Louisiana: The district of retiring Democrat Rep. Cleo Fields, which Republicans made significantly more GOP-leaning will go to a December runoff between Democrat Patricia Moore and Republican Gabe Firment. One of the most stunning results of the night was Democrats' multiple apparent victories in North Carolina, where House candidates were boosted by Sen-elect Roy Cooper's strong performance at the top of the ballot. Democrats are on track to flip several seats that were rated as likely or even solidly Republican by Cook Political Report, likely unseating Republican Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore. They are also likely to unseat Rep. Richard Hudson, the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee. Virginia Foxx, who chairs the House Rules Committee, is behind by about 100 votes. In all, the state's House delegation could go from a 10-4 Republican majority to a 9-5 Democratic one. Between the lines: The North Carolina result is the product of a brutal 2024 gerrymander in which GOP state legislators diluted most solidly Republican districts to draw out several House Democrats. They redistricted again last year, only to put Democratic Rep. Don Davis in more hostile territory. GOP Rep. Greg Murphy — whose district was packed with more Democratic voters to make Davis' seat redder — barely hung on Tuesday night. Former Democratic Rep. Kathy Manning, who was one of the Democrats drawn out in 2024, told Axios that Tuesday's result was "absolutely" a result of GOP redistricting backfiring. The bottom line: Republicans "tried to break the laws and go against these norms in your massive authoritarian power grab," DNC vice chair Shasti Conrad told Axios. "How did that turn out?"

events.title: WIPEOUT: GOP LOSES HOUSE AND SENATE
events.summary: Republicans lost deep-red Senate seats in South Carolina , Kansas and Texas as well as House seats nationwide, AP projects, giving Democrats control of both chambers of Congress. Why it matters: President Trump made himself the face of the GOP campaign for control. Now his party is losing all over the map, and he's distancing himself from the outcome. Data: AP; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Former President Obama wrote on X: "Tonight, the American people sent a clear message — they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face." Zoom in : Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won election to U.S. Senate from Michigan, AP projects, adding to the Democrats' already rushing blue wave. In Texas, James Talarico secured a history U.S. Senate seat, defeating Trump-backed Republican opponent, Ken Paxton. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott conceded to Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the Texas governor race. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton flipped the country's longest-held Republican Senate seat, ending a 94-year drought. In Maine, Susan Collins conceded to Troy Jackson in the Senate race. In Minnesota , Democrat Peggy Flanagan won election to U.S. Senate, AP projects. In South Carolina, Sen. Darline Graham will lose reelection to Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, AP projects. In Iowa, Democratic nominee Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson to flip the Senate seat vacated by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, AP projects. Data: AP; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Zoom out: Former Gov. Sherrod Brown (D) defeated Sen. Jon Husted (R) in Ohio, AP projects. Earlier in the night, Democrat Roy Cooper defeated Trump's handpicked candidate, Michael Whatley in North Carolina while Democrat Jon Ossoff won reelection to U.S. Senate in Georgia, AP projects. In North Carolina's 11th House district, Jamie Ager flipped the seat for Democrats. The seat is held by retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards , who ended his reelection bid after the House Ethics Committee recommended he be censured. Between the lines: The results tonight were a clear national test of Trump's second presidency , following war abroad, economic anxiety at home and sweeping changes in Washington. "I am absolutely willing to accept those results," Trump said in an interview with The New York Times. "We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out." Yes, but: Trump wrote on Truth Social he plans to criticize the candidates that lost. He also posted an image of a red hat with the word, "VETO." Earlier in the night, Trump raged on social media about the results. He made Fox News the subject of his ire by critiquing Fox's political polling , calling it "a hit job, and every answer is 'BULLSHIT!'" He also texted on-air guests to rage against Jessica Tarlov, a Fox co-host and Democratic strategist he called "DUMB AS A ROCK." This came hours after he criticized multiple Democrat candidates as voters went to the polls. The intrigue: Tuesday night's results created some historic moments beyond control for Washington and Trump's ire. Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate after besting former GOP Sen. John Sununu in the New Hampshire race. There will be three Black women serving in the U.S. Senate for the first time in history after Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton won the Senate race in Illinois. She will join Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Delaware) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland), who became the first two Black women to serve simultaneously in 2025. What we're hearing: Voters identified the cost of living and government corruption concern as the two top issues in this year's election, according to exit polls from AP . Cost of living skyrocketed thanks to the Iran war and the president's tariff policies. Trump himself was deemed corrupt and dangerous in a poll of registered voters prior to the election. The bottom line: Republicans have largely given Trump a free hand in Washington since his return to the White House. Democratic control of even one chamber of Congress will open the door to investigations, subpoenas and even more legislative gridlock.

events.title: El-Sayed becomes first Muslim U.S. senator
events.summary: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's closely watched U.S. Senate race, the Associated Press projected. He will become the nation's first Muslim senator. Why it matters: El-Sayed's win shows how an unapologetically progressive candidate can win in a battleground state President Trump carried just two years ago. The two candidates competed for the seat vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, with Republicans hoping to flip a seat Democrats have held for decades. But the GOP failed in its endeavor — and already lost its Senate majority. The race took a stunning turn in its final days, when Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the August primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers . The move sparked furious backlash from Democrats and prompted several of Stevens' staffers, including her chief of staff, to resign. The big picture: El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director, ran on a progressive platform centered on Medicare for All, taxing billionaires and reducing corporate influence in politics. His victory comes after a contentious Democratic primary and a bitter general election campaign that featured personal attacks over his background, medical credentials and Muslim faith. Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent who narrowly lost a 2024 Senate bid, sought to portray El-Sayed as too extreme for Michigan . El-Sayed cast Rogers as a Washington insider aligned with Trump. Trump himself escalated the attacks in the final stretch of the race, questioning El-Sayed's loyalty to the U.S. and making unsubstantiated allegations of extremist ties. El-Sayed rejected the accusations. Between the lines: El-Sayed's win offers progressives a powerful new argument in the Democratic Party's debate over how to win back voters. Zoom out: Both candidates put affordability at the center of their campaigns but offered sharply different solutions. El-Sayed called for universal health care, tackling medical debt and higher taxes on billionaire wealth. Rogers emphasized tax cuts, expanding domestic manufacturing and more transparent health care prices. He also campaigned on stronger border security and immigration enforcement. What's next: El-Sayed will arrive in Washington with an ambitious progressive agenda — but turning campaign promises into legislation will be a different challenge. His signature Medicare for All proposal faces steep political obstacles, even with Democrats winning control of the Senate. His victory also gives progressives a new national figure as Democrats begin looking toward the 2028 presidential election.

events.title: The 5 biggest shockers of Democrats' stunning night
events.summary: In red states and blue, Republicans suffered losses on a scale even Democrats would never have dared to dream about 24 hours ago. Why it matters: Democrats worried that polls showing a blue wave were overestimating the party's strength. It turned out polls underestimated the size of the Democratic romp — by a lot. The margins Democrats racked up in red states were stunning: Georgia: Sen. Jon Ossoff won reelection by nearly 18 percentage points. North Carolina: Former Gov. Roy Cooper won his Senate race by roughly 19 points. Texas: State Rep. James Talarico cruised to victory by approximately 12 points. These weren't nail-biters in competitive states. They were landslides in states President Trump carried just two years ago. 1. The Texas trifecta Democrats won the Texas House, Senate and governor's mansion, giving the party unified control of state government for the first time since 1995. The sweep came alongside Talarico's double-digit victory in the U.S. Senate race. Texas, long the GOP's biggest electoral stronghold, delivered Democrats victories up and down the ballot. 2. North Carolina was a bloodbath The man in charge of steering House Republicans to victory — Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee — lost his own seat. He'll join the ranks of other defeated party leaders — Speaker Tom Foley in 1994 and Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Sean Patrick Maloney in 2022 — who spent so much time trying to build a majority that they failed to protect themselves. The carnage extended across the state. North Carolina's congressional delegation could shift from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to five Republicans and nine Democrats. 3. The ridiculously cheap wins Democrats are leading in districts that received little or no outside spending from the DCCC or House Majority PAC, the party's main House super PAC, according to AdImpact. In North Carolina's 6th, 9th and 13th districts, Missouri's 2nd and Tennessee's 4th, Democratic candidates are on track to win despite receiving little financial support from national Democratic groups. North Carolina's 6th: Democrat Cyril Jefferson didn't spend a dime on advertising, according to AdImpact. Tennessee's 4th: Democrat Victoria Broderick spent just $90,000 on her entire campaign as of Oct. 14, according to her FEC filing. AdImpact has no record of any paid TV advertising. 4. Hispanic voters swung back in South Texas Democrats are poised to control three congressional seats in the Rio Grande Valley that President Trump carried in 2024 — and the margins weren't even close. Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) was leading Republican Tano Tijerina, 66% to 30%. Democrat Bobby Pulido was leading Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, 62% to 38%. Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) was leading Republican Eric Flores, 56% to 40%. The results were a dramatic reversal in a region where Republicans had made significant gains with Hispanic voters during the Trump era. 5. Democrats won deep in Trump country Democrats didn't just flip swing districts — they broke through in some of the reddest corners of the House map. In Tennessee's 4th Congressional District, which Trump carried by 24 points, Broderick was leading Rep. Scott DesJarlais by roughly 200 votes. Two years ago, Broderick received just 26.8% of the vote to DesJarlais' 70%. The bottom line: The wave didn't discriminate. It washed away good candidates and bad, senators, governors and seasoned Republicans alike.

events.title: Dubai Investments raises $529m from first IPO in UAE this year
events.summary: Dubai Investments has raised Dh1.9 billion ($529 million) from the sale of a 20 per cent stake in its subsidiary DIP Holding, in the UAE’s first initial public offering this year. The company set the final pricing at Dh1.12 per share, settling in the middle of the announced range of Dh1.10 to Dh1.15, DIP Holding said on Wednesday in a statement to the Dubai Financial Market where its shares are traded. Dubai Investments offered 1.74 billion shares in its unit, to investors, which implies a market capitalisation of Dh9.7 billion at listing on the DFM. “The pricing reflects a conscious decision by Dubai Investments to offer new shareholders of DIP Holding an attractive entry point, with a good dividend yield and to support long-term value creation for all shareholders,” the company said in the bourse filing. The Dh1.12 a share price also implies a dividend yield of about 7.5 per cent, based on the expected annualised dividend of Dh725 million for 2027 financial year, the company added. The subscription period for the IPO, which began on October 27, concluded on November 3. The IPO attracted strong demand from local, regional and international investors, “witnessing multiple times coverage across the previously announced price range”, the company said without giving the total size of the order book. The final allocation of shares to individual subscribers, and eligible Dubai Investments employees and shareholders, is expected on November 10. Any refunds are set to commence on the same date, the company said. Shares of DIP Holding are expected to be listed on the DFM on November 11. Breaking the lull The transaction breaks the lull in the UAE IPO market, which had been a hotbed for public floats before disruption caused by the regional conflict, with the DFM and the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange both attracting a steady stream of listings over the past few years. The IPO market in the broader Middle East slowed last year, amid the volatility in oil prices and geopolitical unrest. Companies in the region raised $7.1 billion from 61 listings, down from $13 billion a year earlier. UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows. The Iran war , which has severely disrupted economic momentum in region, has further dented investor sentiment, forcing companies to hold plans for tapping the equities markets to raise capital. DIP Holding, which operates the mixed-used master development Dubai Investments Park, said the success of the public offering signals “confidence in the country’s capital markets”. Situated near Al Maktoum International Airport and Jebel Ali Port, Dubai Investments Park is home to primary 1,000 tenants, 5,700 subtenants and more than 150,000 residents. The district was established in 1997 and hosts warehouses, hotels, retail outlets, schools and medical centres, making it one of the largest mixed-use developments in the emirate.

events.title: Our house purchase is at risk from a frozen Revolut account
events.summary: Access to our £37,000 deposit in a savings account is restricted after a ‘routine security review’ My wife’s Revolut account was frozen in what it calls a “routine security review” over a week ago. Nothing has been requested from her – no documents, the source of funds, or ID – yet, as a result, our house deposit of £37,000 in a joint savings account is also restricted. We’re approaching the completion of our property purchase and have given notice on our rental home. Direct debits are bouncing and we’re concerned about our credit records. At one point Revolut also restricted my personal account, so we effectively had no access to any money. We keep being given deadlines for the restrictions to be lifted which are missed, and call centre staff, when we can get through, have little ability to find out what’s happening, or make anything happen. XWF , Oxfordshire Banks have legal powers, under anti-money-laundering regulations, to freeze accounts if a sudden windfall, overseas payment or unusual activity raises concerns. They are not required to warn customers or explain if they suspect foul play, although customers can complain to the Financial Ombudsman Service if they believe a bank acted unfairly. There’s no suggestion foul play was suspected in your wife’s case and things progressed swiftly after I got involved. Accounts were reinstated, nearly three weeks after being suspended, and your wife was offered £175 as a goodwill gesture. Revolut says regulatory constraints prevented it explaining. “We’re sorry our review process took longer than usual, and our communication didn’t reach its usual standards, particularly given the inconvenience during an important life moment,” it says. events.title: Latinos' rejection of GOP boosts Dems in Texas upsets
events.summary: Latino voters helped Democrats break Republicans' decades-long grip on Texas and reclaim both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, casting doubt on President Trump's historic 2024 gains with the fast-growing electorate. Why it matters: Republicans bet Trump's Latino breakthrough two years ago would create a lasting GOP realignment in Texas and beyond. Tuesday's results exposed how quickly those gains could unravel — and raised new questions about Republicans' coalition heading into 2028. Early results show Hispanic voters' shift aided Democrats in capturing a Senate seat and the governorship in Texas for the first time in a generation. Tuesday's results — particularly in South Texas border counties — reflected some of the anger among Hispanics over high prices and the Trump administration's immigration enforcement. "This is what happens when you mess with the Latino community. We are sending a clear message," said Hector Sanchez Barba, president and CEO of the voting group Mi Familia Vota. By the numbers: Early NBC News exit poll results showed Latino voters moving away from Republicans. Democrats' 16-point advantage in Latino party identification grew from 10 points in 2024, according to NBC's polling. Some 43% of Latino voters identified as Democrats, up from 39% in 2024. Republican identification slipped from 29% to 27%. In the early NBC exit poll, 75% of voters nationally described the economy as struggling, while 65% said Trump's policies had made economic conditions worse. State of play: Democrats reclaimed the House and Senate while ending Republicans' statewide winning streak in Texas dating to 1994. Democratic state Rep. James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton , winning a Senate seat Democrats last captured in 1988. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa ousted Republican Gov. Greg Abbott , becoming Texas' first elected Latina governor. Early returns also suggested Latino voters helped Democrats win crucial House contests in Colorado and Georgia. Comedian Cristela Alonzo attends an election night watch party for Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa at Assembly Hall in Austin, Texas. Photo: Joel Angel Juarez/Getty Images What they're saying: "You know how Tim Russert would always say 'Florida, Florida, Florida?' For the last two cycles, I kept saying Texas, Texas, Texas. That's how I feel right now," Voto Latino CEO Maria Teresa Kumar told Axios. Kumar said the Democrats' historic Texas wins changes 2028 and will transform how presidential candidates talk to Latino voters and see Texas as purple. "There was this notion that we're a sleeping giant. Now, we're jumping up and down and waving our fist above the head," Janet Murguía, president and CEO of the Latino civil rights group UnidosUS told Axios. Zoom in: The clearest tests of the Latino shift came in Texas counties that Republicans had celebrated as evidence of their growing strength. Cameron County, which includes Brownsville and South Padre Island: Talarico led by 38 points in early, unofficial returns. Trump won by 6 points there in 2024. Hidalgo County, another majority-Latino border county: Talarico led by 47 points. Trump won it two years ago by 3 points. Webb County, home to Laredo: Talarico led by 49 points; it was Trump +2 in 2024. Context: Trump's 2024 success shattered longstanding assumptions about Latino voters. A Pew Research Center analysis found Trump won 48% of Latino voters in 2024, compared with 36% in 2020. An August Axios-reported poll of 17 competitive House districts foreshadowed the reversal, showing Democrats leading 58%–35% among Latino registered voters. Supporters react during a midterm election night watch party for Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico at the Long Center in Austin, Texas. Photo: Brandon Bell/Getty Image Reality check: A Democratic rebound doesn't mean Latino voters have returned to their old political loyalties. Democrats' 16-point advantage in Latino party identification remains far below their 33-point advantage in 2018, according to NBC. Republicans may have mistaken Trump's appeal for lasting GOP loyalty. Democrats risk confusing a backlash against Trump with renewed allegiance to their party. A September Axios analysis found 62% of Latino registered voters in 17 battleground districts trusted Democrats more to lower prices, compared with 36% who trusted Republicans. Economic frustration gave Democrats an opening without guaranteeing lasting support. The bottom line: Trump's Latino breakthrough reshaped politics in 2024. Two years later, those voters reminded both parties that winning their support once doesn't mean keeping it.

events.title: Ohio just poured onto its existing 125 data center moratoriums. Transparency pushes and grid safeguards could now ‘dominate policy agendas’ nationwide
events.summary: Ohio voters rejected the AI buildout almost everywhere it was on the ballot Tuesday, with at least 14 municipalities passing bans or other restrictions on data centers. The Buckeye State is on its way to becoming the prototype for how American voters respond in the face of mass AI infrastructure expansion. Ohio residents across 18 municipalities voted on 21 ballot measures on data centers on Tuesday—more than half of the 41 data center-related ballot measures across the country. With more than 200 operational data centers , Ohio ranks No. 5 among U.S. states in number of data center projects. According to state data, companies plan to invest up to $40 billion in AI infrastructure in the state by 2030. Plans for AI infrastructure expansion across the country face strong national opposition—including in the form of 125 local data center moratoriums already in place in Ohio. Ohio voters’ decisive stance against the buildout could foreshadow not just future election results, but how stakeholders in the private sector and government respond. “With over 100 Ohio townships adopting moratoria or restrictions, strong voter turnout against expansion would signal to statehouses nationwide that ratepayer protections, transparency, and grid safeguards should dominate policy agendas,” Keith Durkin, a sociology professor and director of the Ohio Northern University Institute for Civics and Public Policy (ICAPP), told Fortune . How did Ohio vote? (function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})(); In central Ohio, all five communities with data center measures on the ballot voted against data centers. In Sunbury, residents appear to have passed a charter amendment banning data centers that use 25 megawatts or more, with 100% of the unofficial vote counted. The measure was aimed at a possible hyperscale Amazon project, though the project’s fate remains unclear, NBC4 reported. Pataskala voters also approved a charter ban on large data centers. In Trenton, a ban passed 80% to 20% . Organizers hope it will keep an 18-building Amazon Web Services data center out of the city, though it likely won’t affect a four-building AWS campus already under construction nearby, the Journal-News reported . In Perry, more than 87% of voters approved a measure requiring developers seeking tax breaks to offer the village financial guarantees. In Wilmington, around 80% of voters rejected rezoning across four separate referendums meant to accommodate a data center project. Results in Oregon weren’t yet available as of Wednesday morning. Ashville residents voted in favor of entirely blocking a data center campus that is already under construction. The bulk of the ballot measures came from 13 municipalities voting on measures to ban or heavily restrict data centers, including “high impact” campuses using more than 25 megawatts of power. Those measures were on the ballot in the municipalities of Conneaut, Defiance, Granville, Grove City, Hubbard, Monroeville, Oregon, Pataskala, Piqua, Sunbury, Trenton, Upper Sandusky, and Urbana. Two measures in Monroe and Sprigg townships, respectively, decided whether zoning restrictions on large data center developments should be implemented as a means to preserve agricultural land. Wilmington voters also decided on four separate referendums on whether to uphold the rezoning of four rural residential sites to light industrial sites to accommodate data center construction. What do polls say about Ohio’s sentiment toward AI expansion? A Gallup poll published in May found about 70% of Americans opposed the construction of data centers in their local areas, and Ohio appears to largely mirror the national sentiment. ICAPP, in partnership with SurveyUSA, found in a poll of 1,650 Ohio adults published last month, that 55% opposed data center construction in the state compared to 22% in support, while 65% opposed tax breaks for data center developments compared to 15% in support, and 57% said they would vote in favor of a proposed state constitutional amendment banning new large-scale data centers exceeding 25 megawatts in power demands. About 20% of respondents said they’d vote against the amendment, and 21% were undecided. Durkin attributes the negative sentiment toward data centers to a confluence of factors, primarily fear of the environmental and economic risks associated with the AI boom that has emerged as a result of little knowledge about data centers. “I’ve never seen any pro-data center advertising. I’ve never seen any op-eds from the industry,” he said. “Everything we know is that humans don’t like uncertainty from social behavioral science, and there’s uncertainty around data centers.”  This skepticism is bipartisan across both Ohio and the country, and it’s allowed Democrats to make data center construction a wedge issue this election, Tatishe Nteta, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, previously told Fortune . Ben Green, assistant professor of public policy at the University of Michigan’s Ford School, similarly argued data centers have become bipartisan because it has struck ideological chords in both parties. Democrats may oppose the campuses because of climate change concerns, but Republicans similarly value environmentalism through the preservation of land. “Democrats and Republicans might talk about that differently, but massive corporations coming in and forcing a community to deal with some type of project and not really giving a community any voice and operating in secrecy—no one’s really a fan of that,” Green told Fortune . events.title: Bitcoin slides as Democratic sweep bets threaten crypto agenda
events.summary: Democrats, who have traditionally favoured tighter oversight of the crypto industry, had been expected to take control of the House of Representatives, a result that is now projected. Bitcoin fell to a seven-week low as early US election results pointed to a possible Democratic sweep of Congress, raising fears of a tougher crypto agenda and political gridlock. Democrats are projected to control the House and Senate, which could stall industry-backed bills like the Clarity Act and bring more scrutiny for digital-asset firms. Crypto markets are also under pressure from a US$6.3 billion Binance hack, weak retail demand, and heavy ETF outflows, while traders buy more downside protection. WASHINGTON – Bitcoin fell to a seven-week low as the prospect of a Democratic sweep of the US Congress began showing up in early US midterm election results, adding political uncertainty to a market already struggling with fragile investor appetite. The original cryptocurrency slid as much as 2.8% to US$75,630.57 in Asia trading on Nov 4 , its lowest level since Sept 17. It pared some losses to trade around US$76,600 as at 12.20pm in Singapore. The move followed declines in US stock futures and the dollar , while Treasuries gained, reflecting expectations that Democratic control of Congress could lead to gridlock in Washington. “Markets react to change, and a blue flip will likely introduce additional scepticism given the party’s historically choke point stance towards crypto,” said Daniel Reis-Faria, chief executive of ZeroStack. “I expect that uncertainty to be temporary.” Major cryptocurrencies began sliding as initial vote counts came in. They are also projected to take control of the US Senate. The digital asset industry has poured money into shaping the political landscape since US President Donald Trump ran for a second presidential term in 2024. Crypto companies contributed US$189 million (S$241.8 million) to political action committees in the 2026 midterm cycle through the first quarter – more than a third of election spending, according to the consumer rights advocacy group Public Citizen. For investors, the immediate concern is that a Democratic takeover could stall industry-backed legislation and bring tougher scrutiny of digital asset firms. The broader macroeconomic implications are less clear. Political stalemate could limit further fiscal stimulus and weigh on speculative assets, though lower Treasury yields could eventually provide support by easing financial conditions. For now, Bitcoin trading offers limited utility as a gauge of broader market sentiment. Crypto has been grappling with the fallout from a US$6.3 billion hack of largest exchange Binance last week and diminished retail enthusiasm amid the artificial intelligence boom. Those pressures make it harder to separate the macro-driven market moves from industry-specific issues already weighing on digital assets. “Overall sentiment in crypto is near-term moderate fear and long-term uncertainty,” said Damien Loh, chief investment officer at Ericsenz Capital. “Near-term fear because it is still tracking overall risk assets, and with the tech sell-off and potentially a restart to the war in the Middle East that is causing some downward pressure.” Democratic control of the Senate, in addition to the House, would put Congress at odds with Trump’s Republican White House. The Trump family’s financial gains from its crypto ventures became a contentious issue in 2026 , helping derail a regulatory Bill seen as critical to the industry. “With the Clarity Act already stalled in the Senate, a change in committee control would most likely mean renegotiation rather than a quick revival, and markets had largely priced that in,” said Rachael Lucas, an analyst at BTC Markets. Bitcoin is down roughly 6% from a high on Oct 29 , before the Binance hack. More than US$1 billion flowed out of US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds on Oct 30 and Nov 2 . Options markets continued to show demand for downside protection across maturities, even as open interest remains tilted towards calls, or the right to buy Bitcoin, in several of the largest expiries. “As a Democratic sweep became more likely, clients shifted from buying upside calls to downside puts,” said Sean McNulty, a derivatives trader at market maker AQC Tech. “Attention is shifting back to interest rates and currencies, which is also driving Bitcoin’s decline today.” BLOOMBERG
