events.title: Swim and gym prices set to rise above inflation
events.summary: Bosses at Perdiswell Leisure Centre in Worcester want to increase its fees from January Inflation-busting price increases are on the way at a large Worcester leisure centre, with its operators blaming energy and staffing costs. The price of an adult swim at Perdiswell Leisure Centre could rise 6.8% – from £7.30 to £7.80 – if the new charges are approved. Fitness class fees would increase by 5.6% to £9.50, while the price of annual memberships would go up 4.9%. Bosses at Freedom Leisure, the site's operator, said staffing and energy bills were rising faster than income as Worcester City Council were asked to approve the new prices. A report on the price hikes, which outstrip the UK's 3.6% inflation rate, revealed energy costs had more than doubled in recent years, despite efforts to slash consumption. If councillors sign them off in a meeting at the end of November, the average fee at Perdiswell Leisure Centre would increase by 5.3% from January. Matt Wickham, from Freedom Leisure, said things are "tough" for the whole leisure industry Hiring the artificial pitch at Perdiswell, which can currently be done for £44 an hour, would cost 10% more, although the council said it would still be significantly cheaper than comparable pitches elsewhere in the city. Matt Wickham, Freedom Leisure's chief operating officer, explained the firm had seen "significant cost increases", with gas prices up by more than 50% over the second half of the year and minimum wages rising year-on-year. "It's really tough because we know people are feeling the pinch in different ways, but our priority is all about offering a value-for-money service to people from all walks of life," he said. He added the government should consider "immediate financial support" to help the leisure industry through the next 12 months and ongoing investment into leisure centre stock. If approved, the increases would also apply at St John's Sports Centre and Nunnery Wood Sports Complex, both of which are owned by Freedom Leisure. Gym-goers at Perdiswell had mixed views on the price increases – with some saying they were not surprised. Sue Guest said: "I've had two hip replacements so I come and do the aqua swim, it's very beneficial to me. "It would be a shame if they increase it, but then they (the operators) have their own expenses as well. "I think it's still reasonable value for money, actually." Colin English, a pensioner, said: "I use the gym quite a lot, I come at least four or five times a week. "They put the price up last year – if they do it again by these sorts of amounts I may have to reconsider because it's getting expensive." Another gym user called Vinny added: "It feels like everything is going up in price at the moment. "I'd never stop going though, this gym is important to me so I really don't mind." A final decision is expected to be made on 24 November, subject to discussions at two city council committees before then. events.title: Business-friendly Texas flips: Democrats end nearly 40-year drought, winning Senate seat and governor’s mansion
events.summary: It’s been nearly four decades since Texas sent a Democrat to the US Senate, and 36 years since one occupied the governor’s mansion. That all changed Tuesday night. While Democrats notched historic upsets nationwide — including in places like Kansas, which broke a 90-year streak — Texas carries outsized national weight given the recent corporate stampede to the state. SpaceX, Tesla, Chevron, and Caterpillar are among the corporate giants that relocated to Texas in search of lower taxes, light-touch regulation, and a business-friendly political climate. “In Texas, we’re welcome,” Chevron’s Andy Walz said after announcing a move from California. Last month, the parent company of the new Texas Stock Exchange raised $155 million in a third funding round meant to lure companies away from the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq. Like Walz, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has cast Texas as a foil to California — a state Musk famously decried as the “state of overregulation, overlitigation, and overtaxation,” and whose billionaire wealth tax on the ballot Tuesday has alienated business leaders. Yet that corporate embrace has proved double-edged. Musk directed roughly $190 million of his $445 million midterm war chest into Texas, largely backing Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott. That deluge offered Democrat James Talarico an irresistible target down the stretch, allowing him to portray the race as Musk’s bid to buy a Senate seat. Abbott, a three-term incumbent, was also called out for being on Musk’s payroll. “Does Texas belong to the people, or is this the billionaires’ world and we just live here?” said Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Abbott to become the first Democrat elected governor since Ann Richards in 1990. “In less than one month, Elon Musk gave Greg Abbott $5 million to try and buy this election so that he can keep buying up Texans’ land, energy, and resources,” she added. Hinojosa, described as “a long shot” by the Texas Tribune and mostly ignored by Abbott for much of the year, also tapped into rising backlash over data center sprawl. She campaigned against what she termed a “Big Tech takeover of Texas land, resources, and schools.” — Shelly Banjo

events.title: Rogue UK energy bosses and brokers face crackdown on mis-selling
events.summary: Exclusive: Ofgem to be given powers to issue fines and rein in bonuses for executives who ‘reward themselves while customers suffer’ Energy bosses in the UK will have their bonuses curtailed when suppliers and brokers break the rules under a crackdown on mis-selling. Through the energy independence bill, which will be introduced on Wednesday, Ofgem will be given new powers to order compensation, impose fines and ban rogue operators that have pushed businesses and households into overpriced contracts. Companies with a business energy supply contract often use a broker to secure their deal, but – unlike the intermediaries who market mortgages or insurance deals – these energy middlemen are largely unregulated. The government said rogue brokers had been able to push small businesses into overpriced energy contracts while pocketing hidden commissions, leaving companies paying more than they should. These energy brokers and price comparison services will now be brought under Ofgem’s remit. The move is expected to save businesses more than £100m a year from hidden commissions and mis-selling. The watchdog will also be given powers to crack down on payments to bosses who have “rewarded themselves while customers suffer”. It follows public outrage over huge bonus payouts to executives despite investigations into the treatment of vulnerable customers . The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh , said: “People work hard for their money. They shouldn’t be ripped off by energy companies or forced to fight for fair treatment when things go wrong. “When energy bosses fail their customers, they shouldn’t be walking away with bumper bonuses while families and businesses pick up the bill.” The bill, which was announced in the king’s speech and is expected to set out more details on the government’s plans to transition to clean energy, comes as ministers face criticism over the green agenda. John Healey recently unveiled more than £3bn of cuts to the energy department’s budget, much of which will pay for higher defence spending. The chancellor also said he would veto new offshore wind projects if they did not lower bills, adding to concerns that the government was moving away from the pro-renewables agenda. However, the government says it is still committed to its target of clean power by 2030. As part of the new bill, local authorities will be given stronger powers to tackle landlords who fail to meet energy efficiency standards, including fines of up to £30,000. Since 2020, it has been illegal to let properties with energy performance certificate ratings below E, unless the landlord can show that it is exempt. The government will also use the bill to introduce a moratorium on fracking by ending new licensing onshore in England. Fracking, which involves pumping liquid underground at high pressure to crack rock and release trapped oil or gas, is controversial because of its links to earthquakes and fears it could contaminate the water table. It was banned by the Conservative government in 2019. However, in 2022, Liz Truss used her brief tenure as prime minister to overturn the ban, prompting widespread anger. The minister for climate transition, Katie White, said the government was “putting communities first and protecting them from the risks of earthquakes and unsafe drilling”. The moratorium will not include lower-volume fracking operations or “proppant squeeze”, which the fracking industry says is not a form of fracking. However, Tony Bosworth, an energy campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said this was an attempt to “creep in through the back door under a different name”. The government said the low-volume activities were not under the scope of the ban and it was not aware of evidence that they posed the same risks as high-volume fracking. Prof Stuart Haszeldine of the University of Edinburgh has said that earthquakes caused by lower-volume fracking can be as large and unpredictable as those caused by high-volume fracking.

events.title: Why pharma firms are going to Earth’s orbit in search of new cancer drugs
events.summary: A space capsule 300 miles above us is growing the tiny crystals of a potential cancer drug in microgravity R oughly 300 miles above our heads, three washing machine-sized capsules are orbiting the Earth. Inside one of them, tiny crystals of a potential cancer drug are being grown in the weightlessness of space. The others are testing heat protection materials and navigation systems for when the capsules plunge back through Earth’s atmosphere at hypersonic speeds. Together, they represent a small but significant step towards what some hope will become a lucrative new industry: manufacturing drugs and other materials in space. The spacecraft belong to California-based Varda Space Industries. On 1 October, it launched two onboard the same rocket, followed by the third on 20 October. With a record three spacecraft now simultaneously in orbit for the first time, the company is edging closer to its ambition of operating a fleet of orbiting pharmaceutical factories. “We’re the first company in human history to launch multiple commercial re-entry vehicles simultaneously, and as the frequency of launches increases, the once ‘crazy future’ of manufacturing products in space is becoming more and more certain,” said Will Bruey, Varda’s chief executive. There are several reasons for wanting to manufacture certain materials in space, one of the most important being microgravity. On Earth, gravity causes particles suspended in liquids to settle, while differences in density create currents. Both can interfere with the growth of crystals. “If you are able to remove those effects, you can make crystals grow in a much more ordered sort of way,” said Dr Meganne Christian, mission manager for in-space manufacturing at the UK-based Satellite Applications Catapult. For pharmaceutical companies, this could open up new ways of formulating medicines, as the size, shape and arrangement of drug crystals can affect how easily drugs dissolve, how stable they are and how they can be administered. In some cases, this could enable drugs that currently require intravenous infusions to be reformulated into more convenient injections. Other materials, such as the semiconductors used in everything from smartphones to electric vehicles, could also benefit from being manufactured in space, where microgravity and the absence of air could help produce purer crystals with fewer defects. “Personally, I would really love to try and make graphene in microgravity,” said Christian. “Theoretically, it is this incredible material, but in practice you get a whole lot of defects in the crystals. It’s a similar story for semiconductors. If you can reduce the number of defects, you can get a much higher-performing material.” Scientists have been experimenting with manufacturing in microgravity for decades, particularly aboard the International Space Station (ISS). But the ISS has predominantly served as a “test kitchen” for scientific ideas and is scheduled to be retired around 2030. “It wasn’t necessarily designed with manufacturing in mind,” said Dr Ryan Reeves, deputy chief scientist for the ISS National Laboratory. Several companies are developing commercial space stations to replace the ISS, while others are designing specialist laboratories and equipment for conducting experiments aboard them. Among them is the UK-based BioOrbit, which recently sent a microwave-sized laboratory to the ISS as a step towards the production of self-injected cancer drugs. However, for large-scale manufacturing and certain industrial processes, “you need to get humans out of the picture, because we’re dirty, we cause vibrations, and we require a whole higher level of safety,” said Christian. This is where Varda’s autonomous factories come in. Known as free-flyers, they hitch a ride into orbit aboard SpaceX rockets, carrying miniature laboratories in which materials can be processed without astronauts. Once the experiments are complete, a capsule separates from the spacecraft, plunges through the atmosphere and parachutes safely back to an uninhabited region of Earth. Varda is among the furthest advanced in demonstrating this approach, having already returned several capsules from orbit. It plans to launch another seven missions in 2027, and a further 10 in 2028. The ability to conduct experiments frequently is particularly important for drug development. “If scientists have to wait 10 years between experiments or even a year, that really doesn’t fit into the speed of modern drug development,” said Michael Reilly, Varda’s chief strategy officer. While Varda’s manufacturing ambitions are focused on pharmaceuticals, other companies are developing similar systems to produce different materials. For example, Cardiff-based Space Forge is exploring a hybrid approach, in which semiconductor crystals grown aboard spacecraft could be returned to Earth and used as templates for growing larger quantities, much like a sourdough starter.

Deputy chief designer Wang Xiang explained the plans last weekend at an event called the Seventh Manned Space Symposium. Chinese state media has posted video of Wang discussing plans to reach Luna by launching two Long March 10 rockets. One will carry a lander named “Lanyue” and the other will hoist a crew capsule called “Mengzhou.” The two craft will meet in orbit around the Moon, where two of the three Taikonauts aboard Mengzhou will transfer to Lanyue and descend to set boot on regolith. In the video, Wang said China plans near-Earth orbit test missions for both vehicles in coming years, followed by an uncrewed visit to the Moon. If all goes well, China hopes to attempt a crewed landing by 2030. The Seventh Manned Space Symposium marked the 70th anniversary of the founding of China's space program and was also pitched as a moment for articulation of the nation’s ambitions in space under its 15 th five-year-plan, Beijing’s blueprint for the years 2026 to 2030. China called off its last moonshot in August, when authorities decided the Chang’e 7 robotic ice hunting mission “ failed to meet launch criteria ” just one day before its planned launch. The orbit required to reach the South Lunar Pole for that mission isn’t always easily accessible, so China plans to try again next year. When China tries to get Chang’e 7, Lanyue, and Mengzhou flying, it will at least have some new standards to apply to their operations after the China Manned Space Engineering Office last week published seventeen of them. One of the standards defines the architecture for Ethernet and Wi-Fi networks on China’s space station and other orbiters. Another governs signage used in orbit, in the hope that a standard means Taikonauts won’t make mistakes. A couple outline procedures for extravehicular activities, and use of a robotic arm to assist Taikonauts on such missions. events.title: Massive blue wave hands Congress to Democrats
events.summary: The News Democrats seized the House and Senate by wider margins that even party leaders had hoped in a wave election that served as a referendum on President Donald Trump. Democratic House candidates took districts Trump won by double digits just two years ago. They flipped Senate seats nationwide, including in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Competitive races haven’t been called in Michigan and Alaska, where Democrats could run up the score further. Trump told The New York Times on Wednesday night that he “was absolutely willing” to accept the results of the election. Democrats racked up stunning victories across the South. In Texas, James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988. Democrat Gina Hinojosa toppled incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the first Democrat to take the governor’s mansion since Ann Richards in 1990. Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina won a Senate seat in his state, pulling off what no Democrat has there in 18 years. In South Carolina, Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham, winning the seat formerly held by Lindsey Graham. Sen. Jon Ossoff held onto his seat in Georgia. Democrats scored victories across the Midwest, too. Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, overcoming a 94-year drought for Democrats in the state. In Iowa, Josh Turek beat Rep. Ashley Hinson to fill retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst’s seat. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown unseated Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Chris Pappas held retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s seat for Democrats in New Hampshire. Republican Maine Sen. Susan Collins conceded to her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson. Polls in Alaska remain open until 1 am EST. Republicans held onto a Senate seat in Florida. Trump, reportedly watching returns from the White House, criticized Fox News coverage before most polls had closed. In a social media post Trump said Republicans would have had a better night if he’d been on the ballot. Democratic surge Democrats won other gubernatorial races in red states. Keisha Lance Bottoms won the gubernatorial race in Georgia, a first for a Democrat in 28 years — a positive sign for Ossoff if he decides to pursue a 2028 presidential bid, since she would appoint his successor. Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, endorsed by Trump, to become the next governor of Ohio. Ramaswamy aired a late attack ad against Acton featuring her estranged mother, who backed her husband when Acton accused him of rape as a child. Ossoff, who Republicans had hoped to unseat this year, easily blew past GOP rival Rep. Mike Collins to win re-election. Pappas prevailed over former GOP Sen. John Sununu in another race that Republicans had initially hoped to contest. In North Carolina, Cooper scored the party’s first pickup of the night. House Republicans are also faltering in Florida, where three seats drawn to elect Republicans have so far gone to Democrats — re-elections for Reps. Jared Moskowitz and Kathy Castor, plus a victory for Rep.-elect Pia Dandiya. The GOP initially redistricted to try to gain four new House seats. All three of the Florida districts that Democrats have won so far on Tuesday night backed Trump in 2024. Urged to embark on mid-decade redistricting by Trump, Florida GOP Gov. Ron DeSantis has warned that his party was losing some of its advantages, driven by voter anger about the war in Iran. David’s view As the night got better and better for Democrats, I started to hear them ask: Had they built a new national majority? Had they banished MAGA for good?Then they reminded themselves: Thinking like that is what got Republicans into this mess. Two Trump victories, and a 2020 loss that kept most of his coalition intact, convinced many conservatives that they had built a new party system that combined working class voters of all races, the social conservatives who made their local parties run, and the business community that rejected Trump after Jan. 6 but came running back in 2024. Who could beat that? Well, now we know. The Trump coalition came apart on Tuesday, with the president decisively unable to put himself “on the ballot” and turn out his unlikely voters. Plenty of signs were there during early voting – especially in North Carolina, a killing field where Republicans lost House and state legislative seats that were gerrymandered to be impossible to lose. (On a map drawn to elect three Democrats, the party is likely to win nine seats.) Democrats didn’t pretend that they had solved all their party’s problems. But they did learn from Trump’s first term, and the way they miscalculated what a fluke he was. Instead of moving to the left, betting that a more excited base could overwhelm MAGA, they nominated candidates who were willing to break with left-wing orthodoxy – Iowa Sen.-elect Josh Turek adopting a more conservative position on gender, Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico becoming a booster of the energy industry. Their base was so furious at Trump that it was relatively easy to turn out. Persuasion was harder, but they got there; Democrats won back northeast Ohio, eastern Iowa, Texas’s Rio Grande Valley, and even parts of Florida that seemed to be racing away from their party. And Republicans couldn’t change the electorate. Trump wasn’t on the ballot, obviously – but for the first time, voters did not credit Trump with good management of the economy or with keeping America out of wars. The snazziest GOP bumper sticker of the Biden years was “I’d take some mean tweets and cheap gas right now.” Without cheap gas, voters weren’t willing to put up with Trump’s AI memes, jokes about men’s asses, and obsession with building a triumphant arch in Arlington. Finally, Republicans had a failure of imagination. Any reporter who covered the 2016 election remembers the disbelief, even anger, from Democrats who were told that Trump could win the Midwest. It was impossible, until it happened. And Republicans who’d been told that Texas could flip in 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022 could not imagine James Talarico – the “God is nonbinary” guy? – breaking the curse. Talarico is on track to lead a Democratic sweep of Texas statewide offices, cutting down some of the most powerful politicians in the state’s history. Democrats held onto the suburban gains they made from 2016 to 2020, then won back many of the place that no Democrat had won since Barack Obama. They are less afraid of Trump than of any time since the week before the 2016 election.

events.title: Singapore equity funds draw record $2.2b as bank dividends bolster local market
events.summary: Singapore-focused equity funds attracted a record $2.2 billion in the third quarter of 2026, with inflows more than double the previous quarter’s level and almost five times the $450 million recorded a year earlier, data showed. Singapore equity funds saw record inflows of $2.2 billion in Q3 2026, as Morningstar said strong market performance and the EQDP revived interest in local shares. Capital Group said Singapore companies paid US$7.6 billion in dividends, up 2.5% year on year, with underlying growth at 9.6% and banks DBS and OCBC driving gains. Investors also moved money into allocation funds and out of bond funds, which saw $1.04 billion in net outflows as rising bond yields hurt fixed-income returns. SINGAPORE – Investors are putting more money into Singapore stocks and equity funds, coinciding with higher dividend payouts from companies listed here, according to the latest data showing record fund inflows and stronger underlying dividend growth in the third quarter. Singapore-focused equity funds attracted a record $2.2 billion in the third quarter of 2026, with inflows more than double the previous quarter’s level and almost five times the $450 million recorded a year earlier, according to findings released on Nov 4 by Morningstar, an investment research and financial services firm. Separately, investment management firm Capital Group’s latest Dividend Watch report, also released on Nov 4, found that Singapore companies in its study paid a total of US$7.6 billion (S$9.7 billion) in dividends during the quarter, up 2.5% from a year earlier. Underlying dividend growth for Singapore companies was stronger at 9.6%, ahead of the global average of 7.5%. This measure strips out special dividends, currency movements and changes in payment timing to give a clearer picture of recurring payouts. Singapore’s dividend growth was overwhelmingly driven by banks, particularly DBS and OCBC, Capital Group said. At DBS, record fee income, buoyant wealth management activity and growing customer activity helped offset weaker margins, allowing the bank to continue returning surplus capital to shareholders. Meanwhile, OCBC benefited from record non-interest income and strong wealth management and trading revenues, the report said. Both reports point to renewed demand for Singapore equities, alongside growth in the cash that companies are returning to shareholders. Morningstar attributed the growing popularity of Singapore equity funds to strong market performance and measures under the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP) to revitalise the local stock market. Arvind Subramanian, senior analyst and research manager at Morningstar, noted that Singapore investors have traditionally looked abroad for their equity and fixed-income exposure, while the local market tended to attract attention mainly during risk-on periods. “The EQDP measures and strong market performance have put Singapore equities back in the spotlight, with Singapore-focused equity funds becoming increasingly popular among investors,” he said. Singapore equities have recorded positive flows in every quarter since the fourth quarter of 2024, when the EQDP was first announced, and the pace has picked up sharply in 2026 so far. LionGlobal Singapore Trust saw the highest inflows of around $1.05 billion, while Amova Singapore Dividend Equity Fund drew about $530 million. Amova Singapore STI ETF added another $280 million, according to Morningstar. Funds combining different asset classes also attracted more money, driven by the strong appetite for equities. Allocation funds, which typically invest across assets such as shares and bonds, drew $2.45 billion in the third quarter, their strongest quarterly inflows in the past few years. This followed $1.83 billion in the second quarter and $1.49 billion in the first. PIMCO GIS Balanced Income and Growth Fund attracted about $870 million, while Allianz Income and Growth drew roughly $530 million. Schroder ISF Multi-Asset Growth and Income and Schroder Asia More+ also recorded notable inflows. The stronger appetite for stocks came at the expense of bonds, as investors pulled more money out of funds that invest solely in bonds. During the quarter, withdrawals accelerated from fixed-income funds, which recorded $1.04 billion in net outflows, data showed. It is also the third consecutive quarter of outflows from fixed income, and a reversal from the $3.36 billion attracted in the corresponding period of 2025. The PIMCO GIS Income Fund, usually among the category’s leading fixed income asset gatherers, recorded a second consecutive quarter of withdrawals, with investors pulling out about $790 million. Rising bond yields have weighed on fixed-income fund returns , as higher interest rates on new bonds make existing bonds with lower payouts less attractive , pushing down their prices. However, higher yields also offer investors more attractive income opportunities.

events.title: GOP's red wall comes crashing down
events.summary: Senate Republicans' worst nightmare came true Tuesday night, as they watched red state after red state fall to a historic Democratic wave . Why it matters: It's hard to remember now, but Republicans started off the 2026 cycle thinking they could expand their majority. They ended the night with what one source called a "huge f**king thumping" — losing or trailing in every toss-up on the map. At the start of the cycle, top operatives saw a red wall of incumbents in Trump-friendly states, an invincible Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine and a vulnerable Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, who provided a path to expanding a majority. By 9pm Tuesday night, top GOP sources were quietly accepting the reality of the return of Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). "Republicans are going to wake up in a different country tomorrow and we are going to have to start from square one to reinvent a party," one senior GOP Senate aide told Axios on Tuesday evening. Between the lines: For the first time since 1972, Republicans lost a Senate seat in the home state of the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee. The defeat of Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) came despite Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) leading the NRSC. Republicans also lost in the home state of the next expected NRSC chair, Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). Zoom in: North Carolina and Georgia were expected to be the premiere races of the cycle not too long ago. Both were called for Democrats before 8:30pm EST. That was just the beginning of the nightmare. In Texas, Elon Musk's more than $150 million infusion wasn't enough to save Texas GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton after Paxton defeated Sen. John Cornyn in a nasty primary. In Ohio, Sen. Jon Husted's (R-Ohio) campaign had a rocky start — and wasn't bailed out by President Trump's publicity campaign about his rear end. Alaska started looking shaky even before a second Dan Sullivan joined the ballot, and Iowa wasn't a given either. In Kansas, alarm bells started ringing over an unprepared Sen. Roger Marshall. In South Carolina, Sen. Lindsey Graham died, and before Republican leaders could blink, Trump crowned Graham's sister, Darline, who had no political experience. And in Maine, Republicans held out hope that Susan Collins could pull out another miracle. A hope that quickly faded as results began to roll in. What we're hearing: "Absolutely brutal night," another senior GOP aide told us. "But also predictable. Signs were there for months. Biggest fear is that the party lacks the introspection, takes away wrong lessons, and doubles down on the policies and behavior that got us into this mess in first place." "Sometimes there are environmental challenges that even the strongest, best-resourced candidate can't overcome. We're seeing those challenges play out in real time tonight," said a third senior GOP aide. Yet another top operative conspicuously shared charts of Trump's dismal approval ratings. The bottom line: Democrats won Senate seats on Tuesday night for the first time in Texas since 1988, in Kansas since 1932 and South Carolina since 1998.

events.title: Airbnb's Brian Chesky says these 3 mistakes made him a 'terrible CEO'
events.summary: Airbnb's Brian Chesky said these 3 mistakes made him a "terrible CEO." David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Brian Chesky said building Airbnb came more naturally to him than running it as CEO. He said he had to rethink how he hired, managed people, and set priorities. Chesky said these three mistakes made him a "terrible CEO." As Airbnb grew from a startup into a global travel company , CEO Brian Chesky said he learned that building it and running it were two very different jobs. Speaking on Monday's episode of the " How I Built This " podcast, Chesky opened up about the steep learning curve he faced as Airbnb expanded. "I think I was pretty much naturally a great founder, and I was naturally a terrible CEO," Chesky told podcast host Guy Raz. Chesky said being a founder came more intuitively to him, while becoming a CEO required a very different set of skills. "When you're a child, you're making things, you're building things . You're practicing being a founder, and so the moment you found a company is probably not the first time you try to make something," Chesky said. He said he had been developing the instincts of a founder since childhood, from designing and taking apart toys to persuading friends to buy what he was selling. But when he suddenly had to become a CEO, he said he found the role "counterintuitive." Here are the three mistakes Chesky said he made: 1. Deferring to more experienced executives Chesky said that as a CEO, he was often advised to hire highly experienced executives and get out of their way. He said he later came to see how that approach isn't the best for a young company: "You've got to hire people just a little bit ahead of you that are smart, hungry, and you got to stay really close to them." Chesky said he also often ignored his own instincts in favor of listening to executives with far more experience than he did, who were often much older than he was. "The hard part for me was sometimes my intuition would tell me one thing, and they'd tell me another. And what do I do when my intuition and their experience collide? Usually I deferred, and that was usually a mistake," Chesky said. He said that those executives who came from much larger companies often struggled to apply what had worked at a larger business to the demands of a smaller startup. "They also come from companies where they didn't build it. They managed it. And now they have to build it," Chesky said. 2. Being a people pleaser Chesky said he found it difficult to hold colleagues accountable when their work fell short. He said he struggled with knowing "when to tell people what to do" and had trouble having hard conversations about an employee's performance. He was "conflict-averse to the point that if somebody wasn't working out, I would not take action," he said. "I felt cautious about being a boss," Chesky said. "I think I was a little bit of a people pleaser . I wanted people to like me." He said he sometimes took on employees' work himself, without realizing he might either be failing to give them enough room to succeed or be propping them up in an unsustainable way. 3. Not saying "No" enough Another mistake Chesky said he made was not saying "No" enough, which left the company without a clear focus. He compared executives pursuing competing priorities to passengers in a car who all want to go somewhere else. "The right way is one way. And one way has to be your way," Chesky said. He said that if an executive takes a team in a direction the CEO does not believe in, the company could be left dealing with the consequences long after that person leaves. "They've gone down a path for two years. Guess what happens? They leave. You might spend five or 10 years fixing or correcting that decision that person made," Chesky said. events.title: Senate goes Democratic in a ‘generational wipeout’ of Trump’s party
events.summary: The News Democrats have secured control of the Senate, a shocking collapse for a Republican majority that started the midterms with what looked like an impregnable red wall of conservative states. There were almost no blemishes for Democrats and few bright spots for Republicans. The GOP lost seats it held in Maine, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, South Carolina, and North Carolina; failed to flip seats in New Hampshire and Georgia; and is now bracing for further losses that could hamper its effort to retake the Senate in 2028, when the map gives both parties pickup opportunities. Other than North Carolina, the GOP-held losses are in states President Donald Trump won handily in 2024. Republicans could afford to lose up to three seats; they’re on track to lose all of their tossup races. Senate seats in Maine and Alaska are also both at risk of flipping. “This is a generational wipeout,” one senior Republican strategist told Semafor. “We are going to have a full-on GOP civil war.” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said his party had pulled off a “generational remake of the Senate map” by winning so many tough states. After touting Democrats’ candidate qualify, he said Americans had reduced the GOP’s red wall to a “pile of bricks.” “Republicans made a choice and followed Trump over the cliff. Some of the time he talked about extraneous things that were ridiculous, but much of the time, he implemented things that raised their costs on electricity, on healthcare, on goods,” Schumer told reporters at a midnight press conference. He said he heard Trump’s remarks saying he’d work with a Democratic Congress but vowed his party is “going to deliver for the people of America with or without the president.” Democrats started Tuesday night with two quick, decisive Senate victories — by Georgia incumbent Jon Ossoff and former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper — that fueled their drive deeper into red territory, to the tune of tens of millions of dollars. Moving Money Around The party’s top Senate super PAC pulled down several weeks’ worth of ads in those two Southern states in recent weeks, per information shared with Semafor, saving $22 million in North Carolina and $11 million in Georgia. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee also scrapped some ad buys in both states down the stretch, decisions that paid off as the party won both seats early on Tuesday night. Democrats felt optimistic about taking the majority earlier in the night than some had expected after the shocking win in South Carolina. Their decision to pull cash out of Georgia and North Carolina helped top Democratic groups approve new Senate spending in states like Mississippi, South Carolina, and Kansas. It also helped the party shore up candidates in the battleground states of Michigan and Maine as Republicans’ deep-pocketed Senate Leadership Fund super PAC poured in astounding sums. “The strength of the Cooper and Ossoff campaigns allowed Senate Majority PAC to re-invest our initial investments into our expanded battleground map. That is a game-changer when Republicans poured money into races,” said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC. Senate Majority PAC spent heavily in Kansas on top of its spending in traditional battlegrounds, while the DSCC put in $500,000 in South Carolina’s Senate race late, according to a person familiar with the buy. That spending followed $500,000 in Mississippi previously reported by Semafor. That was only possible due to the strength of Ossoff and Cooper, who both raised gobs of money and put away their opponents weeks ago. Cooper raised more than $49 million through mid-October, and Ossoff raised more than $100 million. Cooper and Ossoff are both notching considerable, double-digit victories over their respective opponents, Rep. Mike Collins and Michael Whatley. Burgess’s view In Senate races, candidate quality matters. And it can affect all of the other candidates on a party’s slate. Ossoff and Cooper ran such boringly effective campaigns that it allowed Democratic leaders to concentrate their efforts elsewhere. Appointed Sens. Darline Graham of South Carolina and Jon Husted of Ohio proved weak against Annie Andrews and former Sen. Sherrod Brown. And Trump’s decision to back Ken Paxton in Texas blew up spectacularly for Republicans. Notable Republicans were preparing to move their focus away from Georgia and North Carolina as early as September, as we first reported .

events.title: ‘Buckle up’: A defiant White House pins blame elsewhere
events.summary: The News The White House began Tuesday night with cautious optimism. As Democrats started racking up victories, President Donald Trump’s advisers grew more candid — and defiant. Trump spent the weeks before the midterms traveling across the country, hosting 30 events across 20 states in just over a month as he urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” What resulted was a midterm repudiation of Republicans that, as election night wore on, some in the White House were unwilling to own. “President Trump was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot,” a White House official told Semafor, arguing that he “did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves.” Trump himself echoed the sentiment in a Tuesday night social media post : “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The early results on Tuesday night made clear that Trump’s aggressive campaign push wasn’t enough to surmount public frustration with the Iran war and his tariffs’ effect on the cost of living. Democrats quickly flipped North Carolina, held onto New Hampshire and Georgia — and then flipped long-scarlet South Carolina. Trump officials and people close to the White House quickly acknowledged that a massive blue wave was coming. One Trump administration official emphasized how much the war has directly affected Americans. That conflict amplified voters’ frustration as gas prices climbed, and many in Trump’s base felt betrayed by a president who’d campaigned on launching no new wars. Another Trump ally went even further, describing the war as a “disaster” and lamenting that “the Republican party doesn’t understand the Trump coalition, even though it’s 10 years in.” Officials’ efforts to pin their stunning midterm setback on other GOP leaders suggest that the White House has no plans to seek conciliation with ascendant congressional Democratic majorities. “Regardless of how today plays out, President Trump’s resolve to stop the Radical Left is only going to become stronger,” the White House official added. “Buckle up.” Trump told The New York Times late Tuesday that he would accept the results of the election. Preparing for the Worst In the past few weeks, some administration officials have begun looking to hire lawyers to preempt Democrat-led investigations — an early sign that they knew Tuesday night’s results might not go their way. To that point, some advisers indicated to Semafor that the results rolling in so far were not surprising to them. Trump has often pointed over the past months to historical data showing that the party holding total control of Washington tends to perform poorly in midterm elections. Even before polls across the country closed, the White House began circulating talking points highlighting Trump’s efforts on the trail. That underlying message — that the president did what he could to help — largely persisted inside the administration as the losses mounted. One adviser told Semafor that Trump’s thinking remains along those lines: that he did what he could. Several Trump allies also argued to Semafor that poor candidate quality was partly to blame for Republican defeats, though the president openly endorsed several of the candidates who fell short. Main Character Syndrome Trump certainly made himself a central figure in Tuesday’s election. Democrats looked to amplify his calls for voters to pretend he was on the ballot, believing that voters were so dissatisfied with the administration that a midterm referendum on Trump would reward them. Trump watched the election results roll in from the White House East Room alongside Cabinet members, senior staff, and political advisers, another White House official told Semafor. At times, he took to Truth Social to rage against Fox News’ coverage of the evening. Some staffers ordered in from the Cheesecake Factory, an apparent nod to the now-famous quip from former President Barack Obama about Trump’s decorating. Shelby’s view Tonight’s results are a warning sign for the Republican Party as it tries to look past Trump. And they’re likely to surface a question that some of his aides knew they’d inevitably face: whether the coalition that pushed Trump to power can be reconstituted, and what the party will stand for after Trump leaves office. Some Republicans I’ve texted with tonight are already confronting that question. In the weeks and months ahead, anyone in the GOP who’s eyeing a 2028 run will need to look at the midterm results and find ways to run with a different message than Trump — while not angering him or his base.

events.title: Trump turns his ire toward Fox News on election night
events.summary: President Trump lashed out at Fox News on election night, attacking the network's personalities, polling and coverage as voters awaited midterm election results. Why it matters: Trump, who has repeatedly dined with Fox News patriarch Rupert Murdoch and hired talent from the network, has come to expect favorable coverage. But Fox's editorial decisions this election cycle suggest it isn't always willing to oblige. The latest: Under the shadow of a burgeoning blue wave, Trump wrote minutes before midnight Tuesday that "FoxNews [sic] bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse." Driving the news: Trump began the night by criticizing Jessica Tarlov, a Fox co-host and Democratic strategist, saying he'd "go somewhere else" until she was off the air. He reportedly went so far as to text her co-host, Greg Gutfeld, to complain. His ire then turned toward Fox's political polling , claiming, "Every question is a hit job, and every answer is 'BULLSHIT!'" Around half an hour later, he posted that Fox's ratings were down "because they're spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!" Trump pointed to a "new CNN Poll" as an alternative, touting data demonstrating his strength among MAGA Republicans. But the two CNN polling segments he posted earlier in the night were both well over a month old. State of play : Trump's rocky relationship with Fox News has been a source of tension this election season and in previous elections. Fox's coverage of Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has fueled tensions for months, Axios' Alex Isenstadt recently reported . Republicans reportedly worried that Fox was undercutting efforts to brand El-Sayed as far outside the mainstream. In late October, Trump posted that Fox was "spending far too much time putting on the OPPONENTS of Republican Party Candidates, people that love our Country, and have Great Policies and Ideas." He added, "That's the only reason this Race is close, if it is indeed close." The White House and Fox did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Meanwhile, Trump's former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, now a Fox pundit, appeared on the network's election night coverage and said she had just spoken with the president. Reality check: Murdoch, while he is a conservative, has always been passionate about the news business. Fox News did, after all, spark Trumpworld's ire by calling Arizona early for former President Biden in 2020. Zoom in: Fox News' business imperative means focusing on long-term credibility over short-term access and ratings — which took a downward turn last month in the lead-up to the election. The ratings decline could suggest some Republican viewers tuned out as pre-election polls pointed to possible Democratic gains . But for Trump, who has tried to make it a referendum on his popularity, it's personal. Victorian retail stores are actively monitoring jerry can and fuel purchases and reporting suspicious transactions to investigators, police have revealed. The alliance comes amid a wave of arson attacks across Melbourne linked to the extortion of business owners by organised crime gangs. Overnight, a luxury and sports car workshop at Springvale in the city's south-east joined the long list of hospitality, retail and car dealerships to be targeted by offenders. Police said an alarm alerted the owner of Etuners Motorsports to a fire at his Aspen Circuit premises just before midnight. "He subsequently called a friend to assist," Detective Inspector in charge of the Arson and Explosives Squad, Chris Murray, said. "On arrival, the premise was fully engulfed ... I think it took around about an hour to suppress the fire." The workshop was substantially damaged. The fire caused substantial damage to Etuners Motorsport. ( ABC News: Ethan White ) Inspector Murray said police were looking for three people — a driver and two masked offenders wearing hoodies who lit the fire. He said there was a drive-by shooting at the same business last week. "It's a reputable, successful business and therefore organised crime, if they are involved, are looking to exploit that," he said. Inspector Murray said detectives would examine the business's recent client list to see if there were any possible links to the incidents. Fuel monitoring scheme 'paying dividends' Inspector Murray said police had made hundreds of arrests in recent months after numerous firebombings across the city. He said Victoria Police had recently met with representatives from the retail sector, forming an alliance in which stores would actively monitor the sale of jerry cans and fuel. Any suspicious purchases would be reported to detectives. "That's paying great dividends for us," he said. "[Police] have once again raised the stakes and we have increased both overt and covert patrols all around the state. "My message is, if you want to roll the dice, there's every chance you're going to get caught." Detective Inspector Chris Murray says Victoria Police has formed an alliance with the retail sector to detect suspicious purchases of jerry cans and petrol. ( ABC News ) Inspector Murray repeated his warning to young offenders to think carefully before agreeing to carry out an attack for a crime gang. "The stats are pretty dire at the moment — we've got two individuals currently on life support in the Alfred hospital, we've had 20 offenders with serious injuries as a result of the act of arson and we've had one death," he said. He also warned that young offenders were finding themselves in situations which they could not easily walk away from. "We see this time and time again. If they dip their toe in the water and take one of these jobs on, the reality of trying to then remove themselves and say, "I've had enough" is very, very difficult," he said. "We've had families threatened, we've had individuals threatened." events.title: Australian banks lift interest rates
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australia's banks lift mortgage rates in wake of RBA's fifth cash rate hike this year Australia's banks have lifted rates across a range of variable home loan products, business and personal loans and savings accounts. ( AAP: Joel Carrett ) Australia's big four banks have all lifted their interest rates on mortgages and savings accounts. They are responding to the RBA's decision to hike the cash rate to 4.85 per cent. These rate rises will take effect from mid-November, Australia's lenders will apply higher interest rates to variable mortgages in response to the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) decision to hike the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent on Tuesday. RBA governor Michele Bullock announced the cash rate was lifted to tackle persistent inflation in the Australian economy. "It is going to make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer. Their spending can't grow very quickly because their incomes aren't growing very quickly," Ms Bullock said. Set by the RBA, the cash rate is Australia's official interest rate charged on unsecured overnight loans between banks. Put simply, it is how much it costs banks to borrow from each other. When the RBA lifts the cash rate, it becomes more expensive for lenders to borrow from one another. Macquarie Bank was the first to respond, telling customers it would raise interest rates across its variable-rate home loan products by 0.25 per cent within an hour of the RBA announcement, saying customers had until November 19 before the higher rate kicked in. The next day, the big four banks all announced they would lift interest rates on variable home loans by 0.25 per cent. "A 0.25 per cent per annum increase to variable home loan rates will increase monthly repayments by approximately $79 on a variable home loan of $500,000 for an owner occupier loan with principal and interest repayments," ANZ said in a statement. Westpac, NAB, ANZ and CBA will apply the new rate from November 13. Westpac's chief executive, consumer, Carolyn McCann said the majority of its customers were ahead in mortgage repayments. In statements, all of the banks said customers under financial strain should contact their bank as soon as possible. Those with money in the right savings accounts will enjoy earning more interest when banks lift their rates in the middle of the month. But as the ABC has revealed , banks have been slower to pass on rate rises to savers and often require customers to meet a number of conditions before they can "unlock" the highest rates on offer. Comparison site Canstar said if those conditions were not met, customers reverted to a base rate of around 0.10 per cent. Not using the right account, missing monthly minimum deposits or not meeting withdrawal conditions on the account could cause the rate to plummet to the base rate. events.title: Britain’s housing market unlikely to recover until 2028, says Savills
events.summary: House prices forecast to fall by 1.5% next year as Middle East war keeps mortgage rates higher for longer Britain’s sluggish housing market is not expected to recover until 2028 as higher mortgage rates linked to the war in the Middle East deter buyers and weigh on prices. The property firm Savills said average house prices were expected to drift lower during the rest of 2026 and fall by 1.5% in 2027, as the prolonged conflict undermines buyers’ confidence and keeps mortgage rates higher for longer. Improving economic prospects and mortgage affordability are expected to support a recovery from 2028. Savills expects house prices to rise by 15.8% – or £56,500 on average – over the five years to 2031, with values starting to recover in the second half of 2028. Nationwide said last week that UK house prices had risen by an annual rate of just 0.5% in October, the slowest pace in more than two years. The average price for a property in the UK stood at £273,566, the lender said . The Bank of England is widely expected to increase interest rates from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, putting further pressure on mortgage rates, after UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September. More than 2.3m UK households face a sharp rise in mortgage payments as they come off fixed-rate deals in 2027. Emily Williams, the director of residential research at Savills, said: “The drawn-out conflict in the Middle East has pushed back the prospect of meaningful mortgage rate relief, which will weigh on buyer sentiment and affordability. “We expect this will suppress activity and put pressure on prices next year. But this is unlikely to trigger a sharper correction. “Most homeowners have already absorbed higher borrowing costs since late 2022, with relatively few still needing to refinance directly from rates below 2%, and the labour market remains resilient.” The strongest five-year house price growth in percentage terms is forecast across northern England, Wales and Scotland, supported by relative affordability and economic prospects, according to the prediction. Savills expects first-time buyers to lead the recovery from 2028, helped by deposit affordability and government initiatives, which include the Your First Home scheme . It expects house price growth to accelerate in the second half of 2028, reaching 3.5% for the year as a whole.

events.title: How wall-climbing robots could help Gulf energy producers recover from attacks
events.summary: US technology company Gecko Robotics is deploying a new generation of wall-climbing robots across Adnoc's energy facilities to detect structural weaknesses and assess damage, after the Iran war exposed vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure across the Gulf. The company, which unveiled its Raptor robot exclusively to The National at Adipec in Abu Dhabi, is also considering manufacturing the machines in the UAE as it expands its partnership with Adnoc , including a new agreement with Adnoc Onshore. "When you think about that as it relates to post-attacks, that's where you should be able to think about Gecko's ability to understand what sort of damage has occurred, so that it increases how quickly you can get assets back up and running," Jake Loosararian, the company's chief executive and co-founder, told The National . The robot, which uses sensors and sound waves to identify structural faults without taking facilities offline, is three to five times faster than its predecessor and can collect millions of data points during inspections. The company claims it is up to 50 times faster than competitors' robots. Energy under threat Since the beginning of the Iran war , energy infrastructure has been attacked across the region. Demand for the robotics firm's services has been high, with large contracts awarded for military applications. The company is also expanding its military business, signing a $300 million agreement with the US Navy last week for robotics applications. The military is using robotics and AI to improve the readiness and performance of critical assets, a concept that also applies to energy infrastructure during regional conflicts, Mr Loosararian said. The technology provides data on "what to fix, how to fix it", while helping extend equipment lifespans and maintenance cycles, he added. Meet Raptor Raptor, Gecko's new wall-climbing robot, scans the surface and captures millions of data points during its inspections. "Raptor allows for a 50 x reduction in the cost of data collection, while also increasing the fidelity by roughly the same order of magnitude," he said. The robot is said to save time and money for companies, which do not have to take facilities offline for assessment; the advanced monitoring technology uses sensors and sound waves for detection, which is fed back to the digital layer that maps the assets. The company is focused on safety and building "better tools" for people. "Robotics are essential to ensure that resilience and readiness is possible in a world where we don't have a lot of these skilled workforces. And by the way, we should be building technology that makes people safe. And that's exactly what these robots are doing," he said. Changing priorities Mr Loosararian said energy companies need to adopt the latest technologies if they want to lead the sector. "If you don't have a path that leads you towards a more AI-native, robotic-native way of running infrastructure, you are operating in the ancient past, and that ancient path will lead you to demise," he said. "The energy companies that are looking more and more like tech companies are going to be the ones that win the day." UAE manufacturing ambitions Gecko is considering manufacturing robots in the UAE as demand grows, allowing it to develop and test the technology closer to the energy facilities where it is deployed. The company already deploys tens of robots a day in the region. "There's an abundance of energy infrastructure in the UAE," Mr Loosararian said. Building technology close to operating facilities would help avoid "the death of a lab", where equipment developed in controlled environments fails to perform as expected in real-world conditions, he said. The UAE is also seeking to expand local robotics manufacturing as part of its industrial development strategy. "Robotics is feeding a lot of sectors today, and it's enhancing and expediting production. It's becoming a big demand, not just for the production part, but also in ease of doing business for the end users," Ibtisam Al Saadi, acting assistant undersecretary for the industrial development sector at the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology, told The National . She said interest among young Emiratis in robotics programming and manufacturing was growing, alongside locally manufactured drones and 3D printing. Gecko's expansion also includes an agreement with Adnoc Onshore, expected to be announced on Wednesday, to deploy robotics and AI models for critical infrastructure.

events.title: House Republicans torch each other over "brutal" midterms losses
events.summary: SHREVEPORT, La. — The GOP's election-night defeat has unleashed a wave of finger-pointing inside the House Republican conference, with members questioning whether Speaker Mike Johnson or any of the other top deputies can survive next week's leadership elections. Why it matters: Johnson spent months insisting Republicans would defy the odds and keep the House. But after losing the majority, he cast the defeat as all but inevitable, an explanation unlikely to satisfy Republicans ready for a new leadership slate. One House Republican told Axios that every member of GOP leadership will face a challenger because of the election results. Another said the losses have created a major opening for Republicans looking to challenge the current leadership team. A third said they no longer see a path for Johnson to remain atop the conference. Driving the news: At Johnson's election-night watch party in his hometown of Shreveport, the mood grew increasingly somber as it became clear Democrats would secure the House majority. Johnson remained offstage until just before 11pm Eastern time, even after networks projected Democrats would win control of the chamber. In a soundtrack to the GOP's election-night defeat, "White on the Ground" by the Kruse Brothers played over the speakers to a subdued crowd just before Johnson took the stage. "It's only happened twice in 90 years that a sitting president has picked up or held seats for his party in that first two-year cycle," Johnson told supporters Tuesday night. "It's very, very difficult to overcome, and it looks like history will be kept here tonight." Behind the scenes: House Republicans were already privately unloading on their leaders Tuesday night, with some arguing the scale of the party's losses demands a change at the top. "I think Iran, ICE, inflation, fuel prices, lack of focus on pocketbook issues all played a part of this," one member told Axios. Asked for a vibe check, one member simply texted Axios: "Brutal." The scale of the losses was underscored by the defeat of NRCC Chair Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) — the man tasked with preserving the Republican majority who couldn't hold onto his own seat. Zoom in: Johnson spent months crisscrossing the country in a last-ditch effort to save Republicans' fragile majority, traveling to more than 40 congressional districts across 22 states. Johnson publicly insisted in October that he intended to remain the top House Republican even if his party lost the majority, but he has yet to formally declare any plans to run for minority leader. Trump praised Johnson in an interview with Politico on Tuesday, but stopped short of endorsing him for the job. "He's going to have to make that decision," Trump said of Johnson. What we're watching: House Republicans are scheduled to hold leadership elections Nov. 10, with candidates required to declare by Nov. 6. Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) are also being floated as potential contenders.

events.title: Democrats poised to claim a House majority bigger than they’d hoped
events.summary: The News House Democratic leaders are preparing to welcome moderate members from across the country and a majority big enough to manage comfortably and contain a restive progressive wing. After years of seeing hardline Republicans torment Speakers Kevin McCarthy and Mike Johnson by maximizing their leverage in a slim House majority, Democrats are poised to make large enough gains to insulate themselves against unruly blocs in their caucus — particularly on the left. It might still be days until the full size of the majority is known. But Democrats are pushing into redder territory; in a shocking development for the GOP, its House campaigns chief, Rep. Richard Hudson, was on track to lose his deep-red North Carolina seat as of late Tuesday night. Democrats were leading late Tuesday in several of the Texas seats that House Republicans redrew at President Donald Trump’s behest to be more favorable to their party. They were ahead, too, in all four of the Florida seats that Republicans redrew. And in Ohio, where Republicans attempted to draw out Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur, the veteran lawmaker was leading her race; other Republicans, like Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, were trailing in early returns. Democrats have dealt with jitters for months now that an incoming progressive left could vote against Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ speakership bid, but the cushion provided by a larger House majority could all but moot a rebellion from the left both in an internal caucus election and the full speaker vote. The mood was jubilant at Jeffries’ watch party in Washington, DC, on Tuesday night, with cheers for every flipped race as TV networks called the House for Democrats surprisingly early in the night. Jeffries and Democratic leaders had taken a personal interest in defending redistricted territory and in recruiting candidates to run in redder seats. “Today begins the great American Comeback. In the North, in the South, in the East, in the West, in the Midwest, from sea to shining sea, people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,” Jeffries said Tuesday night. “They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January.” ‘How to Lead’ Centrist Democrats are already trumpeting their role in recapturing the House majority. “I am feeling really good. New Dems are showing how to lead,” said Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill., who chairs the New Democrat Coalition. The majority of the DCCC’s “Red to Blue” candidates this cycle were backed by the centrist bloc, which put substantial resources behind its candidates, too. Democratic leaders still face huge questions about how they’ll run the House floor and counter Trump. They’ve talked up an early agenda centered around reversing cuts to Medicaid and restoring lapsed healthcare tax credits, but could face pressure from the progressive left to put up a more ambitious plan. The jockeying for influence is already beginning. Leading up to Tuesday evening, Democrats from across the ideological spectrum were preemptively laying claim to their roles in helping flip the House and their visions for what a Democratic majority might be capable of doing. Progressives like Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, said they wanted to vote on legislation that they would dare the Senate to filibuster or Trump to veto. “This is a mandate to deliver big change. No complacency,” he said in a statement. But with the House majority likely padded by redder territory this cycle, Democrats will face fierce internal resistance to progressive policy ideas like Medicare for All. Most candidates from purple districts, with the exception of some backed by the Progressive Caucus, have shied away from such ambitious proposals. Fred Wellman, one of those candidates who took operatives off-guard by triumphing in a red district in Missouri, told Semafor he wanted “to work towards a Medicare for All system, but right now we need to stop the bleeding.” “A lot of people were doubting us, and all I have to say at this point is ‘I told you so, you should’ve listened,’” he quipped. Nicholas’s view For all of the drama over individual races this cycle, Republicans across the country couldn’t outrun the overall environment. With diesel and gas prices still spiking through Election Day, and Trump’s approval rating sagging, voters were ready to punish Republicans. Democrats are on track for a majority far bigger than the 10-seat margin they’d publicly predicted heading into Tuesday. Now comes the hard part. Most in the party put aside their ideological differences over the last few years in pursuit of recapturing the House, but Democratic leaders are going to face tough decisions about their legislative agenda, all set against the backdrop of the 2028 presidential election.

events.title: India’s EloElo nabs $80M from NBCUniversal to bet on the country’s rising microdrama market
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. More than 118 million users watch microdramas every month as the serialized format has taken off in India. EloElo’s Story TV is one of the top apps for microdramas, with over 33 million active users , according to analysts. Banking on that scale, the company has raised $80 million in Series C from Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal. This round brings its total fundraising to $130 million, with a valuation of $500 million. As people spend more time on platforms hosting verticalized videos, serialized content has become popular in multiple geographies, including the U.S., China, and India, with Hollywood celebrities like Issa Rae, James Franco, and Kim Kardashian investing in and starring in the format . Given India’s massive internet population of more than a billion and the country’s appetite for entertainment content, it presents a big market opportunity, with analysts expecting the industry to cross $3-$4 billion in annual revenue by 2030 . Last year, dedicated apps like Story TV, Kuku TV, and Quick TV were among the top downloaded video streaming apps in the country. Founded in 2020 by former Flipkart exec Saurabh Pandey, the Story TV platform has taken off in the last few years with a catalog of over 5,000 titles in six languages. Pandey told TechCrunch that because of the snackable content format, users log 95 minutes on the app on average through multiple sessions in a day. “I fundamentally believe that the next billion users will probably not grow up on a diet of watching television; they will grow up on a diet of watching content on their phones, right? And this content has to be, and this entertainment, designed very differently. It’s not going to be appointment viewing. It’s going to be within certain slots throughout the day. And a lot of this was earlier solved for short clips, but serialized storytelling was never solved,” Pandey said about the microdrama format. He believes that there still will be a place for big-screen viewing with family or friends, but the majority of entertainment consumption would be done through mobile. All microdrama platforms compete against platforms like YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok, where creators are posting content for free. Some of them are also creating a way for creators to post serialized content . Pandey thinks that producing quality content on the platform will entice users to choose StoryTV over other free platforms. The company points to its partnerships, such as the one with Indian TV production company Balaji Telefilms, to produce content. The company offers different kinds of subscriptions ranging from monthly, quarterly, and yearly to unlock content. It also offers some free content supported by ads, which might not be as lucrative a medium to make money as subscriptions, according to reports . Monetization is a challenge in India, as users often stick around for free content, but few convert to paid users. A report from analyst firm Redseer indicates that more than 40 million people have paid for microdrama at least once, but only 15-17 million users pay for it on a monthly basis. A separate survey by Ormax Media suggested that 72% of people haven’t ever paid while consuming microdrama . All microdrama platforms want to have enough supply to engage different audiences and want to involve AI to solve that. Some platforms, like Google-backed Kuku, want to improve workflows and create more content , and some platforms like Dashverse’s Shortfree want to use video AI models to create serialized clips . At the moment, StoryTV falls into the first camp with its Dolphin AI platform. Started as an internal tool to improve video creation, the company is now planning to make the tool widely available. It can act as an editor with templates and an array of models to create images, audio, and video, according to its website. EloElo’s vision is to have people use this tool for marketing campaigns and ads as well. Notably, while Indian platforms like Pocket and Kuku have built AI tools and given them to creators, it is likely to accelerate their content pipeline. But at InVideo, there hasn’t been a scaled effort to provide a good alternative to CapCut or Instagram Edits to creators from India. Pandey believes that human involvement is still paramount to producing good stories, and AI tools are still creative directors for steering. “My belief in involving AI is that AI is a really fast race car where AI is the engine, but you need an extremely capable Formula One driver to be on the steering wheel. That, for me, is the creative director or the showrunner. AI is supposed to work with them, augmenting their skill set. AI can help write stories, but so far the best stories I have loved have all had a very high human x AI element to it,” he said.

events.title: Josh Turek delivers flips control of Senate with Iowa upset
events.summary: Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson in a major upset Tuesday, becoming the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Iowa since 2008, the AP projected and sealing Democratic control of the chamber. Why it matters: Turek's victory delivers Democrats control of the Senate — and signals a political backlash against Republicans in a state Trump won comfortably just two years ago. The big picture: Turek's victory breaks the GOP's hold on both of Iowa's Senate seats for the first time since Democrat Tom Harkin left office in 2015, marking a major breakthrough for Democrats in a state that has shifted right. State of play: The Cook Political Report rated the race a toss-up after moving it left during the campaign as mounting frustration over rising costs, Trump's tariffs and the Iran war put Republicans on the defensive. Zoom in: Turek, a Council Bluffs state lawmaker and Paralympic medalist, built his campaign around affordability and appeals to working-class and independent voters. He criticized Trump's tariffs and other administration policies that he argued were hurting Iowa farmers and families. He also made government ethics and corruption a central theme, including support for a ban on congressional stock trading. Between the lines: Republicans had held both of Iowa's U.S. Senate seats since Harkin retired, while GOP candidates have increasingly dominated statewide races. The bottom line: Turek's win offers Democrats a potential roadmap for competing in increasingly Republican states — and raises questions about the GOP's political strength heading into 2028.

( ABC News: Fletch Yeung ) Major Australian retailer David Jones's days could be numbered, as shopping centre Westfield confirms the department store chain has not paid rent since September and is in breach of its contracts. A decision on the future of David Jones could be made within the next 24 hours. The ABC understands the three-person board of the 188-year-old retailer will need to meet imminently to decide whether to put David Jones into administration. Scentre Group, the owner of Westfield, issued a stock market update, revealing its financial exposure to the embattled department store. David Jones has a network of 43 stores in Australia and New Zealand. ( AAP: Dan Himbrechts ) It noted the chain occupied space at 17 Westfield locations and said David Jones had paid "all rent up to 30 September 2026". Scentre CEO Elliott Rusanow said David Jones had not paid rent since September and was "therefore in breach". Lifeline rejected, says Westfield owner Mr Rusanow today said the shopping centre group had offered a lifeline but was knocked back by the private equity owners of David Jones. "We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital Partners that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading and that offer has disappointingly been rejected by them," Mr Rusanow said. David Jones was acquired by Anchorage Capital Partners from South African group Woolworths Holdings in late 2022. Scentre's ASX filing noted that David Jones had provided $45 million in bank guarantees for its stores across the Westfield Australia and New Zealand portfolio, of which Scentre's share was about $30 million, equivalent to eight months' gross rent. David Jones's key lender has chipped in extra cash to the store to stock up ahead of Christmas. ( ABC News ) David Jones has a network of 43 stores across Australia and New Zealand, with flagship stores in Sydney and Melbourne CBDs, with about 50 million in-store visits a year and 5 million customers, according to its owners. "The fact that we've had this massive shock has meant that we're poorer and that's what people are feeling," she said. The ABC has contacted David Jones CEO Erica Berchtold directly for comment.
