events.title: Asian equities and US stock futures slump amid blue sweep in US polls
events.summary: Live updates: Follow the latest news on US midterms US stock futures and Asian equities tumbled along with the dollar as early results from the midterm polls rippled through markets, threatening President Donald Trump’s agenda as the Democratic party looked poised for a sweep. Futures for the benchmark S&P 500 index slid 1.06 per cent, at 6.30am time, giving up an earlier 0.5 per cent advance, as early election results started rolling on Wednesday. Futures fell 1.9 per cent on the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100, and dipped 0.7 per cent on the Dow Jones index. The US dollar fell against its group of 10 peers. While futures fell, US Treasuries benefited, with the yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note declining seven basis points to 4.89 per cent, according to Bloomberg data. Stock-index futures slid amid investors concerns that Democratic control of the House and Senate would result in tighter regulations and closer scrutiny of the tech-heavy sectors, including artificial intelligence companies. Treasuries, however, stand to gain as political haggling in Washington is bound to limit government spending, easing borrowing concerns. “Early headlines and prediction markets are suggesting a rising probability of a blue wave,” Bloomberg quoted Andrew Ticehurst, a senior rates strategist at Nomura Holdings, as saying. “That scenario is generally regarded as being negative for the dollar and positive for US Treasuries. Markets are reacting consistently with that in early Asia trading.” A blue wave in US politics refers to a large electoral victory for the Democratic Party, whose traditional political colour is blue. Asian stocks In Asia, equity benchmarks slid, reversing earlier gains and taking their cue from US stock futures. MSCI's broadest ⁠index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan fell 0.5 per cent. South Korea's Kopsi slid 3.6 per cent, giving up its earlier gains of more than 3 per cent. Japan's Nikkei index fell 3.5 per cent, while the Hang Seng index in Hong Kong slipped 0.22 per cent. China’s Shanghai SE index also retreated by 0.21 per cent, while stocks in India dropped 0.13 per cent. "Markets appear to be pricing in the possibility ​of ⁠a stronger-than-expected Democratic showing, which could reduce expectations ‌for further fiscal stimulus," Reuters quoted Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo in Singapore, as saying. Historic sweep Democrats were projected to win big in Tuesday's midterms, flipping both a Senate seat and a House of Representatives seat in North Carolina and picking up a governorship in Georgia. As of 9.45pm Washington time, Democrats were projected to win 45 Senate seats compared to Republicans' 36, with 19 races still to be called, according to AP. Democrats have also flipped the North Carolina seat with a win by Roy Cooper. The party needs 51 seats to gain a majority. The Democrats have also taken control of the US House of Representatives, CNN and CBS projected on Tuesday, in a momentous development that will reshape the course of Mr Trump's final two years in power. The Democrats only needed to flip three Republican-held seats to take control of the chamber and initial results showed they had easily surpassed that threshold. Control of the House means the Democratic will block Mr Trump's legislative agenda and open investigations into his administration's policies.

events.title: Emaar offers Dh15 a share for 100 per cent control of Emaar Development
events.summary: Dubai property developer Emaar Properties intends to make a voluntary cash offer to acquire up to 100 per cent of the shares in its listed unit Emaar Development that it does not already own. The biggest listed developer in the emirate is offering Dh15 ($4.08) per share to investors to take full control of its subsidiary. The proposed offer is subject to approval by Emaar Properties’ board, the company said in a filing on Wednesday to the Dubai Financial Market, where its shares are traded. The offer covers shares not already owned by Emaar Properties and its indirect wholly owned subsidiary, Emirates Property Holdings, according to the bourse filing. With the construction unit valued at more than Dh60 billion at current share price, the potential transaction could cost Emaar Properties as much as Dh12.6 billion, according to Bloomberg. Emaar Properties, the developer of the landmark Burj Khalifa in Dubai, currently owns just over 79 per cent of Emaar Development. Emaar had previously announced plans to increase its ownership of Emaar Development. In March 2022, its board approved a proposal to raise its stake in the subsidiary by up to three percentage points. Emaar raised Dh4.82 billion from the sale of a 20 per cent stake in its development business in November 2017, which at the time was the largest Dubai listing in three years. Emaar Development, which also trades on the DFM, is the property development arm of Emaar, specialising in residential communities and build-to-sell projects in Dubai. Its portfolio includes developments such as Dubai Hills Estate, Arabian Ranches, Emaar South and The Valley. The latest move comes as Dubai continues to navigate the economic fallout from the Iran war, which is now in its ninth month. The company’s ownership structure also shifted in May, when investment company Dubai Holding became the largest shareholder in Emaar Properties after acquiring a 22.27 per cent stake in the developer from the Investment Corporation of Dubai (ICD). One of the largest real estate developers in the Middle East, Emaar has a portfolio spanning residential, commercial, hospitality and retail assets across the Middle East and North Africa, Asia and Europe. Emaar, which has 90,000 units under production globally in 18 markets, is weathering the wave of geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds on the fundamental strength of its business. In September, Emaar founder Mohamed Alabbar said that the property market in Dubai was set for a “nice balance” next year despite softening due to the Iran war, as the sector goes through a period of adjustment. In June, Emaar said it would unveil an “extraordinary” Dh200 billion megaproject in Dubai, set to house nearly 150,000 people. Emaar Properties reported a nearly 9 per cent annual increase in its second-quarter profit, as revenue rose during the period despite geopolitical uncertainty. Net profit attributable to owners of the company for the three months to the end of June climbed to Dh3.7 billion ($1 billion), while revenue for the three-month period rose 18 per cent to Dh11.5 billion. In the first half of 2026, net profit surged 22 per cent annually to Dh8.7 billion, as revenue rose 21 per cent to nearly Dh24 billion. Emaar Development also reported a sharp rise in second-quarter profit to Dh2.6 billion, up 43.5 per cent. Revenue for the period surged 32 per cent to Dh6.5 billion. First-half profit rose 48 per cent to Dh5.5 billion and revenue climbed 34 per cent to Dh13.3 billion. Its property sales during the period reached 22.4 billion.

events.title: Chinese stock investors stay on the sidelines even as state intervention gathers pace
events.summary: Leveraged traders trimmed holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October Chinese investors refrained from bets on stocks this week, even after Beijing unveiled a litany of measures to shore up confidence in the world’s second-largest equity market. Leveraged traders trimmed their holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October, according to official data. The retreat in retail enthusiasm contrasted with the government ramping up its efforts to prop up stocks, including liquidity injections through two monetary tools and reported suspensions of new share sales to keep a lid on supply. The divergence illustrates investors’ unease over whether the latest bout of government interventions will drive sustained gains in the markets, which are grappling with weak domestic demand and the fallout from an AI stock rout in the US. Investment banks including Bank of America and Macquarie said that state intervention might stabilise sentiment, but would fall short of fuelling a fresh rally.

The house of Zen on Tuesday announced its Q3 2026 results, which saw it grow revenue 45 percent year-over-year to $13.4 billion. The company’s Data Center segment won $8.5 billion of revenue, up 97 percent year-over-year. Sales of silicon in AMD’s client and gaming segment slid eight percent to $3.7 billion, a worse fall than the five percent fall that helped to sink Intel’s share price . Intel, AMD’s great rival in the x86 market, offered revenue guidance of $15 billion to $16 billion for its next quarter, which would represent almost no growth. AMD, by contrast, told investors it expects around $17 billion of revenue next quarter. CEO Lisa Su predicted even better days are ahead. “We think 2027 is going to be a very strong momentum year for both the CPU business as well as the data center AI business,” she said on the company’s earnings call. “We have said the overall company will grow greater than 80 percent, and for the data center CPU business, we will about double, and for the data center AI business, it will significantly more than double.” Su said AMD is confident its supply chain can meet that demand. “We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year,” she said. “We are also deepening our collaboration with our supply chain partners and investing alongside them to secure the long-term capacity our growth will require.” The CEO added that AMD has “strong confidence in our ability to sustain exceptional revenue growth for years to come, with earnings growing even faster.” If those predictions are correct, AMD will likely accelerate away from Intel to become the leading provider of x86 processors after years of challenging Chipzilla's lead. Intel would still have higher overall revenue, due to its foundry operations, but in terms of revenue earned from selling chips, AMD would become the market leader. AMD is arguably already the server CPU technology leader, and while it is second to Nvidia in the GPU market has trounced Intel. Even AMD's declining client and gaming revenue has an upside because it was the gaming part of the portfolio that created the problem. PC chip sales rose seven percent year-over-year to $2.9 billion. Su said strong sales of Ryzen mobile processors drove that growth. “Commercial is becoming a larger part of our client business as large enterprises adopt Ryzen PRO PCs across their employee base,” she said, pointing to strong adoption at the world’s largest banks, automotive companies, and healthcare concerns. Big corporate buyers are often a source of bigger profits and/or steadier revenue, so AMD looks to be taking the cream off the top of the PC market rather than scrounging for SMB and retail scraps. Investors liked what they heard, sending AMD’s share price up by around five percent in after hours trading.

( ABC News: Matt Garrick ) China Southern Airlines will suspend its direct flights between Darwin and China. The direct route between Darwin and Guangzhou launched less than a year ago. The airline's final scheduled flight to Guangzhou will be on December 3. China Southern Airlines will suspend its direct Darwin to China flights after a year of operation, making it the latest in a suite of scrapped international routes out of Darwin. The Darwin to Guangzhou route launched in December last year and will cease at the end of its current season, with the final flight leaving Darwin on December 3. It was the only flight operating directly between China and the NT, and the farthest-reaching route out of the Territory. A spokesperson from the Airport Development Group (ADG), which operates Darwin International Airport, said the call was a commercial decision by China Southern. Direct flights from Darwin to Guangzhou were only introduced in December last year. ( ABC News: Matt Garrick ) "Although ADG is disappointed by the airline's decision, decisions regarding individual routes and service schedules are commercial decisions made by airlines," they said. "Travellers from Darwin continue to have connectivity to China and other international destinations through established hubs including Singapore, Denpasar and Dili." The flight is the latest in a series of short-lived international routes out of Darwin. In 2025, Qantas launched a direct flight between Darwin and Singapore while AirAsia introduced services from Darwin to Bali and Kuala Lumpur. By June 2026, Qantas had reduced its Darwin to Singapore flights to cover the peak tourism season only, while AirAsia had pulled out of Darwin entirely. Darwin International Airport continues to connect passengers to Singapore, Denpasar and Dili. ( Facebook: Darwin International Airport ) The ADG spokesperson said it is exploring other international flight routes out of the Territory capital. "ADG continues to actively engage with airline carriers and other aviation partners about opportunities to strengthen Darwin's international connectivity," they said. Announced in August 2025, the Darwin to Guangzhou route was heralded as a boost to tourism which would deliver 52,000 seats between the two cities each year. In April this year, Tourism Minister Marie-Clare Boothby led a delegation of tourism operators to Guangzhou for talks with travel agents. "This mission was about showing that we are serious about growing our share of the Chinese traveller market," she said at the time. Marie-Clare Boothby said the Darwin to China route was about growing tourism in the NT. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi ) "China — and particularly Guangzhou and the wider Guangdong province — offers the Territory a high-value and highly concentrated market." Northern Territory Chamber of Commerce CEO Glen Hingley, however, says the axing impacts more than just the tourism industry. Mr Hingley said stakeholders across the NT needed to collaborate, making flight routes in and out of Darwin viable for trade as well as tourism. "It's important that for these airlines when they make decisions to come here that they're not just looking at passengers, they're looking at the freight opportunities," he said. Glen Hingley says airline operators should be looking at freight opportunities as well as passengers. ( ABC News: Marcus Kennedy ) "We're the only destination that was flying a 737, the rest of Australia has wide-bodied aircraft, so they're able to make it work from a freight perspective." Mr Hingley said there was ample opportunity for the NT aviation industry and that overcoming the challenge of its small population required cooperation across sectors. "We've got to not operate in silos, whether that's different government agencies, different industry bodies, different industry sectors, and of course the airport," he said. "We're shouting at clouds if we're waiting for the federal government to intervene.

events.title: Talarico flips Texas Senate seat in historic Democratic breakthrough
events.summary: Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' closely watched U.S. Senate race, delivering a historic breakthrough for Democrats in a state Republicans have dominated for decades. Why it matters: Talarico's victory ends the nation's longest Democratic drought in statewide elections and flips a critical Senate seat as Democrats fight for control of the chamber. The Austin-area state representative becomes the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. His win also marks the first Democratic victory in a Texas statewide election since 1994, a stunning reversal in a state President Trump carried by nearly 14 points in 2024. What they're saying: "We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We just showed that a politics of division is no match for the politics of love," Talarico told thousands of supporters in Austin. "And we just sent a message to every billionaire mega donor, every trillionaire megadonor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system in this state, in this country — power belongs to the people." The big picture: The race became the nation's most expensive Senate battle after Texas Attorney General Paxton defeated longtime incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary, with massive spending from both parties . Republican leaders had warned that Paxton's nomination could jeopardize the seat, and the party poured enormous resources into defending it. On the campaign trail: Talarico, a former public school teacher and Presbyterian seminarian, built his campaign around affordability, public education and criticism of wealthy donors' influence over politics. Paxton, a three-term Texas attorney general and close ally of President Trump , emphasized immigration enforcement and conservative policies. Between the lines: Paxton's candidacy exposed divisions within the Texas GOP, with party leaders initially warning that nominating the attorney general could endanger a seat Republicans had held for decades. Paxton defeated Cornyn in the May Republican primary runoff after securing Trump's endorsement, setting up the costly general election battle. His campaign was also shadowed by years of legal and ethical controversies, including his 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House. The state Senate later acquitted him. The backdrop: Democrats have spent decades trying to turn Texas blue, with former Rep. Beto O'Rourke coming within roughly 220,000 votes of unseating Republican Sen. Ted Cruz in 2018. Talarico's win marks a breakthrough for a party that has repeatedly fallen short in statewide contests, even as Texas' population and political landscape have changed. What's next: Talarico will take office in January.

events.title: ‘Not enough energy’ for the world due to geopolitical tensions, says Ducab chief
events.summary: The world needs to diversify its energy sources as geopolitical tensions put pressure on supplies and costs, the chief executive of UAE cable maker Ducab has said. Charles Edouard Mellagui warned that higher prices for raw materials could ultimately reach consumers’ bills. Speaking to The National at Adipec 2026 in Abu Dhabi this week, Mr Mellagui said oil and gas alone would not be enough to meet growing demand. “We have to prepare ourselves to add more energy [sources] because oil and gas are not enough,” he said. “We will need solar. We need wind. We need nuclear. We need battery storage.” He said geopolitical conflicts were putting the global energy system under strain, disrupting the movement of materials and equipment needed to maintain and expand supplies. “Given the geopolitical situation and crisis worldwide, there is not enough energy for the eight billion people in the world,” Mr Mellagui said. “That’s why we see the crisis going through the roof.” He added that geopolitical tensions “exacerbated” the problem and pushed countries to become sovereign in terms of energy. However, he believes the UAE was well prepared. For residents, the pressure could eventually be felt through costs, he said. “At first, they will see it in the bill because if you have raw material going up, of course, at the end of the day, the price will escalate.” Factories stayed open Despite disruption to international trade, Mr Mellagui said Ducab continued manufacturing cables used to carry electricity to homes, businesses and major infrastructure. He credited government support and the availability of ports, roads, lorries and trains for helping the company receive materials from overseas. “We have been able to bring raw materials from all over the world ... and we are able to produce the cable, and we did not close [our operations even] for a single day,” he said. He added that geopolitical tensions can make it difficult to bring the raw material to manufacture and to export, complicating the whole supply chain, while also highlighting the importance of producing locally. Ducab buys more than 40 per cent of its raw materials locally. Mr Mellagui said domestic suppliers had an important role in supporting production when importing became more difficult. “When you cannot import, or you import in a difficult situation, what matters is your ability as a country to produce locally,” he said. The company would still need international suppliers, he added. Local manufacturing was only one part of securing supplies. More equipment made in the UAE Mr Mellagui's comments followed Adnoc ’s announcement on Sunday about offering more than Dh60 billion ($16 billion) in local manufacturing opportunities through 2030. This includes electrical and automation systems, pumps, chemicals, piping and other equipment. Adnoc said producing more of these goods locally would shorten delivery times and reduce exposure to global supply disruptions. Mr Mellagui said demand from major businesses could help strengthen local manufacturers. Delivering power to growing communities New homes, industrial developments and AI data centres are adding to the need for electricity and the infrastructure that carries it. Mr Mellagui said several energy sources would be needed to meet demand. Ducab has supplied cables for major UAE projects including the Al Dhafra Solar Project, Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park and Barakah Nuclear Energy Plant . Alongside expanding generation, the industry needed to reduce electricity waste, Mr Mellagui said. Ducab is developing cable designs intended to minimise those losses. He added that energy needs to be secure and available, but also affordable. Rising raw-material costs can push prices up further along the supply chain. AI ‘paying the bill back’ The growth of AI has increased attention on the electricity consumed by data centres. Mr Mellagui said the technology is now helping energy companies become more efficient. “AI is paying the bill back,” he said. “It has learnt, developed, consumed a lot of power, a lot of energy, and now, we are asking this AI to restitute to us what it has learnt.”

events.title: Journalist quizzed over 'nail in the coffin' remark at Jones trial
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Alan Jones trial hears journalist said police involvement would be 'nail in the coffin' for story Journalist Kate McClymont has given evidence for a second day. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) A journalist who broke stories on allegations against broadcaster Alan Jones has been quizzed in his trial for a second day over messages she sent to a complainant's mother. Kate McClymont wrote to a mother of one of the complainants that police involvement in the case would be "the nail in the coffin" for the story. Mr Jones denies indecently assaulting or sexually touching several young men who reported their allegations to the journalist and then later police. The journalist who broke stories alleging Alan Jones had indecently assaulted several men told the mother of one complainant that police involvement in her son's matter would be "the nail in the coffin" and she hoped "shit does hit the fan" for the radio host. NSW Sexual Violence Helpline on 1800 424 017 NSW Victims Services on 1800 633 063 Bravehearts (support for child sexual abuse survivors) on 1800 272 831 Child Protection Helpline on 132 111 MARS Australia (for men affected by rape and sexual abuse) on (07) 3857 1222 National Survivors Foundation on 1300 124 433 Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. Sydney Morning Herald chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont has been questioned about her stories on former 2GB host Alan Jones, who has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching in the NSW Local Court. Ms McClymont has been cross-examined for a second day, and has been asked about text messages she sent to the mother of one young man, Complainant A, who alleged he was 17 when Mr Jones kissed him without his consent. The Downing Centre Local Court trial heard Ms McClymont had already published her first story with allegations about Mr Jones when she came into contact with Complainant A's mother, who told the journalist that her son had made a statement to police in 2018, but asked that it was not investigated further at that time. In a snippet of a recorded phone call between Ms McClymont and the complainant's mother, Ms McClymont can be heard saying, "this would be an absolute nail in the coffin if the police were involved". Ms McClymont's messages have been the focus of Wednesday's evidence. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) "That's just brilliant, oh I am breathless," she tells the mother. Questioned about the intent of that comment, Ms McClymont said she did not mean "killing Mr Jones". "On the Friday, the police had said we have received no complaints about Alan Jones and we have not looked at him," she told the court. "The fact that someone has come forward and said we went to police and made a statement… as far as the story goes this is a significant event. "It is the nail in the coffin for the story." Alan Jones has pleaded not guilty to all charges. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) In March 2024, Ms McClymont texted the mother again, to let her know police were looking into other allegations against Mr Jones. "All I want to say is Alan Jones is the subject of a police investigation!!!!" Ms McClymont texted the woman. The court heard a later text said, "I hope the shit does hit the fan for him!" and finished with a smiley face and two 'poo' emojis. The defence has suggested previously that Ms McClymont did not like Mr Jones and was part of a media conspiracy along with broadcaster Ray Hadley and author Peter FitzSimons to bring down the former radio host, by unearthing false allegations against him. Hadley has given evidence in the criminal trial of his former 2GB stablemate. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) The court also heard Ms McClymont was tipped off by a NSW Police media unit officer, on her private phone, about Mr Jones arrest in November 2024. Asked if the purpose of that was so that journalists and photographers could be there to capture the moment, Ms McClymont said that it was. The journalist said she declined to provide transcripts or recordings of her private conversations with confidential sources to police, because her sources had not given her clearance to do so. She did end up providing the interviews under court subpoena, the court heard.

events.title: Fake jobs and malicious code used by hackers in largest crypto-heist
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Binance investigation uncovers fake job plot involved in $9 billion crypto-heist Binance has investigated the hack on its assets. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic ) The crypto-exchange platform at the centre of a $9 billion cyber attack says hackers used job interviews and malicious code to steal the funds. The company says the hackers appeared to take their first steps towards the breach as early as June. It says 98 per cent of the affected assets have been recovered by drawing on its own funds. The world's largest crypto-exchange platform says attackers used fake job interviews and malicious code to steal $US6.6 billion ($9 billion) in funds. The attack on Binance, believed to be the largest cyber attack in the cryptocurrency sector's history, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply. The FBI has attributed the four-hour attack on October 29 to North Korea-affiliated hackers. North Korea has denied the allegations, with the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un calling the claim "absurd rhetoric". Almost $9 billion in cryptocurrency was hacked from exchange company Binance, but who was behind the attack? Binance said the hackers began their plans as early as June. It said they first targeted a platform engineer by getting them to download a virus-laden version of the widely known programming software Homebrew. Binance's cybersecurity teams identified the malware and removed it, but the hackers had already had time to harvest information about the engineer and his colleagues. Zhao Changpeng is the founder and chief executive officer of Binance. ( Reuters: Benoit Tessier ) In September, the attackers approached another Binance engineer through a legitimate job-search platform, offering him an interview for a position in a fictitious company. After building trust with the subject through sharing social media photos and videos, they asked the engineer to download a test exercise as part of the interview process. The exercise contained malware that deployed "sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques", Binance said, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version. That malware was critical to the success of the attack, as it allowed the hackers to establish a connection with Binance's internal systems. Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic ) On October 20, the attackers used the access they had gained and an internal AI tool to gain control over software used by two other engineers. Nine days later, they triggered malicious code that initiated the attack. According to Binance, 98 per cent of the affected assets have been replenished by drawing on its own funds, with the remaining amount involving little-traded currencies that are harder to acquire. It said around one-third of the stolen assets had been frozen, meaning the attackers could not use them or convert them to another currency. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Salmon Tasmania is seeking an emergency permit to treat farmed fish with florfenicol to prevent a disease outbreak that caused mass mortalities last year. If approved, some fishing areas would be temporarily closed to prevent export bans being imposed by countries that have zero tolerance for antibiotics in wild seafood. The lobster industry is opposed to the closure plan, with one outraged fisherman saying the salmon industry could face large-scale protests. Tensions have escalated between Tasmania's salmon industry and the wild seafood sector over plans to close some fishing areas when antibiotics are used in salmon pens. Salmon Tasmania has applied for an emergency permit to use florfenicol to treat farmed fish affected by a bacterial disease that caused mass mortalities in 2025 . A separate emergency permit issued late last year had to be revoked in March after traces of florfenicol were detected in wild seafood more than 10 kilometres away. The new permit application includes a plan to shut wild fisheries for up to six weeks if they are located within the same zone as salmon pens treated with antibiotics. The closures are designed to avoid trade bans being imposed by countries that have zero tolerance for antibiotics in rock lobster, abalone and other wild seafood. The Tasmanian Atlantic salmon farming industry has been hard hit by disease. ( Tassal ) Under the "Wild Fisheries Market Access Plan", Salmon Tasmania would also provide financial support to affected commercial fishers to ensure they were no worse off. events.title: Alpha Dhabi expects hospitality to play key role in international portfolio
events.summary: Alpha Dhabi Holding is open to seeking more opportunities in the hospitality sector as part of its push to grow its international portfolio, a senior executive has said. The company, which is part of Abu Dhabi's International Holding Company (IHC), generated Dh7.7 billion ($2.1 billion) in revenue from its overseas portfolio companies in the first nine months of 2026, which is more than 13 per cent of its total revenue, it reported this week. “We will remain central to our investment approach alongside disciplined international expansion,” Alpha Dhabi Holding's chief investment and strategy officer Derek Nicholson told The National on Tuesday. “Our hospitality is an area where we can grow internationally … we look for opportunities that build on our capabilities and we're not here just to expand, for its own sake,” he said. Alpha Dhabi, which manages a portfolio of more than 250 public and private investments across 45 countries, has two hospitality units – National Corporation for Tourism and Hotels, and ADMO Lifestyle, the latter of which expanded in Egypt by acquiring the Nammos brand. The Egypt venture is a “model where we are the owners of the IP [intellectual property]”, Mr Nicholson said. He said this was an asset model to expand internationally and had given the group diversification “but we will continue to remain selective and focused on where we believe that we can generate long-term value”. Alpha Dhabi's net profit attributable to owners of the company for the nine months that ended on September 30 jumped nearly 41 per cent year-on-year to Dh7.78 billion, as revenue grew 6 per cent to about Dh58.3 billion. Last week, Alpha Dhabi Holding said it had signed an agreement to commit $1 billion for investments in artificial intelligence companies around the globe, investing through the Alpha Wave Global-managed fund Alpha Wave III. Mr Nicholson said Alpha Wave III was a “long-term investment theme” that also showed the “quality” of the companies New York-based Alpha Wave Global could source. Those companies include AI majors OpenAI and Anthropic, and Elon Musk's SpaceX. The venture fund will give Alpha Dhabi indirect exposure to the tech heavyweights. “When [Alpha Wave Global] approached us with Alpha Wave III, we decided that we wanted to continue our commitment to this sector,” Mr Nicholson said. “We see multi-trillion dollar investment over the next three to five years, and this is a theme where we think there are still opportunities to find best in class companies that are leaders in the sector.” In August, Alpha Dhabi , which was established in 2013, doubled its shareholding and capital commitment in its private credit joint venture with the UAE capital's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Company.

events.title: Stratton's win sets up Senate first for 3 Black women
events.summary: For the first time in history, three Black women will serve simultaneously in the U.S. Senate when Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton takes office in January. Why it matters: It took over 235 years for two Black women to serve in the U.S. Senate at the same time. Two years later, that number will grow to three. Driving the news: Stratton won election to the U.S. Senate on Tuesday, defeating Republican Don Tracy, per AP. She'll join Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Delaware) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland), who were both elected in 2024 and became the first two Black women to serve simultaneously in 2025. The Stratton campaign did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. By the numbers: Stratton will become the sixth Black woman to serve in the U.S. Senate and the second from Illinois, where Carol Moseley Braun became the first Black woman ever elected to the chamber in 1992. Former Vice President Kamala Harris became the second Black woman elected to the Senate in 2016. Former Sen. Laphonza Butler became the third to serve when California Gov. Gavin Newsom appointed her in 2023, but she was never elected. The bottom line : Stratton and Sen. Tammy Duckworth will make Illinois the first state represented by two women of color in the Senate simultaneously. Go deeper: Juliana Stratton wins Illinois U.S. Senate race, making history

events.title: Oil rises on Iran war uncertainty after Trump’s Republicans are routed in midterms
events.summary: Vote counting was under way in the US midterm elections, with Democrats snaring majorities in both houses of Congress for the rest of Trump’s second term. Oil prices rose as traders watched the Iran war, after Democrats won control of the US Congress in the midterms and investors weighed Trump’s next move. Brent and WTI gained 0.7% after earlier falls. Priyanka Sachdeva said Trump’s mixed signals cut trader confidence, but Strait of Hormuz risks still support prices. US strikes on Iran were described as limited. Crude stocks fell by 5.27 million barrels, far below forecasts, which analysts said was broadly supportive for oil. BEIJING – Oil prices rose on Nov 4 in a volatile session as investors awaited Washington’s next move in the war with Iran, after Democrat s captured control of US Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans in the midterm elections. Brent futures rose 76 US cents, or 0. 7 %, to US$104. 36 a barrel at 3.30pm Singapore time . US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 63 US cents, or 0. 7 %, to US$96. 72 , reversing earlier declines. In the previous session, Brent settled at its lowest level in nearly four weeks as traders weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran. “President Trump’s conflicting signals, with military strikes continuing alongside statements downplaying further escalation, have made it difficult for traders to build strong directional conviction,” said Priyanka Sachdeva, head of market insights at Phillip Nova. “I believe some profit-taking and reduction in speculative long positions are justified, particularly after the sharp rally in October,” she said. “However, the underlying supply disruption risks around the Strait of Hormuz have not disappeared. An unexpected drawdown in US crude inventories is also offering some fundamental support,” Sachdeva added. The US had carried out “defensive” strikes on Iran’s Qeshm island targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets, a US official said on Nov 3 . Another official said the strikes appeared limited and did not signal a return to major combat operations. Markets remained on watch for any progress in talks to end the US-Israeli war with Iran, as Qatar stepped up mediation efforts to avert an escalation of attacks after the US midterm elections. A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Nov 3 that Iran and the US remain far from a deal to end their war . US President Donald Trump told the Financial Times on Nov 3 that the US had no immediate plans to strike Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” Trump said in the six-minute telephone interview. Meanwhile, crude stocks fell by 5.27 million barrels in the week ended Oct 30, market sources said on Nov 4 , citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Eight analysts polled by Reuters had expected, on average, a rise of about 880,000 barrels in crude inventories. Petrol stocks rose by 1.43 million barrels, while distillate inventories fell by 1.19 million barrels from a week earlier, the sources said. “Diesel inventories remain tight, while petrol stocks rose more than expected. The data are broadly supportive of oil prices,” Haitong Futures said in a note on Nov 4 . Official data from the US Energy Information Administration is due at 10.30am EST (11.30pm Singapore time) on Nov 4. REUTERS

events.title: Dollar dips with US midterm results in focus
events.summary: The yen strengthened to 158.30 per US dollar in early trading. SHANGHAI/SINGAPORE – The dollar fell against most major currencies on Nov 4 ahead of results from US midterm elections, with investors bracing for a potentially strong Democratic showing. The first results in the US midterm elections began trickling in, with Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff winning reelection in Georgia in the first major race to be called. The question of whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress from Donald Trump’s Republicans, though was likely still hours away from a definitive answer. The euro firmed 0.2% to US$1.1212, while the yen strengthened to 158.30 per US dollar in early trading. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of six currencies, edged down 0.2% to 101.7. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 4 basis points to 4.919%. “Given the Democrats are favoured right now, our expectation is that they will take control of both the House and the Senate,” said Carol Kong, currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. “If that pans out, the US dollar could sell off further from here, because a Democratic sweep would limit government spending over Trump’s term.” As of 7.30 pm ET (8.30am Singapore time), US media outlets had projected winners in a handful of House races after polls closed in 10 states, with voting still under way across much of the country. Kong said investors were also watching the risk of an escalation in the Middle East depending on the election outcome. “If the Republicans do lose control of the House and the Senate, what will the President do? He previously flagged that he will restart a bombing campaign in Iran after the election, so we are watching that very closely,” she said. “If he does ramp up the aggression in the conflict, then we could see oil prices jump sharply higher, and that will support the US dollar.” Oil prices were little changed at US$103.85 a barrel after easing about 1% on Nov 3 to the lowest in nearly four weeks. The market is weighing talks to end the wars in Iran and Ukraine against worries that recent attacks in both conflicts could further disrupt supplies. Sterling edged higher to US$1.3440, with traders eyeing the Bank of England’s policy announcement on Nov 5 . The central bank’s Monetary Policy Committee is expected to raise interest rates for the first time since August 2023. China’s offshore yuan last traded at 6.6673 per dollar, stabilising after suffering its biggest one-day drop since May 15 on Nov 3 , when the People’s Bank of China raised the amount of foreign currency that financial institutions must hold in reserve in a move to slow the yuan’s rally. events.title: AMD sales forecast tops estimates on soaring AI chip demand
events.summary: Fourth-quarter revenue will be US$17 billion (S$21.7 billion), plus or minus 3%, the chipmaker said in a statement on Nov 3. AMD forecast fourth-quarter revenue of US$17 billion, above estimates, as strong AI chip demand and data centre sales stayed high. The result calmed worries about an AI bubble. AMD shares rose about 6% after the report, and the company’s value hit US$1 trillion in September. AMD’s data centre sales nearly doubled to US$8.5 billion, but PC and gaming sales fell 8%. Gross margin is set to narrow to about 55%. CALIFORNIA – Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), a key challenger to Nvidia in AI chips, gave a revenue forecast that exceeded analysts’ estimates, indicating that demand for data centre processors remains strong. Fourth-quarter revenue will be US$17 billion (S$21.7 billion), plus or minus 3%, the chipmaker said in a statement on Nov 3 . That compares with an average analyst estimate of US$16.3 billion. The outlook provided fresh evidence that AI spending is sustainable, potentially helping soothe jittery investors. Under chief executive Lisa Su, AMD has become one of the most important suppliers of processors and computers that operate at the heart of AI facilities, underpinning a flood of new services. “Our fourth-quarter outlook reflects accelerating revenue and earnings growth, driven by strong demand across our data centre portfolio,” chief financial officer Jean Hu said in the statement. AMD shares gained about 6% in late trading after the report was released. Even with recent turbulence, the stock has more than doubled in 2026 . The company’s valuation reached US$1 trillion in September, putting it in an elite group. The data centre growth has helped AMD offset a slump in the personal computer market , where rising memory chip costs have slowed production and depressed user demand . Intel, AMD’s top rival in that field, suffered its worst stock decline in decades after a downbeat earnings report last week. One possible weak spot for AMD: Its gross margin will narrow to about 55% in the fourth quarter. That measure – the percentage of sales after removing production costs – had been 56% in the previous period. AMD’s third-quarter sales rose 45% to US$13.4 billion. Profit climbed to US$2.09 a share, minus certain items. Analysts on average had predicted revenue of US$13.1 billion and earnings of US$1.97 a share. AMD continues to deliver record results and now boasts sales that are twice as big as they were two years ago. It has also been outperforming long-time nemesis Intel in the market for central processing units, or CPUs. But it is still well behind Nvidia in so-called AI accelerators, which are used to train and run artificial intelligence models. Sales at AMD’s data centre business nearly doubled to US$8.5 billion. Analysts had predicted a total of US$8.2 billion. PC and gaming-related sales shrank 8% to US$3.7 billion. Like other makers of components for PCs, AMD is suffering from a side effect of the data centre boom. AI servers require a massive amount of memory. That has cut into the supply of chips available for laptops and desktop machines – and forced prices up. AMD is debuting new product ranges in both the CPU and accelerator markets. The Santa Clara, California-based company is also taking on Nvidia more directly with its Helios server design. But Nvidia, the largest chipmaker and world’s most valuable company, has not been standing still. It is updating its own line-up at a fast pace and branching out into everything from software to networking to complete computers. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Gold steadies as traders track Iran talk prospects, US midterms
events.summary: The precious metal’s movement has been choppy this week on conflicting signals on the progress of US-Iran talks. Gold stayed near US$3,930 as traders watched US-Iran talks and US midterm elections for clues on interest rates, inflation, and fiscal policy. Oil swung on mixed signals from diplomacy, with fresh mediator proposals and reported US strikes on Qeshm raising tensions, but hopes of a peaceful deal eased prices. Gold has fallen about 25% since late February and nearly 7% in October, as higher energy costs and tighter policy hurt demand for the non-yielding metal. Gold held a decline as traders tracked diplomacy efforts in the Middle East and the outcome of US midterm elections for clues on the path for interest rates and American fiscal policy. Bullion was hovering around US$3,930 an ounce, following a modest retreat in the previous session that came after a jump of almost 2% on Nov 2 . The precious metal’s movement has been choppy this week on conflicting signals on the progress of US-Iran talks, making the impact of energy prices on inflation difficult to gauge. Oil continued to fluctuate after shifting in a range of around US$5 a barrel on Nov 3 . Tehran and Washington are reviewing fresh proposals from mediators on how to resolve their differences and avoid a return to all-out war, according to a diplomat briefed on the matter. That came after limited US air strikes reportedly hit targets on the Iranian island of Qeshm inside the Strait of Hormuz on the night of Nov 2 . Oil prices had soared over October on worsening tensions but sharply reversed course this week on signs the White House was willing to allow more time for a diplomatic resolution. Crude and gold have mostly moved in opposite directions in recent weeks, with elevated energy prices fuelling expectations of tighter monetary policy – a headwind for the non-yielding metal. The precious metal slumped almost 7% in October, slipping below the US$4,000 an ounce threshold at the end of the month when a retreat from artificial intelligence prompted investors to liquidate bullion holdings to cover losses elsewhere. It is down around 25% since the US-Iran conflict erupted in late February, as accelerating inflation has spurred tighter monetary policy. Americans are casting their votes in midterm elections that will determine who controls the House and the Senate. The outcome is likely to shape the US fiscal policy outlook, indirectly affecting gold. Spot gold was 0.2% higher at US$3,938.47 an ounce at 8.17am in Singapore, while silver was steady at US$49.81. events.title: Democrat Roy Cooper flips North Carolina Senate seat
events.summary: Democrat Roy Cooper has defeated President Trump's handpicked candidate, Michael Whatley, flipping one of North Carolina's two GOP-held U.S. Senate seats. Why it matters : Cooper, the popular two-term governor, delivered Democrats one of their best shots at flipping a Republican-held Senate seat. Even in a state that voted all three times for Trump, Cooper has never lost an election. The big picture: While the race was originally expected to be tight and expensive, Cooper consistently widened his polling lead throughout campaign season. His name recognition boosted his chances against Whatley, a lawyer who served as Republican National Committee chair but had never run for office himself. As enthusiasm lagged behind Whatley, GOP-aligned super PACs canceled their ads and redirected spending to more promising states, even as Trump still campaigned for Whatley in North Carolina. Catch up quick: Cooper will succeed Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who decided not to seek reelection after clashing with Trump over the "big, beautiful bill" and its associated Medicaid cuts. Trump had threatened to back a primary challenger against Tillis. On the trail: Cooper focused his campaign on affordability, blaming Republicans for high gas prices and tying GOP policies to inflation. Meanwhile, Whatley centered his platform on helping execute the Trump agenda, despite the president's historically low approval rating. Whatley attempted to paint Cooper as the "soft-on-crime candidate" and continued to recite a debunked claim that Cooper is responsible for freeing Decarlos Brown Jr. , the man accused of stabbing and killing a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee on Charlotte's light rail. Trump alleged North Carolina had become "one of the most violent" states under Democratic leadership while campaigning for Whatley. What's next: Cooper will take office in January. He will be the first Democrat to represent North Carolina in the Senate in over a decade.

events.title: Democrats beat back GOP Senate challenge in N.H. with Pappas win
events.summary: Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former GOP Sen. John Sununu in the New Hampshire Senate race, AP projects, becoming the first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate. Why it matters: Pappas' victory keeps the seat in Democratic hands and could boost the party's chances of taking control of the Senate. Driving the news: Pappas led Sununu 61% to 38% with 20% of the votes counted. He'll succeed retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) in January. Catch up quick: Republicans saw New Hampshire as a top pickup opportunity, with Senate Majority Leader John Thune campaigning for Sununu in the competitive race, despite polls showing Pappas ahead. Most polls compiled by the New York Times in the weeks before Election Day showed the Democratic Pappas leading Sununu by 5 to 8 percentage points. Zoom in: Although President Trump endorsed him, Sununu has shown daylight with the president, criticizing his trade war with Canada and his so-called anti-weaponization fund — and he backed Trump's primary opponents in 2016 and 2024. Still, prominent New Hampshire Republicans — including Don Bolduc , the Trump -endorsed 2022 Senate nominee — endorsed Pappas in mid-October, accusing Sununu of being too beholden to the president. Between the lines: Republicans welcomed Sununu's entry into the race because of his family's long ties to New Hampshire politics. Sununu served in the Senate from 2003 to 2009 before losing to Shaheen in 2008. His brother Chris served as governor for eight years. Senate GOP Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) posted on X in October 2025 that Sununu's decision to run catapulted New Hampshire to "a top-tier U.S. Senate race." The bottom line: Pappas' win reflects a preference New Hampshire voters expressed in pre-election polling : They wanted a check on Trump's power. events.title: Google responds to political backlash over removing search from schools that ban AI
events.summary: Politicians including Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized Google following reports that the company would restrict search at schools that ban AI. Google responded to the outrage, saying that Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search will be turned off by default, and schools can choose to turn one or all of them back on. Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the New York Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." Google is playing defense on Tuesday after a political backlash to its new policy surrounding use of artificial intelligence in schools. In a blog post titled "Designing responsible AI for learning," Google said it's bringing AI into its Classroom offering with a product called Guided Learning. The New York Times published a story saying that the company will turn off search for schools that reject AI entirely. Following the Times' story, prominent left-leaning politicians, including Sen. Bernie Sanders from Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced their outrage on social media. "Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," Mamdani wrote on X. Sanders wrote that "Google is threatening schools," referring to the policy as "extortion." Google responded later in the day. In a post on X , the company said its new policy was meant to give schools more choice over how students interact with AI. Google said its Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook and search are turned off by default, and that "schools are in control," with the ability to turn them as they see fit. "We are also updating Search for schools to make it better for learning," Google wrote. "Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don't get quick answers to schoolwork." The company's post didn't explicitly respond to the claim that access to search requires use of AI. However, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." A Google spokesperson referred CNBC to the X post when asked for comment. Google's broader practices have come under fire in recent years, with the company losing antitrust cases over its search and advertising businesses. Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan aggressively pursued Google and other tech giants, including Meta and Amazon . Khan said in a post on X on Tuesday that Google's new AI for learning policy highlights "the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service." It's the latest controversy related to the impact of technology on children and the role leading internet companies are playing in delivering information. In August, Meta reached a landmark $16.7 billion settlement in its child safety trial after a number of state attorneys general accused the company of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by apps like Facebook and Instagram . The same month, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens after state attorneys general launched an investigation into the company's safety practices, with Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, a Republican, filing a lawsuit in June. The nonprofit Common Sense Media recently gave Google's AI overviews an " unacceptable risk " rating. Last month, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo., launched an inquiry over Google's push of AI into classrooms. Google introduced AI overviews as a search function in May 2024 . — CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos contributed to this report. WATCH: Meta settled its child safety lawsuit. Now comes the hard part.

events.title: Canva announces layoffs, job changes for about 22% of workforce
events.summary: Some 1,271 people, or 22% of Canva’s staff, will lose their jobs, change roles or relocate to central hubs, chief executive Melanie Perkins said. Canva will cut jobs and change roles for 1,271 staff, or 22% of its workforce, after growth slowed for the first time in 10 years. Chief executive Melanie Perkins said the company must become simpler, with smaller teams, fewer niche roles, and more work centred in Sydney. Perkins called it “the hardest moment in our 13-year history” as AI and wider software industry changes push firms to do more with fewer workers. SYDNEY – Canva announced job cuts and a sweeping overhaul that will impact more than one-fifth of the workforce, as artificial intelligence forces a structural reckoning at one of Australia’s highest-profile technology companies. Some 1,271 people, or 22% of Canva’s staff, will lose their jobs, change roles or relocate to central hubs, chief executive Melanie Perkins said in a note to employees posted on the firm’s website on Nov 4. The sweeping changes at Canva, an online design and publishing platform, mirror a broader upheaval across the software industry. Investors have wiped billions of dollars from the value of these firms amid concerns new technology like Anthropic PBC’s Claude will cannibalise their business. Artificial intelligence is allowing people to do more on their own without speciality programmes, while companies are using AI to operate with fewer workers. “New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use,” Perkins wrote in the note. “I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough.” Perkins, who co-founded Canva with Cliff Obrecht and Cameron Adams, did not specify how many of those staff would lose their jobs. But after the firm’s growth slowed for the first time in a decade, Perkins said Canva needs to become a simpler business and return to running small, empowered teams. There will be fewer niche specialisations, she said. She described the reorganisation as “the hardest moment in our 13-year history”. Sydney will become the main base for more of Canva’s product teams. Perkins said more people will work face to face, and most hybrid staff will spend two to three days in the office a week from January. Canva has been preparing for a potential listing, and the overhaul leaves the company in a delicate financial balance. After hitting a US$40 billion (S$51.2 billion) high in 2021, Canva’s valuation tumbled to roughly US$26 billion a year later during a broad tech sell-off. While Canva’s dollar worth subsequently rebounded, the effect of more recent tumult is not yet clear. While the AI era has led to widespread job losses, investors are also questioning when, or even if, the vast associated investments will deliver a financial dividend. Firmus Grid in October scrapped a planned Australian initial public offering of up to US$5.5 billion, turning a rising star of the AI data-centre boom into one of the biggest deal flops in recent memory. Nextdc shares plummeted in October after the data centre operator said it was considering force majeure options and cut earnings guidance. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Republicans underperform as first midterm votes are counted
events.summary: The first midterm votes counted on Tuesday night suggest a tough night for Republicans, in line with polling that has put Democrats well ahead in the battle for Congress on the strength of public frustration with President Donald Trump’s agenda. In Indiana and Kentucky, where most polls closed at 6 pm ET, Democrats ran well ahead of their early vote totals two years ago. They were competitive in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, outside of Indianapolis — where Trump won by 17 points in 2024 — and in Kentucky’s 6th District, which went for Trump by 15 points. Neither of those seats was a Democratic target at the start of this election cycle, but both races saw later investment as the environment appeared to degrade for Republicans. Indiana Rep. Victoria Spartz, an erratic candidate in the 5th District who has underperformed the party before, faced a last-minute spend from the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a green energy PAC working to beat Republicans who voted to revoke energy credits last year. House Majority PAC, the Democrats’ super PAC, spent nearly $400,000 for their candidate, JD Ford. The Kentucky seat became a target after Rep. Andy Barr left it to run for Senate. Republicans nominated former state Sen. Ralph Alvarado, while Gov. Andy Beshear campaigned for Democratic nominee Zach Dembo, a federal prosecutor. Republicans expected their numbers to improve as Election Day votes came in, but in both Indiana and Kentucky, the party’s vote share has universally fallen since 2024. Indiana Democrat Beau Bayh, the son and grandson of former senators, led in the early count for secretary of state, the one statewide race his party was competing for. Yet Democrats remain wary about overreading the meaning of early votes, recalling that they banked votes for Kamala Harris two years ago before getting overwhelmed on Election Day. — David Weigel

events.title: Canva layoffs: design giant to cut or relocate more than 1,200 jobs in major restructure
events.summary: Chief executive Melanie Perkins describes job cuts as ‘without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history’ in email to staff Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Canva is cutting or relocating more than 1,200 jobs, representing 22% of its global workforce, as part of a major restructure that includes laying off staff who helped build the Australian-founded design platform. The changes mirror a trend across the technology sector, where software companies are fighting to stay competitive against cheaper artificial intelligence disrupters while aggressively embedding AI tools themselves. Canva’s chief executive, Melanie Perkins, said in an email to staff on Wednesday that the restructure was “without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history”. “For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs,” she said. “Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today.” The restructure will affect 1,271 people, according to the company, as it focuses on “collapsing layers” and bringing “more teams together in person”. “We know relocating is a big decision for those being asked to consider it, and we’re committed to making the process as smooth as possible with comprehensive support,” said Perkins, who did not specify the exact number of job losses. Those leaving Canva will receive at least six months of salary and retain healthcare coverage for a further 12 months in countries where workers receive that benefit. They can also keep their laptops. Those leaving can also apply for US$10,000 (A$14,000) grants to start their own ventures. Get the most important news as it breaks The graphic design company is one of Australia’s most successful startups and has long been touted as a candidate for a blockbuster listing on the Nasdaq. But it has now added to a wave of restructures in the technology sector, which has included 1,600 redundancies at the software company Atlassian , and job losses at Afterpay’s owner, Block, and at WiseTech Global , another software company. While established software companies have rejected the threat of a “SaaS-pocalypse” , a term used to describe the idea that AI becomes so advanced that specialised software becomes redundant, many have overhauled their business models in response or aggressively adopted AI tools. Unlike Atlassian, Block and WiseTech, Canva did not mention AI in its restructure announcement.

The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms. It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff. The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said. "For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office. Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn. Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products. "New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday. Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013. events.title: UOB’s Q3 net profit jumps 182% to $1.25b but misses estimates; shares fall over 5%
events.summary: UOB is the first bank to report its third quarter earnings on Nov 4, after all three banks saw shares fall on Nov 2. UOB’s third-quarter net profit jumped 182% to $1.25 billion, helped by an 81% drop in credit loss provisions, but it still missed Bloomberg’s $1.38 billion estimate. UOB said it is pushing wealth, transaction banking and selective growth in digital infrastructure and energy, while aiming to double wealth income by 2030 and keep loan growth steady in 2027. SINGAPORE – UOB’s third-quarter net profit jumped 182% to $1.25 billion from $443 million a year earlier, largely due to a sharp drop in provisions for potential loan losses. But compared with the previous quarter, its net profit fell 15% from $1.48 billion. It also missed the $1.38 billion forecast among six analysts polled by Bloomberg. They fell over 6% before the noon trading break, but moderated to close 5% down at $38.44. The jump in UOB’s net profit was a result of several factors. For one thing, UOB set aside $258 million for credit and other losses in the three months ended Sept 30, a sharp reduction of 81% from $1.36 billion a year earlier. Net interest income, which measures the difference between what a bank earns from lending and pays on deposits, rose 1% year on year to $2.28 billion. Net fee income in the third quarter hit a record $733 million, a 19% increase from the same period a year ago. It also marked a 10% increase over the previous quarter. This rise came on the back of strong growth in wealth, cards and loan-related activities, UOB noted. Customer-related treasury income also reached a new high, reflecting robust client engagement and demand for hedging solutions, it added. Meanwhile, assets under management grew by 3% over the same quarter in 2025 to reach $204 billion. UOB chief executive officer and deputy chairman Wee Ee Cheong said: “The group continued to see healthy customer activity across our businesses this quarter, with strong growth in wealth management, healthy loan growth and record fees and customer-related treasury income.” For the first nine months of 2026, wealth income rose 13% from a year ago, while card income was up 25% year on year. Wee said at a media briefing that the bank has also been reshaping its wholesale banking business, by investing in its transaction banking capabilities, strengthening the regional network and deepening sector coverage. Wholesale banking loans grew 9% year on year, with trade loans recording a robust 31% growth. Transaction banking also remained an important driver of the franchise’s performance, UOB said. Total expenses fell to $1.6 billion, a 4% decrease over the previous quarter, in line with income moderation. Wee said this financial performance reflects the strength of the bank’s diversified franchise and customer relationships, with over eight million customers in the region. “As connectivity across ASEAN strengthens, customers increasingly value banking partners that can support them across their business, personal and wealth needs,” he said. Non-performing loan ratio also fell to 1.5%, although non-performing assets rose slightly, especially in Greater China. Responding to media queries, group chief financial officer Leong Yung Chee said: “You do see recovery in Greater China asset quality issues, but they are recovering slower than what we have seen in the US portfolio. “We intend to manage that very actively, and we will see that gradually decline in terms of non-performing loan numbers.” When asked about the portfolio exposure to real estate and hospitality, Leong said that it has declined. “We are growing in some of the other non-real estate sectors such as digital infrastructure, energy sectors. These are higher-growth areas. So some of our loan growth that you are seeing in these markets are from these areas,” he said. When it comes to artificial intelligence-related financing, Leong said the amount currently constitutes less than 5% of the loan book. These short- and long-term loans are evaluated under the bank’s credit processes and borrower profile assessments. “(AI) is one of the areas where it’s exhibiting the strongest growth across industries. But we’re also not immune to, or ignorant about what’s happening across the AI-related financing space,” he said, referring to credit default swaps that have risen. “We have to be very selective about which ones we do, but we cannot ignore that this is a very exciting and high-growth area right now.” He also commented on the high interest rate environment. “Deposit rates have all been creeping up lately, which is very good for consumers, but from a funding cost and net interest margin, it applies pressure and compression,” he said, although he noted that these will adjust when benchmark rates firm up, which takes one to two quarters before it shows up in financial results.

events.title: Graduates are managing AI - but are they learning much else?
events.summary: Managing AI agents is a big part of Lotte Underwood's job Published 4 November 2026, 00:04 GMT Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR. Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing. She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation. A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media. Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others. "A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood. AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts , but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's. Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement. Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI. "My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel. Debra Maxwell is looking for "AI disruptors" Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company. CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI. "We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell. "We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way." Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role." If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier. Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires. For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer , external , it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building. Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%. Cian Clinton uses around ten AI agents for work tasks Cian Clinton, who joined consultancy Valliance last September after graduating from a Bachelor of Science in 2024, says the incorporation of AI into his role makes him feel less like a graduate, and more like an equal team member. He uses around 10 AI agents daily for different tasks. "Your ideas and your creativity are a lot more valued because you actually get to implement those firsthand, and the responsibility you take on is a lot greater because of that," says London-based Clinton, 23. "I am now taking on responsibilities which would usually take me four or five years to get to." His career progression, he believes, will now be faster as a result. "AI is killing the 'pyramid' approach…progression is no longer based on your knowledge bank. Now it's more based on your critical thinking and understanding of the processes," says Clinton. There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers. But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?
