events.title: Stocks rally, dollar dips after Democrats’ midterm sweep
events.summary: The greatest market reaction may come not from who wins Congress, but from how decisively they win and how far the result deviates from expectations, said an analyst. Democrats won the US midterms, taking both chambers and raising fears of tighter AI rules, slower data-centre growth and more political gridlock, Reuters said. Global stocks fell, led by AI shares in Asia and weak Nasdaq futures, as investors sold risky assets and moved into bonds for safety. The dollar weakened against major currencies, while yen and Swiss franc rose; oil stayed choppy as traders weighed war talks and supply risks. LONDON – Global stocks and the dollar recovered on Nov 4 from lows hit overnight after Democrats won control of both the Senate and the House in the US midterm elections, which has fuelled fears that rapid AI sector growth could be hamstrung by regulatory scrutiny. In a major setback to US President Donald Trump and Republicans, Democrats scored sweeping victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations. The breadth of the party’s success was underscored by gains in districts long considered safely conservative, highlighting a political shift that caught many investors off guard. “Democrats pulled off a double victory in the US midterm elections that few saw coming at the onset of the year. The blue wave means the federal government is sure to be divided on most issues,” said Deborah Cunningham, chief investment officer, global liquidity markets at Federated Hermes. “That typically creates a blockade against new legislation – an environment that broad financial markets traditionally view favourably as variables decrease.” Opinion polls have shown Democratic voters favouring more control over AI, and investors expect the Democratic-controlled Congress to apply more scrutiny to the sector. AI stocks in Asia initially led the decline in equity markets, while bonds and safe-haven currencies such as the Swiss franc gained. By the time the bulk of the midterm results had filtered through in the European morning, equities had turned higher. MSCI’s All-World index was up 0.13%, while Europe’s STOXX 600, which has acted as a hedge against AI-related risks, was up 0.5%. US stock futures also edged into positive territory, having fallen by as much as 2% overnight. “Overall, these results have had a mild impact on markets so far. Investors will move on from trading the uncertainty of the election results to trading the reality of what they mean for policy,” XTB research director Kathleen Brooks said. “This is bad news for Tesla and SpaceX on Wednesday, but the semiconductor names, the backbone of the AI trade, could brush off concerns about AI regulation and continue to move higher after Tuesday’s stunning rally for the sector,” she said. The AI boom has helped propel global markets in recent years, driven by heavy spending from tech giants racing to build data centres and expand computing capacity. That has made investors acutely sensitive to anything that could derail the technology’s rapid expansion. The election outcome could also hold broad implications for the US fiscal outlook as well as sectors such as defence, healthcare and banking. Futures on the small-cap Russell 2000 index, which is more exposed to the US domestic economy, were last up 0.7%, having lost 1% earlier. Treasuries rallied as investors expect gridlock in Washington to cut government spending, with AI regulation also possibly slowing growth and reducing the need for rate hikes. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note was down 3 basis points on the day at 4.92%, having fallen as much as 6 bps to a low of 4.89% overnight, which, in turn, weighed on the dollar. “Bonds are coming out as the clear winner as markets put the AI trade on the chopping block and embrace the higher possibility that further tax cuts are put on ice and government spending slows,” said Prashant Newnaha, senior rates strategist at TD Securities in Singapore. In currencies, the dollar weakened broadly, leaving the euro up 0.4% at US$1.133 and the pound up 0.5% at US$1.348. The yen and the Swiss franc – both safe-haven currencies – also notched up gains. The Swiss franc was the standout performer, with the dollar down 0.6% against it at 0.8163 francs. The dollar also fell 0.4% against the Japanese yen to 158.12. In the oil market, prices were choppy on Nov 4 after they hit a four-week low in the previous session as investors weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran against worries that recent attacks in both conflicts could further disrupt supplies. Brent crude was down 0.4% on the day at US$103.17 a barrel. REUTERS

events.title: The brutal 2026 attack ads even rivals had to respect
events.summary: Top party strategists may hate seeing one of their candidates gutted by a brutal ad. But they can still admire the hit. Why it matters: A record $11.6 billion has plastered political ads across screens of every size in the country during the 2026 midterms . Only a handful of those earned the grudging respect of operatives on both sides. 📺 Zoom in: Multiple Republican strategists singled out the "brutal" series of ads attacking Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kans.) over lawsuits against patients with overdue medical bills — some of whom were later arrested . Against the advice of his own team, Marshall released a self-directed ad answering the attacks. In Nebraska , an ad highlighting a past vote by former Gov. Pete Ricketts to pardon a man convicted of rape was singled out by both parties as one of the cycle's most damaging. Ricketts is expected to win re-election to the Senate. In Maine, an upbeat jingle hit Democratic nominee Troy Jackson for having children with his second cousin. "If he'll f**k his own family, he'll f**k yours too," the radio ad said (among other things). Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) called for the ad to be taken down. And in Florida , Rep. María Salazar (R-Fla.) turned on her own party leader, criticizing President Trump over ICE's aggressive enforcement tactics, saying some immigration policies had "gone too far." The intrigue : Even hardened operatives are dealing with a new frontier: AI-generated attack ads that can make up scenarios and put words in an opponent's mouth. In Michigan , a Republican-aligned super PAC used AI-generated imagery to depict Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a fabricated family photo and playing a game with cards referencing "Death to America" and 9/11. In Texas, GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton's team used AI to depict Democratic candidate James Talarico defacing a Bible with a crayon and saying: "In the beginning God was non-binary, and he wasn't a Christian. And God said, 'let there be six genders,' and there were." 🤺 Between the lines: An attack ad helped spark this weekend's blowup in the Michigan Senate race. Rep. Haley Stevens' (D-Mich.) shocking decision to withdraw support from El-Sayed grew out of their public dispute over an ad she called antisemitic. El-Sayed ultimately disavowed the ad but said Stevens wasn't welcome at his events, and she endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) on Sunday. The other side: It's hard to imagine a bigger backfire than Vivek Ramaswamy's (R) ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent for Ohio governor, Amy Acton (D). It could prove fatal for his gubernatorial bid, and Republicans worry it could hurt Sen. John Husted's (R) re-election chances too. The ad sparked immediate bipartisan backlash. Ramaswamy doubled down before pulling it off-air. One internal GOP poll had Acton's lead grow by 6 points after the ad ran.

events.title: Children use AI to speak video games into existence
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Children use AI to create video games with hopes of building hub in regional Queensland Bailey Francois says the workshop was a "really cool" experience. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) Children as young as eight have used Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create their own video games. The Bundaberg program focused on creativity rather than coding ability, allowing more people to be involved. Organisers hope to create a game development hub so regional kids do not need to leave their hometown to work in the industry. It sounds like fun — the cacophony of dings and pings, revving engines, and other video game effects punctuated by the occasional cheer or groan as children play. But this is no arcade. These Bundaberg children, aged eight-13, are taking part in a new gaming development workshop. You would be forgiven for thinking they had undergone extensive coding training to create these video games. Instead, they talked the games into existence using artificial intelligence (AI). The children's creativity was boundless, producing racing, quest and trivia games. Celebrating the wins was a major part of the workshop. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) Bailey Francois, 13, said AI made their ideas come to life. "Basically you can either speak to it [the AI language model] and it converts that into text," she said. "Or you can type it out, which I find a bit difficult, if you want to create a long paragraph." Bailey was one of about 20 young people who took part in the games development workshops in Bundaberg last month. The children 3D-printed, decorated and wired their own controllers. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) Participants used 3D printing to produce a console and learned how to wire a controller, before brainstorming their game idea and instructing the AI. "Game design is game design. Game design isn't animation or coding or these other things. It's its own discipline," organiser Don Meadows said. Mr Meadows grew up in Bundaberg but moved overseas to pursue his passion for game development. "There's not a games industry [in Queensland]," he said. "You move overseas and you don't come back. I'd love to come back and I'd love to start an industry here." Organisers Don, David and Ronnie. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) Queensland University of Technology (QUT) senior lecturer Cody Phillips said the Australian industry generated about $600 million in revenue each year. "Australia is definitely punching above its weight in terms of global industry presence," Dr Phillips said. "But we're not really seeing too many titles coming out of regional Australia." Luke Wogandt rated the workshop 10/10. ( ABC News: Grace Whiteside ) Dr Phillips said AI was "a new frontier" in creating opportunities. "A lot of people are building and creating games without being formally employed within the games industry," he said. "There are virtually no barriers to somebody publishing their own game." But he also believed the technology needed stronger safeguards. "There's a lot of copyright legislation that still needs to be worked out," Dr Phillips said. Alekai Sprague, 11, said it was incredible to discover what AI could be used for. Alekai Sprague says it was wonderful seeing his imagination come to life. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) "It just shows how much a simple AI can do, instead of having to learn to code and do everything yourself," he said. "It's quite a wonderful thing, watching your imagination … come to life in a game." Chase McGibbon, nine, said he was keen to keep developing games as he grew up. "I really want to try to build a game when I'm older," he said. Chase McGibbon says everyone's games were fun and different. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) The workshops were the brainchild of Mr Meadows and Bundaberg creative David Quarrell. Mr Quarrell said with creativity the main driver of game design, AI made it accessible to everyone. The idea started with Mr Quarrell's 16-year-old son, Oscar, who cannot read or write — but was able to talk to AI. "The AI didn't stop. It didn't get confused. It took everything that Oscar had said as a prompt and it filtered through all of these 'ums' and 'ahs' and it got the core substance from it and it created something," Mr Quarrell said. "We've removed the need for reading and writing and we've just allowed his imagination to be captured." The organisers are aiming to build a gaming hub in the region to encourage young people to work in the industry without leaving their hometown.

events.title: CrowdStrike's new kill switch can stop rogue AI agents in their tracks, CEO says
events.summary: CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said the company's new technology allows businesses to stop rogue AI agents, prevent them from restarting and cut off their network access. Kurtz says he sees AI agent safety as a major growth opportunity for CrowdStrike, pointing to growing enterprise demand and an expanded partnership with Anthropic. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said Tuesday that the cybersecurity company can now shut down rogue artificial intelligence agents. CrowdStrike's new kill switch , announced Tuesday at its Fal.Con Europe conference, allows security teams to terminate misbehaving agents, prevent them from restarting and cut off their network access. It is designed to give humans more power over artificial intelligence models and systems, as concerns about how to control agents grow. "Everyone is building AI agents, but they never had the off button, and now they do," Kurtz told CNBC's Jim Cramer on " Mad Money ." "It's going to be an incredibly important part of making sure that AI agents run and operate safely." The AI Kill Switch, as CrowdStrike calls it, is part of the company's Falcon Guardian platform, which monitors AI agents operating within an organization. The technology, which is available immediately, is aimed at addressing AI safety concerns surrounding the rapid adoption of AI agents. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing AI development over safety concerns, a position backed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman . Kurtz argued at the time that slowing AI development would not eliminate existing security risks, which he said underscored the need for safeguards as companies deploy autonomous systems. Kurtz said Tuesday that CrowdStrike's new kill switch represents a significant shift in cybersecurity, which has traditionally focused on protecting companies from external threats. As businesses rely more on AI agents, he argued that security providers must also ensure those systems operate safely within their own organizations. "Enabling agents to work safely is a massive market opportunity for CrowdStrike," Kurtz said. "We have AI capabilities to prevent these breaches from happening on the outside, and we also have the capabilities to make sure that agents are basically doing what they are instructed to do." The CEO compared the technology to airbags in cars, arguing that safeguards are necessary even when AI systems are designed to operate correctly. "If they go outside of those guardrails at runtime, we can kill those agents," he said. CrowdStrike is seeing growing demand for its security tools as businesses adopt AI. Kurtz pointed to CrowdStrike's partnership with Anthropic to protect its Claude Cowork product: He said enterprise customers had pushed for CrowdStrike's technology to be integrated before they deployed Anthropic's offerings. "Our customers went to Anthropic and said, 'We need CrowdStrike before we can deploy AI,'" Kurtz said. "I think it says volumes that customers would not roll out AI without CrowdStrike." events.title: Strand bookstore to pay nearly $1.5 million over Covid loan tied to Sen. Wyden's wife
events.summary: The Strand, the iconic New York City bookstore, agreed to pay nearly $1.5 million in a civil settlement for accepting a Covid government loan that was off-limits because the store is owned by the wife of Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C. The Strand applied for the $932,350 loan in February 2021 from the Paycheck Protection Program administered by the Small Business Administration, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office said. Store owner Nancy Bass Wyden certified on the loan application that "the spouse of a Member of Congress does not directly or indirectly hold a controlling interest in the applicant," Pirro's office said. The Strand , the iconic New York City bookstore, agreed to pay nearly $1.5 million in a civil settlement for accepting a Covid government loan that was off-limits because the store is owned by the wife of Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C. The Strand applied for the $932,350 loan in February 2021 from the Paycheck Protection Program administered by the Small Business Administration , U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro 's office said Tuesday. Midterm elections 2026 live updates: Economy, inflation and voter concerns Trump focuses on Reflecting Pool in final public speech before midterms How the 2026 midterms could affect defense, healthcare, crypto and AI stocks DOJ asks Supreme Court to block California counting disputed mail-in ballots "Ms. Wyden's certification was knowingly and materially false and Strand was not eligible for the second draw loan it received," the office said. The Strand will pay $1,482,560 to settle the case. There was no determination of liability by the store, Pirro's office said. The Strand, in a statement, said the store made an "unintentional" mistake in applying for the loan, and said it was unaware at the time the funds were barred to businesses owned by the spouse of a member of Congress. Bass Wyden's husband, who has served in the Senate for more than 30 years, is a staunch critic of President Donald Trump , who appointed Pirro to the post of top prosecutor in the District of Columbia. Bass Wyden is the granddaughter of Ben Bass, founder of the Strand, whose flagship store is in Greenwich Village. Congress authorized the forgivable PPP loans when it passed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act in March 2020. In December 2020, Congress provided additional funding for the PPP loan program with separate legislation, which "included a prohibition against businesses obtaining second draw PPP funds if a member of Congress or their spouse directly or indirectly held a controlling interest in the PPP loan applicant," Pirro's office said. In a statement Tuesday, Pirro said, "The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren't eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator." Her office noted that the False Claims Act, which the Strand was alleged to have violated, "allows the government to establish liability based on reckless disregard and permits the government to recover more than its actual losses," which is what occurred in this case. The civil settlement resolved claims brought under a so-called qui tam lawsuit, which allows private whistleblowers to sue on behalf of the U.S. government and receive a portion of any recovery. The qui tam action in this case was filed by a corporate entity, Blockquote Inc., in U.S. District Court in Washington. Blockquote, whose owners were not disclosed by Pirro's office, will receive a total share of about $148,256 in connection with the settlement. The docket for Blockquote's lawsuit is sealed from public view. The Strand, in a statement after CNBC requested comment from the store and Bass Wyden, said the restriction that the store violated was passed by Congress between the first and second rounds of the PPP. "Unfortunately, the bookstore's accountant and the bank administering the loan were not aware of this change when the second-draw application was processed," the Strand said. "We stand by the facts: the circumstances arose during an unprecedented and rapidly changing public health emergency, the mistake was unintentional," the store said. "We hope this matter will be viewed objectively and in its proper context, with the understanding that the application of justice should always be fair, impartial, and free from political considerations," the store said. A spokesman for Sen. Wyden's office said the senator and his wife do not discuss her business, and that he had no involvement in the loan or settlement.

( Pexels: Jonathan Borba ) Design giant Canva has announced a restructure affecting 1,270 jobs, pointing to slowing growth and "new technology" changing how people create and use products. Sydney will be made the primary hub with some staff asked to relocate. A package for outgoing employees includes at least six months' salary and other supports while they find other work. More than one in five jobs will be affected at software company Canva as it restructures amid slowing growth and rapid technological change. Canva co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins told staff in a memo the restructure was the "hardest moment in our 13-year history". The changes will affect about 1,270 jobs, or 22 per cent of its global workforce. Ms Perkins said Canva's growth had slowed "for the first time in a decade", arguing small changes would be insufficient to prepare the company for its next phase. Canva said "new technology" was also changing how people created and used products. The company did not explicitly mention AI in the announcement. As part of the changes, some employees may be asked to relocate, with Sydney becoming the primary home for Canva's product teams. It currently has operations in Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth, and operates in 37 countries. "From January, we expect most Hybrid Canvanauts to spend around two to three days in the office each week, depending on what makes sense in your area," Ms Perkins said. Atlassian cuts nearly 500 jobs from Australian workforce Atlassian's Australian workforce will account for 30 per cent of the tech giant's global job cuts, with the freed-up funds to be invested in AI and enterprise sales. A package for outgoing employees includes at least six months' salary, health and wellbeing support, and the removal of the one-year equity vesting cliff for some recently hired staff. Canva will also offer $US10,000 grants through a new fund for departing employees who want to start a business or pursue a community project. The company said it had explored a range of alternatives and had come to the "difficult conclusion that small changes won't be enough". "We need to re-found Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community," Ms Perkins said. Sydney will become the primary home for Canva's product teams. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) Canva grew out of a Perth-based startup founded by Ms Perkins and Cliff Obrecht, later joined by co-founder Cameron Adams. It became one of Australia's biggest technology success stories, growing into a global design platform used by hundreds of millions of people. Job cuts have become increasingly common across Australia's tech sector, including Atlassian's 1,600 jobs slashed earlier this year . Atlassian said AI would allow it to reduce headcount and redirect resources. Block, which owns Afterpay and logistics software company Wise Tech Global, also announced major workforce cuts. events.title: "I Voted" stickers become tributes at ICE memorials
events.summary: Voters in Minneapolis and Houston are among those leaving "I Voted" stickers at memorials for people killed by federal immigration agents. Why it matters: The tributes highlight how the Trump administration's unpopular immigration crackdown is motivating voters this election cycle. Zoom in: In Minneapolis , people are placing stickers on memorials for Alex Pretti , an ICU nurse, and Renee Good , a writer and mother, who were killed by federal agents in January. In Houston , voters have covered a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo , a construction worker and father who was fatally shot by ICE agents in July, with stickers and handwritten messages like "I voted for you" and "Por usted" — "for you" in Spanish. A voter places an "I Voted" sticker on a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Photo: Mark Felix/Bloomberg via Getty Images Ronaldo Salgado, Araujo's oldest son, placed his sticker on his father's memorial in the first week of early voting and hundreds followed him, the Houston Chronicle reports . "I am beyond touched that this community and that the entire city is voting with my dad in mind ... I didn't realize it would grow this big," he told the Washington Post. The big picture: These midterms are testing whether President Trump's 2024 gains with Latino voters have lasted. National polls in the lead-up to Election Day showed Latino voters swinging back toward Democrats , with immigration as a key area of disagreement with the administration. In an October NBC News/Telemundo poll , 67% of Latino voters said Trump's enforcement has gone too far, 31% said they or someone close now carries ID because of ICE concerns, and 27% know someone detained or deported. events.title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday. The system, called FlashProve , is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model. It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using. Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model. In particular, the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results. FlashProve could also be used to verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model. “A developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model,” the researchers write. “How can a user verify these claims?” To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a “fingerprint” of each model they release that can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. Crucially, the fingerprints don’t reveal a model’s weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. That means labs could publish the fingerprints without giving up their most valuable asset, enabling the system to work with commercial models, too. The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device. As part of the announcement, researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub . Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab. “This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda,” researchers explain in the announcement post. “We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.summary: JetBlue has raised its checked bag fees for the third time in less than a year as fuel costs continue to eat into its profits. Fees will be as much as $70 for a first bag for many economy-class passengers flying during peak travel times like holidays or during the summer. Other airlines raised baggage fees earlier this year. Welcome to the era of the $70 bag fee. JetBlue Airways has raised the price of checking a bag for many customers for the third time in less than a year as high fuel costs continue to eat into the industry's profits. Checking a first bag for travelers booked in economy will now be $50, up from $45, if purchased more than 24 hours before departure during a nonpeak travel period. If it's paid within 24 hours of departure, the fee will be $60. During a peak period, such as during the holidays or the summer, it will be $55 if purchased more than 24 hours before departure, up from $49, and $70 for within 24 hours of departure. There are exceptions to the checked bag fees, such as for customers who hold a co-branded JetBlue credit card or who hold elite frequent flyer status. "We're adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs," JetBlue said in a statement. "This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one." The price of jet fuel, airlines' biggest cost after labor, has roughly doubled this year since the start of the Iran war in February, costing airlines billions and driving up the price of tickets. Jet fuel was going for $4.44 a gallon on Tuesday for the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Other airlines often follow when one carrier raises fees. Major U.S. airlines did so earlier this year after JetBlue raised its bag fees. The changes were reported earlier by the Thrifty Traveler blog . events.title: Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, the New York Times reported Tuesday. The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout. For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said. Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years , according to the International Energy Agency. Most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment, told Bloomberg last week . In some cases, these delays are already costing some data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s. Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets. In 2025, OpenAI followed Musk’s lead with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April. In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines. Currently the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity. Converted jet engines come with trade-offs, though: They’re less efficient and pollute more than turbines designed for conventional gas plants, and it takes more of them to make the same amount of power, according to the Times. That may ultimately make converted jet engines a short-term play with some experts saying that efficiency and environmental concerns may grow in importance in a year or two. events.title: Nasdaq ends higher as AI heavyweights rebound ahead of midterm results
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, in New York City, on Nov 2. Nasdaq rose 0.83% as AI stocks rebounded, with Microsoft, Amazon and Nvidia up. Apple fell 1.9% after warning that memory chip costs would lift holiday-quarter margins. The Nasdaq 100 is now in a correction, more than 10% below its 6 October record, as investors worry AI spending is rising faster than near-term cash returns. Markets also watched the US midterm elections, seen as a possible shift for fiscal policy, regulation and tax. Traders expect the vote to reduce a major market overhang. NEW YORK - The Nasdaq ended higher on Nov 3 as AI heavyweights rebounded ahead of US midterm election results, while Apple fell after the iPhone maker joined the list of Big Tech companies whose quarterly results failed to impress investors. Apple dropped 1.9% after it warned that the cost of memory chips would continue to rise, pressuring its holiday-quarter gross margin. Memory-chip maker Micron Technology gained 2.6%, while Nvidia rose 2.3% after falling in the last four sessions. The broader Philadelphia chips index jumped, while AMD rose ahead of its quarterly report due after the bell. Microsoft and Amazon each moved more than 2% higher. “This is a rotation from safe tech, like Apple, into riskier tech, like chipmakers,” said Jay Hatfield, chief executive officer at Infrastructure Capital Management. “It’s clear dip-buying in a higher-risk, Nasdaq-driven market.” The Nasdaq 100 on Nov 2 ended more than 10% below its Oct 6 record-high close, confirming that the tech-heavy index has entered a correction as investors worry that massive investments in AI infrastructure are outpacing near-term cash generation. The S&P 500 is down about 3% from its record-high close on Oct 6, and it remains up over 10% in 2026. Oil prices eased as investors weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran against worries about additional supply disruptions from recent attacks in both conflicts. Iran and the United States are still far from a deal to end their war, a senior Iranian official told Reuters. The S&P 500 climbed 0.36% to end the session at 7,568.92 points. The Nasdaq gained 0.83% to 25,372.01 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.38% to 51,787.04 points. Six of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by consumer staples, down 1.76%, followed by a 1.75% loss in materials. AI-powered analytics software provider Palantir Technologies forecast revenue above estimates for the last three months of the year after topping third-quarter expectations. Its shares dipped. American voters will deliver a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term in the Nov 3 midterm elections, with polls and nonpartisan analysts favouring Democrats to wrest the House from Republicans, while control of the Senate remains uncertain. “Markets will assess potential implications for fiscal policy, regulation, taxation and government spending. This will be good to put behind us as it has been an anticipated volatility event for quite some time,” said Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. Morgan Stanley analysts said in a note earlier this week that the elections should help remove a major market overhang. They believe a US market correction that began in June is in its “final innings.” Gartner dropped 13.2%, while US-listed shares of Thomson Reuters and Shopify fell 9.9% and 8.7%, respectively, after all three reported quarterly results. Declining stocks outnumbered rising ones within the S&P 500 by a 1.6-to-one ratio. The S&P 500 posted 10 new highs and one new low; the Nasdaq recorded 57 new highs and 251 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was relatively light, with 16.6 billion shares traded, compared with an average of 17.4 billion shares over the previous 20 sessions. REUTERS

events.title: North Korean fake job interview led to $6.3B Binance heist
events.summary: North Korean cryptocurrency thieves tricked a Binance software engineer into downloading malware onto their work-issued computer during a fake job interview process before last week's record-breaking $6.3 billion heist . In an incident report published on Tuesday, the cryptocurrency exchange said several techniques - including social engineering via fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method” - led to the October 29 security breach. “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” the incident report said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.” Over the weekend, the FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus Group , known for combining espionage with massive cryptocurrency heists . The Pyongyang-backed crew is also highly adept at job market scams - both posing as IT workers , who are then hired by Western companies , and as potential employers to lure software engineers into downloading malware and infecting corporate devices . With the recent Binance attack, the Norks used the latter. The attack prep began back in June with a supply chain attack when one of its engineers downloaded a malicious Homebrew installation . While the malware was detected by the security team, the device was replaced, and all affected credentials rotated, “Engineer A’s role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker,” the report says. Three months later, the social engineering part of the attack happened. In September, another software engineer was contacted via a “legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone purporting to be a project director who arranged a series of job interviews for the Binance engineer with the fake company. During the first round - a live video interview with the engineer and a fake HR rep - the interviewer “shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust,” according to the report. “This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.” The second interview with someone purporting to be the CEO of the phony company was conducted on a “popular social chat app,” and toward the end, the CEO instructed the engineer to download an “assignment” containing a malware-laced code repository. The code executed on his work computer during the setup process, which kicked off a series of unauthorized activities. According to Binance, the malware replaced a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version, which executed commands and established communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The attackers also took steps to hide the malicious script and evade detection, and it worked. Binance’s endpoint security tools did not immediately detect the malware. Here’s the script: CREATE /opt/homebrew/Cellar/pyenv/2.8.0/libexec/pyenv_ MODIFY pyenv_ → 3,414 B DELETE .../libexec/pyenv (3,344 B) ← remove the valid pyenv RENAME pyenv_ → pyenv (3,414 B) ← replace it with a malicious version DELETE /opt/homebrew/bin/pyenv (3,414 B) ln (create a new symlink) + spawn zsh Then, on October 20, the miscreants used the compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain access to the computers of wallet DevOps engineer A and another wallet software developer, Engineer C. Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer, which the Norks soon discovered. On October 29, the attacker accessed Engineer C's computer, used the stolen credentials from Engineer A to deploy a container, and triggered a script to launch the cryptocurrency-stealing attack. As of Tuesday, Binance said it has rebuilt the compromised wallet system and internal AI tool, and replaced all of the affected devices. It also decommissioned all credentials and tokens assigned to the compromised engineers, and is working with law enforcement, blockchain intel firms, and security researchers to trace and freeze the assets. The crypto exchange has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to conduct a cybersecurity review of the incident, and recommend additional protective measures. Binance said it’s also working to establish a security research fund and initiatives with AI companies and security shops to focus on AI security in blockchain environments.®

events.title: Singapore’s rise as a wealth hub mirrors Asia’s changing fortunes: Julius Baer Asia head
events.summary: Singapore’s cross-border wealth is expected to grow at a compound annual rate of 9% between 2025 and 2030, from about US$2.1 trillion (S$2.7 trillion) to US$3.3 trillion. Singapore has become Julius Baer’s second-largest global hub after Switzerland. Its workforce grew from 34 in 2006 to more than 1,350 this year. Asian wealth is changing from preservation to diversification, succession planning and family governance. Younger heirs and tech founders want global equities, alternatives and discretionary portfolio management. Julius Baer says Singapore is a leading safe haven because of neutrality and strong governance. Cross-border wealth there may rise 9% a year to US$3.3 trillion by 2030. SINGAPORE – More affluent families from around the region and globe are turning to Singapore to manage their wealth as their focus shifts from preserving fortunes to diversifying investments, succession planning and transferring wealth to the next generation, Julius Baer’s Asia head Jimmy Lee told The Straits Times. The Swiss private bank serves clients across more than 25 markets from Singapore, where its workforce has grown from 34 employees in 2006 to a multinational workforce of more than 1,350 in 2026. Since it set up shop here 20 years ago, Singapore has grown to become Julius Baer’s second-largest global hub after Switzerland. “Singapore’s rise as a global wealth management centre has mirrored the evolution of wealth across Asia,” said Lee, a veteran private banker w ho b ecame the bank’s head of Asia-Pacific in 2016. Two decades ago, wealth management in Singapore was primarily focused on wealth preservation, he said. Many clients were first-generation entrepreneurs who had built their businesses through challenging economic conditions and were focused on protecting capital. Portfolios were often concentrated in familiar regional markets, with equity trading playing a central role. Alternative investments, sustainability and philanthropy were less prominent considerations. Digital assets had yet to emerge as an investable asset class, he said. Meanwhile, Singapore was strengthening its regulatory framework and financial infrastructure, helping to establish its position as a trusted financial centre. Today, the landscape has become more diverse and client priorities have evolved alongside it. The rich have shifted their focus from wealth preservation to diversifying investments, succession planning and transferring wealth to the next generation, says Jimmy Lee, Julius Baer’s Asia head. A new generation of wealth holders, including second- and third-generation family members, as well as entrepreneurs from sectors such as technology, fintech and e-commerce, are placing greater emphasis on diversification across geographies and asset classes, Lee said. Interest in global equities, alternative investments and thematic opportunities has increased, while discretionary portfolio management – where a licensed portfolio manager makes buying and selling decisions on clients’ behalf without requiring prior approval for each trade – has become more widely accepted. As intergenerational wealth transfers continue across Asia, families are also taking a more structured approach to managing wealth. Succession planning, family governance and long-term stewardship have become increasingly important alongside investment performance. “Singapore’s development reflects many of these trends. Supported by a stable regulatory environment, financial resilience and a deep ecosystem of financial expertise, it has become an important centre for wealth management and family offices in the region,” Lee said. More than a quarter of Julius Baer’s global business today originates from Asia, spanning clients, assets under management and talent. Lee said the bank’s presence in the region reflects two decades of sustained investment and commitment. “Building long-term relationships in Asia requires local expertise, continuity and a willingness to invest through market cycles. We view our presence here as long-term, underpinned by the belief that enduring client relationships are built through consistency, proximity and a deep understanding of local markets,” he said. Singapore is also an important centre for innovation for Julius Baer, which in 2021 established Launchpad, its dedicated innovation lab in the Republic, to test and incubate disruptive tech solutions, including digital assets and generative AI. Lee said that as client needs continue to evolve, Singapore will remain central to how the bank develops new capabilities and delivers the next generation of wealth management. In a new report on Asian safe havens, Julius Baer said market volatility driven by artificial intelligence, rising geopolitical tensions and growing government debt has prompted investors to rethink how best to protect their wealth. Traditional safe-haven assets, including US Treasuries, gold and the Japanese yen, have delivered mixed results in 2026.

Ballistic Ventures, the cybersecurity-focused venture capital firm co-founded by former Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein (pictured above, second from the right), is seeking to raise $490 million across two new funds, TechCrunch has learned through regulatory filings. The San Francisco-based VC firm filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission this week to raise $360 million for its third flagship fund, matching the size of its previous fund raised in 2024, and another $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund B. Neither fund had recorded any sales at the time of filing. The fundraising plans come as the growing use of artificial intelligence has raised concerns about more sophisticated cyberattacks. The rise of AI agents has also created new opportunities for cybersecurity startups and the venture capital firms backing them. Founded in late 2021, Ballistic Ventures’ founding team includes Schlein, former AT&T Cybersecurity president Barmak Meftah, and Roger Thornton, who co-founded security companies Fortify Software and AlienVault. The firm has backed companies, including Talon Cyber Security, acquired by Palo Alto Networks , and Pangea, bought by CrowdStrike , alongside startups such as Armadin , GetReal , Nudge Security, and Oligo Security. Ballistic’s ties to storied venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins, where Schlein spent more than two decades, help set it apart from rivals, a cybersecurity investor at another VC firm told TechCrunch. Its investment strategy, however, is similar to those of other cybersecurity-focused investors, including Forgepoint Capital and Ten Eleven Ventures, the person said. In 2022, Ballistic announced its $300 million debut fund and raised another $360 million for its second flagship fund two years later. It also raised about $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund A, per PitchBook data. The new Fund B is targeting a similar amount. U.S. cybersecurity startups raised $11.5 billion in 2025, the highest since 2022, a recent report by JPMorgan Chase said, citing PitchBook data. AI-enabled companies accounted for about 72% of U.S. cybersecurity venture deals through May this year, compared with 36% in 2019, the report said. Separately, Microsoft, in its annual Digital Defense Report released last month, warned that hackers are increasingly using AI for activities ranging from phishing and social engineering to malware development. The technology is allowing attackers to operate faster and at greater scale, even as many of their underlying techniques remain unchanged. events.title: Microsoft improves Windows 11 performance on 8 GB PCs as RAM prices keep climbing
events.summary: With RAM getting more expensive, Microsoft is putting more effort into making Windows 11 run better on systems with just 8 GB of memory. Microsoft said on Tuesday that it was "raising the bar for 8 GB Windows 11 PCs," following a renewed focus on memory optimization earlier this year . The changes come as Redmond continues pushing more expensive Copilot+ PCs, which require at least 16 GB of RAM, amid a memory crunch fueled by AI infrastructure demand. Now, Microsoft says a low-end machine with its 8 GB of precious RAM will be up to 20 percent more responsive and 40 percent faster at multitasking thanks to improvements made in memory management. The tweaks are relatively simple, as Microsoft explained, and seem more about adjusting back to the reality that its flagship operating system needs to function on the hardware people can actually afford to purchase if and when they’re forced to upgrade. Windows 11 will now keep up to 2 GB more active data in memory before shunting it to slower storage, as one example. In another instance, Windows will connect directly to Edge when the browser is already running in the background, allowing it to launch up to 33 percent faster, according to Microsoft. Microsoft apps are also being made more efficient, with Teams able to enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which Microsoft said will make it launch "up to 20 percent faster." Memory efficiency is also being improved by tweaking things like Widgets, which will only load when used instead of always being on, and decreasing the time when Edge tabs go to sleep from two hours to 15 minutes by default. Microsoft said it’s enabling third-party apps to make use of those tweaks, too. Microsoft also included benchmark data in the blog post from a recent bit of research it commissioned. The benchmark report compares a range of 2026 Windows machines with models from 2021, finding that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8 GB of RAM performed about as well as a 2021 Dell XPS 13 with 16 GB across selected workloads. What that means, says Microsoft, is that “the complete PC, not memory capacity alone, shapes the experience.” In other words, please buy some new Windows hardware, even if it’s expensive - we’re begging you. Software optimization can only do so much. “For many people, 8 GB is a great fit for the things they do every day,” Microsoft EVP of Windows and devices Pavan Davuluri wrote in the blog post. “Demanding workloads, such as 3D modeling, advanced video editing, or large-scale data processing benefit from 16 GB of memory or more.” It’s no surprise Microsoft is improving the performance of lower end systems at the same time it’s subtly asking users to buy newer kit, even if it’s just an 8 GB machine - Microsoft may have done well in the past two quarters, but it’s no thanks to Windows devices. Microsoft’s Q4 2026 earnings in late July saw the company rake in cash more broadly, while simultaneously reporting a 7 percent decrease in Windows OEM and devices revenue. Likewise, in its fiscal Q1 2027 results, reported just last week, Microsoft again brought home a mountain of net income, with adjusted earnings reaching $36.4 billion, up 18 percent from the same period last year. Windows OEM and devices revenue, however, was down a whopping 22 percent . It’s hard to think of a reason beyond the fact that hardware prices have shot up with more force than a SpaceX rocket - memory prices are likely to actually make it to Mars, unlike Starship - leaving both consumers and enterprises to stretch those upgrade cycles. If you need to get the most out of that 8 GB Windows 11 PC, you’ll find the latest improvements in 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later. Microsoft is also encouraging users to keep its branded apps up to date, as “some improvements arrive through app updates or through Microsoft Store.” ®

events.title: AI ‘godfather’ Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI
events.summary: Nobel winner warns the tech could be near to triggering major incident such as power or banking shutdown One of the “godfathers of AI”, Geoffrey Hinton, has said it could turn out that humans would have been better off never developing the technology as he warned it could trigger a large-scale incident this year or next, such as a temporary blackout of financial or power systems. The Nobel prize-winning computer scientist told the Guardian he is not a “doomer” about the technology that is underpinned by his groundbreaking research into artificial neural networks and believes AI has the potential to lead to a “wonderful future” but he said “it might be that we would have been better off never developing it”. Hinton, 78, said that within a decade and possibly sooner, humanity will know whether it can manage the technology’s risks and enable what he called “radical abundance” or whether “we fail to manage the risks and … have a huge gap between rich and poor, huge cultural problems, massive unemployment, just society being torn apart”. Hinton was speaking before a screening of a new feature-length documentary, AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About – a title suggested by an AI chatbot – featuring him and his former Google colleague Demis Hassabis. Hinton tells the documentary makers: “I feel I have a duty. I’ve got a reputation that makes me a spokesperson and I need to burn it all on this.” Speaking to the Guardian, Hinton took aim at the risk-taking by the leaders of some of the major AI companies who continue to release ever more powerful AI models as they race for supremacy and market-share, saying he didn’t trust Sam Altman , the chief executive of the ChatGPT maker, OpenAI, “at all”. “I think [Mark] Zuckerberg and [Elon] Musk and Sam Altman, they understand the risks, and they don’t give a shit. They’d rather have the money. That’s my belief.” The London-born computer scientist, who grew up in Bristol and spent much of his career at the University of Toronto, said it was “extremely worrying” that Altman was in charge of one of the handful of frontier US AI companies currently leading a race with China to develop the most powerful AI. Altman insisted in September: “the world should trust we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing and because we feel the magnitude of this”. Hinton has been working on AI for about 44 years and in the 1970s coined the concept of the neural network – a mathematical system that could learn and gain experience much like humans do. In 2023 he quit Google to speak freely about AI risks, warning : “If these things get carried away with getting more control, we’re in trouble.” He said he viewed incidents this summer in which OpenAI AI agents conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website as akin to 1979’s partial nuclear meltdown at the Three Mile Island power station in Pennsylvania – effectively a warning shot. “Either later this year or next year we’ll see Chornobyl, and that may be enough to make people really pay attention,” he said. This Chornobyl-type of event would not be a nuclear incident, according to the examples he gave, but rather could include an AI-enabled attack on the electricity-generating system that “causes a massive brownout” or an incident that brings down the financial system for a week. “Can you imagine what would happen? We could recover from it [but] that would make them sit up and take notice.” Asked who “they” were, he said: “world leaders other than Trump”. The US president, Donald Trump, has said he “ totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme ” to control AI and wants frontier AI companies to regulate themselves, amid concern that rules could hinder the US in its AI race with China. Hinton backs a tougher plan endorsed by the president of Finland and 32 other countries, including Singapore, Germany, Canada and Australia, for mandatory testing of frontier AI models, independent evaluation and intergovernmental common standards. The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he will use the UK’s G20 presidency next year to seek agreement on a “single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks”. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Hinton said: “We need something like the American FDA for drugs where the companies have to give very good statistical evidence to an independent authority that [the AI model] does more good than harm before it is released. We discovered with thalidomide [a drug developed in the 1950s that caused severe birth defects] that releasing and then suing them isn’t the right way to do it. What the big tech companies are saying is treat it like we treated thalidomide.” Hinton’s role as one of the progenitors of AI has led to comparisons to Robert Oppenheimer, who was central to the creation of nuclear weapons. One of Hinton’s friends even bought him an Oppenheimer-style hat.

events.title: Midterms raise new election security questions
events.summary: The midterms are raising fresh questions about the federal government’s role in election security, and where to draw the line between protecting the vote and intervening in the electoral process. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, once a leader in election security, has scaled back its work in President Donald Trump’s second term, raising concerns about the government’s ability to identify and respond to foreign interference. The Justice Department announced its “ largest monitoring effort in history ” today, deploying observers across all 50 states, though a federal judge has ruled that monitors cannot be sworn law enforcement officials or make arrests. The Michigan Attorney General’s Office contacted the DOJ after receiving reports that the department’s monitors were speaking with poll workers in Dearborn and Flint, actions outside the scope of their duties. The disputes could continue after polls close, if legal challenges prolong the fight over election results. — Lauren Morganbesser

( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) A former adviser to the NT infrastructure minister says she disclosed shares in gas firm Beetaloo Energy before starting the role. She worked for the minister when the NT government struck a gas supply agreement with Beetaloo Energy. It comes weeks after the ABC reported the NT deputy chief minister spruiked Beetaloo Energy without publicly disclosing his relative worked there. Further links between the Northern Territory government and gas producer Beetaloo Energy have emerged, with a former ministerial staffer insisting she disclosed her shareholdings in the company before starting the government job. Sonia Harvey was hired by the office of NT Treasurer and Infrastructure Minister Bill Yan in March 2025, after working for Beetaloo Energy (formerly Empire Energy) as "government and community relations vice-president" for three years until July 2024. Ms Harvey said she left Mr Yan's office in September this year for "personal reasons", having advised him on infrastructure and logistics policy. Sonia Harvey left Bill Yan's office in September 2025. ( Supplied: Linkedin ) That same month, the ABC reported NT Deputy Chief Minister Gerard Maley had been spruiking Beetaloo Energy without publicly disclosing that his sister-in-law worked at the firm. Beetaloo Energy's share register shows throughout Ms Harvey's tenure in Mr Yan's office, she held 62,500 shares in the company, which would be currently worth around $13,750. The ABC does not suggest any wrongdoing by Ms Harvey, who said she disclosed her Beetaloo Energy shareholdings "as part of [a] pre-employment check". "I have complied with the relevant requirements applying to ministerial staff, including in relation to the declaration and management of conflicts of interest," she said. During Ms Harvey's time in Mr Yan's office, the NT government signed an agreement with Beetaloo Energy , securing appraisal gas from its Beetaloo Basin fracking project for the NT energy grid. Gerard Maley signed the gas appraisal deal with Beetaloo Energy in December last year. ( ABC News: Matt Garrick ) Appraisal gas is extracted by companies during the testing phase of a project. At the time, Beetaloo Energy chief executive Alex Underwood said the appraisal deal had enabled the firm to reach a final investment decision on its Beetaloo Basin project. The appraisal deal was signed after both Beetaloo Energy and Tamboran Resources inked 10-year gas supply agreements with the former NT Labor government in 2024, amid concerns about ongoing gas supply shortages in the territory. The details of this latest gas deal have been kept secret by the Country Liberal Party government for "commercial in confidence" reasons. The NT government has spruiked the Beetaloo Basin gas reserve as key to the territory's future. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Ms Harvey said she was not privy to any information regarding the Beetaloo Energy gas supply appraisal agreement and said she had "no engagement" with the company while working in Mr Yan's office. According to her Linkedin profile, Ms Harvey's connection to the NT gas industry goes back to 2015, when she founded and became chief executive of the gas-focused Energy Club NT. Infrastructure contracts awarded during tenure During Ms Harvey's tenure in Mr Yan's office, the infrastructure minister announced tenders relating to the Beetaloo Basin, including a $68 million contract for the design and construction of stage three of the Carpentaria Highway upgrade — a service road connecting the Beetaloo Basin to the NT's main highway. In total, the federal and NT governments have allocated a combined $262 million to the Carpentaria Highway upgrade. The territory contributed $52 million, of which $15 million was allocated in the 2025-26 financial year, an NT Department of Logistics and Infrastructure spokesperson said. In May 2025, Mr Yan also announced a contract worth more than $900,000 for "technical advice" to help with planning for the Territory Energy Link — "a proposed multi-user, multi-asset infrastructure corridor stretching from Elliott to Darwin". "It will connect the Beetaloo to Darwin and the world," he said at the time. Bill Yan announced tenders relating to the Beetaloo Basin while Sonia Harvey was working in his office.

events.title: Hiding inside Palantir’s skyrocketing quarter is a foreboding signal
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. The data analysis company Palantir delivered such a huge third-quarter earnings report on Monday that its press release even bragged that the numbers were “crushing consensus expectations.” Yet retail investors were lukewarm on the company on Tuesday, with the stock trading slightly down. That’s because Palantir’s enterprise sales, its big growth area, showed signs of slowing. First, the good news for the company’s investors. Revenue grew 96% from a year earlier, and 20% from the previous quarter, to $2.31 billion, beating analysts’ expectations of $2.18 billion. It was the first time Palantir has topped $2 billion in a quarter. Palantir also reported adjusted earnings per share (profit per share, excluding certain one-time items) of 44 cents, compared with analysts’ expectations of 41 cents. The company even raised its revenue guidance, or forecast, for the full year. Normally, that alone would send a stock soaring. The clincher was that Palantir’s U.S. commercial revenue surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time ever. The company reported $984 million in commercial contracts (up 148% from the year-ago quarter), versus $953 million in U.S. government revenue. The reason for all this love from enterprises? They are signing up for the company’s AI software that can run frontier models and custom-train open-weight models securely, without sharing any of their data and business processes with outside AI labs. Plus, Palantir has long offered what is today known as “forward-deployed” software engineering, in which its own engineers work directly with customers to customize the software. However, Palantir also revealed a less-than-rosy signal: Even as enterprises are moving faster than ever, they are often signing short-term trials. “What Ryan and I are seeing on the front line and commercial is this much quicker interaction, much quicker to deployment, shorter duration of the contract but then an ability to expand that contract dramatically,” CEO Alex Karp (pictured above) told Wall Street analysts on the quarterly earnings call. Palantir is experiencing one of the unique phenomena of AI in the enterprise right now. Corporations are willing to quickly try AI software, skipping the usual bureaucracy, but they are also more willing to cancel contracts. Karp used one off-color metaphor after another to describe how unconcerned he was about holding onto his enterprise business. “We’ve gone from being the most attractive person in the physics department to being the captain of the football team, kind of thing,” he said, describing the influx of prospective corporate customers flowing in. “Conversely, you know, once you go Palantir, you don’t go back, and that’s just how it is, and you see it in our numbers.” The numbers don’t yet confirm Palantir’s long-term success. While the company closed a hefty $1.46 billion of total contract value from U.S. enterprises in the quarter, that’s actually a decline from the record $2.13 billion in the previous quarter. That suggests slowing sales, at least in the most recent quarter. The next earnings will show whether Palantir has solidified its role as a rising U.S. enterprise AI provider. Historically, many enterprises sign their biggest tech purchases in the final quarter of the year. Karp and his team certainly sound confident. They increased guidance for U.S. commercial revenue to be “in excess of $3.559 billion, representing a growth rate of at least 143%.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Anthropic BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters At Fireworks Forge, a celebration of specialized models British fintech Revolut slashes AI coding costs 10x by cutting out Claude and going self-hosted 17 hours ago GhostBSD 26.2 takes the fright out of FreeBSD with a friendlier installer 21 hours ago Forget retraining - AI can now tweak another AI's weights 1 day ago Architect creates open source replacement for VM migration tool VMware has hidden 1 day ago AI could break legal systems by finding previously hidden loopholes 1 day ago Nvidia doesn't seem to care whether open or closed models win out as long as its hardware is powering the infrastructure. "We love closed models," CEO Jensen Huang said. "There's a solid place in the world for closed frontier models. But the world has so many good ideas … The idea that all of us would be based on general intelligence is not logical." Speaking with Lin Qiao, CEO and founder of Fireworks.ai , at the company's Forge event in San Francisco on Tuesday, Huang wasn't ready to throw Nvidia's cloud customers, which help deliver the proprietary AI of Anthropic and OpenAI, under the onrushing open model bus. But having come to the defense of open weight models in July to push back against protectionist pressure from the leadership of Anthropic and OpenAI, Huang recognizes the economic and strategic appeal of AI services that are more affordable and less locked-in. Most of the value in the world, he said, is captured in specialized intelligence, which is to say AI models trained on specific domains of knowledge. "The opportunity for artificial superintelligence is already here," he said. "By taking an open frontier model, adapting it, and providing it with your domain knowledge, your access to your specialized tools, and the proper evaluation, you should be able to create essentially a superintelligence." That aligns with Fireworks' business – offering a platform for companies to train and run models tuned to their specific needs. Coincidentally, that platform just received an infusion of 25,000 Nvidia GPUs to support its expansion in Europe . Huang's endorsement of open models also fits with Qiao's introductory remarks about the need for the AI frontier to be open. But he largely avoided echoing Qiao's focus on the cost savings allowed by working with open models. In her introductory remarks, Qiao stood on stage backlit by a slide composed of ten headlines highlighting the extraordinary cost of unchecked token spending. "Cost is out of control," she said. "Business cannot scale without borrowing a lot of money." That theme was echoed in a subsequent session helmed by Kay Zhu, co-founder and CTO of AI workspace Genspark, titled Gen-1 Slides: Frontier Quality Without Frontier Costs. Gen-1 Slides, Genspark's model for generating slide decks, was built atop MiniMax M3 and tuned to deliver results comparable to Anthropic's Opus 5 at 1/17th the cost – $0.30/M tokens compared to $5/M. Asked what might become commonplace next year but seems unlikely today, Huang said this year's breakthrough has been agent harnesses that turn AI models into agents. He added, "I would say the big breakthrough we'll talk about next year, maybe this is a little self-serving, is how Open Shell has enabled every company in the world to deploy agents safely, confidently." Given the nod to make a second prediction, Huang added, "I would say that the second big breakthrough for industry would be hardware in the loop. And hardware in the loop basically is robotic systems." Given Nvidia's evident interest and investment in robotics , that would be fortuitous.

events.title: Trump says he’ll cut Israel aid, teeing up a fight
events.summary: President Donald Trump said today that the US plans to end around $4 billion in aid to Israel after this year, though the country will still be able to buy weapons. The surprise announcement came as voters fanned out to cast ballots in the midterm elections, including in races where anti-Israel sentiment is shaping the results. Trump said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed with the plan; Netanyahu has said in recent months that he wants to gradually reduce the country’s reliance on congressionally-approved US aid. But there’s a domestic calculus to the announcement, too, as some in the Republican Party grow increasingly skeptical of US aid to Israel. “It’s a bad talking point,” Trump told Fox News earlier today. On the other hand, Trump’s plan sets him on a collision course with Israel’s supporters in Congress, who could approve the aid against his wishes. — Shelby Talcott

events.title: Orbital Matter 3D-printed the first rigid beam in the vacuum of space
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. A satellite built by the German startup Orbital Matter 3D-printed a half-meter long beam out of a custom plastic material, in what executives called a first for a free-flying spacecraft in orbit, and a step toward constructing large structures in space. The company’s small satellite, Replicator 2, was launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission this summer, with four of the company’s 3D printers onboard. Each printer can create a rigid, cylindrical beam by extruding coils of resin that are cured by an ultraviolet light, which the company analogizes to cement and water. This technology matters because future spacecraft will need to be larger in order to generate more electrical power and radiate a more heat into the vacuum of space, particularly if they’re going to serve as orbital data centers. But they’ll still need to fit into the tight confines of the fairing on top of the rocket that carries them into orbit. If spacecraft are able to construct their own structures in orbit, the power and heat-dissipation challenges may get a lot easier to solve. “Replicator 2 is the first proof that we can simply build the array in space, at whatever size the mission demands,” said Jakub Stojek, CEO and co-founder of Orbital Matter. The company is partnering with the European Space Agency and Thales Alenia, a leading European satellite builder, with which it collaborated on Replicator 2. Today’s large structures in space are origami projects — large solar arrays or telescope mirrors are folded up and then deployed on orbit. That’s a tricky engineering project, and so the idea of making and assembling those structures in space is appealing. NASA has funded some efforts at the idea, notably a mission with the company Redwire that 3D-printed structural beams in a vacuum chamber in 2023 but never got off the ground. Two of Orbital Matter’s printers are designed to deploy a flexible solar array, but an anomaly led one of the printers to fail. Still, the boom that was created successfully deployed the solar array, and is an important proof of concept. Previous 3D-printing efforts in microgravity were limited to the pressurized environment onboard the International Space Station. “That’s why we put so many printers on this single satellite. We preferred to learn in orbit and adapt the software as needed rather than waste years testing every possibility on the ground,” Orbital Matters CTO Robert Ihnatisin told TechCrunch. The boom’s length is limited by the amount of resin carried onboard the satellite, and the company’s engineers believe that 100 meter booms are feasible. For comparison, SpaceX’s Starlink V2 satellites — among the most powerful mass-produced satellites in orbit — uses solar arrays that are 20 meters long. Orbital Matter was co-founded in 2022 by Ihnatsin, who previously worked at 3D-printing company FormLabs, and Stojek, and raised a $3 million seed round. Now, Orbital Matter is working on another demonstration mission, scheduled for launch in 2028, that will test a larger version of its printer on a bigger satellite that the company hopes will deploy a solar array that can generate 5 kw of power. That will be a “stepping stone” toward larger deployments of 100+ KW per wing by 2030. The company is also collaborating with satellite builders that are considering incorporating its PADS (printer-assisted deployment system) into their spacecraft to extend solar panels, antennas, or other components. events.title: Haley Stevens requests U.S. marshals' protection after death threats
events.summary: Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens has requested U.S. marshals' protection after the Democrat told authorities she had received death threats for endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in the swing state's hotly contested Senate race, two senior Trump administration officials tell Axios. Why it matters: Stevens' surprise decision Sunday to switch her endorsement to Rogers over Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed was the biggest political story of the midterm campaign's final days. Stevens — who lost to El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate primary — was widely criticized by Democrats after siding with Rogers, and her top staff members resigned. "She has received death threats and reached out to the Marshals Service," one of the officials said. "There's a process to go through but she's a member of Congress and we expect her request will be fulfilled." Zoom in: Stevens' support for Israel and his criticism of the Jewish state was a major dividing line in their primary campaign. Stevens objected to El-Sayed's ties to controversial progressive streamer Hasan Piker and an ad by a PAC tied to Piker's uncle, Cenk Uygur, blaming Israel for rising grocery prices. El-Sayed disavowed the ad, but Stevens said she believed he hadn't done enough to address her concerns and didn't want her help on the campaign trail. The dispute came to a head when she was told she was no longer welcome at El-Sayed's campaign events. Stevens announced her endorsement of Rogers after appearing with him at a church service on Sunday. Stevens could not be reached for comment Tuesday. The big picture: The political environment in Michigan has been volatile this weekend. On Monday, the New York Post reported a former El-Sayed staffer was one of several anti-Zionist activists federally indicted for allegedly terrorizing members of Michigan's Jewish community. On Sunday, a conservative Jewish activist was attacked by a progressive activist at a University of Michigan event where organizers were criticizing Islam. On Friday, U.S. officials announced the arrest of a Michigan man for allegedly threatening FBI director Kash Patel. Stevens recently clashed with an anti-Zionist activist whom she accused of trying to intimidate her over her support for Israel.
