events.title: Car finance compensation payments explained
events.summary: Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, although some may be offered an early settlement. Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed. Who could receive car finance compensation? The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024. The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period. In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them. The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much. Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan. Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders. How much compensation could victims receive? Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement. The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn. How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered. The FCA has announced some claimants might be offered an early settlement, but only if it as good as what would be paid under the current proposed central scheme. What do victims need to do to claim compensation? Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything. The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company. The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts. Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation . The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain , external . lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster some people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, if the agreement began on or after 1 April 2014 and you complained by 30 June 2026 some of those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027, if the agreement began before 1 April 2014 there are exemptions , external , and anyone who does not hear from their lender by the dates set out, isn't necessarily owed compensation those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees. FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers. When will drivers receive compensation and who will pay? Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027. But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme. Consumer Voice said the scheme left "too many people short-changed" . The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance. The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled for 16 February to 3 March.

events.title: Apple's Mac business is booming, but the memory market has other plans
events.summary: Apple says it sold more Macs in fiscal 2026 than in any previous year, but soaring memory prices are threatening to spoil the Cupertino-based gadget maker's record-breaking run. The warning came during Apple's fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call on Monday, the first since John Ternus took over as CEO . "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus told analysts. Apple has already raised prices across much of its hardware lineup, including Macs and iPads in June and iPhones in September. Those increases, along with existing inventories and cheaper components elsewhere, have softened the blow. Unfortunately for Apple, memory prices haven't finished climbing. "For the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs," Ternus said, adding that Apple expects to pay more for memory beyond the end of the year. Mac buyers haven't been deterred so far. Apple pulled in $10.8 billion from Macs in the September quarter, up 24 percent year-on-year, following $10.35 billion in the June quarter, up nearly 29 percent year-on-year. The MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro accounted for much of the latest growth. "We have never sold more Macs in a fiscal year than we did this time," Ternus said. Whether Apple can keep enough of them on shelves is another matter. COO Sabih Khan said the company had already experienced supply constraints across iPhone, Mac, and iPad during the September quarter, largely because of limited availability of advanced chipmaking capacity. Now memory is taking over as the chief headache. "For the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory, as demand has been higher than what we expected," Khan said. Apple isn't sitting idle. Ternus revealed that its manufacturing purchase obligations jumped by $33 billion between June and September as it bids to secure supplies, although he offered no indication of when the memory crunch might ease. Higher memory costs are also squeezing Apple's margins. CFO Kevan Parekh said gross margin fell by roughly one percentage point between the June and September quarters, excluding tariff effects, entirely because of memory costs. The damage would have been worse without existing inventory, cheaper non-memory components, and those price hikes. Apple expects its gross margin to fall from 47.9 percent in the September quarter to between 45 and 46 percent in December, primarily because of higher memory costs. Costs associated with rolling out Siri AI will also weigh on the figure. Parekh said Apple had "reluctantly" raised hardware prices, but supply constraints made it too early to assess how customers were responding. Meanwhile, Ternus is keen to sell customers on the Mac as an AI machine, particularly for running models locally. "Mac mini and Mac Studio in particular are pushing the boundaries of local private AI," he said, pointing to workloads that previously would have been difficult to run on desktop hardware. Apple has also refreshed its Mac lineup with M6-powered machines and a touchscreen MacBook Pro, giving customers more reasons to upgrade, provided there's enough memory to build the things. Not that the wider business is struggling. Apple reported September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent year-on-year, while iPhone revenue climbed 17 percent to $57.6 billion. Services brought in $31.6 billion, up 10 percent. Apple forecasts revenue growth of 7 to 10 percent in the December quarter despite the supply constraints. Even with memory prices running wild, it isn't expecting to go hungry. ®

events.title: Drivers may get compensation offers before car finance saga ends
events.summary: Drivers may be offered compensation from lenders ahead of the next legal battle in the car finance mis-selling saga. Regulator the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it would welcome lenders making settlement offers as long as customers were not given a worse deal than under its proposed central scheme. That scheme is facing a legal challenge, to be heard in February, with resulting compensation unlikely to be paid until late next year. But Barclays has confirmed it will make early compensation offers from now, with others expected to follow suit. The FCA said it would still only expect a minority of claimants to be made early offers, with most having to wait for the outcome of next year's court case. Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA's general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said: "Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. It's clear they want the choice. "Anyone who wants to wait can, and there's no obligation to agree to the offer. We'll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means." The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. But millions of drivers who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024 will be entitled to compensation after the loans were mis-sold. They mostly related to when car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them. Average compensation payouts of about £829 are expected to be made related to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period. Car finance compensation payments delayed until next year Published 1 day ago Compensation will cost the industry up to £9.1bn, including administrative costs. Individual payouts will vary, depending on the degree of harm each driver faced. With huge compensation payouts inevitable, some lenders have already set aside millions of pounds to cover the cost. Barclays has decided to start making compensation payments early, potentially to start clearing the cost off its balance sheet. It pointed out that claimants had already faced "a considerable wait". "By making these early settlement offers, we are giving some customers the option of receiving redress sooner, rather than waiting for the legal challenges and any subsequent FCA action to conclude," said a Barclays Partner Finance spokesperson. "Each offer will be calculated using the FCA's redress scheme methodology. We will clearly explain how it has been calculated and what accepting a full and final settlement means, so customers can decide whether accepting the offer is right for them." The lender said claimants would start to be contacted directly "in the coming weeks". But it stressed not all customers whose complaints were acknowledged on or before 1 October 2026 would receive an early settlement offer. Guidelines on whether to accept an offer The FCA has published a factsheet to help drivers , external work out whether they should accept early settlements from lenders. It will include a list of lenders who are making early offers, to ensure claimants with other lenders are not scammed. The regulator said lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes: Being able to keep any payment, even if the final settlement under the central scheme after the legal challenges proved to be smaller Claimants would not be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge meant they would have been paid more Accepting an offer takes you out of the scheme and stops any further input from the financial ombudsman The Finance and Leasing Association, which represents lenders, said: "We want to see consumers receive the fairest outcome in as timely a way as possible and recognise that, in some cases, that may point to early settlement, while in others it may be appropriate to await greater legal certainty." But Kevin Durkin, solicitor advocate and director at HD Law, who represented Marcus Johnson who won his case in the Supreme Court, said he had "real reservations" that fair compensation would be offered. "These are only heightened by reports that just a small number of claimants will receive what could be lowball offers. I fear this is crumbs from the table, for some customers who are highly likely to be owed more, while the vast majority will receive no offer at all," he said. The main proposed FCA scheme remains partially suspended, pending legal challenges in February. Consumer group Consumer Voice said the proposed compensation scheme left "too many people short-changed".

events.title: Higher oil prices boost Saudi Aramco profits despite disruption from attacks
events.summary: Ore. Governor Projected winner Tina Kotek • D 3 hours ago Neb. Senate Projected winner Pete Ricketts • R 3 hours ago Election 2026 live results: Mississippi Senate race separated by dozens of votes Saudi Aramco is reporting a 35% increase in third-quarter net profit, boosted by higher oil prices and the sale of a stake in a Malaysian company FRANKFURT, Germany -- Majority state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco on Tuesday reported a 35% increase in third-quarter net profit as earnings were boosted by higher oil prices and the sale of its stake in a Malaysian refining and petrochemical company. Net profit rose to $36.3 billion from $26.9 billion in the year-earlier quarter. Adjusted net profit, which leaves out the sale of a stake in PRefChem to Malaysian state oil company Petronas, rose 9% to $31.2 billion. The company also benefitted from high profit margins at its refineries turning crude into useable products such as diesel fuel. Saudi Aramco sold its oil for an average of $95.20 a barrel during the quarter, compared to $70.10 in the year-before quarter, the company said in a news release. Oil prices surged after the outbreak of the Iran war due to disruption of supply and uncertainty about the course of the conflict. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Captain identified after deadly Florida Learjet crash 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say After the war began in February, Saudi Aramco was able to use its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu to maintain a significant share of its oil exports despite disruption of tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz due to the risk of Iranian attack. The pipeline was attacked Sept. 10 but has resumed flows. Saudi oil is now also being transported through the strait using a U.S.-protected corridor near the coast of Oman. Exports have continued despite attacks on Aramco facilities by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. The company is a major source of revenue for the Saudi government as it invests in projects aimed at diversifying its economy. events.title: Long-term demand for LNG will continue to rise, Adnoc Gas CEO says
events.summary: Demand for gas will continue to rise as the world requires more energy to power the development of artificial intelligence, the chief executive of Adnoc Gas has said. Severe disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz has shut down about one fifth of the world’s monthly liquefied natural gas supply since the Middle East conflict started in February, adversely affecting some countries in Asia, Shell said in its latest LNG outlook. But Fatema Al Nuaimi told Adipec on Tuesday: “Gas is going to continue to grow and demand is going to continue in the long-term.” Ras Laffan in Qatar, the world's largest LNG refinery, was severely damaged by Iranian missile attacks. QatarEnergy declared long-term force majeure on contracts with buyers in China, South Korea, Italy and Belgium. However, global demand for LNG is projected to increase by around 65 per cent by 2050, to nearly 700 million tonnes a year, Shell said in its report. A key driver for growth comes with the rising development of new data centres to power AI technology. “We have these new demand hubs from AI … about 9.5 million tonnes of LNG required just for SpaceX,” Ms Al Nuaimi said. “We are an ambitious nation when it comes to building AI hubs to attract the biggest names in artificial intelligence and for this to be materialised, energy is required.” Abu Dhabi is investing heavily in AI infrastructure to support the growth of the technology. Among the projects is the 1-gigawatt Stargate UAE project being developed by Abu Dhabi-based AI company G42 in partnership with technology giants OpenAI, Oracle and Nvidia. It will lie within the 5GW UAE-US AI Campus in Abu Dhabi. ⁠Ms Al Nuaimi called for flexibility and co-operation in ​managing gas contracts to adapt to changing market conditions. “Contracts are very rigid, written with terms and conditions, and no matter how you craft them, they are not fit for different circumstances that face us in the market. So it's important for us to be flexible and to work together eventually.” Adnoc Gas on Tuesday also announced the singing of a five-year agreement to supply up to 1.6 million tonnes of LNG to France's TotalEnergies, as the Abu Dhabi company expands its share of the global market. The agreement comes as Adnoc scales up a new global LNG trading platform that combines the marketing activities of Adnoc Gas and investment arm XRG with the commercial capabilities of Adnoc Trading . Adnoc Gas supplies about 60 per cent of the UAE’s sales gas needs as well as end customers in more than 20 countries.

events.title: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
events.summary: The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found. Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report. The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic. "This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation. Quiet quitting was popularised on social media shortly after the pandemic . Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more. So you still show up for work, but no more helping out with additional tasks or checking emails outside work hours, instead focusing on work-life balance and "acting your wage". Yet, far from being just a talking point on TikTok, the Resolution Foundation said the findings in its report were "consistent" with the idea of quiet quitting. 'I was working 60 hours a week so I quiet quit' Published 31 August 2022 The percentage of those surveyed willing to go the extra mile to help their employer has sunk from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025, according to their survey of 4,656 adults. Meanwhile, those who were not even "fairly" satisfied with their roles has sunk to one-in-four, the lowest level on record. In addition, workers are less likely than 10 years ago to say they have an interesting job, with 63% of those surveyed saying so, down from 74%. "Workers today are indeed a little less committed to their employers, and a little less intrinsically drawn to work in general, than workers were a decade ago," the report added. This shift over the last decade "may have contributed to weak productivity growth", which has slowed since the financial crisis and weakened again after the pandemic, the Resolution Foundation found. Workers were also more focused on pay than in the past, which it said was "perhaps unsurprising... given the flatlining living standards of the past decade". Sir John Curtice, politics professor and co-editor of the report, said the analysis does not mean that young people have "become more 'work-shy', nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs". "But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financially rewarding and have flexible work hours," he added. Are you quiet quitting? Tell us how and why. events.title: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
events.summary: Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period. The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000. The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance". Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres. Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September. It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen . Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold. As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo. Ternus said he was "thrilled" by the early reaction to the foldable phone. Chief operating officer Sabih Khan said the company was working hard to get the Duo "into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible". Apple's results for the three months to 26 September did not include sales of the Duo, which was released at the end of October. Nevertheless, Apple said it had sold more iPhones globally over the last year than ever before. iPhone revenue for the quarter rose 17% to $57bn (£42bn). Sales of Mac computers also grew over the three months by 27% to a record $10.7bn. Overall, Apple's sales between July and September rose from $102bn to $114bn. Pre-tax profit also increased, from $32.8bn to $36.1bn. However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and watch, fell by 10% and 7%, respectively. Khan said that most Apple devices were still experiencing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with advanced nodes. Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allow Apple devices to operate more quickly, most of which it has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan. Khan said the problem was expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products. Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of devices to store data like apps, photos and text messages. Much memory storage runs through data centres, which have experienced a boom in demand for space as AI chatbots and platforms - including those developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic - have become popular. Watch: Would you buy Apple's $2,000 foldable phone? Storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple. Earlier this year, Cook referred to a sudden increase in data centre costs as a "thousand year flood". Apple has lifted prices on nearly all of its hardware products by around 20%. Sunil Krishnan from Aviva Investors told the BBC's Today programme that Apple posted "a reasonably solid set of results" with a "pretty good performance" from its iPhone business. While there were concerns over the company's guidance on profit margins and the cost of memory chips, Krishnan added that in the broader context, "margins well north of 45% for a very well-established company, I think, are pretty impressive". However, Apple's share price fell by 1.8% in after-hours trading. events.title: How We’re Covering the Midterms — and the Aftermath
events.summary: Early voting for the midterms in New York last month Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images This has been a midterm election cycle unlike any other. Wealthy donors spent staggering sums . Both parties moved to redraw congressional district lines . President Donald Trump and his allies relentlessly questioned whether the results could be trusted even before a single ballot was counted. At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit that said the federal government would contest any outcome in which Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent in Alaska, was not victorious. Newsrooms, including ours, have tried to plan how we will cover an election in which the losing side refuses to accept the will of the voters. Was the Alaska lawsuit a single data point or a harbinger? As we prepare to write about Nov. 3 and beyond, we find ourselves in the uncomfortable position of trying to game out what might happen in the future — not our strong suit. The record shows that journalists are pretty good at telling readers what happened, particularly if we have some time and some data to sift through, and much less good at forecasting the future. Help Us Report on Key Election Issues ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something? Send Us a Tip And yet we have to plan. Over the past few weeks we have prepared our reporters and editors to cover every scenario we can imagine. None of us have forgotten the chaos of 2020 when Trump was urged by advisers to send the military to seize voting machines in states he had lost. The Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol as lawmakers gathered to certify Joe Biden’s victory underscored the sense that literally anything was possible in the aftermath of elections. We will have reporters on the ground in 11 key states covering voting, with even more in Washington, D.C., and others on standby. Our reporters have detailed what experts will be watching . But elections are no longer confined to Election Day (early voting and voting by mail constitute a huge share of the electorate). And our plans for covering voting stretch back many months. Over the past year, we’ve tried to use the techniques of accountability journalism to add new facts to this pivotal moment in American history. We have focused considerable attention on the mechanics of elections, a once-arcane issue that has become a central aspect of the MAGA movement’s argument that Trump’s 2020 loss was “rigged” by his opponents. We examined how the Trump administration depleted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency , the arm of the federal government charged with safeguarding election systems. We discovered that Department of Homeland Security officials had asked CISA to obtain a voting machine and hack it without informing the manufacturer of any vulnerabilities found. The plan wasn’t acted on, but its existence made CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. CISA and DHS didn’t respond to our questions, but a White House spokesperson said Trump “has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.” Another story looked at how delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures endangered the validity of mail-in ballots in rural counties , typically Republican strongholds, during this year’s primaries. The Postal Service said such delays are less likely in the general election. One of our most detailed election stories traced the career of Cleta Mitchell , a lawyer who spearheaded the legal attacks on the 2020 results. Mitchell leads a coalition of what she calls “election believers” — people who scour the voting results for errors that they believe point to larger conspiracies. Changes she’d hoped Trump could push through before the midterms, such as compelling states to turn over confidential voter information to the Justice Department, have been blocked by the courts . But she has nonetheless become the voice of a well-funded national movement, one which has the president’s ear. When Trump is weighing what to do in the aftermath of this week’s vote, our reporting strongly suggests that Mitchell will be among the people he listens to. We asked to speak with Mitchell multiple times. She declined but told us in an email: “​​​​What we focus on is making sure the election process is accurate, transparent, and honest. The ONLY steps I’ve urged the Administration to take are those that will give the voters — ALL voters — confidence that the outcomes are correct.” A White House spokesperson said she has no official role in election policy but is an effective private advocate. We have also spent time doing the traditional work of investigative reporting, looking closely at candidates’ records in public office. A newsroom like ours can’t cover every race, so we focus our resources on areas where we have particular expertise. Our team in Texas has covered state Attorney General Ken Paxton for years, and we kept our focus once he announced he would run for the U.S. Senate. One story looked at his travels, revealing that only 1 in 6 of his nearly 1,000 out-of-state trips were linked to his official duties. Texas taxpayers paid $3.3 million for Paxton’s security detail to accompany him. (Paxton didn’t answer our questions, but his office said he “faced numerous security threats.”) That has become an issue in the Senate campaign. Another opportunity arose from an investigation that was seemingly not related to the midterms: our examination of the Trump administration’s handling of the Justice Department. We began many months ago to look for promising cases that had been dropped and found out the FBI had been looking into pay-to-play allegations involving prominent Democratic and Republican members of Congress. The case included a bipartisan list of political figures such as Susan Collins , the Republican senator from Maine running in a closely contested race this year, and James Clyburn , a leading Democratic representative from South Carolina who’s also on the ballot this year. Our first story revealed that Collins helped a little-known defense contractor win millions in federal contracts while the company’s CEO helped bankroll her 2020 reelection effort through a donation made via a shell company. Our second story revealed that the FBI was looking into interactions that Clyburn and Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, had with the same contractor. Collins has denied all wrongdoing. “A donation would never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Clyburn’s office said. Graham’s communications director wrote that “any allegations of quid-pro-quo behavior … are simply false.” The FBI stopped examining the allegations after Trump purged the bureau. Our coverag

events.title: Broadcom denied names of cloud providers backing VMware merger challenge
events.summary: Euro cloud trade association CISPE can keep the identities of members backing its VMware merger challenge confidential from Broadcom following a ruling by the EU General Court. Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe filed an action last year seeking to annul the European Commission's approval of Broadcom's acquisition of the cloud and virtualization giant. CISPE believes the Commission erred in allowing the purchase to go ahead without imposing any conditions on Broadcom to protect the many European cloud providers and their customers who depend on VMware's software. Broadcom sought access to redacted information identifying members supporting the action, arguing that it needed the information to challenge the action's admissibility. CISPE says the ruling allows the case to proceed without disclosing those identities to Broadcom. "It is a procedural ruling on confidentiality rather than a decision on the substance of the case, but it removes the immediate obstacle to the action moving forward," a CISPE spokesperson told The Register . CISPE argued that identifying the members, which are or have been VMware customers, would expose them to a significant risk of retaliation because of Broadcom's market power. Those members had supplied information about their commercial relationships with VMware. As far as the case itself goes, CISPE says it warned the Commission that Broadcom would use VMware's pre-eminent position in the private cloud market to rewrite licensing terms and reshape the market in its favor. Just a month after Broadcom's acquisition concluded in November 2023, partners were informed that VMware's channel program was to end in early 2024, and that Broadcom was also ditching the majority of VMware's Cloud Services Providers , keeping only a select few that had the largest turnover. Despite Broadcom CEO Hock Tan publicly stating that inflating prices was not his strategy, that is what happened. AT&T says that Broadcom proposed a 1,050 percent price increase , for example. Meanwhile, nine out of ten respondents to a recent survey of VMware customers said they were considering moving to alternatives. CISPE, which represents 48 cloud infrastructure service providers across the EU, says fewer than 20 European providers remain authorized to offer VMware-based services, down from more than a thousand. Commenting on the latest ruling, CISPE Secretary General Francisco Mingorance declared it a good day for the organization and for the rule of law in Europe. "The case matters even more today than when we filed it. In the three years since the European Commission waved this deal through without conditions, Broadcom has dismantled the European VMware channel ," he said . "Those excluded have until 31 March, 2027, to sell their infrastructure or their customers to a competitor chosen by Broadcom, or to close. This is the foreclosure the European Commission was warned about." We asked CISPE what outcome it hoped to achieve, nearly three years after the acquisition closed. "The immediate objective is to have the Commission's unconditional clearance annulled, on the basis that it failed to properly assess the effect of the acquisition on European cloud providers and the VMware channel," CISPE's spokesperson told The Register . The Commission did impose conditions concerning interoperability with rival hardware, but CISPE argues these did not address the risks to cloud providers. "We appreciate that it's a long shot (although there is precedent)," the spokesperson continued. "We have (along with others) also filed a competition complaint with the Directorate-General for Competition against Broadcom for its actions post-merger." The precedent referred to is the EC approval given to the merger of Sony and BMG's music divisions in 2004, which was ruled to be not of "the requisite legal standard" two years later. The deal was subsequently reassessed and re-cleared. "Ultimately, we want to do whatever we can to bring Broadcom to the table to negotiate and ideally end some of its most egregious practices so that European cloud providers can once again support cloud customers in a commercially fair and viable manner," the spokesperson added. The Register asked Broadcom to comment The European Commission declined to comment on procedural matters . ®

events.title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
events.summary: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators .  Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage. An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay. In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.  A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).  Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.  The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.  A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?” Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.  During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.  There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.  Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.  Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.” One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.  It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.  “Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior. Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. events.title: The US-China thaw may not outlive the Trump era
events.summary: Andy’s view The prospect of steep losses for Republicans in today’s midterms and the lame-duck presidency that ensues regardless raise a fundamental question about the outlook for a budding US-China détente. Can warming superpower ties outlive the Trump era? I wouldn’t count on it. It’s not that an election humiliation would crimp US President Donald Trump’s diplomatic style. On the contrary, there’s every expectation it would give him even greater incentive to build his legacy on the world stage. But the current thaw is so much an artifice of his own unabashed admiration for his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping. And a backlash is brewing. Trump boasts of a “great friendship” with the Chinese strongman — they’ve held two summits so far this year, with plans of another meeting in Shenzhen this month, and a fourth in Miami in December — speaks of a G2 to manage global affairs, and waves away strategic concerns that might strain the bromance. (Asked about reports that Chinese satellite imagery was used by Iran to kill US troops, Trump told reporters on Air Force One: “They basically do what we do.“) Yet US policy on China remains very much in play, and debates will surely heat up after the midterms as the race to succeed Trump gets under way across both parties. Although Republican hawks have largely fallen silent in Trump’s second term, within the Beltway a bipartisan tough-on-China consensus is intact. Foreign policy elites complain that Trump is ceding the Western Pacific to Beijing (Evan Feigenbaum of the Carnegie Endowment mocks the administration″⁣s “ reverse pivot from Asia ” as the Pentagon diverts warships and marines to the Gulf.) Tech hawks accuse Trump of throwing away the US lead in AI by greenlighting exports of advanced Nvidia chips to China, or turning a blind eye to illicit transfers. The Taiwan lobby is outraged at his transactional approach to the island. Moreover, such criticisms are likely to intensify if an angry Trump, smarting from midterm defeats, focuses even more of his attention on deal-making with Xi. Ali Wyne, a US-China specialist at the International Crisis Group, sees bipartisan frustration at Trump’s China policy winding up like a coil, ever more tightly as he gives ground to Xi, and eventually unspooling “violently and unpredictably.” The next president, Wyne told me, will inherit a weaker hand vis-à-vis China and is likely to be “far more permissive of competitive and even confrontational actions.” Certainly, Trump’s successor — from either party — won’t have nearly the same latitude to manage China ties; one former American diplomat calls the president “ his own China desk officer .” (Of course, there’s always a chance that Trump himself will flip before he steps down, as he did at the end of his first term when he blamed Xi for unleashing the pandemic on the world and wrecking his reelection chances.) The late Henry Kissinger, the architect of Nixon’s 1972 opening to China, observed that “America has no permanent friends or enemies, only interests.” In Trump’s ardent pursuit of Xi, critics suggest the US president forgot that lesson. Once Trump goes, a return to a colder, harder, more calculating is in the cards. Notable In a recent op-ed for The New York Times, Thomas L. Friedman argues that as the world’s leading AI superpowers, with shared interests in safeguarding against AI’s risks, the US and China may be pushed toward “ mutually assured collaboration .”

events.title: What's on the line for health care in the midterms
events.summary: Voters are about to decide whether public backlash against the health care industry translates into meaningful policy shifts. Why it matters: Health care has never been more expensive, and it's not going to get any cheaper without significant intervention. The big picture: It's hard to see Democrats not making health care affordability a top priority in the next Congress, regardless of whether they win only a narrow majority in the House or sweep both chambers in a blowout. But the party isn't aligned on an agenda, and a strong showing by progressives could drag things leftward. Reality check: Any Democratic victory — no matter the size — will be tempered by the realities of split government, with President Trump still in office for the next two years. Larger Democratic majorities may bring greater leverage in negotiations over spending packages or raising the debt limit. And the boldest changes will probably be reserved for the campaign trail, as 2028 presidential contenders begin to vie for the party's nomination. Here's what we're watching: Medicare for All vs. moderates: What happens in Michigan's Senate race — and Maine's, to some extent — will almost certainly shape how much sway progressives have in the next two years. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has made Medicare for All central to his campaign, unabashedly supporting the idea in a race that could determine which party has control of the Senate next year. The same is true of Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine's Senate race, though Jackson has a lower national profile than El-Sayed. But Medicare for All supporters looking for a vote on the measure face an uphill battle : Despite the policy's growing popularity among the public, moderates unwilling to abolish private insurance will make up a sizable portion of any Democratic majority. The doctors-turned-politicians: Doctors are on the ballot in key races this year, and the question is how much public trust translates into votes. El-Sayed, an epidemiologist who went to medical school but isn't a practicing physician, is one example. There's also pediatrician Annie Andrews, who's mounted a strong challenge to Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, and Ohio governor candidate Amy Acton, who has focused on pediatrics and preventive medicine. "We've seen in our research over the last six-plus years that [doctors are] among the most trusted potential candidates for office, hands down," said Erik Polyak, executive director of 314 Action. MAHA on the line: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s "Make America Healthy Again" movement has focused its attention largely on the Iowa governor's race in the final weeks of the election, going all in for Republican Zach Lahn, who's pledged to take on Big Agriculture interests and the use of farm chemicals. Calling it an "existential" vote, MAHA Action founder Tony Lyons told MAGA influencer Steve Bannon that the race will be "the test of what's possible in a state, of whether we can actually take the country back from these corrupt companies, from these corrupt politicians, and really protect people." California's tax plan: Golden State voters will decide the fate of a controversial one-time wealth tax on billionaires, with most of the proceeds to be used to fund health care services. The money is intended to partly make up for Republican cuts to federal Medicaid spending but the tax is opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, a likely 2028 Democratic presidential contender. The measure tests voter sentiment in one of the bluest states to tax the super rich in order to fund health benefits — a potential prelude to a national debate over expanding the federal government's role in health care and how to fund it. Abortion ballot measures: Voters in four states will determine what reproductive rights in their states look like, another round of post-Roe abortion policymaking via ballot initiatives. Nevada and Virginia will consider constitutional amendments protecting the right to abortion, while Missouri will weigh a measure backed by the state legislature to repeal a 2024 pro-abortion rights amendment. Idaho voters will determine the fate of a state law guaranteeing a right to abortion until fetal viability, generally considered to begin around 23 to 24 weeks into a pregnancy, or after that in the case of a medical emergency.

events.title: I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining.
events.summary: A flash flood along the Rio Ruidoso on July 30, 2025 Three summers ago, over Father’s Day weekend, my family and I went camping in the Lincoln National Forest, just a few hours drive north of our home in El Paso, Texas. It’s a beautiful area that’s long served as a getaway for the region, with skiing in the winter, and golf and hiking in the summer. My daughter played under the trees, and I rode my bike down mountain trails that, I noticed, seemed concerningly dry.  The next evening, after we left to drive home, two fires started in forests surrounding the town of Ruidoso, New Mexico, around 25 miles away from where we’d been. I watched horrifying videos online of fire lapping the mountains behind the village’s strip malls and parking lots. The fires were eventually suppressed by a combination of human effort and the late summer monsoon season. But when the downpour of rain hit the burnt landscape around Ruidoso, it created another problem: Recurring floods then ripped through town, damaging homes and infrastructure, and leading to emergency rescues. The following summer, the scene repeated. On July 8, 2025, monsoon rain hit a burn scar and quickly swelled the Rio Ruidoso and its tributaries. Three people — two of them children — lost their lives.  Reporter Abe Streep, a member of ProPublica’s Southwest office, and I met in Ruidoso to report on what happened. Ruidoso is a place built on tourism, with a paid (rather than volunteer) fire department staff and its own disaster manager. How could two children and a man be swept to their deaths in a place that appeared equipped to handle such disasters?  In two stories ProPublica recently published, Abe answered those questions. He found that, after the 2024 fires, experts warned the town of increased flash flooding risks . Initially, local and state leaders considered a relocation plan for some homes and businesses that would get people out of harm’s way, but the project faltered. Instead, village leaders continued promoting tourism to the town, and the mayor even chastised residents for warning of floods on social media. Abe also reported that, while local and state officials insisted the emergency response to the flood was admirable, first responders say the three deaths could have been avoided . The responders told Abe that village leadership left them understaffed and inadequately equipped to contend with the flooding. The Village of Ruidoso did not respond to detailed written questions about its emergency response, and it has not publicly released a report on rescue efforts during the flood. Reached by phone, the fire chief, Cade Hall, disputed our reporting but declined to provide specifics. Mayor Lynn Crawford has said protecting the village includes balancing public safety with tourism, the lifeblood of its economy. But in an interview last year, Crawford said to Abe and me: “Who’s to blame? I didn’t start the fire.” My role as a photographer was to document Ruidoso as the story unfolded — to visualize the people and place at the center of it. It’s a role I’ve had countless times in my career, but this story hit unexpectedly close to home. I could imagine my own family caught unaware in a similar situation, trying to escape the El Paso summer heat but instead navigating an unfathomable disaster. A crumbled trailer and debris from flash flooding in Ruidoso on Aug. 1, 2025 The crumbling house at the Riverview RV Park on Sept. 10, 2026 When Abe and I started reporting, we met people from the community and out of town who tried to help. I watched as New Mexico National Guard service members loaded sand bags into families’ cars, people prepared hot meals for those who had been displaced and volunteers handed out donated supplies from collection centers.  Supplies inside a Salvation Army makeshift distribution center and a sandbag distribution point facilitated by the New Mexico National Guard last summer While we were reporting one afternoon, it started raining. Fear swept through me. Our phones lit up with flood warnings from the National Weather Service. We knew we should take them seriously. Abe and I sought refuge in a local brewery perched high above the river basin. Before we knew it, the water from that thin little creek of Rio Ruidoso became a torrent. The rushing water rose quickly. It swept through the river valley right under the brewery, carrying what looked like trees and debris with it. A woman watches the Rio Ruidoso rise from inside a brewery in downtown Ruidoso last summer. Two people venture close to the river as a flash flood began to subside last summer. Still, I wanted to photograph the river up close. I left the safety of the brewery and let the heavy rain cover me as I moved closer to the river. As I made photos that afternoon and throughout the rest of the trip, questions about my own safety ran through my mind: Would the water keep rising? If it did, could I get to high ground? And, notably, would I have enough warning? In hindsight, I realize these questions were largely about whether I could trust the systems in place to keep me and others safe. And as Abe kept reporting over the next year, the more those questions felt valid.  Last month, Abe and I traveled again to Ruidoso. The town felt lighter and less ominous. Much of the ruin had been removed or rebuilt. Grass and sagebrush sprouted on a burn scar. Tourists wandered around a lively downtown on a Friday afternoon. People seemed to be moving on from the terror of the previous year. Downtown Ruidoso on a Friday afternoon this summer A mule deer and an elk wander behind downtown Ruidoso. New growth on a burn scar above Ruidoso But Stephanie and Sebastian Trotter still carry the scars of the day. They lost their two children, Sebastian Rowan, 7, and Charlotte, 4, in the Ruidoso flooding.  There is now a memorial for them and Benjamin “Tim” Feagin, the third person who died, at the RV park where they had been camped. But I wanted to see for myself the places where each of them was found. I felt that making photos of those places could help people connect with the reality of their deaths as well as their lives. So, early one morning, I walked along the floodplain trying to find the locations Abe had shared with me.  I got to the bridge where a firefighter found Sebastian Rowan. There was no marker, no indication that anyone’s body had been found there.  Then I went looking for the area where Charlotte was found. I wandered under pine and cottonwood, through knee-deep grasses and wild sunflowers. Crows cawed overhead, and the early morning sun broke through the trees. I stood there for a while, admiring the beauty, awed by the sadness of the river’s trickle. Rio Ruidoso, near where the body of Sebastian Rowan was found The post I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining. appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: What not to watch on Election Day
events.summary: Ben’s view National election days in the United States of America are biennial festivals of noise over signal. This is the day of maximal public attention to television and online news, on par with wars and natural disasters and the World Cup finals. Hundreds of millions of people are watching TV and YouTube closely, chattering and analyzing on social media. Media companies — like ours — will be there to keep you company, of course, in our case with superb analysis and a thoughtful afternoon livestream . And yet: There’s no other day where the volume of nonsense so outweighs the quantity of new information. In the old days of print journalism, before websites, social media, and even cable news required that reporters broadcast nonstop, Election Day was a blast. Political reporters could sleep late, have a long lunch, even catch a movie. In the afternoon, you’d drop by a polling place for a little “B-matter” — some color and an ambiguous quote or two to bulk out a story in the early edition. “Voters lined up around the block at P.S. 87 on the Upper West Side to cast their ballots. ‘It sure is crowded here,’ said Bob Smith, 70.” That sort of thing. Too Online The modern Election Day media contains three things: anecdotes about how many people are voting; anecdotes about chicanery and hoaxes; and, long after that, results. Early voting trends and stories about how long the lines are in reliably red or blue districts are tempting to use as data points — but are notoriously misleading. You can only vote once, and it doesn’t count more if it comes in early, rather than if you wait until Tuesday to stand on line. Then there are the anecdotes. One, inevitably, will be that a voting machine somewhere in the US is on the blink. The influencers will be all over it. X, in particular, is now hyper-charged to reward engagement. A video — real or manipulated — of a machine in Pennsylvania or Arizona appearing to refuse to accept votes for one candidate is engagement gold. When you see these posts, remember that the US election system is wildly decentralized, secure, and largely offline, and that this story circulates every year. There will also be hints and rumors of poll-site interference or intimidation. Both parties have a maximal incentive to play up anything like this, both as an early warning in case it’s real, and to motivate voters in any case. This is a global phenomenon: Recent elections in Israel and Brazil were marked by wildly viral claims of misconduct — foreign funding of Arab voters in Israel’s case, polls being kept open too late in Brazil’s — that evaporated the next day when they were no longer relevant. Media companies, of course, have our own incentives to keep you engaged. There will be nonstop panels on TV and livestreams, analysts repeating analysis of days-old polls, and — come afternoon — figures from exit polls suggesting that Hispanics are voting in large numbers, or that the economy is a major issue. (These exit poll analyses are both largely useless and often corrected in the days after the election, but they fill the air.) So, Election Day is a good day to sleep late, see (if you haven’t yet), and, of course … watch our livestream . Then when the polls start closing at 6 pm EST, the news arrives: Numbers start rolling in to replace the chatter. And, on their heels, often, litigation. Room for Disagreement There could be substantive news to follow if the Trump administration acts to disrupt voting on Election Day, as some suspect will happen. A group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates “have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has ‘war-gamed’ how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots,” ProPublica reports .

events.title: Could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe?
events.summary: France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments. With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital. Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon , Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros. Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars. Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING. Battle for investor capital heats up That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France , Germany and Italy , whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances. With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%. The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028. Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade. Could France's debt crisis spread across Europe? In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance." Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market." That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow. 'Bond abundance' helps drive up yields Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance." Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest. Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together. Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down. AI is much hyped, frequently feared, and possibly overrated European companies could also feel more pain Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022. The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period. Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments. Regional governments paying the price for AI The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom. A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise. "Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

events.title: Trump vanishes from GOP campaign ads
events.summary: Data: AdImpact; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Republicans on the ballot this cycle have all but stopped mentioning President Trump in their campaign ads , according to an Axios analysis of broadcast advertising data from AdImpact. Why it matters: Trump has tried to make the 2026 midterms a referendum on his presidency. His party has run the other way. The big picture: Ads from both parties in Senate, House and gubernatorial races have shifted from a heavy focus on Trump during the primaries to a much greater emphasis on the economy in the general election. Both parties have also leaned much more heavily into health care, with a noticeable increase among House Republicans. By the numbers: The drop-off is steepest among Republicans, and especially in House races. Trump appeared in 66% of House Republicans' primary ads but shows up in just 3% of their general election ads. In Senate races, Republican ads mentioning him fell from 77% to 22%. Governor's races saw the same shift: Republican ads mentioning Trump fell 34 percentage points. Democrats have also pulled back from Trump, though less dramatically. Trump appeared in 45% of Democratic primary ads, but just 18% of their general election ads. Zoom in: Republican candidates are mentioning some of Trump's signature issues less than during the primaries. The share of Republican ads mentioning immigration has dropped 20 percentage points in Senate races and 14 points in House races. Ads referencing law enforcement fell from 11% of Republican Senate primary ads to 6% in the general election, even as their mentions of crime increased. Data: AdImpact; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Between the lines: Candidates often lean on the country's most prominent political figure in primaries, then pivot to policy issues in the general election. But this year's drop-off stands out given how hard Trump has pushed to tie himself to the midterms. He has urged voters to pretend he's on the ballot and essentially demanded ads running during the Republican midterm convention in September feature him. Of note: In this analysis, primary ads are broadcast ads that aired before a race's primary. General election ads aired between the primary and Oct. 26. The trends may be even more pronounced in ads running through Election Day. The bottom line: Most Republicans have been too scared to tell Trump how unpopular he is, Axios reported . But their ad receipts don't lie.

events.title: Is a post-midterm deal with Canada possible?
events.summary: Trade watchers are waiting for Tuesday’s elections to pass to ascertain whether a US-Canada deal is actually imminent. President Donald Trump’s repeated insistence that a deal is close “matters for a couple of key states” like Michigan , Washington Council Ernst & Young’s Blake Harden told Semafor. “So it’s hard to know if it’s the midterms that are motivating that from the White House and whether that calculus changes after.” Both countries have signaled little change in their positions since talks collapsed, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pledging “our teams will work over the coming weeks” to advance the ball. The US and Canada may have “more room to make a deal” post-election, Harden said, or “could actually get more dug in” without an “action-forcing event.” The White House is keeping details of talks closely held. “The Trump administration welcomes continued engagement with Canada as we work toward finalizing the details of a deal that will deliver meaningful results for the American people,” a White House official told Semafor. — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: UK.gov lacks understanding of climate impact, says watchdog
events.summary: Public bodies in the UK expect higher operating costs and energy charges as a result of climate changes and the transition to lower carbon energy, but few have a good picture of the risks, according to government auditors. A new report from the National Audit Office (NAO) says some public bodies expect financial impact from the risks they identified, although bodies were often not able to cost these – even approximately. "Bodies anticipate costs to arise from damage to assets and infrastructure, driven by physical damage from extreme weather, as well as from chronic shifts to higher temperatures and more precipitation. Bodies also expect higher maintenance and repair costs, potential asset upgrades, and transition costs. Many bodies expect increased operating costs, including energy charges. Bodies controlling significant property or infrastructure are particularly concerned with decarbonization and adaptation costs," the report stated. His Majesty’s Treasury (HMT) has set out rules for climate-related financial disclosure in larger central government bodies' annual reports, which produced their first set of reports for the 2025-26 financial year. Other rules for disclosure have been in place since 2022. However, the NAO found [PDF] that understanding of the risks in the impact of climate change – increasing temperatures, higher risk of flooding, higher winds and longer droughts – was poor, as was insight into costs of moving to a low-carbon economy. "Bodies did not articulate transition risks as well as physical risks in the strategy disclosures. In the disclosures we reviewed, while several transition risks were listed, few specifics were given, unlike physical risks, which were explained in greater detail," the report from the watchdog stated. "The transition risks most frequently identified included the financial cost of transition, and supply chain disruption. Anticipated transition costs included the costs of: switching to lower-carbon energy sources, including investments in new technology; complying with new regulations; and of fluctuations in the price and availability of materials, water, energy and specialist skills," it added. Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "UK public services will need to adapt to the impacts of climate change. Parliament needs clear information on the resilience of infrastructure, service provision and finances to climate change, and on how these risks are being managed." "Although public bodies are still learning how best to report their most pressing climate risks, the requirement on all large central government bodies to make such disclosures from 2025-26 is an important first step. We expect this reporting to become more useful over time." Earlier this year a report from Global Action Plan, a climate charity, claimed 84 percent of proposed datacenter developments were in areas that are already water stressed or projected to be water stressed by 2040. Water consumption by datacenters could intensify strain on the UK’s water systems already stressed by climate change, it argued.®

events.title: Fired general accused of being source for Wall Street Journal, NYT
events.summary: The Pentagon's former top military planner is under federal investigation and may face a court-martial for allegedly leaking to reporters from the Wall Street Journal and New York Times, according to three sources familiar with the controversy. Why it matters: Former Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last week after being accused of misconduct as part of the department's war on leaks. Sylvia failed four polygraphs and admitted to the incidents during two interviews on video that lasted more than a total of two hours, according to details from an internal Pentagon report shared with Axios. "The president has no tolerance for leakers, so Sylvia's termination is the first step in the accountability process, not the last," one of the sources said. Zoom in: Starting in the fall of 2025, the sources said, Sylvia gave information without authorization to reporters Michael Gordon of the Wall Street Journal and Greg Jaffe of the New York Times. Neither reporter is suspected or accused of doing anything illegal, improper or unprofessional in their reporting. Journalists often rely on confidential sources in reporting on issues that involve institutions where insiders aren't authorized to speak publicly. The report states Sylvia admitted to more extensive contacts with Gordon in 2025 and 2026, when the general allegedly shared classified information about Ukraine and Iran with the reporter. The Justice Department is investigating that. Only one discussion with Jaffe appears in the investigative report, concerning Hegseth's unexplained purging of military leaders. Sources said the unauthorized communication by Sylvia potentially violated the Uniform Code of Military Justice's prohibition of "conduct unbecoming of an officer." Behind the scenes: Sylvia allegedly admitted to first disclosing information to Gordon in the fall of 2025 when the two met in the Pentagon and discussed unspecified information about Ukraine, the sources said. After the Wall Street Journal and other outlets were barred from the Pentagon, Sylvia met Gordon at the Silver Diner in Arlington, Va., to give information about a book the reporter was planning to write, the report said. "Major General Sylvia relied on notes he took while reviewing a classified secret report to orally brief Gordon on assistance to Ukraine," said the report, which emphasized that Sylvia didn't receive clearance to discuss the sensitive information. A separate legal analysis of Sylvia's conduct alleged that the general also discussed "munitions stockpiles and high-level interagency discussions with Iran" that were classified, according to a source briefed on the document. Then, "sometime in June or July," Gordon sent Sylvia a message on the encrypted app Signal, the report said. "Sylvia is unable to recall exactly what was in that message" the report said. "But he believed it had something to do with Iran. He stated that he did not respond to the message and instead deleted it." While deleting the message, Sylvia allegedly told military investigators that "he believed he deleted the entire message thread with Michael Gordon. This erased Signal messages and Signal phone calls that would have been recorded in Signal on [Sylvia's] personal phone." Sylvia "indicated multiple times he was comfortable with what he told Gordon about Ukraine assistance," the report said without elaborating. The intrigue: Sylvia's case has led to some friction in the Pentagon after the Joint Staff initially issued a positive statement about the general immediately after he was terminated. The Joint Staff retracted its statement after senior Defense Department officials sent word that Sylvia had been fired for allegedly leaking. A source familiar with the investigation said the Joint Staff should have known better. "You don't get four polygraphs deep without the head of the Joint Staff being briefed at some point. Why wasn't he flagged, what red flags flared up?" the source said. "Their first statement, they gave him a farewell — you know, 'We wish you well in your future endeavors' — and had to retract that information after the truth came out," the source said. "So there's a level of culpability within the Joint Staff that I think is a critical part of this they need to answer for." What they're saying: The Joint Staff declined to comment and referred questions to the Justice Department. The New York Times and Wall Street Journal declined to comment. Sylvia could not be reached for comment. The Defense Department referred Axios to a statement by Assistant Defense Secretary Sean Parnell, who said last week that "classified information is not personal property. Leaking it for personal, political or professional gain is a betrayal of the trust placed in those responsible for keeping it."
