events.title: Venezuela seeks more investment in energy sector as it reforms hydrocarbon law
events.summary: Venezuela is seeking more international investment in its energy sector, with the partial reform of the country’s hydrocarbon law representing a “paradigm shift”, its hydrocarbons minister said on Tuesday. “The new framework allows private participation in primary activities through mechanisms such as the production and exploration contracts and provides guarantees such as dispute resolution and different frameworks that improve conditions for attracting this investment,” Paula Henao told delegates at Adipec in Abu Dhabi. Venezuela's oil sector suffered for years as a result of sanctions that hampered the flow of investment into the country. The oil-rich nation is seeking more investment since the ousting of president Nicolas Maduro earlier this year. Mr Maduro was captured and arrested in a US-led operation in January, with Donald Trump's administration taking control of Venezuela's oil industry. “The main obstacles to large-scale investment continue to be sanctions,” Ms Henao said. The country has signed 80 commercial agreements with international companies over the past year despite continuing challenges, she added. In September, Venezuela signed an energy agreement with France’s TotalEnergies. Details on the scope and value of the agreement were not disclosed. US company Chevron has also revealed plans to invest $7 billion to double its Venezuelan oil production to 600,000 barrels per day over seven years, while North American Blue Energy Partners plans to invest up to $100 billion across 17 Venezuelan oil projects. US oil producer Continental Resources also signed a memorandum of understanding with the state-owned oil and gas company PDVSA to jointly develop the Ayacucho 2 block in Venezuela’s Orinoco Belt, one of the world’s largest deposits of heavy crude. Abu Dhabi’s XRG, Adnoc's international energy investment unit , was awarded an offshore natural gas project in the South American country alongside global oil major bp and Qatar’s UCC in August. Venezuela is one of Opec’s founding members, alongside Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq and Kuwait. Home to the world’s largest proven oil reserves, the country produces about 1.1 million bpd of crude, with most exports flowing to China and India, according to Rystad Energy. While that accounts for just around 1 per cent of global oil trade, the output is distinctive, with more than 67 per cent classified as heavy crude.

events.title: Charted: Why early midterm results can be misleading
events.summary: Data: AP via The New York Times and Axios research; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios The first votes counted Tuesday night will almost certainly look redder than the final result, and control of the House and Senate could take days to settle. Why it matters: Early leads can create false impressions of who's winning and suspicion when those leads vanish. Election night is really election week. By the numbers: AP didn't call control of the House until seven or eight days after Election Day in each of the past three elections . The Senate was settled by 10:44pm on election night in 2018 and at 12:06am the next morning in 2024 . In 2022, it took four days , and in 2020, it wasn't called until Georgia's January runoffs , two months later. State of play: Republicans hold 53 Senate seats . Democrats need a net gain of four for a majority. The red head start: In every national election since 2018, the House and Senate votes counted by 9pm ET were 4 to 9 percentage points more Republican than the final result, an Axios analysis of AP and Edison Research vote counts found. It's mostly geography. Fast-counting Florida and other right-leaning states report first. At 9pm on election night 2022, Florida accounted for 40% of all Senate votes counted nationwide. By 11pm, more House races had been called for Republicans than Democrats in all four elections, including 2018 and 2020, when Democrats won the House. The tilt fades, slowly. At 6am Wednesday, the national House count was still 2 to 3 points more Republican than the final, largely because California, Washington and Oregon count for days. Data: Axios research; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios Zoom in: Each state tilts its own way, depending on which ballots and which counties it counts first. States that count early and mail ballots first tend to start bluer than they finish. States that count Election Day votes first start redder. Ohio, Nebraska, Texas, Kansas and Iowa start blue. Sherrod Brown and Bernie Moreno were tied at 9pm in 2024 with half of Ohio's votes counted. Moreno won by 4. Independent Dan Osborn led Sen. Deb Fischer at 11pm in Nebraska with half the votes counted in 2024. Fischer won by 7. Beto O'Rourke led Ted Cruz at 9pm in 2018 with nearly half of Texas counted. Cruz won by 3. In 2020, Kansas Republican Roger Marshall was down by 8 points at 9pm, even though he'd eventually win by double-digits. Michigan swings both ways. Elissa Slotkin led Mike Rogers by 13 points at 9pm in 2024, trailed by 3 at midnight and won by less than half a point. Maine starts red and counts slowly. In 2020, Susan Collins led by 18 points at 11pm with 16% counted. She won by 9. Alaska is the slowest and starts out redder. In 2020, Sen. Dan Sullivan led by 28 points at 6am ET with 37% counted. He won by 13. Election-night results include Election Day ballots and some early and absentee ballots. The rest are counted in the following days. Rural mail often goes through Anchorage, and weather can slow it, with domestic ballots accepted up to 10 days after Election Day if postmarked on time. If no one wins a majority of first choices, Alaska will run its ranked-choice tally on Nov. 18. Data: AP and Edison Research via The New York Times; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios Watch the clock (all times ET): 6pm — The first votes: Parts of Indiana and Kentucky close, giving us the first House returns. 7pm — The red head start: Polls close in the key Senate states of Georgia, South Carolina and most of Florida and New Hampshire. Fast-counting Florida gives Republicans an early boost in House races. 7:30pm — North Carolina and Ohio close: Watch for early Democratic leads in Ohio that could shrink as more votes come in. 8pm — Four more key races: Maine closes, along with most of Michigan, Texas and Kansas, the rest of New Hampshire and Florida's Panhandle. 9pm — Peak red mirage: Iowa, Minnesota and Nebraska close, along with the rest of Michigan, Texas and Kansas. Historically, the national House count looks most Republican between 9pm and 11pm. 11pm — The West Coast: California, Oregon and Washington begin reporting, bringing millions of votes and pivotal House races into the picture. The early Republican tilt should begin fading. About 1am Wednesday — Alaska: The last polls close, and initial results are expected. Election-night results include Election Day ballots and some early and absentee ballots, with others counted in subsequent days. The bottom line: Early leads aren't necessarily predictive. The closer the race, the longer voters may have to wait to learn who won.

events.title: New FCA rules bring ESG rating providers into UK regulation for the first time
events.summary: New UK rules for environmental, social and governance (ESG) rating providers will raise standards in the market, helping investors to make better informed decisions. The new framework brings ESG rating providers into FCA regulation for the first time, covering a market that plays an important role in investment decisions. The rules are designed to improve the transparency, reliability and comparability of ESG ratings, helping build confidence in the information investors rely on. The regime applies to firms or organisations providing ESG ratings and assessments to ensure reliability across the market. The FCA has published guidance to help firms understand whether they may be in scope. Laura Dawes, director of authorisations and sustainable finance at the FCA, said: 'Trusted information is essential for well-functioning markets. These rules will help improve transparency and raise standards across the ESG ratings market while supporting competition, innovation and growth. 'Firms should check now whether they are in scope and start preparing for authorisation. We'll continue to provide practical support to help them prepare.'The new framework introduces requirements covering transparency, governance, systems and controls, the management of conflicts of interest, and engagement with users of ESG ratings and rated entities. It is designed to be proportionate to firms' size and activities and is informed by international and existing standards. Firms that may be in scope should start preparing now. ESG rating providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027. The FCA will provide webinars and access to its Pre-Application Support Service to help firms prepare. Firms should now: understand whether the framework could apply to their activities review the final rules and guidanceconsider whether they need FCA authorisationstart preparing for implementationengage early with FCA support servicesNotes to editorsRead the FCA’s Policy Statement and final rules, PS26/22, ‘ESG ratings: final regime’.The new framework takes effect on 29 June 2028. From that date, firms providing ESG ratings in the UK will need FCA authorisation and to have the relevant permission before carrying on that activity, unless an exemption applies.ESG rating providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027. We are staggering application periods and encourage firms to apply as early as possible within their window. ESG ratings generally assess how companies or other entities, assets, or financial products perform against environmental, social and governance criteria. They are used by asset managers, lenders, benchmark administrators and others to inform capital allocation decisions and manage risk, among other uses. The approach is shaped by international standards, including recommendations from the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO). The final rules follow the FCA’s consultation, CP25/34, which opened on 1 December 2025 and closed on 31 March 2026. The regulatory framework follows government legislation bringing the provision of ESG ratings within the FCA’s remit in October 2025. 95% of respondents to the government’s consultation supported the move. The regime regulates how ESG ratings are produced, governed and communicated. It does not prescribe a particular sustainability view or methodology. There is strong investor demand for ESG information. The FCA's Financial Lives Survey 2024 found 72% of adults with investments or a defined contribution pension wanted their investments to do some good as well as provide a financial return.

events.title: Three questions that will define AI's political power
events.summary: The 2026 midterms bring the first test of voter sentiment on the AI race, offering a window into how a niche policy debate is transforming into a wedge issue ahead of a presidential campaign cycle. Why it matters: The results will reveal whether explicitly campaigning on AI regulation — or aligning with tech moguls like Elon Musk — is a winning political strategy or a liability for 2028. One thing is already clear: Candidates increasingly can't afford to have half-baked AI agendas. Here are three major questions about the future of AI politics and policy, and the races we're watching on Election Day for answers. 1. Did AI break through? A different kind of AI political spending has emerged in the midterms. Instead of supporting or opposing candidates based on their AI positions, some groups want to make AI policy itself a campaign issue. Guardrails Alliance, a pro-regulation advocacy group, recently launched ads targeting Republicans and Democrats over their positions on AI in Arizona, Montana, North Carolina and California. The organization backed Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who said AI was the most important issue heading into Election Day, tying it explicitly to jobs and affordability. Democratic group Tomorrow Together also launched ads against Republicans' AI track record in Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania. Meanwhile, competing AI groups Public First and Leading the Future spent more than $50 million through affiliated super PACs in nearly 50 races, but their TV and digital ads largely avoided the very issue they're trying to influence: AI. These races could offer an early test of whether explicitly campaigning on AI is a viable political strategy heading into 2028. 2. Did Elon Musk help or hurt candidates? Elon Musk's political spending, involvement in DOGE and ties to the Trump administration have made him both a powerful political backer and a target for Democratic attacks. He was the biggest donor in the midterms by far, contributing more than $400 million. Races we're watching include: Texas' 10th District: Republican Chris Gober, who represented Musk in connection with DOGE, faces Democrat Caitlin Rourk. Kansas' 1st District: Democrat Lauren Reinhold has leaned into her experience with DOGE, criticizing Musk's influence over the federal government in her challenge against Republican Rep. Tracey Mann. Ohio Senate: Republican Jon Husted has benefited from spending by Musk's America PAC in his race against Democrat Sherrod Brown. Texas Senate: Musk-affiliated spending has made the contest between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton another test of his political influence. These races could help answer whether Musk's money helped elect Republican allies or gave Democrats a useful target. 3. How loud will the AI safety movement be in the next Congress? A handful of candidates aligned with stronger AI safeguards could help determine whether the next Congress has a more vocal bloc pushing back against the industry's efforts to limit regulation. Races we're watching include: Michigan Senate: El-Sayed wants a new Cabinet-level federal agency to regulate AI and a ban on superintelligence. He has used Musk's political involvement to attack Republican Mike Rogers, who has benefited from Musk-affiliated political spending. Colorado's 8th District: Democrat Manny Rutinel sponsored the nation's first comprehensive AI bill. California's 11th District: Democrat Scott Wiener's AI transparency legislation was at the center of a regulatory fight that divided the industry, offering a preview of battles in Washington. Minnesota's 2nd District: Democrat Matt Little would add another voice to the push to ban data center construction and nondisclosure agreements at the national level. These are some of the races that will help determine the size and influence of the AI safety movement's congressional coalition, an important indicator of where the fight over AI regulation is headed in 2027 and beyond. The bottom line: Many factors will shape the outcomes of races across the country. But competing AI factions will be quick to claim victories, explain away losses and draw lessons about what worked ahead of 2028.

events.title: Elon Musk's next target: a major shake-up of America's wireless market
events.summary: Elon Musk is looking to shake up America's wireless industry, potentially bringing the first major new competitive threat in years to a business dominated by three companies. Why it matters: The cellular industry has seen enormous technological change, but relatively little disruption to its competitive structure. Musk has the money, spectrum and satellite network to attempt something different — though he faces daunting obstacles. Driving the news: SpaceX is assembling the pieces to become a major U.S. wireless carrier, potentially building its own terrestrial network and buying available spectrum. The moves are meant either to build the capability to bypass existing carriers or to bring them to the table for a deal that would allow Musk to strike a deal for wholesale access to their networks. Musk may have reason to move quickly while the current administration and its regulatory appointees remain in place, a reason some analysts have cited in the context of proposals for a merger between Tesla and SpaceX . What they're saying: Blair Levin, a former FCC chief of staff who now heads policy at Optimal Advisory, says Musk's financial resources distinguish him from previous challengers. "For the first time, there is an entity capable of scaring investors in the traditional big three," Levin told Axios. Unlike Dish, which faced serious financing constraints, SpaceX can draw on capital markets that have rewarded Musk's ambitious plans. The latest : SpaceX has held talks with EchoStar about acquiring Boost Mobile or gaining access to its network arrangements, according to a Washington Post report Monday. That could provide a quick route to customers and infrastructure, although approval of such a deal is far from a foregone conclusion if Musk's businesses are drawn into a regulator quagmire after the midterm elections. The Post reported that Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile have all rebuffed Musk's efforts to gain access to their networks. State of play: Musk also has a path to maneuver around them. SpaceX has agreed to multibillion-dollar spectrum deals , including a low-band variety useful for reaching customers indoors and supporting a traditional cellular network. The company could build its own network using towers and smaller rooftop antennas, though doing so would require substantial investment and time. The big picture: America's wireless industry has spent much of the past two decades consolidating. T-Mobile once played the scrappy challenger, shaking up the industry with aggressive pricing and the elimination of unpopular practices. But its 2020 acquisition of Sprint reduced the number of major nationwide carriers from four to three. Regulators tried to preserve a fourth competitor by requiring the sale of Boost Mobile to Dish Network, which planned to build a nationwide network. That effort never delivered the competitive alternative envisioned, leaving Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile firmly entrenched. The intrigue: Musk would be moving from a business where SpaceX enjoys enormous technical and economic advantages to one where the established players have spent decades building infrastructure, acquiring customers and learning how to serve them. In terrestrial wireless, the big three carriers have spent decades investing in towers, spectrum, indoor coverage and the countless small improvements that make their networks reliable. Building such a network isn't simply a matter of spending billions on infrastructure, Craig Moffett of MoffettNathanson said in a recent podcast interview. It also means catching up on decades of work filling in coverage gaps in stadiums, airports and other difficult locations. The catch: Even if Musk can assemble the necessary infrastructure, it's far from clear that becoming a nationwide wireless carrier would be a particularly attractive business. Moffett questions why SpaceX would want to enter an industry where even the established carriers struggle to earn attractive returns on their investments. Between the lines: Success will depend on fundamentally lowering the cost of providing service or creating something for which consumers are willing to pay extra. SpaceX has floated the idea of using Starlink rooftop equipment as small cellular base stations, potentially reducing some of the costs of building a traditional network. The political backdrop: Musk's plans come as Washington faces a potentially significant shift following Tuesday's midterm elections. While SpaceX is likely to face significant political and regulatory risks due to Musk's ties with Republicans, analysts aren't sure that will translate into opposing a wireless deal that adds competition to the market. The bottom line: Musk has repeatedly succeeded in industries where established players doubted his ambitions. But this time he's the outsider, trying to overcome the advantages of companies that have spent decades building the networks he wants to challenge.

events.title: Democrats could learn wrong message from a blowout victory
events.summary: Democrats are poised to romp in today's election — easily winning the House and, according to most forecasts, flipping the Senate too. Yet the party itself is less popular than the IRS . Even the GOP has a better brand. Why it matters: There's a difference between a blowout and a mandate. Confusing the two could tempt Democrats to overread the results and forget the serious credibility problem they still face heading into 2028. The big picture: Democrats have done a lot of things right to position themselves for a big night. They recruited candidates who've put red state Senate races that seemingly were beyond reach, within their grasp. Many of those candidates vastly outraised their Republican opponents. But polls across the board still show a lesser-of-two-evils election — or as one Republican tied to President Trump's political operation described it, a contest of which party voters hate more. Voters are more eager to disempower Trump than to empower Democrats. By the numbers: Just 29% of registered voters have a positive opinion of the Democratic Party vs. 38% who view the Republican Party positively, according to a pre-election NBC News poll . The same poll showed Democrats with a 7-point lead in the congressional generic ballot, 52 to 45. And nearly 6 in 10 voters who plan to back Democrats in the election said their vote is about stopping Trump and Republican policies — vs. 4 in 10 who said they were more motivated to help Democrats enact their policies, per an October CBS News/YouGov poll . Zoom in: Many Democrats say they're determined not to repeat the mistake they made after the last midterms in 2022. They defied predictions of a red wave and saw it as an endorsement of Joe Biden and their party — when voters actually were increasingly angry. The post-2022 takeaway ultimately laid the groundwork for Trump's return to the White House after the 2024 election. Democrats won the House in the 2018 midterms — and went on to impeach Trump the following year. This time, presumed House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) isn't talking about another Trump impeachment — his 100-day agenda is focused on affordability. Zoom out: Other Democrats warn that it's been easier to run against Trump when he's actually in office. Making him the face of the election didn't work in 2024, and it might not in 2028, either. At the Third Way gathering in South Carolina earlier this year, Democratic strategist Jim Messina told a crowd of operatives and party leaders, "We have no economic message. And if we don't get one, we're not going to win" in 2028. Flashback: The 2006 midterms also featured a Democratic uprising against an unpopular war and an unpopular president. Democrats flipped the House and Senate in a major rebuke of President George W. Bush. But the party that year had a net-positive party image of 4 points in NBC polling. Today, it's 23 points underwater. Two years later in 2008 — with anti-Bush and anti-war backlash still running hot — Democrats harnessed Barack Obama's talents and calls for "change" to win back the White House. But a midterm blowout in 2026, if it materializes, will offer no guarantee the party will find an equally talented standard-bearer in 2028. What they're saying: "It's not great for the Democrats ... for 2028," Bill McInturff, one of the pollsters who conducted the NBC survey, said of the Democratic Party's lousy image. "But I don't see it as a barrier for how well they can do in 2026 when midterms are about Trump and these economic numbers." The bottom line: Ultimately, many top Democrats believe it will take a new presidential nominee — and likely one who wins in November 2028 — to fully repair the party's damaged brand. Axios' Alex Thompson and Holly Otterbein contributed to this story.

Credit unions could benefit from several ideas put forward today by the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) aimed at helping the sector grow, innovate and meet the changing needs of their members. Credit unions, which are member-owned and typically focus on savings and personal loans in a specific occupation, community or area, have over two million members in the UK. Building on the joint PRA and FCA 2025 Mutuals Landscape report, this discussion paper examines whether the regulatory framework remains proportionate as the sector evolves, and explores how credit unions can expand access to financial services and improve outcomes for the members they serve. Options the regulators are seeking views on include: Removing some requirements on internal audit and regulatory documents for smaller credit unions, cutting red tape without compromising stability; Creating a risk-based framework for larger, more complex credit unions, giving them more flexible capital requirements; Applying relevant rules for smaller deposit takers, such as the standardised approach for risk weighted assets, to replace the current simple leverage ratio they report on; Applying a simplified version of the Basel framework, streamlining capital add-ons for large credit unions with specific exposures, and applying a simple capital buffer for absorbing shocks in stress periods; What barriers there are to credit unions offering new products and services, including how shared-service organisations and third-party organisations can best support investment, technology and operational capability; Giving credit unions additional guidance on FCA expectations around working with third-parties to provide important services; Whether changes to FCA fees could reduce regulatory costs and support sustainable growth; Providing credit unions a path to convert into building societies, bringing the benefits of a framework more tailored to specific lending and a wider range of funding tools; Reviewing the current framework for solvent exit, providing further flexibility to transfer business or restructure in an orderly manner. Shoib Khan, Director of UK Deposit Takers at the Prudential Regulation Authority, said: “Credit unions are a vital part of our financial services sector, and we have scope to make their regime even more proportionate and growth-friendly. We want to have an open, transparent dialogue with firms, and I look forward to seeing their honest feedback.” Sheree Howard, Executive Director of Authorisations at the Financial Conduct Authority, said: “Credit unions provide valuable support to millions of members, including many who may otherwise struggle to access affordable financial services. As the sector evolves, it is important that the regulatory framework keeps pace, enabling credit unions to innovate, grow and meet the changing needs of their members while continuing to deliver good outcomes for consumers. We want to hear directly from the sector about what is working well, where barriers remain, and how the regulatory framework may need to adapt to support a strong, sustainable future for credit unions.” The regulators are encouraging firms to offer their feedback on the options presented and whether there are other options which have not been included. The possibilities at this stage give more options to firms with very different business models, growth trajectories and risk profiles.

events.title: Republicans keep Senate hopes alive, mindful of the majority’s power
events.summary: Republicans can lose up to three seats today and still keep the Senate majority. Any further losses, however, carry immense consequences. Most in the party are already clocking North Carolina as lost to the Democrats. Losing the Senate would deprive Republicans of control over President Donald Trump’s nominees — including lifetime judicial appointments. And provided the House flips Democratic, Republicans could see a procession of impeachment trials for Cabinet members — and perhaps even the president. “The two oldest members of the Supreme Court are both Republican [appointees]. We want to make sure that if one of them decides to retire, or both, in the next two years, that President Trump can make an appointment that will get confirmed in the United States Senate,” Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., told Semafor on Monday amid a day of campaigning in Iowa. Republicans can quickly table impeachment trials with a simple majority if they keep Senate control; just two years ago, a Democratic majority dismissed the impeachment of then-Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas. Next year, if Democrats claim the majority in both chambers, the GOP can’t expect quick dismissals. “We’re going to need to be able to make sure that those are dealt with quickly in the Senate and are not allowed to be dragged out, which is what you’d have with a Democrat majority,” Barrasso added. The national mood is poor, and Republicans are fighting it out deep in red territory. They are hoping a pair of eleventh-hour dramas in Alaska and Michigian — and their most battle-hardened incumbent — will help bail out their embattled Senate majority. Republicans’ best pickup opportunity at the start of the cycle has faded away in Georgia. But GOP leaders see Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ surprise endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers as fueling their best chance in Michigan since their last Senate win in 1994. Stevens’ endorsement “brings more energy and more attention to that race, and it’s going to help in Michigan,” Barrasso said. “That is going to be a positive influence for the Republicans in the race tomorrow, and in turn I believe is going to generate more turnout and more votes for Mike Rogers.” The last batch of Michigan polls still show Democrat Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Rogers, though they won’t take into account Stevens’ stunning turn over the weekend. If Republicans somehow flip the Michigan seat, Democrats would have to net five pick-ups elsewhere, which would mean winning a majority of races in eight GOP-held states: North Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Maine, Alaska, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa. Alaska has been one of Democrats’ core focuses since the start of the year, and the race still looks close. Republicans are praying that enough Alaskans saw The New York Times’ story on Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign allies working to recruit a spoiler candidate who might siphon votes from GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. “The more people that know about the situation, I think the more it’s going to help Sen. Dan Sullivan. I believe he wins the race,” Barrasso said. Asked if Peltola would be seated if she wins, Barrasso demurred: “We’re not there yet. I believe Dan Sullivan is going to win.” He also predicted GOP Sen. Susan Collins would defeat Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine, holding a seat she has occupied since winning it in 1996. Barrasso has been to Kentucky, Iowa, Michigan, Texas, and Ohio over the past few days. He said that Trump’s rallies are critical to stoking turnout by the GOP base in a cycle that’s typically brutal for modern presidents. “Nobody can get out a crowd or energize a crowd like President Trump,” Barrasso said. — Burgess Everett

events.title: OpenAI pushes policy rebrand to a skeptical audience
events.summary: The News OpenAI’s attempt to rebrand data centers and set a new tone for AI policy discourse after the midterms is landing with a thud in some circles, including with members of Congress. The company’s latest policy push is multi-pronged. It involves calling data centers “compute campuses” and seeking community input on their buildouts. It likens AI rules to speeding limits for cars, arguing that AI helps people in their daily lives, and pushing for global AI standards, as Axios first reported. If initial reactions from AI safety advocates are any indication, AI and tech companies have a long way to go to convince both voters and Democrats, who will likely hold more power in Washington after Tuesday, that their efforts are sincere and not just an attempt at face-saving. “If they think they can change the AI debate with Orwellian name changes, they are setting themselves up for failure,” said Brad Carson, former Oklahoma Democratic congressman and co-founder and president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, a group pushing for AI guardrails. “AI will be the number one issue in 2028,” Rep. Greg Casar, D-Tex., posted on X . “And anyone looking to OpenAI’s lobbyist for advice will lose.” Still, OpenAI’s top lobbyist, Chris Lehane, is betting the company’s refreshed positions — on data centers and AI policy that puts people in control of the technology — will be “durable,” even if it’s in a “lonely position,” he told Semafor in an interview. “People are going to wake up in November and December and January, and there’s going to be hundreds and hundreds of state bills out there. So does Congress and the White House want to cede control of all of this?” he said, adding that OpenAI plans to push for a mandatory AI testing bill that can get 60 votes by connecting members across the aisle. OpenAI still supports certain state AI laws as well, recently endorsing two frontier AI safety bills in California, he said. He also said OpenAI spoke with Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif. on the AI “kill switch” bill the Democrat proposed in July, and said he would soon have “next steps” on making OpenAI’s products safer for teen users. Lehane said OpenAI’s views are meant to offer an alternative to extremes around AI. He argued that embracing a middle path would avoid the US ceding ground to China by being outright opposed to data centers, echoing the White House’s argument for a light touch on AI regulation. His argument isn’t doing much to win over skeptics. “[Lehane is] trying to get the best deal out of the Trump administration that he can before Democrats take over,” Alex Bores, the New York State assemblyman who became a top target of the AI industry in his run for Congress, told Semafor. “But it’s nice to see him say this debate is about control, and that the American people need a stake in what’s happening.” Room for Disagreement If Democrats want to get anything done on AI policy next year, they’ll need to work with Republicans — regardless of control of Congress. And that will inevitably involve moderation and compromise, as well as working with AI firms. “I’d expect others to follow [OpenAI’s lead],” Joseph Hoefer, chief AI officer at Monument Advocacy, told Semafor. “This is where the political calculus is inevitably heading. The industry had a good run making the case for a lighter touch, but the polling shows the limits of that strategy … and a hands-off message gets harder to sustain when voters are asking who’s in control.” Hoefer said that for AI companies looking to buoy continued AI sector growth, “the goal is to give lawmakers a case for AI investment they can defend back home.”

events.title: Russian strikes choke Ukraine’s economy as steel shuts down and grain exports stall
events.summary: Ore. Governor Projected winner Tina Kotek • D 3 hours ago Neb. Senate Projected winner Pete Ricketts • R 3 hours ago Election 2026 live results: Mississippi Senate race separated by dozens of votes Ukraine's economy is struggling as Russia's air war targets industries, logistics networks and ports needed for exports KAMIANSKE, Ukraine -- The furnaces are cold, the factory floor deserted, and twisted metal litters the grounds of Kamet Steel, a vast industrial complex that once helped power Ukraine’s economy but closed after a Russian attack . Across the country, grain — a key export — piles up in fields and silos as farmers struggle to find routes safe from airstrikes and wait for prices to rise. Russia’s intensified air campaign is slowly strangling Ukraine’s economy, targeting industrial and energy plants and the logistics networks, railways and export routes that keep it afloat. The near-daily strikes with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones disrupt production and drive up transport costs. As a result, Ukraine’s government faces a deepening cash crunch as the air war chokes its revenue from steel, agriculture and other key sources. The damage ripples across interconnected sectors just as Kyiv faces uncertainty over future U.S. support . Ukraine’s central bank last week forecast a 0.4% economic contraction in 2026, reversing its previous projection of 1.8% growth, due to the attacks and a surge in global energy prices. Gov. Andriy Pyshnyy said the bank had also raised its inflation forecast to 12.5%, from 10% in July. Ukraine spends some 40% of its gross domestic product on defense — far beyond what it can cover alone, notes Torbjörn Becker, director of the Stockholm Institute of Transition Economics. Raising taxes only would bring in a fraction of what is needed. Missile strikes have halted steel production across Metinvest Group, the country’s mining and metals giant. Kamet Steel, in the industrial city of Kamianske, accounted for more than a quarter of Ukraine’s steel output in 2025. The complex employed thousands producing steel and pig iron for domestic construction. It also supplied semi-finished steel to Metinvest’s facility in Bulgaria for the market there and elsewhere in Europe. But five ballistic missiles struck the site on Sept. 5. Its closure has hurt Ukraine’s industrial economy, affecting construction, mining, engineering, energy and logistics. Ukrzaliznytsia, the national railway operator, relies heavily on steel transport and other freight revenue. Businesses that rely on the plant could lose jobs and face bankruptcy, said Oleksandr Tretyakov, Kamet Steel’s CEO. European Union trade restrictions could hinder recovery by narrowing the market for Ukrainian steel exports, he said. “This is the worst situation since the Second World War,” Tretyakov said, noting that steel once accounted for about 6% of Ukraine’s GDP. “It did,” he said. “Right now, it’s zero.” Agriculture accounts for up to 60% of Ukraine’s foreign currency earnings, making it critical to the wartime economy. But Russian attacks on Black Sea shipping have sharply reduced traffic through Ukraine’s deep-water ports just as farmers need cash to prepare for the next planting season. Ukraine’s Black Sea trade has collapsed with attacks on ports, vessels and logistics infrastructure, according to maritime data and analytics company Lloyd’s List Intelligence. There were only 21 ship arrivals at Black Sea ports in August, down about 90% from a year earlier. Soaring insurance premiums and the constant threat of Russian strikes deter shipowners. Dozens of sailors have been killed in attacks this year. “All our developments and all the innovations we achieved will be crossed out by this situation and we will need to start from zero later,” said Volodymyr Scavinskyi, trade director at Nibulon, one of Ukraine’s leading agricultural exporters. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Captain identified after deadly Florida Learjet crash 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Ship traffic from Ukraine's lower-capacity ports on the Danube River to the Black Sea has surged, even under the threat of Russian bombardment. But it is costly. The Danube delta's Sulina Channel is too shallow for the largest vessels, and dozens of ships often wait days to enter or leave the river. Record low Danube water levels due to drought also constrain the route. Barges that once carried 1,500 tons are loading only 800 to 900 tons, Scavinskyi said. Nearly twice as many barges are needed to move the same volume, raising costs. Transporting each ton of corn from central Ukraine to Spain cost up to $50 earlier this year. Now, it can reach $150, he said. “It’s still risky and you don’t have any guarantees that your voyage will be successful,” Scavinskyi said. For Olena Shelest, commercial director at HarvEast, a major agricultural holding, the immediate challenge is finding buyers.

events.title: Raspberry Pi hikes prices again, barely a month after the last round
events.summary: Raspberry Pi has announced yet another round of price hikes, this time adding $80 to the cost of its 16GB Pi 5, which now sells for more than three times its original launch price. The latest bump, announced by Raspberry Pi boss Eben Upton, takes the 16GB Pi 5 to a whopping $385. The 16GB Compute Module 5 variants are also getting $40 more expensive, although the Raspberry Pi 500+, which packs the same amount of RAM, has escaped this particular round. Upton blamed a familiar culprit: soaring memory costs, worsened by a lack of alternative suppliers for 16GB DRAM and ongoing shortages of other components. "Unfortunately, a lack of alternative supply for 16GB DRAM, compounded by other ongoing component shortages, means we now need to make further price increases on some of our highest-density products," Upton wrote. It's becoming an expensive habit for Raspberry Pi customers. The 16GB Pi 5 cost $120 when it launched in January 2025, which seems almost reasonable now. Raspberry Pi added $25 in December, another $60 in February, and a further $100 in April . With today's $80 increase, buyers are being asked to cough up $265 more than they were less than two years ago, a price hike of 221 percent. And it's barely been a month since Raspberry Pi raised prices on its 2GB Pi 4 and Pi 5 models by $12.50 apiece, taking them to $67.50 and $77.50 respectively. The repeated markups come despite Raspberry Pi reporting record first-half results in September. Revenue jumped 90 percent to $256.9 million, while gross profit rose 79 percent to $59.4 million. Gross profit per board climbed 53 percent to $12.20, helped partly by memory purchased before prices went through the roof. That stockpile advantage has since largely disappeared. For customers unwilling to pay nearly $400 for a single-board computer, Upton advises buying something with less RAM, using an older Pi, or optimizing applications to make do with less memory. He also warned that some sellers are exploiting the shortages by charging inflated prices or offering products that aren't what they appear to be, urging customers to stick to approved resellers. “We’re aware that a few bad actors have been taking advantage of the current memory supply circumstances to sell Raspberry Pi products at inflated prices or shift products that aren’t what they seem,” he said. There is, apparently, some good news, as Raspberry Pi continues to insist the increases are temporary. "As we've said from the beginning, the current memory landscape is difficult but ultimately temporary, and we look forward to rolling back our price increases when memory costs fall once again," Upton wrote. That could be a long wait. Micron has previously warned that memory shortages could drag on into 2028 or beyond, so anyone hoping to see a $120 Pi 5 again probably shouldn't hold their breath. ®

events.title: Oil prices fluctuate after US strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island
events.summary: Oil prices dropped on Tuesday evening following a sharp rise in the morning after reports of a US strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island revived concerns about an escalation of the conflict and further disruption at the Strait of Hormuz . Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world’s oil , was trading 1.72 per cent lower at $102.97 a barrel at 6:16pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was down 1.03 per cent to 95.47 a barrel. Both benchmarks rose sharply earlier in the day, with Brent reaching nearly $107 a barrel. The gains followed a sharp slide on Monday, when both Brent and WTI plunged more than 7 per cent. US forces struck Iran ’s Qeshm Island on Monday night, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday. The WSJ cited US officials, who described the attacks as defensive measures aimed at preventing Iran from targeting commercial vessels in the strait. Iranian state media said there were several explosions on the island, which is at the mouth of Hormuz. It was the ​latest in a series of limited attacks carried out by the US in recent weeks, the WSJ report said. Smaller scale strikes have been carried out and kept secret to avoid indicating any US intent to resume its major military campaign against Iran , the report added. “Overnight US strikes renewed uncertainty, leaving crude near $105 per barrel this morning and the diplomatic opening vulnerable,” said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD. The latest military action comes as the US goes to the polls on Tuesday for midterm elections. It also puts the focus back on the risk of supply disruption, a day after US President Donald Trump reportedly said he wanted to give diplomacy with Iran more time before considering renewed military strikes. “For oil, the decisive question will be whether the midterm elections can align the political pieces to pave the way for more normal supply conditions – or push that prospect further away,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote. “The clearest downside scenario for crude is credible de-escalation of geopolitical tensions followed by improving supply flows. The clearest upside scenario is renewed disruption while inventories continue absorbing the shortfall.” While the US midterms could change expectations rapidly, “they cannot, by themselves, reopen shipping routes, repair damaged infrastructure or reverse the AI impact on broader economies”, she added. The Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route connecting the Gulf to global markets, carried about a fifth of the world's crude oil and natural gas supplies before the conflict began in late February. Oil prices hit a six-month high at the end of October on Hormuz strikes and the probability of the conflict escalating again after the midterm elections. "Energy prices have been at lofty levels for a while, at least from our perspective. Oil trading above $100 and European natural gas above €90 is difficult to reconcile with current market realities," said Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer. "We are in an extraordinarily noisy week due to the midterms, and in a phase where the complex energy supply chains are normalising. Given this setting, today’s exceptional market fever and wild price swings should not come as a surprise. We maintain our cautious view on oil."

events.title: FCA sets expectations for firms making car finance settlement offers
events.summary: Research shows consumers want the choice, rather than wait for the legal challenges to conclude. Almost 9 out of 10 (89%) car finance customers who have complained or are considering doing so want the choice of an offer of compensation now, rather than waiting for the legal challenges to the FCA's compensation scheme to conclude. 86% would be comfortable making the decision, and 61% say they’d accept an offer in line with the scheme. Timing matters for many: 77% say receiving compensation sooner would make a great deal or fair amount of difference to their financial situation.The survey findings are being released today alongside the FCA's expectations for lenders who want to make settlement offers to those owed compensation under its scheme, while legal challenges continue. This comes as Barclays Partner Finance confirms it will make settlement offers to some of its customers owed compensation.The regulator supports lenders making settlement offers, as long as customers are offered no less than they would receive through the scheme.Lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes that they will keep any money received, even if the outcome of the legal challenges means they would have received less. However, they also wouldn’t be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge means they would have been paid more. As consumers can reject an offer and leave their claim to be dealt with under the scheme, these offers can’t be referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service for review.Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA’s general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said:'Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. And it’s clear they want the choice.'Anyone who wants to wait can, and there’s no obligation to agree to the offer. We’ll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means.'To help consumers make informed decisions, the FCA has published a factsheet (PDF) that lenders must share with customers when making settlement offers. Not all lenders are likely to make offers, and those that do may only make them to some customers owed compensation. The FCA will regularly update its website with lenders making settlement offers to help consumers check whether an offer is genuine. Firms are expected to notify the FCA if they plan to make offers.Payouts under the motor finance compensation scheme were due to start this year. The scheme is currently partially suspended, pending the outcome of legal challenges due to be heard between 16 February and 3 March 2027. Under the partial suspension, firms must keep preparing for the scheme and continue progressing complaints as far as possible, but do not need to calculate or pay compensation under the scheme until the legal process concludes.Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained should complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website on how to complain for free. There is no need to use a law firm or claims management company, which may charge up to 36% of any compensation, including VAT.Notes to editorsResearch conducted by Kantar, surveying 1,000 motor finance customers online between 25 and 28 June 2026. Findings cited are based on a subset of 590 respondents who said they had made or were considering making a motor finance complaint.Barclays press release.Statement confirming motor finance legal challenge to be heard in February 2027.Statement on the partial suspension of the motor finance scheme and what it means for firms and consumers.

events.title: Final_FINAL_v7.docx is not a version control strategy
events.summary: The Register and LucidLink are hosting a dinner for senior technology, infrastructure and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair. The subject is one most of them will know from their own shop, where the same file lives in several places at once and nobody is quite sure which copy is current. Most organisations have a folder that proves it. There's a file called final, another called final2, and then the one people are actually using, which somebody emailed to a contractor last Thursday. It's mildly funny until two people spend a week editing different copies and one of them loses the argument. Meanwhile the storage bill picks up another copy of everything, and each team that builds its own way round the problem gives IT another place it can't see into. Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers at the table, and nobody is there to give a presentation. Because the evening is held under the Chatham House Rule, people tend to say what really happened, like the team that quietly built its own sync service because the approved one was too slow, or the leaver who could still open a file share months after going. From there the conversation widens out to unstructured data that won't stop growing, the duplicate storage piling up, the security risk of access scattered across all those copies, and how to modernise without binning the storage and governance the business has already paid for. Drinks start at 6.30pm, then it's dinner around one table until 9pm. Places are limited. Request your place at the November 24 dinner Places go by invitation and each one is confirmed personally. events.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
events.summary: Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric". Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history. This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy. Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor. The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group. "The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said. Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack Published 4 days ago Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far Published 5 days ago But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied. The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025. Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said. The country has consistently denied such claims. Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace". Kim Yo-jong: North Korea's heir apparent? Published 16 June 2020 Who is Kim Yo-jong? Video, 00:02:32 Who is Kim Yo-jong? Published 16 June 2020 Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack. Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users. The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday. The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday. That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes. "Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added. The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals. Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack. The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach. events.title: Forget retraining - AI can now tweak another AI's weights
events.summary: The outputs of AI models are the result of a complex interplay between neurons, weights, training, and inference, and are therefore difficult to follow. But in some ways they're starting to look more like open books. Recent work by Anthropic safety fellow Joshua Fonseca Rivera has revealed how certain neurons in a neural network can be associated with a specific persona . Now, computer scientists from MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) have found that frontier AI models like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra can rewrite the weights of another model directly, as opposed to indirectly through training, and alter their behavior. "We find early signs that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading, writing, and reasoning about neural network weights," said Rikiya Takehi, a PhD student at MIT CSAIL, in a social media post . "Instead of training, models may treat raw weights like readable, editable code: diagnosing failures and patching them directly." To demonstrate that, Takehi and colleagues Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to make it better at math. Astra changed only 0.016 percent of the model's weights, reducing its reasoning loops and improving its math performance by as much as sixfold on the MATH-500 benchmark, while boosting its instruction-following score on the IFEval benchmark roughly threefold. There was no training using gradient descent ; Astra just revised the numerical values that constitute Qwen's weights. "All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops," the researchers wrote in a blog post . "It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming. "Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights." Astra's ability to program weights extends to being able to write a neural network from scratch, zero-shot. The researchers told Astra: "write, from scratch, the weights of a policy network that plays [Breakout] as well as possible." And it did so. Takehi suggests this technique shows promise for improving models without the consequences of catastrophic forgetting , which can occur when a model is revised to include new knowledge. More generally, the authors expect Weight-Space Programming will open the door to new ways to understand models and optimize them, and to implement recursive self-improvement. The technique may also prove useful for reducing model sycophancy and improving interpretability and alignment. The next step, the authors say, involves building a benchmark and a harness for carrying out Weight-Space Programming on LLMs. "We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline," they say. ®

events.title: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
events.summary: 'I've always looked in bins for clothes' Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket. On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters. Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it. Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come. During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist. Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor." Darryl Baker takes the clothes for herself and her children, and to sell In addition to finding clothing for her children and her nephews and nieces, she keeps some for herself. Others she donates or sells, including recently getting £30 for a men's Barbour jacket. Darryl has joined the ranks of so-called dumpster divers – people who rummage through commercial bins for treasures. Motivations include saving money, giving items to charity and disgust at how often perfectly usable items are being consigned to waste - or a combination of all three. Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years. "I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever." Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds. "Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says. Jeff Ferrell sells some of what he finds, and gives away other items Jeff looks for discarded metal to sell at a scrapyard which, he says, earns him around $150 (£110) every two weeks. His wife sells his other finds, such as "an antique or piece of jewellery", on eBay. Through savings and selling the more valuable items, he estimates his finds are worth "tens of thousands of dollars a year". 'If something catches my eye, I'll grab it' While dumpster diving may have been considered taboo in the past, it's now something many people are proud to do and post about online. Millie Diamond, a London-based stylist, posts videos on Instagram of her rummaging through bins. But she has a very specific aim - to unearth fabrics and clothing that she can salvage and refashion into new items, some of which she then sells. Millie Diamond turns dumped textiles and clothes into new outfits She estimates that one dress she found was worth £600. "I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it." Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes." 'I haven't bought shampoo for years' For Charlotte Bayford in Essex it's all about timing. Her best finds come when students at Essex University head home for the summer and ditch anything they don't want to take with them. This includes half-filled toiletries. "I haven't bought shampoo for eight years," says the 44-year-old sales assistant. "I'd say that has saved me some money." Like other dumpster divers, Charlotte gives a lot of her finds to charity. But she has also filled her house with salvaged objects, and sells on some valuable items. Food, as long as it remains sealed, is fair game too. "I've found tins of Heinz baked beans, perfectly fine. I'm quite happy to eat those," Charlotte says. Charlotte Bayford gives some of her finds to charity But is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law? Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita. "Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges. In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land , external . In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances. "In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says. "But there is no general rule that something is free to take simply because it has been put in a skip or bin.

events.title: Adnoc’s XRG to buy Australian LNG stake for $1.5bn
events.summary: XRG , the international energy investment unit of Adnoc, has agreed to acquire Shell’s stake in an Australian natural gas project for $1.5 billion, as the company seeks to diversify its portfolio amid disruption to global energy markets caused by the Iran war. Abu Dhabi-based XRG will buy the stake in Australia's North West Shelf LNG project, marking its first investment in the country's gas sector and opening up greater access to customers in the Asia-Pacific region, the company said on Tuesday. The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, will give XRG access to one of the world's largest integrated LNG developments, with liquefaction capacity of 14.3 million tonnes per year and 4.4 trillion cubic feet equivalent of remaining resources. XRG has been actively increasing its portfolio of investments globally and plans to double its asset value over the next decade. Launched in 2024 as an international lower-carbon energy and chemicals investment company, with an enterprise value exceeding $80 billion, it has acquired stakes in several global gas projects. The latest acquisition strengthens XRG's position in the Asia-Pacific region. The North West Shelf project has been operating for more than four decades and plays a key role in the country's domestic gas supply and energy exports. The asset has supported domestic energy supply, jobs, international trade, and Australia’s emergence as a leading global energy exporter, XRG said. “This investment advances XRG’s strategy to build a leading international gas business serving growing demand across Asia-Pacific. The North West Shelf combines immediate production, strategic infrastructure, and future upstream development opportunities, making it a strong fit with our long-term ambitions,” said Mohamed Al Aryani, president of international gas at XRG. “XRG understands the importance of balancing export success with local energy needs. We believe continued investment in the North West Shelf can help sustain domestic gas supply, support regional energy security, create jobs, and deliver lasting economic benefits for Australia.” XRG said the project offers a combination of existing production, strategic infrastructure and opportunities for future upstream development. The company, which is wholly owned by Adnoc , has an enterprise value of more than $150 billion and invests across natural gas, chemicals and energy solutions.

events.title: Cities Worldwide Build and Scale AI Services With NVIDIA Physical and Agentic AI
events.summary: Cities generate enormous amounts of data from cameras, sensors and operational systems, but turning it into useful action — for planning, maintenance and public services — remains a challenge. Physical and agentic AI offer new ways to close that gap, from digital twins for infrastructure planning to vision and service agents, while keeping local governments in control of how sensitive data is processed and used. Building on initiatives announced at GTC Berlin , NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own. From resident services to vision agents, cities are adopting NVIDIA agentic AI to deliver faster, more responsive public services. City teams don’t need a massive infrastructure investment to get started building these AI services: depending on the workload, NVIDIA RTX workstations or a small GPU system may be enough. In Spain, 1MillionBot combines open source ALIA models trained at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center with NVIDIA Nemotron and other models in resident-service agents for Madrid Digital (Comunidad de Madrid), Administració Oberta de Catalunya and 150+ deployments across Spain, handling municipal procedures, appointment requests, urban-planning incidents and service inquiries. In the San Francisco Bay Area , LiveX is bringing its AI City vision to life with NVIDIA Cosmos world models and Nemotron open models, and Omniverse and Metropolis libraries on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs. The interactive, conversational AI hosts understand people’s needs, provide answers and take action, and can be tailored to local languages and service needs in airports, hospitals, local events and other public spaces. Vision AI agents can turn existing city camera feeds into operational insights, helping teams identify mobility and safety issues and coordinate emergency responses across city services. In Wrocław, Poland , K2K is building shared AI infrastructure using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Cosmos world reasoning models, and NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) to transform existing camera streams into actionable intelligence for mobility, safety and event response — using the same infrastructure across several city functions. In Malaysia , ITMAX bundles infrastructure and agentic AI applications into long-term managed services for cities, including for traffic management. Built with reference to Cosmos, Nemotron and the Metropolis VSS blueprint, ITMAX’s SamurAI V2 vision agents are scaling on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs to support 17,000+ cameras by 2027. ITMAX integrates TeraSim, an open source traffic simulation platform from Laplace Intelligence , to test signal timing, reducing peak-hour corridor travel times by up to 26%. Plan and Operate Critical Infrastructure With Digital Twins Beyond public-facing services, digital twins can help cities expedite infrastructure planning, minimizing disruption to local communities. City digital twins can also serve as a real-time operational simulation to facilitate faster decision-making. At Dangote’s Lekki refinery in Nigeria, Honeywell Technologies’ Forge Plant Cognition uses Nemotron-powered AI agents to understand operational data. A digital twin of the plant and its processes, built using Omniverse libraries, is also planned to support simulation and training. The platform, built on Dell PowerEdge servers with NVIDIA RTX PRO accelerators, helps operators identify bottlenecks, anticipate equipment and process issues, and optimize plant performance. In Taiwan , Linker Vision and Dutch architecture firm MVRDV are using NVIDIA Omniverse and Nemotron to build environmental, social and governance agents that can assess the environmental impact of various urban planning scenarios, simulating 15-year outcomes of an urban forest canopy in 10 minutes — increasing design iteration speed from two weeks per iteration to less than an hour. Cities can extend AI to more services by building on infrastructure already in place and adding capacity. Shared resources and managed services can help extend those capabilities across departments and municipalities. At Morocco’s Tanger Med port, Cires Technologies is expanding a sovereign AI factory for planned applications in worker safety, congestion analysis, cargo routing and port operations. Cires Technologies is also building an ecosystem of application providers to develop local models and applications for ports and cities. Beyond city services, Barcelona Supercomputing Center’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme gives startups access to sovereign computing, technical support and training. BSC AI Factory also supports research and innovation for startups — spanning agriculture, medical imaging, knowledge access and speech services. Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress, running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona, where NVIDIA Vice President of EMEA Paolo Guglielmini will deliver a keynote address followed by a panel moderated by Charbel Aoun, director of smart city and spaces for EMEA at NVIDIA. events.title: Open models can do 90% of agentic work at a twentieth of the cost of a frontier LLM: Gartner
events.summary: For-profit model-makers, many of which are spending billions on AI infrastructure, will be chasing revenue from just ten percent of steps involved in agentic AI workflows, according to analyst firm Gartner. “Nine in 10 agent workflow steps are routine, and open-weight models handle them at parity for a quarter of the price of the cheapest closed model,” the firm’s senior director Mark Petty and group vice president Raymond Paquet wrote last week in new document titled “Open-Weight Models Will Run 90% of Enterprise Agentic Workflow Steps.” “Typical operational workflows involve hundreds of routine executions, such as classification, tool calling, passing, validating and reconciling data,” the pair observe, before suggesting open-weight models “can handle hundreds of these routine steps for every one that needs frontier reasoning.” “Against the cheapest closed model at the same score, the open model costs a quarter as much. Against a frontier model run on every step, it costs as little as a twentieth,” the pair add. Those are the best-case numbers, because the analysts admit “Current open models can be more verbose and retry more often, so the saving per task against a frontier model is closer to five or six times.” That’s still a lovely saving, but the analysts rate it as the welcome by-product of moving to open models rather than an end in itself. “Years of workflow history are a large part of what an acquirer pays for in a SaaS company and every routine step sent to a frontier API moves a slice of it outside your perimeter,” the pair wrote. “Open-weights preserve your control. The cost saving is a bonus.” The two analysts therefore offer the following strategic planning assumption: “By 2030, 90% of enterprise operational agent workflow steps will execute on open-weight models.” They argue that enterprises will mostly adopt domain-specific open-weight models, because they do well “in scenarios where a small number of highly stable steps run millions of times a month.” Most models, however, are already commodities. Harnesses, the tools that run agents and manage agents, are the source of value in AI products, because one of their roles is to route work to the most appropriate model for a job, without users noticing any impact. A good harness saves money, imposes strong guardrails, and manages agent fleets. Less powerful harnesses leave users with more to do. The paper suggests frontier models will continue to have a role as the engine of research and development and are effectively capital expense. Open-weight models become an operational expense after frontier models do the heavy lifting. ®

events.title: Aramco posts 34% jump in third-quarter profit despite attacks on energy infrastructure
events.summary: Saudi Arabia's Aramco , the world's largest oil-producing company, has reported a 34 per cent annual increase in its third-quarter net income despite disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on energy infrastructure in the kingdom. Net profit for the three months to the end of September rose to 135.94 billion Saudi riyals ($36.25 billion), up from 101 billion riyals for the same period last year, Aramco said on Tuesday in a statement to the Tadawul stock exchange, where its shares are traded. “Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security,” Aramco president and chief executive Amin Nasser said. “Despite challenges, the flexibility of our system and the strength of a supply network built over decades enabled us to continue delivering reliably to our customers through this extraordinary period.” Aramco's board approved a third-quarter base dividend of $21.9 billion, a 3.5 per cent year-on-year increase, which will be paid in the fourth quarter of this year. Revenue boost The annual quarterly increase was driven by higher revenue despite volatile global energy markets, where prices shifted according to geopolitical headlines. Total revenue for the reporting period rose to $140.5 billion, up from $111.6 billion recorded for the third quarter of 2025. “The increase in revenue was predominantly driven by higher prices of refined and chemical products and crude oil, partially offset by lower volumes sold of crude oil and refined and chemical products,” Aramco said. The company's increased quarterly income provides a boost for Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s biggest economy, which still relies heavily on the sale of hydrocarbons for revenue. Aramco, Opec’s biggest oil producer and the main driver of Saudi Arabia's industrial sector, has faced waves of missile and drone attacks from Yemen’s Houthi militants that have put pressure on government revenue. In October, a Houthi missile attack damaged Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran. The attack caused a fire in an administrative building in the complex. Several crude refining facilities, including those in Jazan in the west and Riyadh, have also been attacked in recent weeks, raising fresh concerns about Saudi Arabia’s energy industry and Aramco’s ability to continue supplying crude oil to its global clientele. The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks on vessels rose in October to the highest level since the US Iran-war began on February 28, is adding to oil exporters’ woes. Overseas storage To avoid Hormuz, Saudi Arabia has ramped up crude shipments from its main export hub at Ras Tanura. The kingdom has relied on its East-West pipeline to pump crude to its Red Sea port. However, the pipeline was temporarily shut down after missiles launched from Iraqi territory damaged a pumping station. Saudi Arabia, which is also facing a Houthi-enforced maritime blockade, is exploring more routes to keep servicing its customers in Asia. “We continue to explore additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes to further strengthen our global supply network,” Mr Nasser said. While the East-West pipeline provides export flexibility, the company remains focused on operations and will continue to invest in projects, Aramco said. Production started at the company's Zuluf crude oil increment project in October. Major upstream projects, including Jafurah phase two, the Fadhili Gas Plant expansion, and the Dammam development project, remain on track, the company said. Aramco's capital expenditure of $10.5 billion in the third quarter is, however, lower than the $12.6 billion reported for the same period in 2025. “Backed by our strong balance sheet, we remain focused on the disciplined execution of priority projects … to unlock new opportunities,” Mr Nasser said. “This is how we will continue to meet the world’s evolving energy needs and deliver value for our shareholders and customers.”
