events.title: Adnoc Gas to supply TotalEnergies with up to 1.6 million tonnes of LNG in five-year deal
events.summary: Adnoc Gas has signed a five-year agreement to supply up to 1.6 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas to France's TotalEnergies, as the Abu Dhabi company expands its share of the global LNG market. The deal builds on a long-standing partnership between the two companies and reflects growing demand for LNG and confidence in Adnoc’s ability to deliver reliable supplies, the company said on Tuesday. “ Global demand for LNG continues to grow, and Adnoc Gas is well-positioned to capture that opportunity,” said Fatema Al Nuaimi, chief executive of Adnoc Gas. “This agreement reflects the strength of our LNG business, the competitiveness of our supply offering and our ability to secure long-term partnerships that support growth, enhance resilience and create lasting value for shareholders.” Adnoc Gas has continued to execute its long-term growth strategy this year, despite operational constraints. The company awarded $8.2 billion in engineering, procurement and construction contracts, part of its largest capital investment, for the second and third phases of the Rich Gas Development project – $3.9 billion for Phase 2, and $4.3 billion for Phase 3, the company said in August. These contracts build on Phase 1, announced in June 2025. The Rich Gas Development is a multi-phase, $13.2 billion capital investment programme by Adnoc Gas to expand gas processing and liquid recovery infrastructure across the UAE. The latest move strengthens Adnoc Gas’s commercial position at a time when demand for LNG is rising across Europe and Asia. Asia remains the main destination for LNG, accounting for about 65 per cent of global imports in 2025, while Europe has become a major buyer as it replaces Russian pipeline gas and manages storage needs, according to the International Energy Agency’s latest gas market report. “Thanks to its perfect location between Europe and Asia, this new supply will enable TotalEnergies to confirm its position as one of the main LNG portfolio suppliers,” said Stephane Michel, president of gas, renewables and power at TotalEnergies. TotalEnergies is both a shareholder in Adnoc Gas and a partner in the Ruwais LNG project. Adnoc Gas said it expects the planned integration of the Ruwais LNG project to significantly increase its production capacity, supporting its ambition to become one of the world’s leading LNG suppliers. The agreement between Adnoc Gas and TotalEnergies comes as Adnoc scales up a new global LNG marketing and trading platform that combines the marketing activities of Adnoc Gas and investment arm XRG with the trading capabilities of Adnoc Trading . The platform is aiming to reach 47 million tonnes per annum of marketable LNG beyond 2030, a level intended to place it among the world’s leading LNG marketing and trading businesses, Adnoc Gas said on Tuesday. Adnoc Gas supplies about 60 per cent of the UAE’s sales gas needs and supplies end-customers in more than 20 countries.

events.title: Architect creates open source replacement for VM migration tool VMware has hidden
events.summary: A cloud architect has created an open source alternative to VMware’s Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK), which the virtualization giant recently withdrew from public downloads. VMware describes VDDK as “a set of libraries and utilities that enable software developers to create applications that can access and manipulate virtual disks” and “a valuable tool for developers of storage and backup applications.” Users, along with VMware’s rivals, had another use for VDDK: migrating VMs to alternative virtualization platforms. In August, VMware restricted access to VDDK downloads to its partners, meaning VMware customers couldn’t access the tool and some of its rivals’ migration tools became less effective. Cloud architect Andrija Panić decided to do something about it. “Many tools that have nothing in common except VMware use the same small library to read a virtual machine’s disks: virt-v2v and nbdkit, the importers in Forklift/MTV, Proxmox VE and Apache CloudStack, and countless in-house scripts,” he told The Register by email. “When public VDDK downloads ended, all of them became harder to install and run.” “I didn’t think it was fair that people’s ability to move or protect their own data should depend on a download page.” He describes the project as “an independent drop-in for libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3, the disk library that VMware backup and migration tools load to read virtual disks. It was written from scratch, using only public documentation and black-box testing, and contains no VMware code.” Panić told The Register he wrote the tool in Go, with a thin C layer that exposes exactly the same C interface, library name and symbol versions as VMware’s code. The tool cannot write disks, just read them for backup and migration purposes. In his email to The Register , Panić said he has successfully tested OpenVDDK on vSphere versions 6.7 U3, 7.0.3, 8.0.3, 9.1.1. He said that tests in his lab with the latter version, accessing OpenVDDK through vCenter and on a standalone ESXi host, saw every disk read match. “Independent testers have reported successful use with Forklift (VMware to KubeVirt, cold and warm), MTV on OpenShift (cold and warm), a Proxmox VE pipeline and custom nbdkit-based tools,” the architect told The Register . “I've received reports of production use, including a German cloud provider migrating a large file server with V2K Migrate and a US-based company migrating to Apache CloudStack/KVM.” Panić was at pains to point out that the reports of successful use are “not independently audited customer endorsements or a guarantee of suitability for every production environment.” As is often the case with FOSS tools. OpenVDDK is not the only option for migrating away from VMware without VDDK. KVM-based OpenNebula has a tool called OneSwap that it says has a 96 percent success rate. Nutanix recently tweaked its “Move” migration tool so it can do the job without VDDK. Red Hat is working on a fix but has provided details of a workaround . Panić made OpenVDDK available under an Apache license, so perhaps Red Hat and others will find it useful as they re-jig their VM migration tools. ®

events.title: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
events.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.  Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).  The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.  It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).  But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.  So one month in, who’s on board? Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period. There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.  The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents). As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.  But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too. In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.  But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.   Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia. But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.  In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.  Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too . One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order , leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month. But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.  People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change. If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. events.title: Toyota shows off SoC that stores model weights and its OS on integrated memory
events.summary: Japanese carmaker Toyota has decided to have a crack at the market for AI processors. Toyota is the major shareholder in a company called AISIN, a manufacturer of automotive components. Both companies are aware that cars are increasingly reliant on tech like image recognition, and that robotics and other forms of “physical AI” will need parts that overlap with cars. AISIN thinks existing chips aren’t a good fit for such roles, because they rely on external memory to store AI models and then generate a lot of traffic between a processor and the model. That traffic, the company contends, makes image recognition and other on-device uses of AI less effective. DRAM is also currently vastly expensive. The company’s response is a system-on-chip built on a 16nm FinFET process, an Arm Cortex A53 dual-core CPU, plus an Arm MaliG31 GPU. The chip includes built-in STT-MRAM, which stores both model weights and an operating system. AISIN and its research partners at Tohoku University say that approach means the chip can go from power-on to kernel startup in 65.7 milliseconds – 38 times faster than is possible if using external memory – and run the Tiny YOLOv3 object detection algorithm on the chip. “To effectively utilize the limited on-chip memory capacity, a hybrid multiplication architecture combining 8-bit and 16-bit multiplication was developed” according to a machine translation of Tohoku University’s announcement [PDF]. “By combining 16x16, 16x8, and 8x8 bit multiplication, the amount of weight data for the AI model was reduced by 53 percent, from 17.7MB to 9.36MB, while maintaining 16-bit precision.” AISIN is an established parts supplier and already sells to Toyota and other automakers but hasn’t said if or when it can get this chip into production. Meanwhile, the likes of Nvidia and Qualcomm very much want to sell their silicon to carmakers, and position themselves as sources of tech and AI smarts that existing automotive supply chain participants can’t match. ®

events.title: EQT seeks joint AI and data centre deals with Saudi and UAE sovereign investors
events.summary: EQT , Europe’s biggest private markets investment firm, is in talks with sovereign investors in the UAE and Saudi Arabia to explore joint artificial intelligence and infrastructure investment opportunities in the Arab world’s top two economies, its global chair has said. The company with $400 billion in assets, which has been raising funds from Gulf investors for decades, is keen to now deploy capital in the region , home to some of the biggest sovereign wealth funds in the world, Jean Eric Salata, told The National . “Here [in the UAE] I would say, and we've also been talking to Saudis as well, looking at opportunities there. Those are the two big areas that we're working on right now,” Mr Salata said of the continuing AI co-investment conversations with sovereign investors. “We're most excited about, which I think aligns with the strategic goals of the UAE, is the whole infrastructure, particularly data infrastructure and data centres, where we have globally one of the largest footprints.” The Stockholm private equity company plans to expand its AI infrastructure footprint in the Gulf through its portfolio firm EdgeConneX, which owns more than 106 data centres across 25 countries, he said. AI opportunity EQT, which currently manages more than $100 billion in digital and energy assets across markets, is the latest global investor looking to the rapidly developing AI and digital infrastructure sector in the region. AI has become a central plank of economic diversification efforts of the oil-rich Gulf economies that have already announced mega AI infrastructure projects. The UAE is leading the way with a planned five-gigawatt UAE-US AI campus in Abu Dhabi, which includes Stargate UAE – a massive 1GW computing cluster anchored by a $20 billion data centre investment. UAE Tech investors Khazna and G42 are working on these projects alongside global leaders such as OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia and Cisco, and investors such as SoftBank. Saudi Arabia, the largest Arab economy, has rolled out Project Transcendence, a $100 billion scheme to scale domestic AI and data infrastructure. The kingdom’s $1 trillion Public Investment Fund has also set up Humain to build out national cloud infrastructure in the country. Qatar’s sovereign arm, the Qatar Investment Authority, has also launched Qai, a $20 billion AI infrastructure partnership, to build out domestic GPU and data centre footprints. Since last year the three Gulf states have announced AI investment plans worth $120 billion, which exceeded 5 per cent of their gross domestic product, according to International Monetary Fund estimates. The sheer scale of investment required for AI development and data centres creates a huge opportunity for global investors such as EQT. The $1.3 trillion Blackstone Group has already struck a $3 billion deal with Saudi Arabia’s Humain, while tech giant Microsoft has committed over $10 billion towards data centres and related infrastructure across UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Kuwait through to 2030. “There are many conversations that are ongoing right now with potential partners, both here [in the UAE] and elsewhere in the region,” Mr Salata said. “This is a sector that is capital constrained and is really, if you think about the AI build-out, the core, the key constraint in building the infrastructure is actually physical. It's the physical constraint around chips, energy, and data centres.” There is no shortage of demand for compute, hence a very strong investment case for building the power generation capacity and rolling out data infrastructure, he said. “I think that's where a lot of investment opportunity is right now for providers of long-term capital that can invest on a 15-year investment horizon,” he said. UAE SWF partnerships EQT opened an office in Abu Dhabi’s ADGM in September, joining the roster of trillion-dollar investors and asset managers including BlackRock, State Street, Blackstone Group, PGIM , Nuveen and Capital Group . A base in Abu Dhabi gives global investors opportunities to expand in the region and work closely with sovereign funds, large family offices and institutional partners. EQT is already working closely with the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, and Mr Salata said the firm is keen to expand that relationship. “They are one of our most important partners, and we're very excited to be working with them in, I would say, ever-increasing dimensions. We not only manage investments for Adia in our funds, but we also do a lot of co-investing together,” Mr Salata said. Adia is one of EQT’s largest co-underwriters in some of the European firm’s largest deals to take companies private in Europe. In June, Adia, along with Abu Dhabi’s $385 billion sovereign investment arm Mubadala Development Company, joined EQT’s £9.5 billion acquisition bid for the UK’s Intertek Group. Over the years, EQT has executed several co-investment deals with Mubadala, including the 2022 acquisition of Envirotainer, a biopharmaceutical industry solutions company. In 2025, Mubadala took a $600 million stake in Nord Anglia Education, and has been “a significant partner of ours all over the world”, he said. Deeping ties Establishing its first Middle East office in Abu Dhabi, Mr Salata said, was necessary to deepen its ties to the region, where it has active relationships with “many of the other sovereign wealth funds”. “The plan is to continue to develop those relationships regionally and use this office as a base to access them on a more regular basis,” he said. Forty EQT portfolio companies already have a presence in the Gulf, and with a local footprint, it expects more investments from regional sovereign investors to flow into those companies. “The logical place for us to start is with our existing portfolio companies,” Mr Salata said. “We really want to try and figure out how we can become more deeply involved in the investment ecosystem here,” he said. Over time EQT plans to bring more of its portfolio companies to the Gulf, and Mr Salata believes that the number will grow two or three-fold over the five to 10-year horizon. The sectors it seeks to invest in are “very much aligned with some of the longer-term trends in the region”, including infrastructure, education and health care, as well as technology and energy, where “the government policy is supportive”, he added.

events.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
events.summary: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines. A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co. , a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “ XCPE ” (named after one of the malware’s core code components). The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group. The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year , residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects. “Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.” The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems . Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness). The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt , also known as Honeygain , which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs . In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source , after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment. It’s unclear what a consent decree would entail, or what terms are being considered. It’s possible the DOJ could change course, the people said. Fox declined to comment. Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward also declined to comment on the deal. “However, we can affirm that this DOJ under President Trump’s leadership will continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy,” he said in a statement. The deal, which would unite Fox’s content empire of news and sports with Roku’s dominant connected-TV operating system, had worried rivals who fear that Fox will favor its own content. Roku’s free, ad-supported channel also competes for viewers and content with Tubi, which Fox owns. Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch has said his “expectation” is to run the two businesses separately while selling advertising across them. Semafor first reported in September that antitrust regulators were widening the inquiry into the deal, days before the two companies confirmed the deeper probe, known as a “second request.” That enhanced scrutiny came in part because of pressure from Newsmax majority owner Chris Ruddy, who bills himself as a Trump confidant and has had a long-running spat with Fox owner Rupert Murdoch, Semafor later reported. events.title: GOP's midterm blame game starts early
events.summary: Republicans don't know if they'll lose big or small on Tuesday, but they're already bracing for an epic blame game. Why it matters: Privately, Republicans acknowledge it's not a complicated version of Clue. The leading suspect: Mr. President , in the Oval Office, with an assortment of weapons — and one war. Returning Republican senators are unlikely to blame President Trump publicly. There's a price for that. And don't expect Trump to shoulder the responsibility. But do expect departing GOP lawmakers to take shots at Trump or his team, and Trump to fire back at Senate Republicans, whom he's never been shy about torching. The irony of Trump's second midterm: With Republicans privately resigned to losing the House, Trump can still credibly claim victory if they hold the Senate. "It's Donald Trump's midterms. He gets all the credit if we win. He gets all the credit if we lose," one national GOP strategist told Axios. The Iran war: From Alaska to Maine, Trump's decision to go to war with Iran — and the resulting spike in gas and diesel prices — has become a major political liability for Republican Senate nominees. "It's not tariffs … it's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton said at a closed-door fundraiser in September, Axios reported last month . Tariffs: Trump's trade policies have compounded Republicans' affordability problems, particularly in farm country, where producers have faced higher costs and uncertainty over export markets. "We need to end this tariff war now," former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) , the GOP Senate nominee, said in an October campaign ad, breaking with Trump over his tariffs on Canada. Bad candidates: Trump's preferred nominees are also drawing blame, GOP strategists tell Axios. Paxton in Texas and Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina have forced Republicans to spend heavily defending races that should have been easier — and where the party had other options. Complacent incumbents: Sens. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) are facing accusations of "arrogance" and "laziness" from Republicans frustrated that their once-safe seats have become late-breaking battlegrounds — exactly the complacency NRSC Chair Tim Scott warned against. Weak governors: Underperforming gubernatorial nominees in Iowa, Michigan and Ohio threaten to drag down Republican Senate candidates. Vivek Ramaswamy, for example, saw his polling crater in the final weeks . Recruitment failures: Republicans couldn't persuade Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp to run for Senate, and in New Hampshire settled for their second-choice Sununu — former Sen. John Sununu — instead of his brother, former Gov. Chris Sununu. Meanwhile, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) landed marquee candidates in Alaska, Ohio and Iowa — though Michigan and Maine proved more difficult. MAGA money: Trump's political operation amassed an enormous war chest, but some Republicans complain the money arrived too late to rescue vulnerable candidates. Distractions: Trump's focus on D.C. construction projects, the Kennedy Center, Sen. Jon Husted's (R-Ohio) backside and the SAVE Act has frustrated Republicans desperate for a closing message focused on the economy. "Reflecting Pool presser was an interesting choice for closing message," another national GOP strategist said of Trump's Monday news conference.

The Stellantis-owned Dodge brand announced its return at the SEMA Show in Las Vegas on Monday. Dodge will once again give the Cup Series four manufacturers, joining Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota in fielding entries to compete in a 36-race schedule that begins in mid-February and crowns a champion in early November. They have a deep passion for NASCAR and its ability to showcase the world’s top brands, and we can’t wait to see Dodge on the racetrack for the Daytona 500 and beyond.” Dodge raced in NASCAR through the 2012 season and left the same month it celebrated the Cup title with Brad Keselowski and Penske Racing. It was Dodge’s first Cup championship since Richard Petty’s sixth of seven titles in 1975. Dodge re-entered the NASCAR Truck Series with its Ram brand in 2026, with eyes on expanding to the premier Cup Series in 2028. Normally, it would have taken Dodge two years to get ready for the Cup Series. But Dodge bypassed part of the timeline required to develop a new engine by partnering with Earnhardt Childress Racing to build Dodge-spec powerplants alongside its regular Chevrolet operations. Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota allowed that unique partnership in part because they believed a fourth manufacturer in NASCAR would be good for the overall health of the racing series. events.title: Final polls, models and markets see a "blue tsunami"
events.summary: The threat of a blue tsunami is bearing down on President Trump's Washington, with virtually every major indicator forecasting a Democratic rout in Tuesday's elections. Why it matters: Expectations for the midterms have soared so high that some Democrats fear disappointment is inevitable, particularly if the party falls short of winning the Senate — a prize that seemed beyond reach just months ago. By the numbers: Five key metrics help distill the extraordinary consensus taking shape on the eve of the midterms. 🔮 95% and 80%: The probability of Democrats winning the House and Senate, respectively, according to election forecaster Nate Silver , whose model projects an average gain of 25 House seats. Silver says Democrats could now withstand a modest polling error and still capture the Senate — a remarkable cushion given the GOP's history of outperforming polls in the Trump era. 🗺️ 7 for 7: Democrats lead in every Senate battleground state surveyed in the final New York Times/Siena polls , including by 11 points in Michigan and seven in Texas. Trump carried six of those seven states in 2024, though five of the Democratic leads — Maine (+6), Kansas (+5), Ohio (+5), Alaska (+2) and Iowa (+1) — remain within the polls' margins of error. 🏛️ 240: The number of House seats Democrats could win under the upper end of Cook Political Report's forecast — potentially their largest majority since the first year of Barack Obama's presidency. Reaching that mark would require Democrats to sweep all 18 toss-up races. Cook already favors them in 222 districts, four more than needed for a majority. 🎲 73%: The probability of Democrats winning both chambers of Congress, according to Kalshi . After correctly favoring Trump in 2024, prediction markets have become a closely watched barometer of political expectations. Nearly $100 million in contracts have traded on Kalshi's congressional control market alone. 📊 +14: Democrats' lead on the generic congressional ballot in the final poll from AtlasIntel , which became the nation's highest-rated pollster after its remarkably accurate 2024 performance. Reality check: Even the pollsters forecasting a Democratic landslide are haunted by the possibility that they're still missing Trump voters. New York Times polling chief Nate Cohn warned that white Democrats were roughly 30% more likely than white Republicans to respond to the final Times/Siena surveys — a slightly wider gap than in 2020, when polls overstated Democratic support. Washington Post pollsters raised similar alarms after finding Democrat Adam Hamilton leading Republican Sen. Roger Marshall by nine points in Kansas, where registered Democrats were more than twice as likely as Republicans to participate. What they're saying: Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson have accused pollsters of deliberately manufacturing the appearance of a Democratic wave to suppress Republican turnout. "They're trying to create this idea of a blue wave and they're using the poll numbers to do it," Johnson said Monday , claiming conservatives distrust polling calls because they believe "it's a psyop." Between the lines: Prediction markets are sometimes touted as more accurate than polls because bettors have money at stake. But their odds often reflect the same polling data and political sentiment, leaving them vulnerable to the same blind spots. In Wisconsin, Kalshi gave state Rep. Francesca Hong a 96% chance of winning the Democratic gubernatorial primary the day before the August election. She lost to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley. In Brazil, Kalshi gave Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro an 84% chance of defeating President Lula ahead of last week's runoff. Lula won, prompting MAGA influencers to amplify baseless claims that the election was rigged. The bottom line: Voters will ultimately deliver the only verdict that counts. But on the eve of the election, the polls, forecasts and betting markets are all pointing in one direction.

events.title: Anthropic's compute tab could top $1T as Q3 revenue nears $17B
events.summary: Anthropic has published a regulatory filing revealing nearly $900 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, with additional estimated payments potentially pushing the total beyond $1 trillion. The Monday filing reports that Anthropic expects to pay nearly $70 billion in contractual obligations by September 2027, with a total of roughly $447.5 billion in commitments expected to be incurred by the end of 2030. That's assuming of course its revenues continue their upward trajectory, which the prospectus warns is far from guaranteed. "In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%," the prospectus reads. "We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all." "Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the filing reads. Which is to say, if Anthropic's revenues don't grow faster than its compute commitments, it could end up falling into a nasty spiral. And while Anthropic has several options, including debt and equity financing, relying on these long term could dilute existing shareholders or force the company to borrow on unfavorable terms. Every IPO filing reads a bit like this because no company can guarantee eternal success and growth. A lot of this filing's language, as damning as it might sound, is therefore just Anthropic covering its butt. However, even though the company is still growing steadily year-over-year, the latest filing shows revenue growth is already slowing. Between Q1 and Q2 of this year, revenues grew nearly 2.5x. Yet in Q3, Anthropic's reported revenues of nearly $17 billion represented an increase of just 46 percent from Q2. In the same period, Anthropic's compute and infrastructure costs grew 77 percent and it kept signing deals that commit it to more expenditure. Last week, we reported that Anthropic's purchase commitments exceeded $800 billion over the next decade or so. Anthropic now says its commitments are closer to $895 billion. Roughly $320 billion of those commitments relate to existing contractual obligations. Another $451 billion covers leases Anthropic has signed, but that have yet to commence, with the company expecting them to begin between 2026 and 2028, although some remain subject to termination rights or other conditions. Overall, however, Anthropic's compute spend is on track to increase substantially over the next few years. And that's not even counting the blank checks Anthropic has written to secure adequate compute, which it values at $150-$175 billion, putting Anthropic's total compute tab at somewhere north of $1 trillion. Anthropic can't walk away from some of this spending because its deals with Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Broadcom, which now total $437 billion, are non-cancellable. Some require payment regardless of whether Anthropic lights up a single GPU. The AI upstart estimates that of its $895 billion in contracts, only about $213 billion worth allow it to avoid payments. The revised S1 filing also offered insights into the company's customer base, including a major reliance on cloud service providers for distribution. The likes of Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are some of the model dev's biggest compute providers, but according to the filing, cloud marketplaces accounted for roughly 44 percent of its revenue in the nine months ended September 30. Anthropic insists that none of its customers account for more than 10 percent of revenue. Yet reliance on hyperscalers for distribution remains a risk because they are all either actively developing competing products or provide access to models from Anthropic's rivals. Despite all the risks in its prospectus, Anthropic believes it can become a sustainable business if it can access enough compute capacity. And by doing so, the prospectus claims AI will reshape the economy "in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet." With so much at stake, how can humanity afford not to spend like a drunken sailor? ®

events.title: Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware
events.summary: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 . In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating. Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday. “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.” One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said. Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices , allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on wa ter systems across at least 12 US states over the summer. The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote. While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted. Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher. One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote. The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote. “If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post. While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

events.title: Another judge blocks DOJ ballot demands in California
events.summary: A federal judge on the eve of Election Day barred the Trump administration from demanding California officials set aside ballots from registered voters it suspects are noncitizens, finding the effort likely violates the Constitution. Why it matters: Courts had already rejected the Justice Department's attempts to force California to separate the ballots. Monday's ruling goes a step further, directly barring federal officials from making those demands even as DOJ turns to the Supreme Court to compel the state to comply. Driving the news: Chief U.S. District Judge James Boasberg ruled Monday that the Trump administration likely violated the Constitution by pressuring California officials to change how they count ballots. His order prohibits the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security from demanding officials set aside ballots or depart from existing state election procedures based on federal lists of suspected noncitizens. Boasberg found that the Constitution gives states and Congress, but not the executive branch, authority over election rules. The federal ban on noncitizen voting does not mean the administration can rewrite those rules. By the numbers: The DOJ claims it identified more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens on California's voter rolls. After Boasberg ordered DOJ to turn over its list, an expert found that at least 22 members of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights — all known U.S. citizens — were wrongly included. The expert found another 66 members were almost certainly on the list. Boasberg found the expert credible and concluded the list's errors posed a real threat to eligible voters. What he's saying: "The President evidently believes that it would be good public policy for more stringent procedures to be put in place," Boasberg wrote. "No matter how strong that policy case may be, however, it does not justify overstepping the bounds of the Executive Branch's limited constitutional authority in this domain." The White House referred Axios to the Department of Homeland Security for comment. DHS and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to Axios' requests for comment. Catch up quick: In a separate lawsuit , DOJ sought to force California and Los Angeles County to segregate ballots from suspected noncitizens. A federal judge rejected that request Wednesday, as did an appeals court on Friday. Monday's ruling is different in that it restricts the federal government from making its demands rather than simply refusing to order California to comply. It also follows a broader nationwide temporary restraining order Friday that prohibits similar demands and threats of prosecution against election workers. Yes, but: Boasberg did not prohibit federal officials from investigating illegal voting or compiling lists of suspected noncitizens. Federal law makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote in federal elections, and DOJ can prosecute people who knowingly break that law. But that doesn't give DOJ the authority to order states to change how they verify voter eligibility or count ballots, Boasberg wrote. California can continue following its election procedures while federal prosecutors pursue illegal voting, Boasberg said. What's next: The Supreme Court could still order California to set aside the disputed ballots.

events.title: These smart glasses promise to turn your silent mouth movements into text
events.summary: The next time you see a software engineer shaping silent words with their mouth, you may have to think twice before asking if they need a mental health day – they might just be wearing a pair of smart glasses that let them talk to their computer without uttering a sound. Subvocal is a Y Combinator-backed startup aiming to produce these glasses, and already has working prototypes to show off in YouTube videos, including one with YC partner Dave Lieb trying them out and being impressed enough to offer funding. The headset isn’t what the final version will look like, the company notes, which is good: The demo headset is obviously 3D printed and far from fashionable. Once the final product is available it should look a lot sleeker, based on mockups on the company’s website. It’s not clear when they’ll actually be released, though the preorder page says it’ll be sometime in Q1 2027 at an early bird price of $499. It’s not clear what the final full price will be. As for how the glasses work, the founders, Georgia Tech computer science students Aarush Yadav and Arnav Kumar, explain in a launch post on YC that the device uses low-powered radio waves projected from the glasses toward a wearer’s face. Those waves are distorted by muscle movements and the change in a person’s face shape as they speak or simply mouth words, which the duo said can be picked up and translated into written text. “We started working on this about four months ago after building the first version at a hackathon,” the pair explained in their YC post. “Since then, we’ve gone from a table full of electronics and antennas taped to our face to a semi-portable board and sleek glasses that can decode open-ended speech at 200+ WPM and a reasonably low error rate even at a small dataset scale.” This is just a proof of concept, and many key details are still missing, like the accuracy rate, battery life, whether it will paired with an app, or what-have-you. “The core thing we wanted to prove first was that the signal exists and that we can decode it,” Yadav and Kumar said. In a Hacker News post announcing the company, Yadav and Kumar explained that they started the project during the hackathon by focusing on using EMG electrodes attached to Yadav’s face. They didn’t win the hackathon, but apparently the demo was impressive enough to earn some initial funding from San Francisco VC firm Afore Capital. Shortly after that, the pair pivoted from EMG to RF sensing, as a commercial dictation product that required sticking electrodes to one’s face was unlikely to succeed. “Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge,” Yadav said. “First we built an extremely low-noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face.” They eventually got to the functional prototype they have now, and pre-trained the AI models doing the speech recognition to minimize setup time. According to the company, Lieb only had to read 20 sentences to calibrate the headset to his speech patterns. “We think silent speech can become the next interface for interacting with computers, replacing voice and the keyboard,” the company says of its goal. “Emails, prompts, messages, code, notes, commands, all at the speed of speech without bothering anyone around you.” With just four months of work under their belts, Subvocal could be a massive hit, ushering in a new era of silent muttering productivity for workers in a variety of industries, or it could flop as it tries to scale. Those interested in finding out can preorder a pair now for $199, with the other $300 not due until the glasses ship. ®

events.title: Nine engineers, 1,211 code updates in a day: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork
events.summary: Nine engineers, 1,211 pull requests in a day: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork Plus a case study where we put everything together by moving our runtime from Python to Rust while live. In January of this year, a small team at Microsoft set out to build Copilot Cowork , an agentic execution layer that performs multi-step workflows on a user’s behalf. That result brings the powerful AI-assisted tools and capabilities developers have today to everyday knowledge workers, all with Work IQ , Microsoft 365 security and governance, cloud execution, and Microsoft’s multi-model architecture. This is the story of how the team took Copilot Cowork from an empty repo to worldwide GA in about four and a half months, then moved its runtime from Python to Rust while it was live. Agents wrote most of the code. Ways of working changed along the way, and the practices other teams can adapt to build like a frontier development team: moving fast while keeping reliability, security, and cost in view. On October 21, nine engineers merged 1,211 pull requests into the main branch of the Copilot Cowork backend. That number would have sounded absurd to the team in January, when a handful of us made the first commit to an empty repo. Agents wrote most of the code, but engineers remained responsible for defining the work and judging the results. Our small team wrote clearer specs, set architecture and security boundaries, and focused its review on higher-risk changes, production impact, and cases where checks or reviewers disagreed. Automated checks and agent reviewers examined every change. Agents could propose changes, but they could not decide what was allowed to happen. We didn’t plan on working this way. But every few weeks, the agents got better, part of our process stopped working, and we adapted. Six practices emerged from those changes. They cover how we specify work, run agents within clear boundaries, test our checks, preserve what the team learns, shape the codebase for parallel work, and set limits on automated loops. They aren’t a recipe for matching our PR count. They are lessons other teams can adapt to build like a frontier development team while keeping reliability, security, and cost in view. We’ll end with the project that puts those practices to the test together: moving the live runtime from Python to Rust. Lesson 1: Write the spec before the code The first commit was made on January 13. From the start, agents wrote the code. In the first weeks, we learned that the agent was rarely what slowed us down. The bottleneck was not knowing exactly what we wanted. A vague request got us code that looked reasonable, survived a quick read, and then did the wrong thing. Fixing it took longer than writing a proper request would have in the first place. So we adopted a rule that still stands today: no code without a markdown spec written first. The spec covers three things: A good spec saves far more time than it costs upfront. But a weak one leads to rework a few days later. The faster agents became at implementation, the more important it became for us to be precise about intent, requirements, and what good looked like. Many of our specs start out spoken. Someone talks through a feature, and an agent turns that into a first draft of the spec, which the human then edits. I think this did more for our speed than any single model upgrade. We launched Copilot Cowork to our first enterprise customers in the Frontier program on March 30. Lesson 2: Run narrow agents inside clear boundaries The next step was running more than one agent at a time. Each works in its own copy of the repo, on one task, from one spec. One agent became five, and five became dozens. Merged PRs per month went from 257 in January to 2,754 in May. Our busiest week before GA had 783. Parallel work went better than we expected for two reasons: Narrow tasks: An agent with one well-defined task makes fewer mistakes than one asked to do a lot at once. Picking the model per task: We treated model choice as a quality-and-cost tradeoff, not a race to use the cheapest model. Some tasks warranted stronger reasoning; for others, a faster, less expensive model gave us the right balance. In Copilot Cowork, the model runs in a container without user credentials. A trusted host outside the container handles identity, policy, approvals, and tools, and every Microsoft 365 operation goes through the host. We didn’t want to limit what the agent could attempt, because a heavily restricted agent isn’t very useful . With our architecture, the model can plan and ask for anything, and the host decides what actually happens. That separation lets us increase the number of agents working in parallel without giving the model credentials or direct authority over operations. The host still applied identity, policy, approvals, and audit at the point of execution. Building that in at the start was much easier than adding it later would’ve been. It also helped in a way we didn’t plan for. The agent only talks to the host through a defined interface, so we could later replace the entire host without changing the agent—which we did when we migrated to Rust. We reached worldwide general availability on June 16, about four and a half months after the first commit, with several models and 16 plugins. Lesson 3: Make checks prove they checked something With agents writing most of the code, nine people couldn’t read every change, and waiting for a human review was becoming the slowest step for every PR. Several engineers each built their own review bot, modeled on how they review code themselves, and the bots competed. When one bot caught a problem another had missed, the bot that missed it got a new rule. Over time, each reviewer built up a large set of rules learned from its own misses. Each one has now been through at least10,000 generations; in each generation, the reviewer runs reviews, then reflects on what it missed and gets better at reviewing code. Today, a useful first review usually arrives within several minutes of a pull request being opened. On a sample of recent merged PRs, the median was about four and a half minutes. Slower, more specialized passes follow: One walks the call graph, looking for code that isn’t wired up and for tests that would still pass if the change were reverted One looks at operational problems like restart safety, metrics, and stale docs One reads every changed file end to end One checks behavior against the code being replaced The author gets quick feedback while the change is still fresh, and the detailed reading still happens. Of course, reviewer agents can still miss things. Once, a group of reviewer agents read a change in one of the most sensitive parts of the product. Each had been told to try to break it, and none found a problem. People on the team then read the same diff and found four blocking issues, all of which were fixed before it merged.

events.title: Trump cuts South Africa, Rwanda from AGOA trade program
events.summary: The News US President Donald Trump plans to remove South Africa and Rwanda from African Growth and Opportunity Act eligibility next year, stripping both countries of duty-free access to the US market under Washington’s flagship Africa trade program. Trump formally notified Congress and both governments of his decision, the Office of the US Trade Representative said Monday, after an annual review determined Pretoria and Kigali have been engaging in “concerning and pervasive” practices inconsistent with AGOA’s eligibility criteria. These include “barriers that undermine American trade and investment” and practices that “pose a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests in the region,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said. The statement also cited corruption in South Africa, while its concerns about Rwanda extended to the rule of law, political pluralism, and human rights. The decision follows months of US tension with both governments. Washington has clashed with Pretoria over Trump’s claims of a “genocide” against white South Africans, which experts have dismissed, and is ending PEPFAR aid to the country. South Africa hoped to use its critical mineral resources as leverage in trade talks. South African Trade Minister Parks Tau said the “decision does not define the broader relationship” between the countries and that South Africa would continue pursuing trade, investment and shared economic opportunities with the US. The trade ministry said it had offered additional concessions and called it “unfortunate that the US is now raising new issues that have not been the basis for discussions.” With Rwanda, the dispute centers on the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo: The US sanctioned Rwanda’s military in March and its defense ministry last week, accusing them of backing M23 rebels and using minerals from rebel-held territory in their supply chains. Know More South Africa has the most to lose as AGOA’s largest beneficiary, exporting about $1.7 billion worth of goods under the program in 2025, including vehicles and agricultural products. Rwanda’s exposure is far smaller, with US imports from the country totaling about $44 million last year. Standard trade will continue, but affected exports could become more expensive, and the damage may spread across southern Africa and impact thousands of jobs . “The loss of AGOA will reverberate through the SADC region as several countries, including Lesotho and Botswana, are part of the South African supply chain that provides goods and products for the US under AGOA,” said Witney Schneidman, a former US deputy assistant secretary of state for African affairs. AGOA, established in 2000, is authorized only through the end of 2028, and Schneidman said this episode highlights the need to modernize it. “China, the EU and South Africa’s other partners don’t turn their trade relations ‘on and off’ as the US does,” he said.

events.title: AI could break legal systems by finding previously hidden loopholes
events.summary: If AI can find the holes in programming code, it can do the same with legal code, paving the way for chaos. Felix Ringe, a visiting fellow at Stanford Law School’s liftlab and legal scholar, suggests large language models (LLMs) have become potent enough that they could break legal systems by identifying exploitable inconsistencies at scale. "Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language," Ringe and collaborator Linus Folkerts argued in a blog post last week. "Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation." Ringe contends that while courts tend to pave over these text vulnerabilities through statutory interpretation, the ability to discover adversarially useful inconsistencies in the law in an automated way risks overwhelming the legal system's ability to bridge the gaps. To buttress his thesis, he points to recent work by other legal scholars that frames laws as vulnerable code, such as " Legal Zero-Days : A Novel Risk Vector for Advanced AI Systems" and " Hardware and Software Bugs in the Legal System " [PDF]. The analogy dates back at least to 1999, with Lawrence Lessig's Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace [PDF] and Code Is Law: On Liberty in Cyberspace . Lessig credits William J. Mitchell, in City of Bits: Space, Place, and the Infobahn (1995), with the idea that code is cyberspace's law, adding that he "drew the metaphor from others as well." Ringe has turned this on its head by proposing that law is code. The analogy between programming code and legal code works reasonably well, up to a point. Law and code both have their share of formatting pedantry and ritual. The mapping breaks down when courts get cast as a runtime environment – non-deterministic trial outcomes don't work for production applications. Discontinuities aside, Ringe's point is that AI models can surface statutory gaps at a scale that may bring the chaos currently seen in the software security ecosystem to the legal world. To demonstrate that, Ringe and Folkerts cite several potential gaps in German law that they uncovered with the help of LLMs, noting that they're only sharing legal exploits they believe could not cause serious harm. For example, an amendment to Germany's Occupational Diseases Regulation (BKV) is subject to a constitutional requirement to cite its statutory authority. But Ringe and Folkerts argue that the amendment omits a required reference. So, in theory, a journalist could request an unpublished statement submitted to Germany's occupational-diseases advisory council under freedom of information rules, challenging a confidentiality provision that the researchers argue may be invalid. Another example cited describes a transit visa rule that may be invalid because the government failed to identify the authority under which the rule was made. "We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems," they wrote. "In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves." Wendy Musell, a San Francisco-based employment law attorney and partner, told The Register that the use of AI in the legal field is expanding rapidly. "Some California Courts, including LA Superior Court, are testing the use of AI as law clerks," said Musell. "Generally law clerks would assist the Court by researching and drafting opinions for the judge's review. That means AI is serving that role in certain courts. Litigators now must consider how AI is analyzing motions and cases. "This is the case even where I personally have found different AI sources to appear to have a slant or bias, and often fail to accurately analyze legal issues. It was just a matter of time before AI came for the legislative process." Eric Goldman, associate dean for research and professor of law at Santa Clara University School of Law, told The Register that Ringe's argument has some merit. "I think the methodology of using AI to identify potential statutory gaps is logical," said Goldman. "However, it will require careful human review to determine if the AI-identified gaps are in fact actually gaps. Statutory gaps also may have no legal consequence, or at least none of significance; and legislatures will often correct any major gaps once they are identified." Goldman said the idea that legislators should use AI during the drafting process is ambitious, at least in the short term. "Legislators often draft laws with a range of goals and priorities, and avoiding statutory gaps is rarely a high priority," he explained. "But many legislatures have legislative counsel who are responsible for converting draft bills into final legislative text, and I could see where legislative counsel could benefit from using AI to identify drafting gaps as part of their standard cleanup protocols." ®

events.title: Trump to Axios: "No rush" to decide on bombing Iran again
events.summary: President Trump told Axios in a phone interview Monday he's "in no rush" to decide whether to resume fighting in Iran . Why it matters: The midterm elections have been seen as an inflection point for Trump on whether to unleash a massive bombing campaign to try to bring the war to an end. But it appears the president, at least for now, will continue on dual tracks — letting negotiations play out while preparing to go back to war if he concludes a deal isn't reachable. What he's saying: "One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially. They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it," Trump said in the interview. Driving the news: Qatari mediators have written a draft agreement outlining a three-day sequence of confidence-building measures aimed at resuming direct U.S.-Iran negotiations, according to regional sources. A diplomat with knowledge of the situation said the Qatari mediators are waiting for feedback from the U.S. and Iran. Qatari mediator Ali al-Thawadi traveled to Tehran on Monday to continue talks on the draft agreement, and the diplomat said progress is building. Trump is giving diplomacy a chance but is clear-eyed about the chances of reaching a deal. "We are talking to them. It's going fine. The problem with them is ... they try and tap, tap, tap [us along]. There's less urgency [on the Iranian side] than you think there would be, but they want to make a deal more than they ever wanted," Trump said. The latest: Hours after the interview, Trump posted on Truth Social: "Oil Prices are DROPPING LIKE A ROCK, down almost $10 a Barrel, A RECORD, because people feel that there will not be a War with Iran. Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!" Between the lines: Trump is weighing three courses of action, backed by three different camps: 1. Make a deal: Vice President JD Vance and White House envoy Steve Witkoff are urging him to move toward a deal because a renewed war might not change the situation for the better. Most Gulf countries support this position and have communicated that to Trump, sources said. 2. Go back to battle: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants to resume combat, as does Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. They argue that Iran can't be trusted to make a deal, let alone abide by one, and that Trump should finish the job militarily. 3. Maximum economic pain: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are advising Trump to maintain the "no war, no deal" status quo and allow the economic pressure campaign to continue, sources said. Ratcliffe told Trump that prolonged economic pain would induce Iran to make more concessions — or create enough instability inside the country that citizens revolt, a source with direct knowledge said. The CIA declined to comment. The other side: Iran's civilian leadership sounded hopeful Monday about the prospects of reaching a deal. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei "granted the government certain authorities" to try to reach an agreement through diplomacy. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that the diplomatic exchanges "have become very intensive." "Qatar and Pakistan are playing very active roles as mediators," he said. "We have presented our conditions and our proposal, and everything depends on Washington's political rationality. If they choose genuine diplomacy, we are ready to engage. But if they intend to engage in deception and military operations, they will face a response more painful and severe than in the past." Araghchi said that if the U.S. accepts Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, then "negotiations will resume." "Otherwise, the current situation will continue, and Iran will not bow down," he said. The big picture: Russia and China are taking an active role in the effort to reach a deal. Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone Monday with Iranian Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Gen. Mohsen Rezaei. The two discussed the efforts to reach a diplomatic agreement. Rezaei, who is very close to Khamenei, was also the recipient of a letter Vance sent recently proposing to resume negotiations. Russia has also offered to be part of any nuclear agreement, including by receiving Iran's enriched uranium stockpile. At the same time, Rezaei's deputy visited Beijing on Monday and met with the Chinese foreign minister. China is also urging the U.S. and Iran to resume direct negotiations to end the war. What they're saying: Vance told reporters Monday that he and Trump "feel pretty good about the prospect of reaching a settlement" with Iran. "We made some progress and we will see if we can make some more," Vance said. He added: "We haven't set deadlines [for resuming strikes]. We want to make sure the Iranians don't rebuild or try to rebuild their nuclear program. We do think there is a pathway there, but it requires a firm and verifiable commitment that they don't rebuild their nuclear program."

events.title: Trump pre-election pitch: Reflecting Pool, pipes and a new promenade
events.summary: President Trump extolled his administration's Reflecting Pool project , dug up debunked claims of vandalism and applauded the new White House helipad in a Monday pre-Election Day speech. The big picture: Trump's deep focus on remaking the nation's capital has taken center stage as the clock ticks down to midterm elections. Driving the news: "The pool is now better and more beautiful than it's ever been before, and we're very proud of it," Trump said in Monday's speech, adding, "We went through a lot with vandalism." But Trump's own Justice Department dropped the vandalism case against former Olympian David Hearn . A judge later killed the case after prosecutors acknowledged that faulty installation caused the damage to the Pool. Trump added the administration was "giving serious thought" to renaming the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to the "Trump Reflecting Pool," before later saying he was kidding. Throughout the speech, he held up printed images he identified as pipes, joints and other Pool materials. He also showed an image that appeared to show "8647" sprayed onto the base of the emptied pool, claiming "that was a Comey phrase" — a reference to his former FBI director and top foe. Zoom out: He also discussed his White House renovation projects, including the recently installed helipad and Scotts Miracle-Gro's lawn restoration after the UFC fight on White House grounds. Friction point: Trump's projects, including his D.C.-area arch and White House ballroom, have been broadly panned by Americans in polling. "This project should be a project that unites all Americans," Trump said Monday of the newly reopened Reflecting Pool, which stood empty for an extended period earlier this year. Zoom in: His pre-election pitch at times sounded more like a typical rally speech, where he touted his immigration policies and war with Iran while slamming Democrats as "a party that hates America." This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime," he said. "The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history." He also reiterated his pitch to distribute $5,000 checks should Republicans win in the midterms. What's next: After inviting Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to speak, Trump then touted his planned " triumphal arch ," detailed plans for a "promenade" from the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River and teased his golf course renovation . "We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that you don't have enough time," Trump said. He ended his closing argument by lauding a "golden age," saying, "We were laughed at like we were stupid people. We were laughed at by every ruler, every president, every prime minister, every king, every queen. But they don't laugh anymore." Axios' Josephine Walker contributed to this report. events.title: Scoop: Senate GOP makes massive bet on streaming
events.summary: The top Senate GOP super PAC has nearly tripled its spending on streaming and social media platforms this election cycle to more than $200 million, Axios has learned. Why it matters : In a record cycle for ad spending, more political money is shifting to streaming, where super PACs have greater freedom to target voters, bargain and experiment — but platforms have more power to set the rules. In some states, streaming and social media have swallowed half of the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) budget, according to a source familiar with the group's spending. SLF's $200M+ total for the 2026 cycle (up from $71M in 2024) includes tens of millions of dollars funneled through the SLF-linked Texas PAC and its affiliated nonprofit One Nation. The other side: The top Senate Democratic super PAC declined to provide a dollar figure for their spending on streaming. "Senate Majority PAC invested more this cycle in digital communications than any previous cycle, running digital campaigns in 12 states," SMP communications director Lauren French told Axios. Zoom in : Streaming and social platforms offer campaigns the power to target more specific audiences compared to traditional broadcast, and make it easier to measure the impact. "Its way more surgical than a linear broadcast buy," Zack Roday, managing director at Think Big, told Axios. But platforms can also set their own rules around which types of ads they want to accept. Some, like Netflix and TikTok, don't allow any candidate or issue ads . Republicans have complained about restrictions on ads that include transgender issues on Disney-owned platforms. Between the lines: Super PACs often pay multiple times what a campaign pays for ads on broadcast TV and radio because of laws ensuring candidates get the lowest rates. Online, super PACs can negotiate directly — and use their fat budgets and sprawling election maps as leverage. SLF works with platforms like SiriusXM, Paramount, Hulu, YouTube and others to lock in discounts based on their overall spending plans, according to the source. Groups can also experiment with different lengths and formats for ads online, breaking the 30-second broadcast mold. What to watch: Streaming ads can also be trickier for outside tracking. While Meta and Google provide public data on political ad buys, not every platform provides that kind of visibility, Streaming buys aren't covered by the same FCC filing requirements as political ad reservations on broadcast TV and radio. Broadcast filings can offer a preview of a group's targets months in advance, but streaming reservations are much harder to see. Although AI is changing the game, and there is a growing industry of companies offering better tracking tools. Super PACs still have to report independent expenditures to the FEC through 24- and 48- hour reports. Zoom out: Strong grassroots fundraising has helped Democratic candidates crush Republicans in dollars brought in directly to candidates. The GOP is hitting back with cash-flush committees and super PACs fueled by ultra-wealthy donors. In addition to super PACs moving more money to streaming, the National Republican Senatorial Committee jumped on a court decisions to coordinate ad buys with campaigns — giving them access to the candidate rate. It also allowed NRSC to negotiate with streaming platforms on behalf of multiple campaigns. The bottom line: It's just the beginning on maneuvering on streaming and coordinated buys. "That is definitely going to be the story of 2028," Kenny Day, senior vice president at IQM corporation, told Axios. He said the Supreme Court decision on coordinated spending "was too late for either party to really take advantage of the allowance of coordinated spending" in the 2026 cycle. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to show that the more than $200 million total from the Senate Leadership Fund included money spent through Texas PAC (not that it excluded that spending).
