events.title: The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The agentic web is here In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts. This new era is being called the agentic web. It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process . —Grace Huckins Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide. They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults. Cheap, proven ways to make roads safer exist, including tightening intersections with planters and lowering speed limits. But government logjams and red tape can make it difficult to roll out these changes. Still, some cities are making impressive progress by investing in public transit, extending curbs, and using cameras to spot danger zones in need of a redesign. Here’s how close we are to eradicating traffic deaths . —Sara Kiley Watson This story is the final part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Subscribe to read the other five instalments in our new Impossible issue . The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble Big AI bills and weak earnings have spooked investors. ( BBC ) + The Nasdaq 100 had its worst day since June on Friday. ( NBC News ) + OpenAI has cut its funding target by $10 billion. ( CNBC ) + What even is the AI bubble? ( CNN ) + Ukraine has blamed Russia, which hasn’t yet accused anyone. ( BI ) + AI will transform cyber warfare. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Binance users withdrew $3.6 billion after the largest ever crypto hack The funds moved when the exchange reopened on Sunday. ( Guardian ) + Binance says it’s covered $6 billion of the stolen $6.3 billion. ( Reuters $) + But the industry’s response has undermined its “decentralized” image. ( Gizmodo ) 4 An AI agent injected drugs into a live mouse’s brain It chose the gene therapy and controlled the needle itself. ( Wired $) + We need real-time tracking of AI agents. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Data centres have made utilities a flashpoint in the midterms Americans are angry over rising electricity bills. ( Reuters $) + Virtual power plants could help. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Apple has overtaken Nvidia as the world’s most valuable company Investors are favouring its restraint on AI spending. ( Bloomberg $) + But critics say it’s entering its “slop era.” ( 404 Media ) 7 Supermarket fridges have overheated in a new wave of cyberattacks Stores in Belgium, Sweden, and Luxembourg were hit. ( Politico ) 8 The first chocolate bars made from lab-grown cocoa are here Startups are cultivating chocolate to tackle a cocoa shortage. ( WSJ $) 9 Hackers hijacked digital billboards in multiple countries to show porn They also criticized security flaws and Egypt’s government.( Gizmodo ) 10 A new 3D map reveals instability in interstellar space The discovery could help explain why stars form so inefficiently. ( Quanta ) Quote of the day “It would be great if all this was just a house of cards.” —Kevin Roose, a technology columnist at the New York Times, tells NPR that an AI investment crash would be preferable to the technology permanently upending work and society. One more thing Useful quantum computing is inevitable—and increasingly imminent Last year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang jolted the stock market by saying that practical quantum computing is still 15 to 30 years away. He also suggested that those computers would need Nvidia GPUs to function. But Huang’s predictions miss the mark—both on the timeline and the role his company’s technology will play.  Quantum computing is rapidly converging on utility. And that’s good news, because the hope is that they will be able to perform calculations that no amount of AI or classical computation could ever achieve. events.title: Getting a big head start on holiday shopping can benefit retailers and consumers alike
events.summary: Does it make sense to wait until late December to wrap up, like these California shoppers did in 2023? Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Amazon, Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers begin their holiday sales as early as October . But there’s no need to rush to buy wool scarves, fuzzy throw blankets and the other holiday gifts on your list the second you spot some tinsel while shopping. As a finance professor who studies how people and companies make financial decisions , I can explain why the holiday shopping season starts so early: It can help retailers attract more customers while allowing cash-strapped shoppers to stretch purchases out across multiple paychecks. And, for people with deeper pockets, buying gifts early can help them avoid the stress that goes with last-minute shopping. Why retailers get such an early start Estimates for spending on holiday gifts, decor and the like between late 2026 and January 2027 range from about US$1 trillion to $1.7 trillion in the U.S. Some 29% of Americans plan to shell out their share of those large sums in early to mid-December this holiday season, while 17% will shop on Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, according to the Bank of America Holiday Spending survey . But many people like to shop for holiday gifts early – meaning before Halloween . Some do this out of necessity : They can’t afford to buy all the gifts they want to give unless they spread the cost over multiple paychecks. For others, it’s more of a preference. In a 2025 survey, about 54% of early shoppers said they want to manage their budgets gradually . In addition, 41% said they buy gifts early to avoid the stress associated with last-minute shopping. Retailers are adjusting by getting an early start on holiday sales and promoting seasonal items. By offering customers deals months before gift-giving commences, they can encourage even more people to join the early birds . And by launching promotions in October, they might secure sales that otherwise would go to their competitors later in the season. A longer selling season offers other advantages to retailers. It may ease pressure on their supply chain and logistics , since they can receive seasonal orders over three months instead of one or two. This minimizes shipping difficulties and lowers warehouse overhead costs. Building more time into the calendar to move seasonal inventory gives retailers more opportunities to sell those items. However, an earlier shopping season does not necessarily increase consumer spending overall. Some purchases may simply shift from December to October. Early birds could buy these Christmas decorations at a discount on Oct. 17, 2026. Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images Beware of some early-shopping pitfalls To make sure that buying gifts long before the holidays occur is a wise move, early shoppers should read vendors’ fine print and research their return policies . Many big retailers are making their return policies more restrictive by shortening the length of time you can return purchases and adding return/restocking fees. In some cases, the deadline you face for returning an item could fall before the holidays. For example, Best Buy’s extended policy takes effect in 2026 only for purchases made on or after Oct. 30. Target similarly restricts its holiday-season returns window to items bought on or after Nov. 1. Amazon extended its holiday return policy in 2026. If you buy an item from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, it can be returned until Jan. 31, 2027, except for Apple products, which can be returned until Jan. 15. Anyone who bought gifts beforehand will likely be subject to a standard 30-day return policy, which will expire long before Christmas. The timing of holiday shopping varies whether you buy gifts online or in brick-and-mortar stores. Anchiy/E+ via Getty Images When buying early makes financial sense Shopping early is smart when the costs of waiting could outweigh the potential benefits of spending your money earlier than otherwise necessary. For example, if a popular wool scarf that was priced at $100 in October is out of stock on Amazon by November, the supply is gone, but demand remains high. If you want to buy it for your mom and ensure it arrives in time, you may need to get it from other retailers. Maybe you can find the scarf on a website but is selling for $150. If time has run out, you might have to pay, say, $30 more for expedited shipping, bringing the total to $180. Clearly, you would have been better off buying it early on at a lower price. But that doesn’t mean you necessarily need to rush to buy a gift weeks or months ahead of when you’ll be placing it under a tree. First make sure that the price is in line with your expectations and what you’re willing to shell out. And you should do some comparison shopping to make sure other retailers aren’t charging less for the same or similar items. Remember, waiting to do your holiday shopping until the last minute can lead to unnecessary costs, like rush shipping fees. The key is to have a budget , recognize when the price is right, and know when to stop shopping. James Malm does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

events.title: ‘Bragawatts’ and why all data-center investing isn’t created equal
events.summary: The News For all the talk of AI bubbles and market crashes, Scandinavian private-equity giant EQT says it’s making a bet that regardless of what happens with the frontier labs, AI is still going to need a massive amount of power, energy, chips, and data centers. “All of a sudden, we find ourselves with $100 billion of energy assets, which are really the limiting factor for AI right now,” said Jean Salata, global chair of EQT, which has $400 billion in assets under management. “A lot of people went out and signed tons of contracts with anybody — they call them ‘bragawatts.’ But signing something and delivering it on time, and with power connected, are two very different things,” Salata said. “Sophisticated investors understand that, but there’s a lot of things happening in the public markets where people are investing in things that they really don’t understand.” EQT is a unique animal in an industry where exits have dried up, a generational bet on software companies looks vulnerable to AI, and higher interest rates have broken the math of cheap leverage and multiple expansion. Since 2018, PE firms have asked their investors for $1.5 trillion more capital than they’ve given back, and the industry is sitting on nearly $4 trillion worth of businesses it can’t sell. EQT has largely stayed out of the private credit and insurance boom that has turned its US rivals into asset-gathering giants — a “beta business,” said Salata, an artisanally crafted Wall Street dig. And it has an unusual backstop: The Wallenbergs, Sweden’s most powerful business dynasty, helped found EQT in 1994 and remain its largest shareholder. The family’s patient approach to ownership is close to the long-hold model that much of private equity is now trying to reinvent. Q&A Liz Hoffman: For a long time, private equity firms could borrow cheaply, ride a rising market, and look like geniuses. It feels like the jig is up, and I know you have some thoughts on that . Jean Salata: Our industry needs to remember what we are meant to be doing, which is delivering returns for our clients. If we’re not doing that, we’re going to end up in a very difficult place. There’s been a lot of attention on the growth in assets under management, a business model that has really benefited from the tailwinds of the private credit run of the last five years. But we’re in an environment where the tide is going out and that means you’re going where there is real value being created. There are something like 10,000 private-equity firms out there. What should that number be? The industry already is consolidating and that will accelerate. This year the top 10 firms in the world have raised 50% of the capital. When you raise smaller funds, people don’t see the carry coming in and so they leave and you get zombie funds. EQT has chosen not to chase those credit tailwinds you mentioned. It doesn’t have the big lending business that Apollo, Blackstone, and others have ridden to huge AUM piles. Do you feel good about that decision? I think there’s a role for private credit, but the question is who’s best positioned to deliver that? We’re good at being an equity investor, being really close to the sectors that we invest in, bringing the best operational talent, bringing the technology and the AI capabilities that we have to the company. None of those are really relevant to the credit business. It’s an origination business. It’s a beta business. Best case scenario, you make 8% return on your money. So, the answer is yes, I think we are happy with the decision. But how do you resist the pressures to be a one-stop shop? Eventually there is a feedback loop. Second-quartile [performance] is, maybe, good enough. But when you start talking about third- and fourth-quartile returns, clients will either stop or reduce the amount that they invest with you. It’s hard to take anything public right now that isn’t a giant AI company and private equity’s track record on returning capital has been abysmal . How does the industry get out of this funk? There are a lot of assets for sale that need to find a home and there aren’t that many buyers. At EQT, we’ve been able to take advantage of where there are pockets of opportunity and liquidity. We had $33 billion of distributions to our investors in the last 12 months, and as a result, we’re continuing to attract capital. There’s this strange incentive structure in our industry, where you sell businesses that you otherwise wouldn’t want to sell because of this finite [fund] life. There’s a bit of frustration on the part of sellers that have sold assets because they need to go fundraising, only to see the buyers make like another 3x on it, which is why you’re seeing these longer-hold vehicles like evergreen structures, open-ended structures, continuation vehicles. But then isn’t the market saying that the 10-year closed-end fund is outdated and should probably go away? One of the reasons we bought [secondaries firm] Coller is we think there is a convergence happening between the primary market and the secondary market. There’s a case to be made for the secondary market essentially becoming the private equity market, as it is in the world of listed equities. Remember, the stock market is a secondary market. Yes, you have some IPOs, but the vast majority of the trading is in existing shares. Where we’re heading in private markets is not quite that extreme, but it’s going to be a much bigger part of the industry. There were $250 billion of PE secondaries deals last year. That’s doubled in the last three or four years and it’s probably going to double again in the next five. One other tension in PE right now is that everyone seems to be in the same trade — the AI trade . Are you worried about correlation? There’s no patents in finance. We’re all moving in a similar direction and it’s going to boil down to execution. A lot of this is about talent. There’s a shortage of really good talent that understands technology and AI, and the ability to attract, to afford, that talent becomes a question of scale. Tell me why all this AI investing is not going to end terribly. There’s a lot of noise right now about data centers — ‘it’s a bubble, the market’s crashing.’ But if you look at the fundamentals of what’s going on in the AI buildout with power, energy, chips, data center demand, we think it’s very fundamentals-based and a very, very attractive opportunity. I don’t want to say we stumbled onto it — the team deserves more credit than that — but we found ourselves in the middle of this in a big way because we were investing in power assets and in data center assets for cloud migration. The pre-AI generation of data centers. Yes. So all of a sudden, we find ourselves with $100 billion of energy assets, which are really the limiting factor for AI right now. Now we are building the industrial AI core for the next generation of data centers, but we’re still only working with the hyperscalers. This is an important point; 92

events.title: Blackstone-backed data center operator tests AI debt fears
events.summary: The Scoop Wall Street is finding out just how expensive things can get in a matter of months. For a look at how much investors’ jitters are reshaping AI-related debt financing, look to QTS, an investment-grade Blackstone-backed data center operator, that just six months ago was weighing a deal to borrow $800 million at a rate of 1.7 percentage points over Treasurys. That deal never went through. And now, that same debt is being shopped to investors at 2.2 to 2.50 points above comparable Treasury yields for a nearly identical offering, according to people familiar with the matter. Both offerings involve the same company, same blue-chip Wall Street backing, and the same collateral — just for a lot more money. Blackstone declined to comment. As debt jitters spread and borrowing gets more expensive, it’s a lesson in just how much sentiment has shifted in such a short amount of time. Know More On Friday, the Financial Times reported that Blackstone told investors it no longer expected Anthropic to get an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its IPO, a reversal of previous guidance about the frontier lab, which is raising billions of dollars to finance its AI buildout. And investment-grade SpaceX’s $40 billion debt launch saw its pricing widen out — reaching an expected 8.75% yield for the riskier portion of its recent debt deal, up from where pricing was discussed just a week earlier, Semafor reported .

events.title: Trump vows to protect Musk, floats pre-emptive staff pardons
events.summary: President Trump said Monday he'd move to protect Elon Musk if Democrats investigate the SpaceX and Tesla CEO after the midterm elections. He also suggested the possibility of pre-emptive pardons for staff and others around him if Democrats pursue investigations. Why it matters: Trump is positioning himself for a combative final two years in the White House, as polls increasingly point to the prospect of a significant blue wave. What they're saying: In an interview for the "Pod Force One" podcast published early Monday, host Miranda Devine asked Trump about rumors of Musk being investigated or having assets seized. "It's talk. But if it is talk, we'll have to protect them," Trump said. Musk has spent nearly half a billion dollars opposing Democrats during this election cycle and recently suggested it would be the end of democracy if they win the White House and Congress in 2028. The intrigue: Beyond Musk, the president made clear he'd consider pardons for his staff and other allies if Democrats pursue them. "I would if I needed to. Sure," Trump said. "I would not even think about it. I'd do it," he added. What's next: Trump also said in the interview that he'd love to run for a third term but "the language is very exacting." While seemingly shutting that door, he suggested there was still time to implement his agenda. "You know, we have more than two years left. That's a long time. You can do a lot in that period of time," he said. Editor's note: This story was updated with additional information throughout.

events.title: Anthropic's IPO prospectus is big on promises, short on answers to tough questions
events.summary: It's official: Anthropic is going public, and boy, are our eyebrows tired from poring over hundreds and hundreds of pages of questionable claims. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music , or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live. Anthropic is going to need to do a lot to make its massive IPO more than just a flash in the pan, as systems editor Tobias Man n and senior reporter Tom Claburn tell host Brandon Vigliarolo on this week's episode. For one, the company has nearly a trillion dollars in compute commitments to pay for, which is going to mean it'll be burning through more cash than a datacenter gas turbine turned up to 11. In addition to its massive spending for the foreseeable future, there's also the fact that much of its computing power relies on customers who are also competitors. In short, we're skeptical, but you probably already knew that. It's El Reg, after all, and we're not just taking what the AI industry claims at face value - if it looks like a house of cards, it probably is. A lightly edited transcript is below: Brandon (00:03) Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register 's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and this week we're focusing on what I think our contributor Carly Page aptly described as the peak of the AI hype cycle we've been in for the past few years, and that's the public release of Anthropic's initial public offering filing. With me to talk this over is our systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn, both of whom I'm sure have plenty to say about this matter. Welcome guys. Tobias Mann (00:34) Good to be here. Tom Claburn (00:34) Good to be here. Brandon (00:36) So, I'm sure we've got a lot to cover. 614 pages is a lot to go through. Tobias, I understand you were combing through this thing with a fine-toothed comb . Talk us through the hard numbers before we get into some of the more wobbly parts of this IPO. Tobias Mann (00:56) Sure. At face value, going into any S-1 filing, it is a kind of mess of risk mitigation, kind of covering your butt. They all pretty much read like a doomsday prophecy. Brandon (01:18) Right. Tobias Mann (01:18) The S-1 definitely did that. events.title: The ANC set to lose South African cities
events.summary: The News The African National Congress is on course to lose control of most of South Africa’s major cities in Wednesday’s local elections, according to polling data, potentially disrupting power dynamics in the national coalition government. Several polls suggest the party’s remaining support is increasingly concentrated in smaller towns and rural provinces as opposition parties make deeper inroads in the biggest cities that drive Africa’s largest economy. The local government vote will decide who runs 250-plus municipalities responsible for basic service provision including water, sanitation, and refuse collection. It is the ANC’s first nationwide test since falling support forced it to share power in 2024 after losing its parliamentary majority — unprecedented in the democratic era. The latest Ipsos poll , conducted between Sept. 12 and Oct. 13, put the ANC’s national support at an “all-time low” of 30%, reflecting just how far its backing in urban areas has fallen. Roughly 30% of respondents in Johannesburg, the nation’s commercial hub, and Tshwane, home of the capital Pretoria, said they would vote for the ANC. And that figure fell to just 10% in the port city of Durban, where the populist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (or MK), which is pressing for sweeping state control of the economy and built around former president Jacob Zuma, is comfortably ahead in polls. Support for the ANC, the party once led by Nelson Mandela, remains near 60% in Limpopo and the Eastern Cape, vast provinces of villages, small towns, and dispersed settlements that remain far less urbanized than Gauteng or the Western Cape, an earlier Ipsos poll showed. “After 30 years of democracy, voting patterns are changing and we are moving into a completely new reconfiguration of the political spectrum,” said Andre Duvenhage, a political analyst at South Africa’s North-West University. The Ipsos survey and several other polls — if replicated on voting day — indicate that most metropolitan municipalities would require coalition governments after the local elections. This broadly matches the assessment of think tank Oxford Economics, which has predicted that voting in six of the eight metros would fail to produce an outright winner, creating the need for coalition negotiations. A poor ANC showing would “upend the power dynamics” inside the national coalition government, said William Gumede, a political analyst and governance professor at the Johannesburg-based University of Witwatersrand. He argued that if the ANC’s share of the vote was close to or fell below the Democratic Alliance, it would force the former liberation movement to treat its junior partner “as an equal power” in policy-making and government decisions. The two parties became governing partners after the 2024 general election for the first time, bringing ideological rivals into the same government where the ANC remains committed to state-led economic transformation policies while the DA has pushed for bigger private investment. Know More Political parties have entered the final stretch of campaigning with failures of local government providing much of the ammunition. Unreliable water supplies, deteriorating roads, corruption, and mismanagement of municipal finances, have left many councils struggling to provide basic services. Companies are increasingly paying for the failures, said Busi Mavuso, CEO of lobby group Business Leadership South Africa, whose members account for nearly a third of the country’s $490 billion GDP. She said businesses are investing in backup water storage, private security, and road repairs to remain operational. “Capital is not sentimental,” she said, warning that investors can redirect money when infrastructure and municipalities fail. That makes the quality of municipal governments formed after the election important to investors, according to Awongiwe Booi, a fixed income analyst at South African lender Investec. “The alignment and performance of the coalition post the election will matter more than the poll results themselves,” she said. South Africa’s eight metros house about 40% of the population and account for an outsized share of economic activity. Tiisetso’s view The theory from an investor’s perspective is that a weaker ANC is better for public finances. That deserves testing. For starters, there is a risk over what the party does to win voters back or retain those largely rural areas, where official data shows that these countryside towns accounted for nearly 60% of the country’s poor in 2023. Under such circumstances the ANC, in its effort to recover voters and shore up support, would have every reason to demonstrate that the government can deliver more on its campaign promises to expand public employment and automatically enrol grant-receiving households for free basic services. The spending pressure is hardly hypothetical, with Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana saying government departments have asked for more than 700 billion rand ($41 billion) in additional spending over the next three years, more than a third of everything the government expected to spend this year. “That money simply doesn’t exist,” he told a local radio station last month. Even so, an electoral decline makes saying no politically harder, creating a longer term political risk. It might just embolden those arguing that a post-President Cyril Ramaphosa ANC should move toward MK Party and Economic Freedom Fighters, a radical left movement advocating for nationalization of mines and banks, and ditch the market friendly DA, which has long struggled to shake off its image seen by many Black voters as a party of white interests. There’s nothing irrational about voters demanding more from a state where a third of the work force is unemployed and ranks highest in the World Bank inequality index. The problem is that political need does not create fiscal space. Room for Disagreement David Omojomolo, Africa economist at research house Capital Economics, said fears about the coalition government stability after the election are overdone, and expects the macroeconomic impact of the vote to be limited, with borrowing costs constraining the recovery remaining on track. His comment rests on the DA, rather than MK or the EFF, picking up the ANC losses, which the polls support in Gauteng. “That should compel the next ANC leader to continue to follow business-and-investor-friendly policies, including the commitment to fiscal consolidation,” he said. Notable Unpaid bills owed to municipalities have grown more than seven-fold since 2011 to nearly 500 billion rand ($30 billion), Investec noted, a measure of the fiscal hole new councils will inherit.

events.title: UAE oil exports surpass prewar levels despite Hormuz disruption, energy minister says
events.summary: UAE oil exports surpassed prewar levels “at a certain time” as the Arab world’s second-largest economy continues to work as reliable supplier to the world, despite Hormuz disruptions. “At a certain time, we did better than prior because of our continuous work,” UAE’s Minister of Energy and Infrastructure Suhail Al Mazrouei told delegates at the Adipec conference in Abu Dhabi on Monday. He did not disclose the timelines or the volumes the UAE exported, but said [we] "did our best to make sure that the prices of commodities do not go very high”. The Emirates shipped 3.94 million barrels per day of crude and condensate in June, the highest monthly total in the past year, and a sharp reversal from March, when the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz cut exports to a record low of 2.13 million bpd, Kpler data showed. “We feel the pain on those consumers, and we understand that if prices go too high, that's going to strike the demand in years … the pipeline helped us a lot over there. Our readiness through the fleets and the ships have helped us tremendously," Mr Al Mazrouei said. The UAE's Habshan–Fujairah pipeline, often referred to as the West–East crude oil pipeline, has the capacity to transport up to 1.5 million bpd of crude oil, representing a substantial share of the country’s total oil exports. In May, the UAE announced the expansion of the West-East crude oil pipeline to be completed by 2027, with the project expected to double export capacity through Fujairah . Mr Al Mazrouei said the UAE was able to “fill in the supply gap” as supplies from other countries reduced due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. “Sometimes even we have filled in the gap ... we managed to oversupply to those countries because there was a significant reduction from many countries.” The country must also be ready for worst-case scenarios since it “cannot predict what’s going to happen", he added. Oil prices volatile Oil prices have remained volatile since the Iran war broke out on February 28, with prices rising to more than $120 per barrel in March as the Middle East war escalated, with Iran hitting energy infrastructure in the region and ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz coming to a virtual halt. Prices fell in subsequent months amid peace talks between the US and Iran to end the conflict and reopen the strait, but surged again amid concerns that the US is preparing to restart the Middle East war and attack Iran. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, is trading close to $110 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at about $100 per barrel on Monday. “When I think about what happened over the last eight months, it's really quite stunning the level of disruption to the global energy system. Crude oil, natural gas, products have all been disrupted. The thing that stood out is how resilient the system has been,” Meg O’ Neill, chief executive of BP, said in a separate panel discussion at Adipec. “If you went back to the start of the conflict, people would have said that oil should have been $150 a barrel by June, and that didn't happen. People said that natural gas prices should have spiked, and they really didn't until the last month or so.”

events.title: Demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments
events.summary: We have seen demands being made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes. Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries as a way to avoid tax. HMRC has sought to tackle this tax avoidance through what has been termed the loan charge and published guidance for those affected.Questions have been raised about the regulatory status of these loans and whether they were ever intended to be repaid.Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they’re unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.Some consumers are, however being sent legal letters threatening potential court action and asking for immediate repayment of the loan. Repayment is being sought after these disguised remuneration loans were sold by the original provider to a third party.Those seeking payment may ask the FCA to agree to a Validation Order. This is the formal permission needed before the loans could be enforced. We would consider any request carefully and our agreement is by no means guaranteed. If a Validation Order is required and not granted, the debt would remain unenforceable.Anyone who receives a demand for repayment of a disguised remuneration loan, and is unsure whether they are liable for the amount claimed, should consider carefully whether to make any payment. We’d encourage them to look at the HMRC guidance and consider taking legal advice.Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.If you are experiencing any difficulties, whether they are health, money or other difficulties, or if you don't understand what is happening, you should raise this with those contacting you.

events.title: Could the US midterms cause a surprise stock market rally?
events.summary: Investors have a lot on their plate. Oil, inflation and interest rates are climbing, while tech stocks are volatile amid growing fears of an AI bubble . Throw in US President Donald Trump's unpredictability, mounting government debt, regional wars and stretched stock valuations, and it’s all getting a bit much. Now comes another challenge: Americans go to the polls on November 3 for the midterm elections , which will determine control of Congress and the direction of Mr Trump's presidency. Yet here’s a curious twist. History shows that midterm elections have typically been followed by a strong run for Wall Street. JP Morgan Asset Management’s analysis shows the S&P 500 has risen in the 12 months following every midterm since 1950. Might history repeat itself? If so, stock market bulls have plenty to look forward to, says Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell. “The past is no guarantee, but the third year of a presidential term is, on average, the best one for the US stock market.” The average third-year gain across postwar presidencies is a stellar 16.1 per cent. No other presidential year averages a double-digit gain, he says. One theory is that presidents have an incentive to boost the economy ahead of the next election. Another is that the midterms often deliver a lame-duck president who struggles to pass legislation, allowing businesses to operate without interference from Washington. Markets are often volatile before the vote, but when the result is known, investors can focus on policy rather than polling, says Jason Hollands, managing director at Evelyn Partners. Gridlock could boost stocks Mr Trump looks on course to lose control of both the House and Senate. If that happened, it could actually help stocks. “A divided Congress would make major new legislation harder to pass. That could limit the prospect of sweeping changes to areas such as tax and regulation,” Mr Hollands says. But investors shouldn’t assume divided government means quiet government. Aliasgar Tambawala, co-chief investment officer at Klay Group, warns that political gridlock brings problems of its own. “A divided legislature may lead to greater disruptions around issues such as the debt ceiling and government funding.” Mr Trump's executive powers, including tariffs, would remain largely intact, while the President retains his veto. Mr Tambawala expects political volatility to persist, but says GCC investors face bigger concerns, notably the situation in the Strait of Hormuz . “A durable resolution would augur well for the region.” Despite recent volatility, the S&P 500 and tech-focused Nasdaq are up around 12 per cent this year, says Tony Hallside, chief executive of STP Partners. Further gains depend on earnings. “Getting the election out of the way helps sentiment, but it does not create earnings growth. If inflation persists or profits fall short of expectations, the historical election pattern will offer little protection.” AI is another concern. Can the technology justify the huge sums being invested by generating sustainable revenue and profits? “Political clarity will not compensate for disappointing commercial results,” Mr Hallside says. Reality checks for investors Madhur Kakkar, chief executive of Elevate Financial Services, warns that markets face formidable headwinds. Brent crude has hit $117 a barrel, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September and may do so again in December, while 10-year Treasury yields are approaching 5 per cent. “Higher Treasury yields give investors a competitive income alternative at a time when US equity valuations remain demanding,” Mr Kakkar says. The S&P 500's Shiller price-to-earnings ratio ended October at 40.88, a level exceeded only during the dot-com boom. On October 29, Alphabet shares plunged 13 per cent, wiping $500 billion off its value after heavy AI infrastructure spending contributed to negative quarterly free cash flow of $9.1 billion. Yet the US economy remains resilient, with third-quarter GDP growing at an annualised 3.4 per cent. Mr Kakkar urges investors to maintain balanced portfolios rather than chase a post-midterms rally. Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial, believes AI and interest rates, rather than politics, will determine whether markets finish 2026 strongly. “Easing inflation and a successful Anthropic IPO could still fuel a year-end rally.” For the GCC, the outlook is firmer than headline figures suggest, he says. The IMF expects Gulf output to shrink 4.8 per cent this year because of the Iran war, before rebounding 9.1 per cent in 2027. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are shipping substantial oil volumes around the Strait of Hormuz, while high crude prices bolster revenue. Non-oil activity remains strong, but a full recovery depends on the strait reopening, which the IMF assumes will begin in March 2027. Mr Mould remains cautious. Inflation is sticky, interest rates may rise, the Middle East war could drag on, oil and equity valuations are high, and the AI boom could end in an investment bust. History suggests the midterms could unleash another Wall Street rally. But with so many risks stacking up, investors may discover that this time, history really is bunk.

events.title: Resilience of Gulf oil infrastructure has its limits
events.summary: Amena’s view The drums of war are beating again, and the oil-exporting states are bracing “for the worst,” as the UAE’s presidential advisor Anwar Gargash recently put it. Eight months into the US-Iran war, one lesson is clear: There is no amount of operational resilience that can shield energy infrastructure from an unresolved political conflict. Renewed strikes will put more of the region’s oil supply at risk. Saudi Arabia and the UAE have demonstrated exceptional levels of resilience, activating contingency plans, carrying out repair works in record time, and keeping customers supplied. Their bypass pipelines have proven the value of planning for the shift from the “just in time” model to the “just in case” approach. The UAE’s 1.8 million-barrel-per-day (bpd) pipeline from Abu Dhabi to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman was once questioned as an investment. Its cost was recovered after just one month of conflict, according to people familiar with the matter. A second link with similar capacity is expected to be completed by July 2027. Saudi Arabia is considering expanding its larger East-West Pipeline and may bring in countries like Iraq and Kuwait that don’t have shipping outlets outside the Gulf. Within the industry, there’s a growing consensus that the pre-war oil flows will not return. More investment will be earmarked for contingencies, reflecting in part the view that reaching a diplomatic resolution to the Iran war is unlikely anytime soon. So far, the global energy system has performed better than expected. Gulf exporters kept their oil flowing despite the risks faced in Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, inventories were released, and some demand was curtailed, all of which combined to limit the oil price spike. But this resilience should not be mistaken for future security of supply, especially as this potential escalation comes at a time when global inventory levels have been drained by around 1 billion barrels. Brent is trading above $110 a barrel, of which perhaps $40 could be attributed to geopolitical risk. While much of the focus is on guessing what US President Donald Trump is planning, the reality for the oil industry is that higher prices may have eroded around 3 million bpd of demand, according to energy industry executives. This assumption is even more pessimistic than the IEA’s forecast of demand declining by around 2.6 million bpd this year. Another rise in prices, or oil prices sustained at this level, will only lead to even more demand destruction. This week, ahead of Abu Dhabi’s flagship energy conference ADIPEC, senior executives and CEOs from the energy industry gathered to discuss the challenges facing the industry under the Chatham House Rule. There was frustration about the lack of policy support, especially from European governments, for investment in the upstream sector and the construction of refineries. Over the past two decades, around 25% of Europe’s refineries were shut down, mainly as a result of policies related to the energy transition. Today, energy executives from European oil majors are pressured to address rising prices of oil products without having the facilities needed to deliver the energy to consumers. If there’s one silver lining from this crisis, it’s prioritizing investments in new supply and abandoning the dichotomy between the concepts of “old energy” and “new energy.” At the opening of ADIPEC on Monday, Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, was asked what the biggest challenge facing his industry is. He replied with one word: “energy.” Another round of war will make that energy costlier, and less abundant. Notable The UAE’s race toward its “Zero Hormuz” strategy runs through Fujairah, where investments can be seen in all directions intended to move the fossil fuels and products that would otherwise be trapped in the Gulf, Semafor reported.

events.title: FBI pins $6.3B Binance crypto heist on North Korean hackers
events.summary: The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the record-breaking $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, pointing the finger at the notorious Lazarus Group as the exchange scrambles to replace stolen funds and reassure customers. In an alert published Saturday , the agency attributed the October 29 attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus, which has made a lucrative career out of relieving crypto exchanges of their digital assets. Pyongyang was already in the frame before the FBI weighed in. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Elliptic had linked the theft to North Korea, with TRM reporting that most of the $6.36 billion haul disappeared in about 20 minutes. Elliptic, which puts the total closer to $6.43 billion, says it has verified that $2.85 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen or seized. According to the FBI, the hackers have started swapping their loot for Ethereum, with investigators expecting them to move the funds through decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms and instant swap services to make the money harder to trace. The agency has published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the theft and is urging exchanges, blockchain analytics firms, and other virtual asset providers to block transactions involving the stolen funds. The FBI's attribution comes days after Binance admitted that hackers had made off with roughly $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. According to the exchange , the trouble started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave the intruders access to a service container and allowed them to authorize withdrawals they had no business making. Binance has since resumed customer withdrawals , which it suspended after the attack, and says it has now replenished about 95 percent of the stolen assets. The remaining tokens are proving harder to replace because of their limited liquidity. The exchange has committed billions of dollars from its own reserves and emergency funds to cover the losses, with co-CEO Richard Teng promising that customers won't be left footing the bill. That hasn't stopped users from heading for the exits. Binance recorded approximately $3.64 billion in net outflows after withdrawals resumed, although the company said this represented only around 2.1 percent of its reported assets. Replacing the stolen cryptocurrency is one thing. Getting it back from North Korea is another, and investigators face the considerable task of tracking billions of dollars as the hackers attempt to move it beyond their reach. TraderTraitor has form when it comes to raiding crypto exchanges. The North Korean crew has previously been linked to a string of cryptocurrency thefts, including the $308 million attack on Japan's DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024 . The group has previously used fake job offers and recruitment exercises to trick employees into handing over access to their employers' systems. As we reported here on Friday , crypto exchange Bitget has now confirmed that the cyberattack where hackers drained $387.5 million worth of digital assets from the exchange’s wallets also has all the hallmarks of a North Korean operation. Its CEO did not go into too much detail, but did say that “IP behavioral patterns and on-chain signatures” suggest it was Kim’s cronies at work. This isn’t Binance's first expensive encounter with hackers, either. Back in 2022, attackers exploited its BNB blockchain bridge and made off with roughly $566 million in tokens. Four years later, the sums have grown considerably. Binance may have the reserves to make its customers whole, but the attackers responsible for the latest raid still have billions of dollars to launder. ®

events.title: Voting Experts Feared “Chaos” on Election Day. So Far, It Hasn’t Materialized.
events.summary: Election workers in Los Angeles County process ballots for the state’s primary in June. Mario Tama/Getty Images As Americans cast ballots on Tuesday, voting experts’ deepest concerns largely didn’t materialize on a mostly routine Election Day. Tuesday’s relative quiet followed an anxious run-up in which the Trump administration pressed forward with unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections. Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting . The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters , an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants. The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats. Help Us Report on Key Election Issues ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something? Send Us a Tip Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. In the days before the midterm, they threatened to prosecute election officials who didn’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens. The administration didn’t explicitly rule out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines. Election experts told ProPublica the cumulative effect of these steps was to ramp up anxiety about the vote and to erode voters’ trust in the system. “The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worried that this would make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.” In an emailed response to questions before Election Day, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement was “not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.” “Paper Trail” Podcast Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “ Paper Trail .” The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.” Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans said they’d expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm. Republicans said they would focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats planned to concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, said Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson. Here are five issues that voting rights experts said they were watching in this year’s election: People arrive to vote early on Oct. 27 in Coral Gables, Florida. Lynne Sladky/AP Images 1. Will There Be Federal Interference? As clocks hit 5 p.m. on the East Coast, there’d been no confirmed reports about federal law enforcement at the polls. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that he hadn’t sent immigration agents to the polls.   Still, an incident during early voting in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates how widespread such fears have been. Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this. He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage . “Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said. It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places. Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there were real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempted to commandeer voting equipment or ballots. “We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown said. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.” A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.” As is routine in federal elections, DOJ monitors were watching over polling places Tuesday. The agency had assured states that its observers would follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. In Michigan, the state attorney general’s office said it received reports of monitors requesting training materials in Dearborn. A similar report came in about monitors’ interaction with election workers in Flint. The DOJ team overseeing Michigan later told state officials that this was inconsistent with the training they received. Similarly, in New Mexico, the secretary of state’s office received reports of Justice Department monitors “asking some unusual questions and questioning voters” in Bernalillo County, a spokesperson told ProPublica, adding that the office later received reassurance from the Justice Department that “it would be addressed.”  This issue also surfaced in August during the primary election in Wyoming, where poll workers reported feeling uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.” Workers prepare ballots to be scanned for counting in Orange County, California, on Oct. 28. Apu Gomes/Getty Images 2. What Effect Will Noncitizen Voter Challenges Have? events.title: Vintage fun: Prodding AI agents using retro hardware just because you can
events.summary: From the department of "pointless but still cool" comes word of some kit being repurposed as a terminal for AI agents. AWS developer advocate Darko Mesaroš has connected a teletype to a modern command-line interface to revel in the delight of interacting with today's AI technology via a combination of a DECwriter and fanfold paper, or the display and keyboard of a computer whose heyday ended 40 years ago. Mesaroš' project involved AWS Kiro , a Command Line Interface (CLI) and agentic coding service. We would, however, contend that this is more about seeing what retro hardware can be made to do. Two problems needed solving: getting data to and from the teletype, and formatting the output to work on a piece of kit from another era of computing. He used Hayes modem emulation to deal with the serial connection, and Agent Client Protocol (ACP) for working with Kiro. Mesaroš used a WiModem232 for the former. The device emulates a standard Hayes-compatible modem and, according to Mesaroš, "Folks initially used this to connect Commodore 64s to BBSes in the modern era" (he started his computing journey with a Commodore 64). The latter, getting the Kiro CLI to work on a Teletype, was a little more complicated. Kiro's CLI isn't really suitable for a teleprinter capable of 30 characters per second, after all. A simple Rust application took Kiro's output (obtained via ACP) and turned it into something that a teletype, or dumb terminal, could handle. As we said, seemingly pointless, but making it work required knowledge of Rust, competence with containers, an understanding of ACP, and more than a little creative thinking. So, while one might argue it is pointless from a technical perspective, it is wonderfully educational otherwise. The repository is available and focuses on Kiro for obvious reasons (Mesaroš is an AWS developer advocate after all), but in a chat with The Register , Mesaroš said the concept was portable. He said, "Any coding assistant or any harness that supports ACP, this should work, right? I built it for Kiro, but it uses the standard ACP protocol, so I could easily plug in Claude Code or Codex. Anything that basically can serve as an ACP server should be perfectly fine. "Blessed be the standards, right?" There might be some issues. "The biggest problem with this thing is that it doesn't really handle packet drops at all," he explained. "Like, if you drop packets, they're just gone. There're no retries. It's just spitting information out." And then there is buffering. Or the lack of it. Mesaroš said, "There's actually no buffering happening here. Literally, it just comes down through the fire hose through this serial device, and the bottleneck itself is the serial device." Mesaroš had toyed with using the GPIO pins on a Raspberry Pi, but settled on the serial device instead, since everything worked "out of the box." "It's kind of cheating," he admitted, "but it's also kind of good." Mesaroš collects vintage hardware, with a stash that ranges from home computers made by Commodore and Sinclair, to a 1974 Data General Eclipse minicomputer and a plethora of Sun hardware. And, of course, an old Decwriter. He is also a dab hand with the soldering iron, having learned the skills to keep old hardware operational. Unlike today's equipment. "I have this big peeve over modern computers, where you just can't fix them," he said, "and it feels like such a waste of resources that when my MacBook dies I just have to drill a hole through it so nobody steals my data, and throw it away." As for Kiro-TTY – or accessing a coding assistant or agent over serial using a decades-old device – he wrote on his blog, "This absolutely serves no purpose." However, it did provide a novel way of working out how the ACP protocol worked. Perhaps not so usefully, it also taught the developer how to debug serial connectivity. "And in general it helps me stretch what I can do in the current age of AI coding, and keeps my curiosity alive." The destination might be pointless from a modern perspective, but the journey getting there is anything but. ®

events.title: Pharma's next cash cows could be specialized treatments
events.summary: Pharmaceutical companies facing a steep patent cliff are concluding the key to future profits may be customized treatments tailored to patients' genes and lifestyles — not blockbusters aimed at large patient populations. Why it matters: The pivot could influence which diseases get treated in the decades to come, and how much the health system pays. The stakes are huge. More than $500 billion in brand-name drug sales is potentially at risk from generic competition between 2026 and 2032, according to the consulting firm Evaluate. The latest: The race is on to find new treatments that each generate at least $2.4 billion in global sales, a new Iqvia Institute report finds. They're increasingly specialty treatments, biologics and rare disease drugs — with a small group of flagship products accounting for an outsized share of industry sales. GLP-1 drugs like Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Eli Lilly's Zepbound now define that elite category. The next wave could include "biological missiles" that combine antibodies with chemotherapy to target specific cancer cells. "As precision medicine continues to advance, similar approaches may extend beyond oncology into areas such as immunology, metabolic disease and neurology," the report states. Reality check: It's not clear whether all of the innovation will cure more people, or just make health care more expensive. Novel RNA drugs and cell and gene therapies are expensive, hard to make and target small groups of patients. Challenges identifying eligible patients and getting insurers to pay for treatments have already revealed a disconnect between promising R&D and patient benefit. Widespread concern over high drug prices will force manufacturers to find more unmet needs and build sales more quickly after a drug's launch, according to the report. Context: Top-selling drugs historically were aimed at large patient populations with chronic conditions like high cholesterol. The ulcer drug Tagamet became the first to exceed $1 billion in sales in 1986. Over time, cancer and immunology drugs became major drivers of growth, followed by GLP-1s, which are sparking huge demand for conditions beyond obesity and diabetes but also driving up health costs. Iqvia found that blockbusters on average maintain a dominant market position for 12.1 years before losing market exclusivity, or nearly 80% of their commercial life. Specialty drugs for rare or complex diseases lasted even longer. Yes, but: A substantial number of top-sellers will lose patent protection and face potential competition from generics between 2028 and 2036. Bristol Myers Squibb's blood thinner Eliquis and Merck's cancer blockbuster Keytruda, which are both due to lose market exclusivity in 2028, accounted for a combined $65 billion in global sales in 2024. Follow the money: The search for new blockbusters is playing out in a highly charged environment. Drugmakers and biotechs not only have to figure out how to grow outside of crowded categories but also how much payers value new classes of drugs, Evaluate says . There's also uncertainty over China , where Western drug giants have invested tens of billions of dollars to bolster their product pipelines. Evaluate predicts that only autoimmune disease drugs will come close to rivaling GLP-1s, because of their potential to treat dozens of conditions. One example is AbbVie's injectable Skyrizi for plaque psoriasis, arthritis, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, which could find more uses and generate more than $33 billion in sales in 2032. Iqvia identifies RNA therapeutics as a potentially important middle ground between traditional "small molecule" drugs for chronic diseases and highly specialized genetic treatments. These drugs can target disease-causing mutations across many genes and conditions, with applications for central nervous system, cardiovascular and kidney disease, as well as rare conditions. The bottom line: The success at innovating while also making sure patients have access to the new treatments "will ultimately determine whether the growth in blockbuster medicines observed over the past 25 years can continue at its extraordinary pace," Iqvia concludes.

events.title: "Arrogance": 3 GOP Senate candidates blasted over costly red-state rescues
events.summary: Republicans are burning tens of millions of last-minute ad dollars to try to rescue three red-state senators who they say ignored months of warnings that their campaigns were in danger. Why it matters: Senate races in Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi are normally GOP layups. This year, Republicans have diverted resources from swing-state battles to defend them. The frustration with Sens. Roger Marshall (Kansas), Darline Graham (South Carolina) and Cindy Hyde-Smith (Mississippi) comes amid broader GOP finger-pointing as polls show a nationwide backlash against President Trump . "Democrats may win these seats in a wave ... but not a blue wave. It's the wave of arrogance [and] laziness ... that washed over these GOP incumbents and made them think they were invincible," said a national GOP operative involved in several key Senate races. By the numbers: National Republicans have spent $33 million in Kansas, $21 million in South Carolina and $2.4 million in Mississippi, according to data compiled by campaign finance expert Rob Pyers. Trump also has spent valuable campaign time in all three states. Behind the scenes: Republicans say the three senators ignored warnings to raise more money and build stronger campaign operations. National Republican Senatorial Committee chair Tim Scott warned all GOP senators in February 2025: "We do not need to spend time and money in places where races should not be competitive." Trump's political operation also warned Senate Republicans that they would need to pull their own weight. The most complaints center on Marshall, who has raised just $7.5 million compared with $19 million for his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton. Republicans blame his strained relationship with the banking and credit card industries — major GOP donors — and a lack of outreach to K Street. Republicans describe Marshall's campaign as overconfident. About a month ago, his team told aides to other GOP senators that the race would be effectively over within 10 days once it released opposition research on Hamilton. It wasn't. Strategists blame chief of staff Brent Robertson for Marshall's weak campaign operation. The campaign only recently tapped veteran Trump operative Chris Grant as part of a last-minute rescue effort. Alex DeGrasse, another veteran strategist recently hired to help Marshall, pointed to millions in spending by national Democrats and said the senator has made "hundreds of stops across all 105 counties in Kansas" and continues to "work hard for the people of Kansas." In Mississippi, Republicans have long viewed Hyde-Smith as a political underperformer. In 2020, she ran six points behind Trump. She has raised just $6.5 million despite warnings that Democratic megadonors, including George and Alex Soros, were preparing to spend heavily against her. Democratic groups have poured $13.7 million into the race. Republicans also fault Hyde-Smith for holding too few campaign events and underestimating her Democratic opponent, district attorney Scott Colom. Hyde-Smith's campaign did not respond to a request for comment. In South Carolina, Republicans fault Graham for failing to tap her late brother Lindsey Graham's donor network and showing little interest in soliciting contributions. In the first two weeks of October, Democrat Annie Andrews outraised Graham $4.2 million to $570,000. Graham spokesperson T.W. Arrighi said the senator "has faced unprecedented headwinds since losing her brother three months ago, and has risen to the occasion." Some Republicans are sympathetic to Graham, a political novice thrust into the Senate after her brother's death who faced a grueling primary and little time to campaign. They blame Trump for pushing her to run. Yes, but: Republicans point to Idaho Sen. Jim Risch, whose campaign required no spending from national GOP groups, as an example of an incumbent who took the political environment seriously. What they're saying: Representatives for the NRSC and the pro-GOP Senate Leadership Fund super PAC didn't respond to requests for comment. What's next: Top Republicans say the party needs to rethink how it deals with complacent incumbents in 2028 — and make clear that its campaign organizations can't be treated like a charity.

events.title: America's changing power grid faces a powerful El Niño
events.summary: A powerful El Niño could bring major shifts in electricity supply and demand across the U.S. this winter, posing new challenges for utilities. Why it matters: The U.S. power grid has far more solar, wind and battery storage than during the last major El Niño, and the ongoing event could reveal whether that changing energy mix has made the grid more resilient or left it vulnerable in new ways. Driving the news: A very strong El Niño is strengthening in the tropical Pacific and is expected to continue into spring 2027, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says. NOAA's latest outlook favors wetter-than-normal conditions across California , the Southwest and much of the southern U.S. this winter, while the northern Rockies and parts of the Great Lakes lean drier and much of the northern U.S. leans warmer. The intrigue: El Niño doesn't affect every electricity resource the same way. A March study found that previous super El Niños were associated with reductions in potential solar power output of nearly 5% in parts of California over 12 months — and more than 10% in the state's north during winter. Vincent Tidwell, chief scientist at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, says a wetter California winter could boost hydropower, while reduced precipitation or snowpack in the Pacific Northwest could cut generation there. Erik Smith, a climate scientist at the Electric Power Research Institute, tells Axios the Southeast is another region to watch for reduced solar generation as El Niño favors cloudier conditions. California now has more than 21 gigawatts of battery capacity , giving the grid another tool to manage fluctuations in electricity supply — one it barely possessed during the last very strong El Niño. The Columbia and Snake river basins accounted for roughly 62% of Western U.S. hydropower generation between 2001 and 2020, according to a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory analysis . Tidwell tells Axios that the Western grid is accustomed to shifting electricity between regions when hydropower conditions differ, helping compensate for shortages. Federal water managers, states and utilities use seasonal forecasts to plan for potential hydropower availability at Hoover and Glen Canyon dams on the Colorado River, Tidwell says. Zoom in: Tidwell expects natural gas to play a larger backup role if El Niño reduces Pacific Northwest hydropower and California solar generation this winter. Other resources, including wind, geothermal and nuclear power, provide additional options, though he says El Niño's effects on wind generation remain poorly understood. The big picture: A very strong El Niño could actually ease some pressure on the electricity system, Smith says. Warmer-than-normal conditions across the northern U.S. could reduce winter heating demand, potentially offsetting some of the pressure from changing electricity supplies elsewhere. Yes, but: Even a very strong El Niño doesn't guarantee specific weather impacts. A severe cold outbreak could still stress the grid despite a warmer-than-average winter, while a few major storms could radically alter regional rainfall and snowpack, Smith says. The bottom line: "We have a lot of confidence in how the averages are going to play out, but we don't have a lot of confidence in the day-to-day, week-to-week, particular weather events that could drive those averages," Smith says. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

events.title: Microsoft's moolah mountain is more massive than ever. It just doesn't want the people who built it
events.summary: Capitalism can seem so perverse. Take Microsoft, which is celebrating record financial performance by inviting 60,000 employees to consider continuing their careers outside the company . Voluntary redundancy may seem to make sense when a company's running out of cash, but Microsoft is dripping with the stuff . Redmond's first quarter for fiscal 2027 was a bonanza for the tech giant. Its Azure business is up over 48 percent y-o-y, revenues are through the roof, and it has so much moolah it returned $10.2 billion to shareholders in the form of dividends and share repurchases. This latter move probably soothed CEO Satya Nadella, who recently suffered, due to the vagaries of C-suite reimbursement and incentive packages, a 6 percent cut in his pocket money . But as he’s also a stockholder with about 0.01 percent of the company, his share of the cash return presumably eased the pain. He won't have been offered redundo. Jenkins, the large wheelbarrow if you please. Microsoft, then, can afford all its employees, each of whom contributed about $1.5 million to SatNad's bottom line in the last full fiscal year. The "massive efficiencies and RoI of AI" make a great line for a company flogging magic LLM juice, but the evidence remains elusive. AI is, of course, still the reason. Nothing else matters these days. It's just that it's not today's AI. Among all the fulsome figures it put on display for Q1 2027, analysts noted that Microsoft's capital expenditure wasn't as spendy as expected. Quite a lot has been pushed into next calendar year, not because it's not there to be spent – Microsoft could build a 1:1 scale model of the Vatican filled with robot priests if it wanted – but because so much it wanted to mash the Buy Now button for was "Out of stock. More expected soon." This is bad. MS added 88 datacenters in its most recent full financial year: fiscal 2026. That’s not enough datacenters for a cloud business expected to grow by half again in 2027, and hugely not enough to do the other thing. Lags in the cadence of deforestation, dewatering and detonation of the planet can't be tolerated. Thus there are contracts signed to get things back on track PDQ, with mucho, mucho, mucho sponduiks. In its most recent Q1 earnings call, Microsoft is hinting, those selfsame analysts say, that it will have to go to the debt market and go into " negative free cash flow " territory in 2028. In other words, as well as spending its own bank, the company will be taking out massive loans. This is why Billy and Bhavya Dev have to go. The cost of borrowing depends on the financial health of the borrower, and that boils down to how much profit you're making from the money you earn. A big round of redundancies, which are very costly in themselves, sits on the books of the year they happen. The hole in expenditure left by the vanished salaries lives on. The capital must flow. Will this work? Last week, we listed the reasons why it might not — price competition between rivals and increasingly powerful local and open weight models, supply side shortages, you know the litany by now. This week is Groundhog week, with fresh stories singing the same songs from different choirs. Any sensible soul, especially developers sitting on the sharp end of AI's forcible insertion into their working lives, will know how uncertain the job market is. Voluntary redundancy is a very high stakes bet, and the game is very different if you're in an organization that's going downhill and may need to get rid of you later with far less cash available than if you're nominally making $1.5 million in a place whose biggest problem is that it physically can't move into a bigger shell. On average, only 5 percent or so of those offered voluntary redundancy take it, which Microsoft HR will have factored in. It's cold outside and snug within, so that may be on the high side. The biggest knock-on of such schemes is cultural, with only the very confident moving on out, a disproportionate loss of talent and role models. Hey, the cost of doing business, right? For those who do decide to leave and watch the fireworks from outside the tent, part of the deal is career development resources. Sounds great, if anyone knows what technical careers will look like if either AI works and does indeed do all the work, or it fails and the global financial system throws a humongous wobble. Or anything in between. So, here's an exercise in very dark humor quite fitting for the Halloween season. Ask your favorite AI what careers will be available for coders made redundant by AI. It will give you a long and plausible list. Then ask it – and yourself – why AI won't be able to do any of those jobs too. Buying a truck and a wrench and calling yourself a plumber is probably safest. Nobody will ever want AI to fix their toilet. ®

events.title: ‘No room for debate’ over human control of AI, says Sam Altman
events.summary: People, not artificial intelligence, must stay in control of the future, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said on Monday. “There are a lot of other things we can debate, but on this one, we think there must be no room for debate,” he said in conversation with The National 's Editor-in-Chief Mina Al-Oraibi. Speaking at the opening ceremony of Adipec in Abu Dhabi, Mr Altman said there “should not be a handoff to AI” and that the technology “needs to be a tool built for people and needs to serve people, not the other way around”. “I can’t believe that this differentiates us from other AI companies, but it does,” he said. “This is a value that we intend to really go fight for. And I wish it didn’t need to be said.” The remarks followed OpenAI's agreements with Abu Dhabi, covering energy, education, investment and government. These include a deal with Adnoc and Abu Dhabi technology group G42 to use OpenAI’s most advanced models on the energy industry’s hardest problems. Mr Altman’s message was that AI has crossed a threshold. By his account, it has gone from trailing the world’s best scientists at the start of the year to mostly outperforming them. Its demand for power is growing just as fast, he said. “AI was mostly not as smart as our smartest scientists, and now it’s mostly smarter than them,” Mr Altman said, adding that AI could now do “a lot of parts” of many white-collar jobs. He said he believed society would “navigate through this all fine”. But he warned that the industry must show it can prevent harm as its systems become more capable. “How do we guarantee, and how do we give the world comfort with that guarantee, that we are going to avoid serious safety and alignment incidents?” he said. “I think that’ll be increasingly important for our industry to demonstrate.” Energy challenge In a quick-fire round, Mr Altman was asked what challenge he faces today. He answered with one word: “Energy.” He said the energy needed for each AI query had dropped sharply, but demand kept climbing . Six years ago, OpenAI’s heaviest internal user consumed about 100,000 tokens a month. Today, that figure is roughly the global per-capita average, and the top user consumes about 500 billion, he added. Costs could fall “in almost every way, except, you know, atoms are still atoms”, Mr Altman said. He called power “the very dominant factor” in how much AI the world can use. He said he hoped AI would deliver “a net gain for energy availability in the world”. Mr Altman also said OpenAI had solved one of the Millennium Prize problems, a set of unsolved mathematics problems. He said the work used 10,000 agents running an upcoming GPT model for about four days, collaborating with “no hierarchy”. The claim could not immediately be verified independently. He praised the UAE as “consistently the most forward-looking country in the world for AI adoption”, saying about 80 per cent of young people in the country were using ChatGPT .
